additions.text: By the end of this week, you can say who you are, how you are and where you are, and name the things in your room with el, la, un, una and their plurals.
_Yo, tú, usted, él, ella_ = I, you (informal), you (formal), he, she. Plural: _nosotros_ = we, _vosotros_ = you all (Spain, informal), _ellos/ellas_ = they, _ustedes_ = you all.
Spanish usually drops the pronoun because the verb ending already shows who is speaking.
Marina and I are flatmates.
Are you (all) the new students?
She is Jimena and he is Raúl.
_Ser_ = who or what you are (name, origin, job). _Estar_ = how you are right now or where you are.
_Cansado_ changes to _cansada_ if a woman is speaking. _Bien_ never changes.
I'm Kofi. I'm from Ghana.
I'm a nurse.
I'm happy, but a bit nervous. (a woman speaking)
We're in the school café.
Every Spanish noun is masculine or feminine, even objects. The ending is a strong clue, but not a perfect rule.
Learn each new noun together with its article: not _llave_, but _la llave_.
The notebook is on the chair.
I have a problem with the key.
The photo is of my grandmother.
Vowel + _-s_; consonant + _-es_; _-z_ becomes _-ces_. The article changes too: _el/la_ become _los/las_; _un/una_ become _unos/unas_.
Some words lose their written accent in the plural: _habitación → habitaciones_.
I need some towels.
The kitchen lights are on.
The maps are at reception.

To spell, say the Spanish name of each letter. _H_ is silent; _j_ sounds like a strong English h; _v_ sounds like _b_.
In Mexico people also say _be grande_ for b and _be chica_ for v to avoid confusion.

By the end of this week, you can choose the right article from a noun's ending, introduce new places and things with un or una, and refer back to them with el or la.
_-o_ and _-or_ are usually masculine; _-a_ is usually feminine; _-ción, -sión, -dad, -tad_ are always feminine.
For words ending in _-e_ or another consonant, there's no rule: memorise the article with the word.
The building's lift is new.
The train station is far away.
Morelos Street is very pretty.
A few common words break the pattern: _el día, el mapa, el tema, el idioma_ are masculine; _la mano, la foto, la moto_ are feminine.
Feminine nouns starting with a stressed _a_ take _el/un_ in the singular, only for sound: _el agua fría_ (still feminine). Plural: _las aguas_.
The language of the class is Spanish.
My brother's motorbike is red.
The water at the market is very cold.
The school's classrooms are small.
_Un/una/unos/unas_ introduce something new: the listener doesn't know which one yet. _Hay_ (there is/are) goes with _un/una_, never with _el/la_.
_Un_ doesn't always mean the number one; often it just means 'a'.
There's a bakery on my street.
I'm looking for a cash machine (any one).
Tlaquepaque is a quiet neighbourhood.
_El/la/los/las_ points to something both people can identify: already mentioned, unique, or obvious in the situation.
First mention with _un/una_, second mention with _el/la_.
There's a juice stall. The stall is next to the entrance.
Where's the exit, please? (of this building)
Guadalajara Cathedral has two towers.

Every Spanish word has one stressed syllable. Words ending in a vowel, _-n_ or _-s_ stress the second to last; other words stress the last. Exceptions carry a written accent.
That's why _canción_ has an accent but _canciones_ doesn't: the stress stays on _-ció-_, which is now the second to last.

By the end of this week, you can describe several things by their colour, size and origin, put the adjective in the right place and give your opinion with gran, buen or mal.
In a noun group, every word agrees: the article, the noun and the adjective all become plural. Numbers stay the same.
Words ending in _-ión_ lose the accent in the plural. Weekdays ending in _-s_ only change the article: _el martes → los martes_.
I need four white plates.
Sundays are long days.
There are two big windows in the kitchen.
Adjectives in _-o_ have four forms (masculine/feminine, singular/plural). Adjectives in _-e_ or a consonant only change for plural.
Nationalities ending in a consonant add _-a_ for feminine: _francés → francesa_. They are written in lower case.
My backpack is small and my books are heavy.
Ingrid is German and her husband is Japanese.
The hotel and the square are very quiet.
Describing adjectives (colour, shape, origin) go after the noun. A few opinion adjectives can go before it.
_Bueno_ and _malo_ become _buen_ and _mal_ before a masculine singular noun; _grande_ becomes _gran_ before any singular noun.
Oaxaca has good weather in March.
It's a great idea: let's go to the market on Saturday.
Today is a bad day for the beach.
After the noun: the basic meaning (big, elderly, brand-new, unique). Before the noun: great, long-standing, another one, the only one.
For people, _mayor_ is a polite way to say _old_.
Rafa is an old friend from university.
It's the only shop open on Sunday.
This alebrije is unique: it's handmade.

Soft _r_ is a single quick tap, like the _tt_ in American _better_. Strong _r_ is a trill: written _rr_ between vowels and _r_ at the start of a word.
If the trill is hard for you, practise _tr_ and _dr_ fast: _tres, dra, tres, dra_.

By the end of this week, you can point to things that are near, a bit further away or far away, ask what something you don't know is, and say who each thing belongs to.
_Este_ = this (near me). _Ese_ = that (near you). _Aquel_ = that over there (far from both of us).
Demonstratives agree with the noun in gender and number, just like adjectives.
This box is very heavy. Will you help me?
Is that picture there for the kitchen?
Those mountains over there are beautiful.
_Esto, eso, aquello_ = this, that, that over there, when you don't name the thing. They never go with a noun and have no plural.
Use _¿Qué es esto?_ to ask about something you don't know the name of.
—What's this? —It's a remote control.
That thing there is for the bathroom.
What's that thing at the window over there?
The owner chooses the word (_mi, tu, su_); the thing chooses the form (singular or plural).
_Tu_ without an accent = your. _Tú_ with an accent = you.
My plates are in this box.
Does your brother live in Monterrey?
Doña Rosa is looking for her glasses.
_Nuestro_ (our) has four forms: it agrees with the thing in gender and number.
_Su_ can mean his, her, its, your (formal) or their. To be clear, say _el coche de Ana_.
Our street is very quiet.
—Is it his dog? —No, it's the neighbour's dog.
Here are your suitcases, gentlemen.

A final _s_ joins the next word when that word starts with a vowel: _mis amigos_ sounds like _mi-sa-mi-gos_.
That linking _s_ is often the only sign that you are hearing a plural.

By the end of this week, you can introduce yourself and other people: who they are, what they do, where they are from and what they are like, using the subject pronoun only when it is needed, together with everything you learned in weeks 1 to 4.
_Tú_ is informal, _usted_ is polite. _Usted_ and _ustedes_ take the same verb form as _él_ and _ellos_.
_Vosotros_ is only used in Spain. In Latin America, _ustedes_ is used for any group.
They are my classmates.
Are you the manager of the hostel?
We are from Campeche.
Spanish usually drops the subject pronoun because the verb ending shows who it is.
Use the pronoun to contrast two people, to make _es_ or _son_ clear, or to answer _¿Quién…?_
I'm Iván. I'm from Valladolid, in Yucatán.
You're the eldest and I'm the youngest. (contrast)
—Who's the new girl? —Her, the girl with curly hair.
Spanish doesn't use _a / an_ with a job: _Es profesora_ = She's a teacher. Add _un / una_ only if there is an adjective: _una profesora muy paciente_.
Nationalities agree with the person and are written in lower case.
Rodrigo is a waiter and his sister is a lawyer.
He's a very creative cook.
Hanna and Jonas are German, from Hamburg.
A checkpoint mixes everything: this week's classes and the nine classes of weeks 1 to 4.
If one row of the table feels hard, go back to that week before you continue.
This is my old friend Carmen. She's an architect and she's from Monterrey.
Those gentlemen are our neighbours: they're two very nice retired doctors.

_J_ always sounds like a strong English _h_. _G_ sounds the same before _e_ and _i_.
Before _a, o, u_, _g_ is soft like in _go_. _Gue_ and _gui_ keep the soft sound: _Miguel_.

By the end of this week, you can say how you and other people feel, say where people and things are, and ask what there is nearby.
_Estar_ + adjective describes a temporary state: mood, health, energy. The adjective agrees with the person (-o / -a, plural -s). _Bien_ and _mal_ never change.
Watch the accent: _está_ (verb, stress at the end) is not _esta_ (this).
Today I'm in a good mood.
Why are you sad?
The soup is cold.
Location always uses _estar_, even for places that never move: _Chiapas está en México_.
_Aquí_ = here (near me), _ahí_ = there (near you), _allí_ = over there (far from both). No _en_ before them.
Mum is in the garden.
My keys aren't there.
The museum is far from the centre.
_Hay_ = there is / there are. It introduces something new and never changes form.
_Está / están_ = is / are (located). It places something already known: with _el, la, los, las_, _mi_ or a name.
In my neighbourhood there are two old churches.
The colourful church is at the end of the street.
Is there hot water in the showers?

_Hay_ is one syllable (like English _eye_). _Ahí_ is two syllables, with the stress on the _í_.
_Está_ (is) is stressed at the end; _esta_ (this) at the beginning.

By the end of this week, you can say your age and other people's, say if you are hungry, thirsty, cold or sleepy, and describe an object precisely: a big talavera mug for coffee.
_Tener_ = to have. Only _yo tengo_ ends in -go; _tienes, tiene, tienen_ have -ie-, but _tenemos, tenéis_ keep the e.
In questions about having something, Spanish often drops the article: _¿Tienes coche?_ = Do you have a car?
I don't have any cash.
Do you have bigger mugs?
English says _I am 25_ and _I am cold_; Spanish says _I have 25 years_ (_tengo veinticinco años_) and _I have cold_ (_tengo frío_).
_Hambre_ and _sed_ are feminine (_mucha_); _sueño, frío, calor_ are masculine (_mucho_). Weather uses _hace_; a cold thing uses _está_.
How old is your brother? — He's twelve.
The children are very hungry.
Are you sleepy? It's eleven o'clock.
In a noun phrase, the article and the adjective agree with the noun in gender and number. The part with _de, con, para_ does not change.
The adjective usually goes after the noun: _a red shawl_ = _un chal rojo_. _De + el_ becomes _del_.

By the end of this week, you can tell from a verb who does the action and when, describe your week with regular present-tense verbs and say who you are, where you are, where you're going and what you have.
Find the conjugated verb, read the person from its ending and the time from words like _ahora_ or _los lunes_.
The Spanish present covers _I work_ and _I'm working_. Requests (_lee_) and wishes (_ojalá que…_) use other forms: just recognise them for now.
You answer the listeners' messages.
On Mondays we share the office.
Stem + ending. _-er_ and _-ir_ verbs share all endings except _nosotros_ and _vosotros_.
_No_ always goes right before the verb.
Don Julio controls the sound.
Do you have breakfast at the radio station?
We get lots of calls.
_Soy, estoy, voy_ end in -oy; _tener_ gives _tengo_. _Ir a_ + place = to go to; _a + el_ becomes _al_.
_¿Adónde vas?_ = Where are you going? _¿Dónde estás?_ = Where are you?
On Tuesday we're going to La Terminal market.
Andrea has been in the studio since six.
Where are you going after the show?

Yo, tú, él and ellos forms are stressed on the stem; nosotros and vosotros forms are stressed on the ending.
_Preparo_ (I prepare) and _preparó_ (he prepared) differ only in stress.

By the end of this week, you can say what you do, what you put, what time you leave and where you're coming from, and say what you want, what you can do and what you order in a café.
_Hacer_ = to do / make, _poner_ = to put, _salir_ = to leave / go out. Only the _yo_ form is irregular: _hago, pongo, salgo_.
_Salir de_ = to leave a place; _salir con_ = to go out with someone.
I always take lots of photos of the façades.
I put my passport in the small backpack.
What time are you leaving the hotel?
_Venir_ = to come. It works like _tener_: _vengo, vienes, viene, venimos, venís, vienen_.
_Venir de_ = to come from (origin); _ir a_ = to go to (destination). When someone calls you, say _¡Voy!_ (I'm coming!).
Mei is coming from the capital on the seven o'clock shuttle.
We're coming from the square and going to the hostel.
_Querer_ = to want (e → ie), _poder_ = can (o → ue), _pedir_ = to order / ask for (e → i). _Nosotros_ and _vosotros_ don't change.
After _querer_ and _poder_, the second verb stays in the infinitive: _Quiero ver…_, _Puedo pagar…_
Do you want to climb Pacaya on Sunday?
We can't pay for such an expensive tour.
My friends always order the Guatemalan breakfast.

_Ie_ and _ue_ are pronounced together in one syllable, quickly: _quie-ro_, _pue-do_.
When the stem doesn't change (_nosotros, vosotros_), there's no diphthong: _po-de-mos_.

By the end of this week, you can choose between tú, usted, ustedes and vosotros, recognise vos, ask well-written, well-intoned yes/no questions, and use everything from weeks 6 to 9 on a trip.
_Tú_ = informal you; _usted_ = formal you (verb like él/ella); _ustedes_ = you all in Latin America (verb like ellos); _vosotros_ = informal you all in Spain.
_Vos_ replaces _tú_ in Argentina, Uruguay and parts of Central America. Its present forms are stressed at the end: _hablás, comés, vivís, sos, tenés_. Recognise them; you can keep using _tú_.
Madam, do you live in San Juan?
Are you from Rosario? (voseo)
Do you (all) want to come to the market with us? (Spain)
A yes/no question is the same sentence with _¿?_ and a rising tone at the end. Spanish opens questions with an upside-down _¿_.
To answer negatively, Spanish often says _no_ twice: _No, no tengo cambio_.
Are you and your sister coming tomorrow?
Hey, can you take a photo?
—Are you cold? —No, I'm not cold.

By the end of this week, you can ask for specific information with the right question word (price, place, time, people) and say what you don't want, don't have or can't do.
Think of the answer first: a place → _dónde_, a time → _cuándo_, a price → _cuánto_.
A preposition goes in front of the question word: _¿De dónde…?_ (Where… from?), _¿Con quién…?_ (Who… with?).
Where is the central market?
What time does the bus to the lake leave?
Who are you going to the volcano with?
_Cuánto_ agrees with the noun: _cuánta agua_, _cuántos días_, _cuántas personas_.
Before a noun, use _qué_. With _es / son_ or to choose between options, use _cuál_: _¿Cuál es tu dirección?_ (What is your address?).
How many pupusas do you want?
What is the hostel's phone number?
What juice do you have today?
Spanish has no word for _don't / doesn't_: just put _no_ before the verb.
With two verbs, _no_ goes before the first one: _No quiero salir_ (I don't want to go out).
I don't drink coffee at night.
There's no lift in the hostel.
We can't go to the lake today.
_No, no quiero._ = No, I don't want to. The first _no_ answers; the second one negates the verb.
_No, puedo_ actually means "No (that's wrong), I can". To say you can't: _No, no puedo_.
—Is there a table for four? —No, there isn't right now.
—Are you coming on the tour? —No, I can't, I'm working.

Yes/no questions rise at the end. Questions with _qué, dónde, cuánto…_ usually fall, like a statement.
Say _no_ and the verb together, with no pause: _noquiero_.

By the end of this week, you can join two ideas to add, choose, contrast or say no to two things, and explain why you do something and what you do it for.
_Y_ = and (adds), _o_ = or (choice), _pero_ = but (contrast). Put a comma before _pero_.
_Y_ becomes _e_ before an "ee" sound (_i-, hi-_), and _o_ becomes _u_ before an "o" sound (_o-, ho-_).
I read stories and sing songs with the children.
Do you prefer the morning or the afternoon?
The library is small, but it has a lot of books.
_Ni_ = nor / or (in a negative sentence): _No tengo coche ni moto_ (I don't have a car or a motorbike).
Keep _no_ before the verb and use _ni_ instead of _y_ for the second thing.
You don't need experience or qualifications.
Today it isn't raining or cold.
My brother doesn't read novels or comics.
_¿Por qué?_ (two words, accent) = why? _Porque_ (one word, no accent) = because.
_Porque_ is followed by a conjugated verb: _porque tengo tiempo_.
—Why do you come by bus? —Because I don't have a car.
I like Tegucigalpa because people are very friendly.
_Para_ + infinitive = (in order) to: _para aprender_ (to learn).
_Porque_ gives the cause (+ conjugated verb). _Para_ gives the goal (+ infinitive).
I'm going to the library to return a book.
I'm saving money to travel to Copán.
What's this box for? —For keeping the pencils.

_¿Por qué?_ is stressed on _qué_; _porque_ is stressed on _por_.
_Y, e, o, u_ are weak and blend with the words around them.
Why aren't you coming?
Because I'm working.

By the end of this week, you can say where you are going, where you are coming from, where you are, who you are going with and what you don't have, explain a route with del… al… and say when and how you do things.
_A_ = to (movement, destination). _En_ = in / at (place, no movement). _De_ = from, or 's (owner).
Key pair: _Voy a Granada_ (I'm going to Granada) / _Estoy en Granada_ (I'm in Granada).
Today we're going to Masaya by bus.
My cousin lives in a yellow house.
These ceramics are from San Juan de Oriente.
_Con_ = with. _Sin_ = without (usually no article after it: _sin azúcar_).
In questions the preposition comes first: _¿Con quién…?_ (Who… with?).
Are you going to the volcano with your friends or alone?
A water without ice, please.
It's a room with a bathroom, but without a window.
_A + el = al_, _de + el = del_: only with masculine singular _el_.
No contraction with _la, los, las_, with _en / con_, or with the pronoun _él_.
It's fifteen minutes on foot from the hotel to the lake.
We're going to the cathedral and then to the convent.
The room key is in the bag.

By the end of this week, you can describe your daily routine with verbs like levantarse, ducharse or acostarse, and say how often you do each thing.
The scale: _siempre_ (always), _normalmente_ (usually), _a veces_ (sometimes), _casi nunca_ (hardly ever), _nunca_ (never).
_Nunca_ before the verb, or _no + verb + nunca_. Never _nunca no_.

My grandfather never drinks alcohol.
_Una vez, dos veces por semana_ = once, twice a week. _Vez_ → _veces_ in the plural.
_Los lunes_ = on Mondays (habit). _El lunes_ = on Monday (one day). _Todos los días_ = every day; _todo el día_ = all day.
On Sundays we have lunch at my mother's.
I water the plants twice a week.
Reflexive verbs: the person does the action to themselves. The pronoun (_me, te, se, nos, os, se_) goes before the conjugated verb.
In the negative: _no me levanto_ (no + pronoun + verb).
I wake up at five, but I get up at half past five.
What time do you go to bed on Fridays?
My children put on their uniforms after breakfast.
_Me lavo_ = I wash (myself). _Lavo el coche_ = I wash the car. The pronoun shows who receives the action.
With body parts and clothes, use the article: _Me lavo los dientes_ (I brush my teeth).

By the end of this week, you can say what you like and love, ask about and react to other people's tastes, use para mí, contigo or conmigo, and present yourself as a flatmate using everything from weeks 11 to 15.
_Gusta_ + one thing or an infinitive; _gustan_ + several things. The pronoun shows who likes it.
Use the article for general tastes: _Me gusta el café_ (I like coffee).
I really like gallo pinto for breakfast.
My flatmate likes horror films.
Do you (all) like walking around the centre?
_Encantar_ = to love (a thing or activity). Don't add _mucho_ to it.
Agree: _a mí también_ (me too) / _a mí tampoco_ (me neither). Disagree: _a mí no_ / _a mí sí_.
—I love the Irazú volcano. —Me too!
—I don't like rain at all. —I do, it relaxes me.
After a preposition: _mí, ti_; the rest are like subject pronouns (_él, ella, nosotros…_).
_Conmigo_ = with me, _contigo_ = with you: one word each. _Mí_ (me) has an accent; _mi_ (my) doesn't.
This Tarrazú coffee is for you.
Are you coming with me to the Central Market?
Without her the house is very quiet.
A flatmate profile uses everything from weeks 11 to 14: questions, negation, connectors, reasons and goals, prepositions, al / del, adverbs, frequency and reflexive verbs.
Add today's classes: _me gusta / me encanta_, and _conmigo / contigo_.
I'm hardly ever at home at weekends because I visit my family.
Where is the flat? Is it near the park?

By the end of this week, you can organise a shopping trip with exact and approximate quantities, say what you put on to go out and explain what hurts after a hike.
Exact amounts: number + noun. _Uno_ becomes _un_ before a masculine noun and _una_ before a feminine one.
For things you don't count one by one, use a container or measure + _de_: _una lata de_ (a can of), _un litro de_ (a litre of), _medio kilo de_ (half a kilo of).
For the picnic I buy a bag of bread and two avocados.
The volcano trail is twenty-one kilometres long.
We need four cans of tuna and a packet of biscuits.
_Poco_ = little / few, _mucho_ = a lot / many, _bastante_ = enough. _Poco_ and _mucho_ agree with the noun; after a verb they never change.
_Todo_ + article + noun = all the / the whole: _toda la tarde_ (the whole afternoon), _todos los días_ (every day).
In Monteverde there are lots of clouds and little light in the afternoon.
We have enough water for the whole hike.
All the bridges in the park are hanging bridges.
_Doler_ works like _gustar_: _me duele_ + one thing, _me duelen_ + two or more. The pronoun already says whose body it is, so Spanish uses _el, la, los, las_, not _mi_.
After the hanging bridges my neck hurts.
Tomás's feet hurt: his boots are new.
With _ponerse_ (to put on), _quitarse_ (to take off), _lavarse_ (to wash): article, not possessive. Use _mi, tu, su_ to describe, to say where something is, or when it belongs to someone else.
It's raining: I put on my raincoat and my cap.
In the hostel we take off our boots at the door.
Where is my torch? I can't find it.

By the end of this week, you can describe an object with several clues until the other person knows which one it is, and compare two things by size, price or weight.
Build the description clue by clue: what it is, what it's like (colour, size, material with _de_), where it is (_que está en…_).
Colour and size go after the noun and agree with it. Location uses _estar_.
I'm looking for a big green plastic umbrella.
It's the white cap that is next to the keys.
My wallet is brown, small and made of leather.
When it's clear what you're talking about, drop the noun: _la negra_ (the black one), _el que está en la mesa_ (the one on the table).
The article still agrees with the hidden noun: _la_ for _la mochila_, _el_ for _el paraguas_.

_Más … que_ = more … than (-er than); _menos … que_ = less … than. The adjective agrees with the first thing you compare.
With a number, use _más de_: _más de cuarenta dólares_ (more than forty dollars).

_Tan … como_ = as … as. _No es tan … como_ = not as … as.
_Mejor_ = better, _peor_ = worse: just recognise them for now.

By the end of this week, you can say and ask the time, the day and the date, talk about your plans with voy a and explain what you want, what you can and what you have to do.
Time now: _es la una_, _son las dos_. Time of an event: _a la una_, _a las dos_. Up to half past, add with _y_; after that, subtract from the next hour with _menos_.
What time is it? It's twenty past six.
The bus to David leaves at quarter to eight.
The farm closes at one in the afternoon.
_El viernes_ = on Friday (one Friday); _los viernes_ = on Fridays (every week). The date: _el 14 de marzo_ (no _on_, no capital letters).
Today is Wednesday, 11 March.
The flower fair starts on Thursday 15 January.
On Sundays the café opens at eight.
_Ir a_ + infinitive = going to (a plan). The present tense tells habits; _ir a_ tells this particular plan.
Tonight we're going to have trout for dinner at the restaurant by the river.
What are you going to do on Sunday?
My cousins aren't going to come: they have a lot of work.
_Querer_ = to want to, _poder_ = can / to be allowed to, _tener que_ = to have to. _No tengo que_ = I don't have to (it isn't necessary), not _I mustn't_.

By the end of this week, you can say what you and other people are doing right now and talk about things and people without repeating their names, using lo, la, los, las.
_Estar_ + gerund = to be doing something right now. Gerund: _-ar → -ando_, _-er / -ir → -iendo_. Special: _leyendo_, _durmiendo_.
My aunt is sewing the dresses for the party.
What are you eating? It smells really good.
The children are sleeping in the hammock.
Present = habits (_cocina todos los domingos_). _Estar_ + gerund = right now (_está cocinando ahora_). _¿Qué estás haciendo?_ = What are you doing?
What are you doing? I'm waiting for my cousins at the dock.
I normally swim in the morning, but it's raining now.
_Lo, la, los, las_ replace a thing or a person (it, him, her, them). Choose like the article: _el → lo_, _la → la_, _los → los_, _las → las_.
The pronoun goes before the conjugated verb: _la tengo_, _no lo encuentro_, _lo está tocando_.
Have you got the red ribbons? Yes, I've got them here.
This hat is my grandfather's. He wears it at every party.
And Marta? I can't see her.
Order: pronoun + _estar_ + gerund: _la está planchando_ (she's ironing it). Negative: _no lo estoy usando_.
And the drums? They're tuning them in the square.
Have you got the phone? No, Lucas is charging it.

By the end of this week, you can build clear sentences to state, ask and deny, describe a place with ser, hay and estar, ask for the information you need and use the classes from weeks 16 to 19 together. It's the end of A1.
Basic order: who + verb + what + when / where. The time can move; the people can't.
_No_ goes right before the verb (or before _lo, la, los, las_).

Yes/no question: normal order + rising voice. Information question: question word + verb + subject (_¿Qué ve la gente?_). There is no _does_ in Spanish.
Where do groups buy their tickets?
Does the museum have an audio guide? No, it doesn't.
_Ser_ = what it is / what it's like; _hay_ = there is / there are (new things, how many); _estar_ = where a specific thing is.
A good description goes: what the place is, what there is, where things are.
Is there a café? Yes, it's next to the shop.
My neighbourhood is quiet. There's a park and two bakeries. The park is opposite my house.

Perfect = present of _haber_ + participle. Use it for a period that includes now (today, this week) or when you don't say when.
In much of Latin America you will also hear the simple past here (_hoy trabajé_). Week 4 looks at this variation.
This morning I went to the central market.

_-ar_ → _-ado_; _-er_ and _-ir_ → _-ido_. After _a, e, o_ write _-ído_ with an accent.

Irregular stems take endings with no written accent: _tuve_, _tuvo_. _Fui_ / _fue_ can mean _I went / he went_ or _I was / it was_.

For _tú_ commands, drop the final _-s_ of the present: _caminas → camina_. Eight common verbs have a short irregular form: _di, haz, ve, pon, sal, sé, ten, ven_.

For _usted_, start from the _yo_ form, drop _-o_ and use the 'opposite' vowel: _-ar → -e_, _-er/-ir → -a_. Add _-n_ for _ustedes_. Special forms: _vaya_, _sea_.
Madam, carry on along this avenue to the traffic light.
Put your card here, please.
Go to the stop opposite. (to a group)

In Guatemala, Central America, Argentina and Uruguay many people use _vos_ instead of _tú_. _Vos_ commands sound like the infinitive without _-r_, stressed at the end: _caminá, vení_. Learn to recognise them; keep using _tú_ yourself.
Wait on the corner, I'm almost there. (vos)
Ask for the bill, we're leaving. (vos)
Negative _tú_ commands use the 'opposite' vowel plus _-s_: _no cruces, no bebas_. Start from the _yo_ form: _no hagas, no salgas_. For _usted_, just add _no_ to the usted form: _no cruce_.
Don't leave your backpack on the seat.
Don't go out without an umbrella, it's going to rain.
Sir, don't worry, I'll help you.
to go straight on
to turn right
to cross the street
the block (Latin America)
the corner
the traffic light
the zebra crossing
opposite
the stop
the station
to top up the card
to get on the bus
to get off at the stop
rush hour (Latin America)
cash
Excuse me, can you help me? (usted)
How do I get to…?
It's two blocks away.
You can't miss it.
_Tú_: stress on the second-to-last syllable (_CRUza_). _Vos_: stress at the end (_cruZÁ_). _Usted_: same stress as _tú_ but a different last vowel (_CRUce_).
pedestrian (no cars)
corn on the cob (Central America and Mexico)
the stall
empty
Reflexive pronouns go before the conjugated verb in every past tense: _me levanté, me levantaba, me he levantado_. With _haber_, the pronoun goes before _he/has/ha_.
In Xela I used to get up at six because classes started at seven.
Yesterday my roommate fell asleep on the bus.
Have you had your bath yet? The hot water runs out soon.

With an infinitive or a gerund, the pronoun goes either before the conjugated verb or attached to the end. Keep the right person: _vamos a acostarnos_. Affirmative commands attach it: _levántate_; negative ones put it in front: _no te levantes_.
There's a trip tomorrow: I'm going to go to bed early.
Wait a moment, I'm doing my hair.
Calm down, don't worry: the bus hasn't left yet.
With the pronoun, the subject changes emotional state: _me preocupé_ (I got worried). Without it, someone or something causes the emotion in another person: _la noticia preocupó a mi madre_.
At first I used to get very tired, but then I got used to the altitude.
The teacher got angry because nobody did the homework.
_Estar_ = a state. _Ponerse_ = a quick change, a reaction (get nervous, go red). _Quedarse_ = the result, how someone ends up (be left speechless, fall asleep), or to stay somewhere.
When he saw the volcano from the window, he was left speechless.
I went red when the teacher read out my essay.
It was raining so much that we stayed at home all afternoon.
to wake up / to get up
to have a bath / a shower
to get dressed
to do one's hair
to go to bed / to fall asleep
to get used to
to get worried
to calm down
to get angry
to get scared
to get bored
to relax
to go pale / red
to get ill
to get dizzy / carsick
to run out of battery
to fall asleep / to oversleep
to be left speechless
When _me, te, se_ meet a verb starting with a vowel, both vowels join into one syllable: _se_asustó_. Listen carefully: the pronoun is short but it changes the meaning.
I got angry with my brother.
Did you go to bed late?
for your mind to go blank
the altitude
beans (Latin America)
to remember
Last night I went to bed late and today I overslept.
When he saw the bill, he went pale.
We're going to relax in the hot springs.
With _gustar_ the thing you like is the subject, so the verb agrees with it: _gusta_ for one thing or infinitives, _gustan_ for plural things. The person appears as _me, te, le, nos, os, les_.
I like the cobbled streets of this town.
Are you interested in seeing how they make the dye?
My parents love having coffee in the square.
_Doler_ (to hurt), _faltar_ (to be missing / to lack) and _molestar_ (to bother) work like _gustar_. Use _el/la_ with body parts, not _mi_. In the past: _me dolió / me dolieron_.
After climbing up to the viewpoint, my legs hurt.
There are twenty minutes to go before the last bus to San Salvador.
The midday heat bothers Rodrigo.
Add _a + person_ to clarify or to contrast, but keep the pronoun: _A Laura le gusta_. React with _a mí también / a mí tampoco / a mí sí / a mí no_.
—I don't like mosquitoes. —Me neither.
You're interested in art, aren't you?
My grandmother's hands hurt when it's cold.

Indirect object pronouns say _to whom_ or _for whom_: _me, te, le, nos, os, les_. They go before the conjugated verb. With _le/les_, Spanish often repeats the person: _le di las gracias a la artesana_.
I lent my umbrella to a lady at the stop.
Can you tell us where the lake is?
indigo
the scarf / headscarf
the hammock
the ceramic mug
the necklace
to dye the fabric
handmade
the souvenir
the back
the knees
the throat
the feet
the hands
to have a blister
Me too.
Me neither.
I do.
I don't.

The final _-n_ tells you the verb is plural: _duele / duelen, gusta / gustan_. It links to a following vowel (_gustan_estas_); before a consonant, say it clearly. The article (_el/los_) is a second clue.
the process
a clue
What do you think? (to a group)
I love you all.
My sister loves necklaces.
The seller explained to us how they make the hammocks.
Does your knee hurt a lot?

Two object pronouns together: the person first (_me, te, nos, os_), then the thing (_lo, la, los, las_). The second pronoun agrees with the thing. Both go before the conjugated verb, with _no_ in front.
—Can you lend me the ladder? —Yes, I'll lend it to you, but give it back to me on Monday.
—Who gave you the keys? —The doorman gave them to us.
_Le/les_ + _lo/la/los/las_ is impossible: _le_ and _les_ become _se_. _Se lo di_ = I gave it to him / her / you / them. Add _a + person_ if it isn't clear.
—And the floor lamp? —I gave it to my sister.
—Did you explain the problem to the removal people? —Yes, I explained it to them yesterday.

Affirmative commands: pronouns after and attached (_dámelo_). Negative commands: before (_no me lo des_). With _ir a_ / _tener que_ + infinitive or _estar_ + gerund: before the conjugated verb or attached to the end, never in between.
Pass me the tape, please. No, don't throw it to me, give it to me in my hand.
The boxes of books? I have to take them up today.
The stress doesn't move when you add pronouns, but the longer word often needs a written accent to show it: _compra → cómpralo_, _dar → dártelo_, _buscando → buscándolo_.
Tell me the address and write it down for me here.
I'm looking for it everywhere.
Before giving it to him, wrap it up well.
the sofa
the floor lamp
the mirror
the bookcase / shelving
the cushions
the blender
the drill
to move house
to pack (for a move)
the cardboard box
the sticky tape
the removal van
the deposit (on a rented flat)
to lend / to borrow
to give back
to give (as a present)
to keep something
Can you lend it to me?
I'll give it back to you tomorrow.
Adding pronouns never moves the stress: _LLEva → LLÉvala → LLÉvatela_. Keep the strong beat on the verb and say the pronouns lightly.
they don't fit (in my place)
to have an owner / to be taken
for whoever asks for them
pupusas (stuffed corn tortillas from El Salvador)
The bookcase? I'm going to leave it for Raúl.
Don't give it back to me yet, I don't need it.
I'll give it back to you on Monday, I promise.
_Que_ joins a noun and a piece of information that identifies it (who / which / that). It never changes, it works for people and things, and the verb after it agrees with the noun before it.
I'm looking for the lady who rents out the room.
The neighbours who live upstairs have a huge dog.
In English you can drop _that_ (the map I bought), but in Spanish _que_ is always needed: _el mapa que compré_. _¿Qué…?_ with an accent asks a question.
Which shop do you like best? —The one next to the park.
I can't find the key that doña Carmen gave me.
_Donde_ = where / in which, after a place. _Cuando_ = when, after a time you have already mentioned. With _el día, el año_ use _que_ or _en que_: _el día que llegué_ (the day I arrived).
This is the school where my father studied.
In the afternoon, when the market closes, the square gets quiet.
I never forget the year I lived in Santa Ana.
_Lo que_ = what / the thing that. It has no noun before it: _Lo que más me gusta es…_ (What I like most is…).
What surprised me most was the volcano.
Sorry, I didn't understand what you said.
Buy whatever we need for dinner, please.
the corner shop
the bakery
the (sports) court / pitch
the bus stop
the all-night / duty pharmacy
the town market
the neighbour across the street
the owner / the landlord
the street vendor
the host family
to greet each other
It's a thing that is used for…
It's a place where…
It's the person who…
What do you call the thing that…?
I can't think of the word.
Relative _que, donde, cuando_ are unstressed and link to the next word. Question words _qué, dónde, cuándo_ are stressed and written with an accent.
the wedding cake
the terrace
Lake Coatepeque (a crater lake near Santa Ana)
The bus I take comes at seven.
That's the court where my brother plays.
What I miss most is food from home.
_más / menos + adjective + que_ = more / less … than. _tan + adjective + como_ = as … as. With numbers: _más de_ (more than).
The bus is slower than the taxi, but it's less expensive.
My street isn't as quiet as yours.
_mejor_ (better), _peor_ (worse), _mayor_ (older), _menor_ (younger) never take _más_. For size, say _más grande / más pequeño_.
This mattress is better than mine: I sleep much better.
The owners are older than my parents.
Past participles work as adjectives with _estar_ and agree: _la cocina está reformada_ (the kitchen has been renovated). Group nouns like _la gente_ take a singular verb.
The second flat is better looked after than the first one.
The people in this neighbourhood are friendlier than in the centre.
_el / la + noun + más + adjective + de_ = the most … in / of. Use _de_, not _que_ or _en_: _el más barato de los tres_. With _mejor / peor_ the adjective goes before the noun.
El Picacho is one of the most visited places in the city.
Of the three flats, this is the least noisy.
_-ísimo_ means very, very: _carísimo, bonitísima_. Watch the spelling: _rico → riquísimo, largo → larguísimo_. Never _muy carísimo_. Exclamations: _¡Qué bonito!_, _¡Qué casa tan bonita!_
The rent is really cheap for such a central area.
What a big balcony! And the view is gorgeous.
the rent
furnished / unfurnished
bills (water, electricity) included
the parking space
security (guards)
the neighbourhood (in Honduras, Mexico…)
bright / dark
central / far from the centre
noisy / quiet
spacious / cramped, narrow
renovated
it works out cheaper
it's closer for me
it's worth it
the only bad thing is…
I'll take it
_-ísimo_ moves the stress to the _í_: _CAro → caRÍsimo_. Exclamations with _¡Qué…!_ start high and fall at the end.
looked out onto a wall
baleadas (Honduran flour tortillas with beans and cream)
El Picacho (a hill and park above Tegucigalpa)
the car (in much of Latin America)
The third one is the least noisy of the three.
My brother is two years younger than me.
What a modern kitchen!

Diminutives: _-ito / -ita_ is the general ending (_casita_). Words ending in _-e, -n, -r_ often take _-cito / -ecito_ (_cafecito, panecito_). Spelling changes keep the sound: _poco → poquito, taza → tacita_.
We live in a little house near the cathedral.
Can you give me a tiny bit more sawdust?
Diminutives can show size, affection (_mi abuelita_) or politeness (_un momentito_ = just a moment). Some are separate words: _el bolsillo_ (pocket), _la ventanilla_ (ticket window).
Come in, madam, sit down for a little while I get your bill ready.
The bread is nice and warm, fresh out of the oven.
Pay at window number two.

Augmentatives exaggerate: _-ón_ (_un problemón_), _-azo_ (_un perrazo_, also a blow: _un portazo_). _-ucho_ is pejorative (_un cuartucho_ = a shabby room). Some _-ón_ words are new words: _el cajón_ (drawer), _el sillón_ (armchair).
This year's carpet is a huge success.
We stayed in a grotty hotel with no hot water.
_algo_ (something / anything) and _nada_ (nothing) for things; _alguien_ (someone / anyone) and _nadie_ (nobody) for people. They never change and take a singular verb.
—Does anyone have a lighter? —Not me, but I think Luis has one.
—Do you want anything to drink? —Nothing, thanks, we've already had coffee.
_No_ + verb + _nada / nadie_: _No vino nadie_. Or _Nadie_ + verb, without _no_: _Nadie vino_. As objects, people take _a_: _No conozco a nadie_, but not after _hay_.
I didn't see anyone in the square: it was empty.
Are you waiting for someone? —Yes, for my cousin.
the sawdust carpet
coloured sawdust
the stencil / mould
the procession
the design
to wet, to dampen
the block (of a street)
the bucket
the torch / flashlight
to stay up all night
the person in charge
Could you do me a little favour?
Just a moment, I'm coming.
Does anyone need anything?
Anything else? —Nothing else, thanks.
Diminutive endings take the stress: _caSIta, cafeCIto_. _-ón_ is stressed and written with an accent (_problemón_), but loses it in the plural (_sillones_).
sweet bread
so that it doesn't blow away
the dove
I don't know anyone on this block.
Does anyone want a nice hot coffee?
Nobody slept all night.
_algún / alguna / algunos / algunas_ = some, any; _ningún / ninguna_ = no, not any (usually singular). Before a masculine singular noun: _algún, ningún_. Without a noun: _alguno, ninguno_.
Is there a cashpoint near the square?
—Are there any tickets left? —No, there are none left.
Before a noun, _mucho, poco, demasiado_ agree (_muchas personas_). With a verb or an adjective they don't change (_es demasiado caro_). _Muy_ + adjective; _mucho_ + verb, noun or _más / mejor_.
There were too many tourists and very little shade.
This hotel is much quieter than the other one.
_cada_ (each, every) + singular noun, never changes. _otro_ (another, other) never takes _un_. _todo el / toda la / todos los / todas las_ = the whole, all.
Each stela has a different story.
We spent the whole afternoon in the park and we'll come back another day.
Spanish uses double negatives: _no_ + verb + _nunca / nada / nadie / ningún_. If the negative word comes first, drop _no_: _Nunca voy_ = _No voy nunca_. Never _Nunca no_.
I've never seen such a tall temple.
No guide speaks German today.
_también_ (too) answers a positive sentence; _tampoco_ (neither / not either) answers a negative one. _ni… ni_ = neither… nor.
—I've never seen a macaw. —Me neither, what colours!
On the bus there was neither wifi nor air conditioning.
the archaeological site
the temple
the grand staircase
the stela (carved stone)
the ball court
the macaw
the cap
insect repellent
the ticket
the tour guide
the shade
it was packed
it was packed to the rafters
there was a bit of everything
it falls short
there's time to spare
The negative word carries the strongest beat: _No voy NUNca_. _ningún_ is stressed at the end; _ninguno_ on _-GU-_. Short reactions (_yo tampoco_) fall at the end.
nothing like it
the leaflet / brochure
plan it well (to a group)
There isn't a single seat left on the bus.
Each student pays for their ticket.
I never saw so many macaws together.

_desde… hasta / de… a_ = from… to; _hacia_ = towards; _hasta_ = as far as; _por_ = through, along, via. Transport: _en bus_, but _a pie_. Location phrases take _de_: _delante de, enfrente de, al lado de_.
From the hotel to the beach it takes ten minutes on foot.
The stop is behind the church, next to a huge tree.
_para_ = purpose, destination, recipient, deadline. _por_ = cause, route, approximate place, part of the day, price. _por_ + noun, _porque_ + conjugated verb.
Thanks for picking me up; this pineapple is for your mother.
In the afternoon we walked along the beach to watch the sunset.

_ser_ = what someone is like (identity, character); _estar_ = how they are now or a change you notice; _llevar_ = what they're wearing (clothes, glasses, beard, hairstyle); _tener_ = body features (_tiene los ojos verdes_).
My aunt is short and very chatty; today she's wearing a flowery dress.
You're so tanned! Did you go to the beach?
the bus station
the pier / dock
the ferry
the seafront promenade
the lighthouse
the ticket office
to have a beard / a moustache
to wear one's hair long / short / tied back
to be tanned / to have dark skin
the sweatshirt / hoodie
the sandals
How will I recognise you?
I'll wait for you in front of…
Where are you now? (on the way)
You've changed so much.
Thanks for coming to pick me up.

Prepositions are unstressed and link to the next word: _para_el_, _hasta_el_; a final consonant moves to the next vowel: _por_el_ sounds like _po-rel_. In fast speech _para_ is often _pa_, but always write _para_.
a compliment
chilled coconut (to drink)
it's huge on me
to dive / to snorkel
I'll wait for you opposite the ticket office at the pier.
She's the girl who's carrying a red backpack.
We bought the tickets for six hundred lempiras.

Use _se_ + 3rd-person verb when the person doesn't matter: recipes, signs, rules. The verb agrees with the thing: _se lava el arroz_ / _se lavan los frijoles_. With no thing, singular: _aquí se come temprano_.
In Nicaragua, gallo pinto is eaten with tortilla and cheese.
The tables are cleaned after each group.
How do you say “spoon” in Spanish?

Rules: _(no) se puede_ + infinitive, always singular. Compare an instruction for anyone (_se corta el pan_), an order to one person (_Marcos, corta el pan_) and a fact about one person (_Marcos corta el pan_).
You can't use your phone in the kitchen.
Can we taste the sauce?
Doña Rosa, how do you turn this oven on?
Sequence: _primero → luego / después → entonces → al final / por último_. _Al final_ = in the end (the outcome); _por último_ = lastly (the last item). _Entonces_ = then, or so.
First you heat the oil and then you add the onion.
In the end the soup turned out delicious.
Cause: _porque_ after the result, _como_ at the start. Consequence: _por eso_ / _así que_ after the cause. Rephrase with _es decir_ (spoken: _o sea_).
As the oven wasn't working, we made the rosquillas in the frying pan.
I forgot the salt, so the rice came out tasteless.
Vigorón is a cold dish, that is, it isn't cooked on the spot.
red beans
ripe plantain
cassava
pork crackling
cabbage
fresh curd cheese
the pot
the frying pan
the knife
the chopping board
the strainer
to soak
to peel
to chop finely
to fry
to boil
to drain
to taste
Pause briefly after sequence connectors and keep the pitch slightly up. With _como_, the voice rises at the end of the cause and falls at the end of the result. Pause before _así que_ and _por eso_.
sweating
the drawer
over the top
the cooking liquid / broth
First, the ripe plantains are peeled.
As we didn't have an oven, we used the frying pan.
Can you pay by card here?
_Si_ + present for a real, possible condition; the result is in the present or the imperative. Never future or subjunctive straight after _si_. Comma when the sentence starts with _si_.
If Saturday dawns clear, we leave at six.
I'll bring two flasks of coffee if there are more than five of us.
If you don't feel well, tell me and we'll stay.
_Si_ (no accent) = if; _sí_ (accent) = yes. _Si_ = maybe it happens; _cuando_ = it will happen or always happens. _Si no_ = otherwise.
—Are you in? —Yes, if it doesn't rain.
When we get to Cartago, we always eat at the market.
If the train is full, we'll wait for the next one; if not, we'll get on now.
Soft requests are fixed chunks + infinitive: _¿Podrías…? (tú) / ¿Podría…? (usted)_; _¿Te / Le importaría…?_ (answer _No, claro que no_ to accept); _¿Me harías el favor de…?_
Don Ernesto, would you mind keeping the key for me until Sunday?
Could you send me the location of the viewpoint?
_Me gustaría_ + infinitive or noun = a polite wish now. The courtesy imperfect (_quería pedirte_, _venía a_) speaks about now. Decline with _Lo siento, es que…_ and offer an alternative.
Good morning, I wanted to ask you what time the park opens.
I'd like a table near the window, please.
I'm sorry, it's just that I don't have a car; if you like, I'll go with you by bus.
the crater
the summit
the viewpoint
the flask
the raincoat
to sign up / to join in
fog
to be cloudy
to dawn clear
a downpour
it's cold up there
to water the plants
to feed the cat
to pick up a parcel
to keep the key
to take out the rubbish
to keep an eye on things
A soft request rises at the end like a question; falling sounds like an order. Stress the í in _podrías_ and _importaría_. Conditional _si_ is weak; _sí_ (yes) is stressed.
it's not worth it
the first-aid kit
let me know (usted)
straight
If there's fog, we'll visit the ruins.
Would you mind watering my plants at the weekend?
I'm sorry, it's just that I work on Saturday.

_Hay que_ + infinitive = general obligation, never with a person. _Tener que_ + infinitive = one person's obligation (conjugate _tener_). _Deber_ + infinitive = what is right, advice, formal rules; no _que_.
To see the coffee fields at their best, you have to go up early.
This week my partner has to cook twice.
You should put on sun cream: the sun is strong.
_No hay que / no tienes que_ = it's not necessary. _No debes_ = you shouldn't, it's not right. _No se puede_ = it's not allowed.
There's no need to book: the tour leaves every hour.
You shouldn't leave food in the room because of the ants.
A natural order: verb + thing + how + where + when. Don't put a lot of information between the subject and the verb.
We roast the coffee slowly in a clay pot.
My brother has been working at a cooperative since January.
Put the most important time or place at the start, followed by a comma, but don't pile everything there. Offer two options with _o_; the answer is one option, not _sí_.
In the afternoon, the cooperative organises a visit to the village.
—Shall we go by bus or on foot? —On foot, it's close.
In high season, you have to book two weeks ahead.
We dry the beans in the sun on the patio in the afternoon.
The volunteers have breakfast together in the kitchen at six.
On Thursday, we visit the processing plant by bus.
the coffee field
the ripe bean / cherry
the coffee-picking basket (Costa Rica)
the coffee processing plant
the hillside
the storeroom
to pick by hand
to dry in the sun
to roast
to do a tasting
to sort the beans
rubber boots
gloves
the hat
insect repellent
sun cream
In a closed choice with _o_, the voice rises on the first option and falls at the end of the second. Pause slightly at the comma after a time or place frame.
to get off
picks you up
the cabin
ants

After a preposition, use the infinitive (_antes de subir_). _Al_ + infinitive = when. An action as subject is an infinitive (_Viajar es…_), not _-ing_. _Acabar de_ = to have just; _volver a_ = again; _empezar a_ = to start.
We left the hotel without having breakfast.
I've just seen a dolphin near the boat.

_Seguir_ + gerund = to keep on / still. A gerund can say how (_llegó corriendo_). _Estar_ + participle = a state, and the participle agrees (_cerrada, cerrados_). With _haber_ the participle always ends in _-o_.
We're still waiting, but the boat isn't coming.
The ticket windows are closed until two.
A boy ran across the street.

Indirect questions follow _no sé, ¿sabe…?, ¿me puede decir…?, dime_. The question word keeps its accent (_dónde, qué, cuándo_) and the verb follows it. Use question marks only if the whole sentence asks.
Do you know how long the crossing takes?
I don't know which one is our dock.
For yes/no questions inside a sentence use _si_ (= whether), without an accent: _no sé si hay asientos_. Not _qué_ or _que_.
Ask at the window whether they take cards.
I don't remember if I locked the car.
Can you tell me if this bus stops at the dock?
the dock / pier
the ticket office
the queue
the ramp
the deck
the crossing
sold out
delayed
cancelled
the sea is rough
the seasonal timetable
the return ticket
ID card / passport
to board
to disembark
to get seasick
Question words inside a sentence keep their stress and accent (_no sé DÓNde_). When _que, donde, cuando, si_ don't ask anything, they're weak and have no accent.
a typical Costa Rican set meal
anxious, on edge
easily
some pills
Can you tell me where the ticket office is?
We're still waiting because the ramp is closed.
I don't know if the ferry takes bicycles.
A finished, measured period → preterite: _trabajé tres años, viví de 2018 a 2021_. A counted total → preterite: _fui cuatro veces_. Not the imperfect, even for long periods.
I did an internship at a newspaper for one summer.
That year we went to the beach three times.
Habits of a period (_siempre, cada sábado, dos veces por semana_) → imperfect. _Hace_ + time = ago, with a past verb: _volví hace dos meses_. Don't mix it with _desde hace_ (still going on).
A year ago I knew nothing about radio.
At university I used to work weekends in a café.

Story: scene and causes in the imperfect, events in the preterite, today with the present perfect where usual; _ayer_ + preterite. Messages: _¿podrías…?_, imperative with attached pronouns, _gracias por_, _para_ + deadline.
As there was a crash on the avenue, the bus was stopped for twenty minutes.
Could you send me the questions by Thursday? Thanks for everything.
The studio keys, give them to Rebeca, please.
the radio station
the recording studio
the script
the presenter / announcer
to be on air
the audience
the guest
to do an internship
the position
the former boss
a reference letter
to work shifts
often
from time to time
twice a week
for a while
recently / not long ago
Regular preterite stresses the last syllable (_trabajé, trabajó_); the present stresses earlier (_trabajo_). Imperfect stresses _-aba / -ía_. Strong irregulars (_estuve, hice_) have no accent.
intense, busy
soaked
just in case
to make everything worse
I came back to San José two months ago.
As it was raining, the bus was stopped for twenty minutes.
Could you send me the script by Thursday?
I introduce myself and name my things
Review of soy and estoy, of the persons (yo, tú, usted…) and of nouns: masculine, feminine and plural.
Review the persons (**yo, tú, usted, nosotros**…) and choose between `soy` and `estoy`.
Review noun gender and rebel words like `el día` and `la mano`.
Turn singular nouns into plurals: `-s`, `-es`, `-ces`.

This week you review your first two classes: how to introduce yourself with **soy** and **estoy**, and how to name people, places and things with their gender and plural. Here you see it in a different way, step by step, for studying on your own.
The persons: who is speaking?

Before the verb comes the person: **yo** (I'm speaking), **tú** (I'm talking to you, informally), **usted** (I'm talking to you, politely), **él** or **ella** (I'm talking about someone else). In the plural: **nosotros/nosotras**, **vosotros/vosotras** and **ellos/ellas/ustedes**.

**Vosotros** is used in Spain to address a group informally. In Latin America people say **ustedes** to any group. **Usted** and **ustedes** take the verb like él and ellos: usted **es**, ustedes **son**.
In Argentina, Uruguay and parts of Central America you will hear **vos** instead of tú, with a different verb form: _vos sos_ means _tú eres_. You only need to recognise it.
The pronoun is often dropped because the verb already shows the person: **Estoy bien** sounds more natural than _Yo estoy bien_.
**-os** is for men or a mixed group; **-as** is only for women: _nosotras_ could be three female friends.
The six persons
_Usted_ takes the verb form of él and ella: **está**, not _estás_.
Soy or estoy?

Both verbs translate as _I am_, but they say different things. With **ser** you state your identity: your name, where you're from, your job. With **estar** you say how you are right now or where you are.
A quick question: can it change tomorrow? If it's your name or your country, it doesn't change: **soy**. If it's your mood or the place where you are, it changes: **estoy**.
To ask someone else: **¿Cómo estás?** (state) and **¿De dónde eres?** (origin).
Ser and estar in the present
How you feel today is a state: **estoy**.
Where you're from is identity: **soy de**.
A place where you are now: **estoy en**.
Every noun has a gender
A noun is the name of a person, a place, a thing or an idea: _la amiga_, _el barrio_, _la llave_, _la paciencia_. In Spanish they are all **masculine** or **feminine**, objects too.

The ending helps: **-o** is usually masculine (_el cuaderno_), **-a** is usually feminine (_la toalla_), and **-ción** and **-dad** are feminine (_la habitación_, _la universidad_). With **-e** or a consonant there's no clue: _el cargador_, _la llave_.
There are few **rebel words**, but they are very common: _el día_, _el mapa_, _el problema_ end in -a and are masculine; _la mano_ and _la foto_ end in -o and are feminine.

From one thing to several: the plural

Look at the last letter. If it ends in a **vowel**, add **-s**: _silla → sillas_. If it ends in a **consonant**, add **-es**: _cargador → cargadores_. If it ends in **-z**, change the z to **c** and add **-es**: _lápiz → lápices_.
The article goes plural too: **el → los**, **la → las**, **un → unos**, **una → unas**. Rebel words keep their gender: _los mapas_, _las fotos_.
Watch the accent mark: _habitación_ has one, but _habitaciones_ doesn't, because the stressed syllable is now the second to last.

Spelling: the names of the letters
At a reception desk, on the phone or in class, people will ask you: **¿Cómo se escribe?** (How do you spell it?) To answer, use the name of each letter: _Ana: a, ene, a_.

Some letters have surprising names: **h** is called _hache_ and is never pronounced; **j** is called _jota_ and sounds strong, from the throat; **ñ** is _eñe_; **v** is _uve_ and sounds exactly like b; **w** is _uve doble_; **y** is _ye_; **z** is _zeta_.
The vowels have very short names: a, e, i, o, u. Always say them short and clear.
In Spanish almost everything is written the way it sounds. The traps are **h** (silent), **b** and **v** (they sound the same) and **ll** and **y** (they sound the same in almost every country).

This week you review two classes that go together: how to tell whether a word is masculine or feminine, and which article to choose depending on what the other person knows. One idea guides everything: **learn every word with its article**.
The ending gives you a clue
Look at the end of the word. Masculine words almost always end in **-o** or **-or**: _el vaso_, _el color_, _el ascensor_. Feminine words almost always end in **-a**: _la plaza_.
Some endings are very reliable: **-ción**, **-sión**, **-dad** and **-tad** are always feminine: _la estación_, _la televisión_, _la ciudad_, _la libertad_.
With **-e** or other consonants there's no rule: _el puente_, _la calle_, _el árbol_, _la sal_. Here only memory works: word and article together.
A famous -or exception: **la flor**. Learn it with a picture: a red flower on the table.

Ending
Gender

**-ción** is always feminine: **la** estación.
**-or** is almost always masculine: **el** color.
Tricky words and “el agua”

Some common words are deceptive. They end in -a and are masculine: _el día_, _el mapa_, _el tema_, _el idioma_, _el sistema_. They end in -o and are feminine: _la mano_, _la foto_, _la moto_, _la radio_.
But not every word ending in **-ma** is masculine: _la cama_, _la crema_, _la forma_ are feminine. So, once again: word and article together.

Special case: some feminine words begin with a strong (stressed) **a**: _agua_, _aula_, _área_. In the singular they take **el** or **un** for the sound, but they stay feminine: _el agua fría_. In the plural they go back to **las**: _las aulas_.
The most useful traps
-a but masculine
-o but feminine
feminine with el
_Tema_ is a trap: it ends in -a, but it's masculine.
_Agua_ begins with a stressed a: in the singular, **el** agua.
_El_ is only for the sound: _agua_ is feminine, and so is the adjective.
Un, una: something new
Use **un, una, unos, unas** when you introduce something **new** in the conversation: the other person doesn't know which one yet. _Hay un mercado en el centro._
**Hay** almost always goes with un/una (or nothing, or a number): _Hay una parada aquí_, _Hay dos bancos_. Never _hay el_ or _hay la_.
You also use un/una to say **what something is like**: _Guadalajara es una ciudad grande_.
The articles
Something new
We know which one
_Hay_ introduces something new: **un** banco.
El, la: we already know which one
Use **el, la, los, las** when both people know **which one** it is: because you've already mentioned it, because it's unique or because it's right there in the situation.
It's the natural flow of a story: first _un_, then _el_. _Hay una plaza con una fuente. La plaza es antigua y la fuente es enorme._
The key question isn't “does it exist?”, but “does the other person know which one it is?”. In a hotel, _¿Dónde está el ascensor?_: there's only one, and you both know it.
Listen to a story in Spanish and count: how many times does it go from _un_ to _el_? It's the most common pattern.
Second mention: we already know which fountain it is, **la** fuente.
The exit of this building is a specific one: **la**.

The stressed syllable
Every Spanish word has one **stressed syllable**: it's said with a little more force. In _mercado_ it's **CA**: mer-**CA**-do. If you move the stress, the word sounds strange or changes its meaning.

The general rule: if the word ends in a vowel, -n or -s, the stress falls on the second to last syllable (_pla-za_, _ca-lle_). If it ends in another consonant, on the last one (_co-lor_, _ciu-dad_). If it doesn't follow the rule, it has a written **accent**: _es-ta-ción_, _ár-bol_.
The stressed syllable explains _el agua_: the voice lands on the first **a** (**A**-gua). In _alarma_ the stress is on _LAR_, so we say _la alarma_.
The written accent marks the stressed syllable when the word doesn't follow the rule: _televisión_, _árbol_, _panadería_. In the plural the accent sometimes disappears: _estación → estaciones_.
Why?
Where does the stress fall?
Stress on the first **a** of each word: **A**-gua, **AU**-la, **Á**-rea.
Here the first a is weak: a-**LAR**-ma, a-**YU**-da. That's why it's _la_.
The stress doesn't move: es-ta-**CIÓN**, es-ta-**CIO**-nes.
mer-**CA**-do, **CEN**-tro: second to last, because they end in a vowel.
ciu-**DAD**, ca-te-**DRAL**: they end in a consonant, so the stress goes at the end.

This week you review three classes: the plural of a group of words, adjectives that agree and the position of the adjective. Here you see it with objects from a craft market, step by step, so you can study on your own.
The whole group becomes plural

You already know how to make a noun plural. Now look at the **whole group**: article or number + noun + adjective. If there are several things, all three words change: _una vela verde → tres velas verdes_.

Numbers don't change (_dos, tres, cuatro…_). From **dos** on, the noun and the adjective are plural. The adjective follows the same rule as the noun: vowel + **-s** (_rojas_), consonant + **-es** (_azules_), **-z → -ces** (_felices_).
Two special cases: words in **-ión** lose the written accent (_una reunión larga → dos reuniones largas_), and weekdays ending in **-s** don't change, only the article does: _el lunes → los lunes_.

What changes
The adjective becomes plural too: consonant + **-es**.

The adjective copies the noun
The adjective says what something is like: its colour, its size, its origin. It always **agrees** with the noun: masculine or feminine, singular or plural.

Adjectives in **-o** have **four forms**: _negro, negra, negros, negras_. Adjectives in **-e** or a consonant have **two forms**, one for singular and one for plural: _verde, verdes_; _azul, azules_; _feliz, felices_.

Nationalities ending in a consonant do change for the feminine: _español → española_, _alemán → alemana_, _inglés → inglesa_. Notice: in the feminine the written accent disappears. And they are written in lower case.
If the group mixes masculine and feminine, the adjective is **masculine plural**: _un vaso y una jarra rojos_.

After to describe, before to give an opinion
The normal order in Spanish is **noun + adjective**: _una casa amarilla_, _un mercado grande_, _un café mexicano_. This is how you describe: colour, shape, size, origin. Always after.

A few adjectives go **before** when you give your **opinion**: _un buen café_, _una mala noche_, _una gran ciudad_. Before a masculine singular noun, **bueno** and **malo** get shorter: _buen_, _mal_. **Grande** becomes **gran** before any singular noun, masculine or feminine.
In the plural there is no short form: _buenos amigos_, _grandes ideas_. And after _es_ or _son_, the adjective is complete: _El café es bueno_.

Four adjectives that change meaning
With some adjectives, the position changes what you say. **After** the noun they have the basic meaning; **before**, another meaning.

_Una ciudad grande_ has a lot of inhabitants; _una gran ciudad_ is important or impressive. _Un compañero viejo_ is old in years; _un viejo compañero_ is a colleague from a long time ago. _Una bici nueva_ has just been bought; _una nueva bici_ is another bike, different from the previous one. _Un sombrero único_ is very special; _el único sombrero_ is the only one, there is no other.
For a person's age, _viejo_ can sound harsh: it is kinder to say **mayor**: _una señora mayor_.
If in doubt, put the adjective **after**: it is almost always correct and has the basic meaning.

Soft r and strong r
Spanish has two **r** sounds. The **soft r** is a very short tap of the tongue, like the _tt_ in American English _better_: _caro_, _claro_, _negro_, _amarillo_, _para_.
The **strong r** is a long trill: the tongue vibrates several times. It is written **rr** between vowels (_carro_, _barro_, _jarra_) and **r** at the start of a word (_rojo_, _regalo_, _rebozo_).
Careful: changing the sound changes the word. _Caro_ (a lot of money) is not _carro_ (car); _pero_ is not _perro_.
Between vowels, one **r** sounds soft and two (**rr**) sound strong. At the start of a word you write a single **r**, but it sounds strong: _rojo_, never _rrojo_.

This week you review two classes: demonstratives for pointing and possessives for saying who something belongs to. Here you see them during a house move: lots of boxes, lots of things and lots of owners.
Near, a bit far, very far
To point, Spanish looks at **distance**. Near you, in your hand: **aquí** and **este**. Near the other person or a bit far: **ahí** and **ese**. Far from both people: **allí** and **aquel**.

The demonstrative agrees with the noun, like an adjective: _este sillón_, _esta lámpara_, _estos cojines_, _estas cajas_. Careful: the masculine singular ends in **-e** (_este_, _ese_) or **-l** (_aquel_), never in -o.

In everyday conversation, **este** and **ese** are the most common. **Aquel** is for things that are clearly far away: _aquel edificio de allí_. In many Latin American countries you also hear **allá** instead of _allí_.
Point with your finger when you practise: hand = este, arm = ese, whole arm and beyond = aquel.

What's this? The forms without a noun
When you don't know the name of a thing, or don't want to repeat it, you use **esto**, **eso** or **aquello**. They are neuter forms: neither masculine nor feminine, and they have no plural.
The most useful question of the week is **¿Qué es esto?** (near you) or **¿Qué es eso?** (near the other person). The answer includes the noun: _Es un abrelatas_.
Careful: **estos** is not the plural of _esto_; it's the plural of _este_. And _esto_ never goes before a noun.

Mi, tu, su: the person and the thing

The possessive says **who** something belongs to. The **person** chooses the word: yo → **mi**, tú → **tu**, él, ella or usted → **su**. The **thing** chooses the form: one thing → _mi_; several things → **mis**.
That's why _mis llaves_ are one person's keys: the **-s** says there are several **keys**, not several owners.
**Tu** (possessive) has no accent; **tú** (the person) does: _Tú tienes tu cargador_.
Don't put an article before the possessive: _mi libro_, not _el mi libro_.

The possessive goes without an article.
Nuestro and the problem with su
With **nosotros** the possessive has **four forms**, because it also agrees with the thing in gender: _nuestro coche_, _nuestra casa_, _nuestros vecinos_, _nuestras plantas_.
With **ellos**, **ellas** and **ustedes** you use **su** and **sus** again. In Spain, with _vosotros_, you use **vuestro, vuestra, vuestros, vuestras**: _vuestra casa_.
**Su** can have many owners: his, hers, yours (formal), theirs, yours (plural). If it isn't clear, use **el / la + thing + de + person**: _la bici de Andrés_, _el coche de mis padres_.
Key question: **¿De quién es…?** / **¿De quién son…?** And answer: _Es de Andrés_, _Son de mis padres_.

**de + person** is enough: no need to repeat.

Linking: a final s joins the vowel

In Spanish, the words in a group are pronounced **together**, without a pause. If a word ends in **s** and the next one starts with a **vowel**, the s moves to the next word: _mis amigos_ sounds like **mi-sa-mi-gos**.

This linking is very common with plural possessives and demonstratives: _tus hermanos_ (tu-ser-ma-nos), _estos objetos_ (es-to-sob-je-tos), _nuestras amigas_ (nues-tra-sa-mi-gas). Remember: **h** is silent, so _tus hermanos_ links too.
For listening: if you hear an **s** before the vowel, the group is plural. _Mi amigo_ and _mis amigos_ differ only by that s.
In writing, the words stay separate: _mis amigos_. Linking is only about sound; never write _misamigos_.
Join the s and the i: _mi-si-jos_. The h is silent.

This week is a checkpoint. You review two new classes (subject pronouns and the verb ser for identity, job and origin) and combine them with the nine classes of weeks 1 to 4. By the end of the week you can introduce a whole group.
Subject pronouns: who does the action
The subject pronoun says **who**: _yo, tú, él, ella, usted, nosotros, nosotras, vosotros, vosotras, ellos, ellas, ustedes_.
**Tú** is for friends, family and colleagues; **usted** is for older people, customers or formal situations. **Usted** and **ustedes** take the verb of _él_ and _ellos_: _usted es_, _ustedes son_.

**Vosotros** is only used in Spain, for a group you're close to. In Latin America, **ustedes** is used for any group. In Argentina, Uruguay and parts of Central America you also hear **vos**, with its own verb form (_vos sos_ means _tú eres_); you only need to recognise it.
Subject pronouns
_Ustedes_ takes the verb of _ellos_: **son**.
With or without a pronoun?
In Spanish the verb already shows the person: _soy_ can only be _yo_; _somos_, only _nosotros_. That's why the pronoun usually **disappears**: _Soy diseñadora. Vivo en Mérida._

The pronoun **appears** in three cases: to **contrast** two people (_Yo soy de Lima y él es de Quito_), to **make clear** who _es_ or _son_ refers to (_Ella es cocinera_), and to answer **¿Quién…?** (_—¿Quién es el profesor? —Yo._).
Repeating _yo_ in every sentence sounds strange: _Yo soy Ana. Yo soy profesora. Yo soy de Puebla._ Better: _Soy Ana. Soy profesora y soy de Puebla._

Ser: who you are, what you do, where you're from, what you're like
With **ser** you say your identity: your name (_Soy Itzel_), job (_Es cocinero_), origin (_Somos de Yucatán_), nationality (_Son alemanas_) and personality (_Eres muy simpático_).
A **job** goes without an article: _Es ingeniera_, not _es una ingeniera_. If you add an adjective, you do use **un / una**: _Es una ingeniera excelente_.

A **nationality** agrees with the person and is written in lower case: _mexicano, mexicana, mexicanos, mexicanas_. Those ending in **-e** have one form for both genders: _estadounidense_, _canadiense_. _Ser de + place_ says the same thing: _Es de Chile_ = _Es chilena_.
Remember the contrast from week 1: with **ser** you say who you are (_Soy médica_), with **estar** how you are today (_Estoy cansada_).

A job on its own goes **without** an article.
Nationalities are written in **lower case**.

J and g: the throat sound
Many nationalities and jobs have a strong sound that comes from the throat, like a stronger English _h_: _Japón_, _japonés_, _jubilado_, _ingeniero_, _argentino_.
This sound is written **j** before any vowel (_ja, je, ji, jo, ju_) and **g** before **e** and **i** (_ge, gi_): _ingeniera_, _argentina_, _Gerardo_.
Before **a, o, u**, **g** is soft, like in English _go_: _gallego_, _uruguayo_, _inglés_. To keep the soft sound with e or i, you write **gue, gui**: _Miguel_, _guitarra_.
The **x** in _México_ and _mexicano_ sounds like **j**: it's an old spelling that has been kept. In _taxi_ or _examen_, on the other hand, x sounds like **ks**.

This week you review two classes: **estar** for states and places, and the difference between **hay** and **está**. Here you see them with new examples and one key question for each decision.
Estar: how you are today
With **estar** you say how a person is right now: their mood, their body, their energy. The question is **¿Cómo estás?** and the answer changes from one day to the next.
The adjective agrees with the person: _Raúl está preocupado_, _Raquel está preocupada_, _los niños están aburridos_. **Bien** and **mal** never change: _Ellas están bien_.
A city or a thing can also use _estar_: _Hoy la plaza está muy tranquila_ talks about today. If you say _La ciudad es tranquila_, you talk about what it is always like.
Before you choose, ask yourself: am I talking about how it is now or how it always is? Now → **estar**.
Estar in the present
The adjective agrees with the person: hermana → aburrid**a**.
_Hoy_ marks a state right now: **estoy**.
Estar: where you are
To say where someone or something is, use **estar en** + place: _Estoy en la plaza_, _Mis gafas están en el bolso_. The question is **¿Dónde está…?**
The words **aquí**, **ahí** and **allí** go without _en_: _Estamos aquí_. Aquí is near you, ahí is near the other person and allí is far from both.
For distance, use **cerca de** and **lejos de**: _El hostal está cerca de la catedral_. With no place after it, just _cerca_ or _lejos_: _El aeropuerto está lejos_.

Word
Meaning
**Allí**, **aquí** and **ahí** don't take _en_.
To say where a place is, use **estar**.
Hay or está?

**Hay** introduces something new, something the other person doesn't know yet: _En la calle hay un cajero_. After _hay_ comes **un, una, unos, unas**, a number, _mucho, mucha_ or a noun with no article: _hay agua_, _hay tres cafés_.

**Está / están** places something known, something that already has a name: _El cajero está en la esquina_. Before it comes **el, la, los, las**, a possessive (_mi, tu_) or a proper name: _Ingrid está en la plaza_.
**Hay** never changes: _hay un banco_, _hay dos bancos_. But _está_ becomes **están** with several things: _Los bancos están en la avenida_.
Quick trick: look at the word before the noun. _Un, una_, a number or nothing? → **hay**. _El, la, mi_ or a name? → **está**.

Hay, ahí and está: an accent changes the sound
**Hay** has just one syllable: the a and the i go together, as in _aire_. **Ahí** has two syllables, _a-í_, and the stress is on the í. The h is silent in both.
The exclamation **¡ay!** sounds exactly like _hay_. That's why context matters: _¡Ay, qué frío!_ / _Hay frío_.
**Está** (verb) is stressed at the end: es-**TÁ**. **Esta** (demonstrative) is stressed at the start: **ES**-ta. Listen and repeat: _Esta calle está cerrada_.
The written accent marks the stressed syllable: **ahí** and **está** have one; **hay** and **esta** don't. If you forget it, you write a different word.

Tener: what you have

**Tener** is irregular. With **yo** it is _tengo_. With **tú**, **él/ella/usted** and **ellos/ellas/ustedes** the e changes to **ie**: _tienes, tiene, tienen_. With **nosotros** and **vosotros** it doesn't change: _tenemos, tenéis_.
With _tener_ you say what you own or what is part of your life: _Tengo dos hermanas_, _¿Tienes coche?_, _La tienda tiene platos muy bonitos_.
In yes/no questions, the noun often has no article: _¿Tienes perro?_, _¿Tienen ustedes cambio?_
Tener in the present
With yo, tener is **tengo**.
With nosotros the e doesn't change: **tenemos**.
Tener for age and feelings
For age, Spanish uses **tener + number + años**: _Mi abuela tiene ochenta años_. The question is **¿Cuántos años tienes?** Don't use _ser_ for age.
For what your body feels, use **tener + noun**: _tener hambre, sed, sueño, frío, calor_. To say it's a lot: **mucha** hambre, **mucha** sed (feminine) and **mucho** sueño, frío, calor (masculine).

With _frío_ and _calor_ there are three ideas: **hace frío** (the weather), **tengo frío** (my body) and **el café está frío** (a thing). In the last one, _frío_ is an adjective and agrees: _la sopa está fría_.
If in English you say _I am_ + age or a feeling, think **tengo**. If you say _I am_ + adjective (_tired, happy_), think **estoy**.

The whole phrase agrees with the noun
A noun phrase has a noun in the middle and words around it: **determiner + noun + adjective + de / con / para…** For example: _una taza grande de talavera_.
The noun is the boss: the determiner and the adjective copy its gender and number. _Un chal rojo_, _una vela roja_, _unos platos rojos_, _unas velas rojas_.
What comes with **de**, **con** or **para** doesn't change: _una taza de barro_, _dos tazas de barro_. And remember: **de + el = del**: _el color del plato_.
The adjective usually goes **after** the noun, the opposite of English: _a blue plate_ = _un plato azul_. Numbers don't change: _para cuatro personas_.

The g in tengo and the j in hijo
**G** before **a, o, u** sounds soft, as in English _go_: _tengo, gato, regalo, globo, gusta_.
**J** always sounds strong, with air from the throat: _hijo, rojo, jarra, viejo_. **G** before **e, i** sounds the same as j: _gente, girasol, mágico_.
To keep the soft sound before e or i, Spanish writes **gu**: _guitarra, hamburguesa_. The u is silent.
If you hear the strong sound before a, o, u, write **j**: _jarra, rojo, jugo_. Before e, i it can be **g** or **j**: _gente_, but _jefe_; you have to learn it with the word.

Reading a verb: who, when and what for

The dictionary gives the **infinitive**: _preparar_, _aprender_, _abrir_. In a sentence, the verb is **conjugated**: its ending tells you who does the action. In _preparamos_, the ending **-amos** means _nosotros_.

The **time** comes from the verb and the words around it. With the present you talk about what you usually do (_los lunes_, _siempre_) and what you're doing now (_ahora_, _hoy_). _Escribo_ can be _I write_ or _I'm writing_.

Finally, look at the **intention**. Almost all sentences **inform**: _Andrea lee las noticias_. Some **ask for something**: _Lee esto, por favor_. Others **express a wish**: _Ojalá que llueva_. For now, you only recognise the last two.
If you don't know who is speaking, cover the stem and look only at the ending: _-o_ is yo, _-amos_, _-emos_, _-imos_ is nosotros.

The regular present: -ar, -er, -ir
Take **-ar**, **-er** or **-ir** off the infinitive and you have the stem: _prepar-_, _aprend-_, _compart-_. Then add the ending for the person.
**-er** and **-ir** verbs are almost the same. Only **nosotros** (_aprendemos_ / _compartimos_) and **vosotros** (_aprendéis_ / _compartís_) differ.
To make it negative, put **no** before the verb: _No trabajo los domingos_. To ask, use **¿?** and raise your voice at the end: _¿Trabajas los domingos?_

**No** goes right before the verb.
Ser, estar, ir and tener
These four verbs are irregular and appear in almost every conversation. Three end in **-oy** with yo: **soy, estoy, voy**. The fourth is **tengo**.
**Ir** is movement: **ir a** + place. With _el_, **a + el = al**: _Voy al mercado_. With _la_ it doesn't change: _Voy a la universidad_. And home, with no article: _Voy a casa_.
Don't mix up **¿adónde vas?** (movement, with _ir_) and **¿dónde estás?** (place, with _estar_): _Voy al estudio_ / _Estoy en el estudio_.
A quick question: is there movement? Then **voy a**. Are you already there? Then **estoy en**.
