_Ir_ is movement: it goes with **a**.
_Estar_ gives the place: it goes with **en**. _Al_ is for _ir_.
With yo: **voy**, like soy and estoy.

The stressed syllable in the present
In the regular present, the stress falls on the **stem** with yo, tú, él and ellos: **PRE**-pa-ro, a-**PREN**-des, **A**-bre, **GRA**-ban.

With **nosotros** the stress moves to the ending: pre-pa-**RA**-mos, a-pren-**DE**-mos, a-**BRI**-mos. With **vosotros** too, and that's why it has a written accent: pre-pa-**RÁIS**, a-pren-**DÉIS**, a-**BRÍS**.
If you put the stress in the wrong place, you can say a different word: _preparo_ (present) is not _preparó_ (past). Listen carefully for the stressed syllable.
The **vosotros** forms have a written accent because the stress is on the last syllable: _grabáis, leéis, recibís_. The nosotros forms don't: _grabamos_.

Hago, pongo, salgo: only yo changes
**Hacer**, **poner** and **salir** are irregular only with **yo**: _hago_, _pongo_, _salgo_. With the other persons they have the regular endings: _haces_, _pone_, _salimos_, _salen_.
They're very useful verbs on a trip: **hacer** fotos, hacer la maleta; **poner** agua en la mochila, poner música; **salir** de casa, salir a las cinco, salir con amigos.
**Traer** works the same way: yo **traigo**, tú traes. For now, you only need to recognise it.
Learn the three together, like a song: **hago, pongo, salgo**. You already know the other forms.
Three verbs with yo in -go
With yo, salir is **salgo**.
With yo, poner is **pongo**.
Venir: where you're coming from
**Venir** is like **tener**: **vengo** with yo, **ie** with tú, él and ellos (_vienes, viene, vienen_) and no change with nosotros and vosotros (_venimos, venís_).
**Venir de** gives the origin: _Vengo del mercado_. **Ir a** gives the destination: _Voy al mercado_. Remember: de + el = **del**, a + el = **al**.
Use **venir** when someone moves towards the place where you are: _¿Vienes a mi casa esta noche?_ If the other person calls you and you go towards them, you say **¡Voy!**
Tener and venir: two twins
With él, venir takes **ie**: _viene_, like _tiene_.
With nosotros there's no change: **venimos**.
**De** + place is origin: _vengo de_.
Quiero, puedo, pido: the boot rule
Some verbs change the vowel in their stem: **querer** (e → ie: _quiero_), **poder** (o → ue: _puedo_) and **pedir** (e → i: _pido_).

The change happens with **yo, tú, él/ella/usted** and **ellos/ellas/ustedes**. With **nosotros** and **vosotros** the stem doesn't change: _queremos, podemos, pedimos_. If you write the six forms in a table, the ones that change draw a boot.

**Querer** and **poder** go with a noun or an **infinitive**: _Quiero un café_, _Quiero subir al volcán_, _No puedo caminar seis horas_. **Pedir** already means _to order / to ask for_: _Pido un chocolate_ (no _por_).
Before you conjugate, ask yourself: is the person inside or outside the boot? Only **nosotros** and **vosotros** are outside.
The boot: the forms that change
Nosotros is outside the boot: **podemos**.
With ella, pedir changes: **pide**.
After _poder_, the verb goes in the **infinitive**.

The diphthongs ie and ue: one single syllable
In **quiero**, **puedo** or **viene**, the two vowels **ie** or **ue** go together in one syllable: _quie-ro_, _pue-do_, _vie-ne_. Don't say _qui-e-ro_.
When the stem doesn't change, the diphthong disappears: _que-re-mos_, _po-de-mos_, _ve-ni-mos_. That's why _pueden_ has two syllables and _podemos_ has three.
**Pedir** has no diphthong: it changes e to i. _Pi-do_, _pi-den_; _pe-di-mos_.
If you hear **ie** or **ue** in the stem, the form is inside the boot: _quiero_, _puedo_. With nosotros and vosotros you write the vowel of the infinitive: _queremos_, _podemos_.

This checkpoint reviews two new classes: **forms of address** (tú, vos, usted, ustedes, vosotros) and **yes/no questions**. It also brings together everything from weeks 6 to 9: estar and hay, tener and the noun phrase, the regular present, ser, estar, ir and tener, and verbs in -go and with a stem change.
Tú, vos, usted, ustedes or vosotros?

To talk to **one person** informally, almost the whole Spanish-speaking world uses **tú**. To show respect, with older people or in a service situation, use **usted**, with the verb for él and ella: _¿Usted es el lanchero?_

In Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and parts of Central America (Guatemala too) many people say **vos** instead of tú. In the present, the vos form is stressed at the end and has a written accent: _hablás_, _comés_, _vivís_. Some frequent verbs: _vos **sos**_, _vos **tenés**_, _vos **querés**_, _vos **podés**_. With vos the stem doesn't change: _querés_, not _quierés_. You don't need to use it: just recognise it.

To talk to **a group**, in Latin America people say **ustedes**, with the verb for ellos: _¿Ustedes tienen cambio?_ In Spain, with friends or family, people say **vosotros**: _¿Tenéis cambio?_ And **don't mix** forms: _vos hablás_ and _tú hablas_ are fine; _tú hablás_ isn't.
If you don't know which form to use with an adult you don't know, start with **usted**. If the other person uses tú with you, you can switch.
Who are you talking to? The verb tener
You're talking to…
Form
With vos, the form is stressed at the end and has an accent: **hablás**.
_Usted_ takes the verb for él and ella: **tiene**.
_Ustedes_ takes the verb for ellos: **quieren**. _Queréis_ is for vosotros.
Yes/no questions

A basic sentence has **subject + verb + information**: _Mei viene a las siete_. The verb agrees with the subject: _Mei y Óscar vienen_, _Mei y yo venimos_. The subject is often left out, because the verb already shows it: _Venimos a las siete_.

To make a yes/no question, write **¿** at the start and **?** at the end, and raise your voice at the end. The order can stay the same (_¿Mei viene a las siete?_) or start with the verb (_¿Viene Mei a las siete?_).

If the question starts in the middle of the sentence, the **¿** goes exactly where the question starts: _Perdón, ¿hay baño en la lancha?_ To answer: **Sí, …** or **No, no …** (the first _no_ answers and the second negates the verb).
In a written message, put the **¿** before you write the question. That way you won't forget it.

Review: weeks 6 to 9

**Week 6.** With **estar** you say how and where you are (_estoy cansada_, _el muelle está allí_). With **hay** you introduce something new (_hay una lancha a las ocho_) and with **está** you place something known (_la lancha está en el muelle_).
**Week 7.** With **tener** you say your age and feelings (_tengo veinte años_, _tengo mucha sed_). In the **noun phrase** everything agrees with the noun: _unas mochilas pequeñas de tela_.
**Week 8.** You read a verb (person, time, intention), conjugate the **regular present** (_trabajo, aprendes, viven_) and use **ser, estar, ir and tener** (_voy al muelle_, _estoy en el muelle_).
**Week 9.** You use verbs with yo in **-go** (_hago, pongo, salgo, vengo_) and those that change their stem following the **boot rule** (_quiero, puedo, pido_; but _queremos, podemos, pedimos_).

Your voice rises in yes/no questions

A statement and a yes/no question can have the same words. The difference is in the melody: in the statement your voice **falls** at the end (_La lancha sale._ ↘); in the question it **rises** at the end (_¿La lancha sale?_ ↗).
The rise starts on the last stressed syllable: _¿Hay sitio para **DOS**?_ ↗, _¿Tienes **FRÍ**-o?_ ↗.
**Vos** forms are stressed at the end: tú **HA**-blas / vos ha-**BLÁS**; tú **TIE**-nes / vos te-**NÉS**. That's why they have a written accent.
In Spanish a question is opened and closed: **¿…?** If it starts in the middle of the sentence, the **¿** goes where the question starts: _Oye, ¿vienes?_

This week you review two classes: question words, which always have a written accent when they ask, and negative sentences with no. Here you use them in San Salvador: in a pupusería, in a hostel and on a city tour.
One word for each kind of information
Before you ask, think of the **answer** you want. A thing? **Qué**. A person? **Quién**. A place? **Dónde**. A time? **Cuándo**. The way? **Cómo**. An amount or a price? **Cuánto**.
The question word goes at the start, after **¿**. If there is a preposition, the preposition goes **first**: _¿**De** dónde eres?_, _¿**A** qué hora cierran?_, _¿**Con** quién vives?_
In a question these words always have a **written accent**. Without the accent they are different words that don't ask anything: _Creo **que** cierra tarde_.
Before you write the question, say the answer quietly: _a las ocho_ → **¿A qué hora…?**

Cuánto changes; qué and cuál are chosen

**Cuánto** agrees with the thing you count: _¿cuánto **dinero**?_, _¿cuánta **agua**?_, _¿cuántos **días**?_, _¿cuántas **personas**?_ With a verb alone, without a noun, it's **cuánto**: _¿Cuánto cuesta?_
**Quién** also has a plural: _¿Quiénes son esas chicas?_ and so does **cuál**: _¿Cuáles son tus horarios?_

**Qué** or **cuál**: before a noun, the usual word is **qué** (_¿Qué bebida quieres?_). With **es / son**, or to choose between things you can see, the usual word is **cuál** (_¿Cuál es tu número?_, _¿Cuál quieres, la grande o la pequeña?_).
Cuánto with a noun
_Personas_ is feminine plural: **cuántas**.
For a piece of information with **es**, the usual word is **cuál**.
No goes before the verb
To make a sentence negative, put **no** right **before the conjugated verb**: _Como carne_ → _**No** como carne_. There is no extra word like English _don't_: just **no**.
If there is a subject, the order is **subject + no + verb**: _Mi hermana **no** trabaja hoy_. The same happens with **hay**: _**No** hay mesas libres_.
With two verbs (**puedo**, **quiero** + infinitive), **no** goes before the first one: _**No** puedo venir_, _**No** quiero esperar_.
First find the verb of the sentence and put **no** right before it. Nothing goes between them.
**No** goes before the verb, not after it.
With two verbs, **no** goes before the first one.
Saying no: short or complete
To a yes/no question you can give a **short** answer: _—¿Quieres salsa? —No, gracias._ Or a **complete** one, with two **no**: _—No, **no** quiero salsa._
The first **no** answers the question; the second one negates the verb. A **comma** goes between them.
Careful: _No, puedo_ (with a comma and no second no) means the opposite, _sí puedo_. To say you can't: _No, **no** puedo_.

The melody of questions: with a question word or yes/no
Yes/no questions rise at the end: _¿Tienes hambre?_ ↗. But questions with **qué, dónde, cuánto…** usually **fall** at the end, like an ordinary sentence: _¿Dónde vives?_ ↘
In these questions the question word sounds **strong**: it's the syllable with the accent. _¿**Cuán**to cuesta?_, _¿**Dón**de está?_ That's why the accent marks the stress.
In negative sentences, **no** joins the verb with no pause: _no-quie-ro_, _no-hay_. If you pause after _no_, it sounds like a short answer: _No. Quiero._
The accent on **qué, quién, cuál, dónde, cuándo, cómo, cuánto** is also written on capital letters: _¿Dónde…?_, _¿Qué…?_ And remember both marks: **¿** at the start and **?** at the end.

This week you review two classes: the words that join ideas (y, o, pero, ni) and the ones that explain a reason or a goal (porque, para). You use them in Tegucigalpa, in a volunteer project with children and books.
Y, o, pero: adding, choosing, contrasting

**Y** adds two things or two ideas: _Hablo español **y** portugués_. **O** gives an option: _¿Vienes el sábado **o** el domingo?_ **Pero** introduces a contrast or a difficulty: _Me gusta el proyecto, **pero** no tengo mucho tiempo_.
Before **pero** you almost always write a **comma**. Before **y** and **o**, in a simple list, you don't.

To sound right, **y** changes to **e** before a word that starts with the _i_ sound (**i-**, **hi-**): _madre **e** hija_, _francés **e** inglés_. And **o** changes to **u** before the _o_ sound (**o-**, **ho-**): _siete **u** ocho_, _mujeres **u** hombres_.
Listen to the next word: if it starts with the same sound (_y-i_, _o-o_), change the connector.

Ni: no to two things
To say **no** to two things, use **no + verb + … ni …**: _No tengo coche **ni** moto_. The first _no_ goes before the verb, as in any negative sentence.
Don't say _no… y…_ for two negative things: _No hablo alemán **ni** ruso_, not _No hablo alemán y ruso_.
It also works with two verbs: _Los domingos **no** trabajo **ni** estudio_.
Two negative things: **ni**, not _y_.
To ask for the **reason**, you say **¿Por qué…?**: two words and an accent on _qué_. To answer, you say **porque**: one word, no accent.
After **porque** comes a clause with a **conjugated verb**: _Quiero ayudar **porque** me gustan los niños_. _Llego tarde **porque** hay mucho tráfico_.
To give your opinion before the reason you can use **creo que** + clause: _**Creo que** es un buen proyecto **porque** ayuda a las familias_.
Question and answer
Form
To **ask**: two words and an accent, **por qué**.
After _creo_ comes **que**.
¿Para qué? Para + infinitive
To say the **goal** of an action, you use **para + infinitive** (the unconjugated verb in -ar, -er, -ir): _Estudio español **para hablar** con mis vecinos_.
The question is **¿Para qué…?**: _¿Para qué necesitas el diccionario?_ — _**Para traducir** un cuento_.

Compare: **porque** looks at the cause, what comes first (_porque tengo tiempo libre_); **para** looks at the goal, what you want to achieve (_para aprender algo nuevo_). After **para**, never a conjugated verb.
Trick: if you can put _para conseguir_ (in order to get) in front, it's **para**; if you can put _la razón es que_ (the reason is that), it's **porque**.

¿Por qué? and porque: where the stress goes
**¿Por qué?** and **porque** are written differently and they also sound different. In the question, the stress is on **qué**: _por-**QUÉ**_. In the answer, the stress is on **por**: _**POR**-que_.
The question _¿Por qué…?_ usually falls at the end, like all questions with a question word. The answer _porque…_ runs on with no pause up to the verb: _porque-tengo-tiempo_.
The connectors **y**, **e**, **o**, **u** are weak and blend with the words around them: _pan y queso_ sounds like _pa-ni-que-so_; _siete u ocho_ sounds like _sie-teu-o-cho_.

This week you review three classes: the basic prepositions a, de, en, con and sin; the contractions al and del; and adverbs of place, time and manner. You use them in Granada, Nicaragua, to get around the city and explain routes.
A, en, de: going, being, coming
**A** marks the **destination**, with verbs of movement like _ir_, _llegar_ or _venir_: _Voy **a** Granada_, _Llego **a** la estación_.

**En** marks the **place** where you are or do something, with no movement: _Estoy **en** Granada_, _Trabajo **en** una tienda_. With transport you also use **en**: _en bus_, _en barco_ (but _a pie_).
**De** marks **origin** (_Vengo **de** Masaya_, _Soy **de** León_) and also the **owner**: _la casa **de** Inés_.
The question tells you the preposition
Question
Preposition
Example
With movement towards a destination: **a**.
A place with no movement: **en**.
Con and sin
**Con** tells you the **company** or what you carry: _Paseo **con** mi hermana_, _un café **con** leche_, _una casa **con** jardín_.
**Sin** tells you what there **isn't** or what you don't carry: _un jugo **sin** azúcar_, _Salgo **sin** paraguas_. Usually you don't put an article after **sin**: _sin dinero_, _sin prisa_.
The five prepositions go **before** the noun or the place. And in questions, they also go first: _¿**Con** quién vas?_, _¿**De** dónde eres?_
Think in pairs: **con** ↔ **sin**, **a** (voy) ↔ **de** (vengo), **en** (estoy).
After **sin**, usually no article.
Al and del: only with el
When **a** or **de** come before the article **el**, they join into one word: **a + el = al**, **de + el = del**. _Voy **al** mercado_, _Vengo **del** parque_.
It only happens with **el**. With _la_, _los_ and _las_ there's no contraction: _a la iglesia_, _de los barcos_, _a las islas_. Nor with other prepositions: _en el lago_, _con el guía_.
With **él** (pronoun, with an accent) they don't join: _Este regalo es **de él**_. And to explain a route, you use **de… a…** with its contractions: _**del** hotel **al** lago_.
Join or not?
**A + el** always joins: **al**.
With _la_ there's no contraction: **de la**.
Where, when, how: adverbs

Adverbs never change: they have no masculine or plural forms. **Where**: _aquí_ (near me), _ahí_ (near you), _allí_ (far), _cerca_, _lejos_. **When**: _hoy_, _mañana_, _ahora_, _temprano_, _tarde_, and to put things in order: _primero_, _después_, _luego_. **How**: _bien_, _mal_, _despacio_, _rápido_.

**Muy** goes before an **adjective** or another **adverb**: _muy bonito_, _muy cerca_, _muy bien_. **Mucho** goes with a **verb** (_Caminas **mucho**_) or with a **noun**, and then it agrees: _**mucho** calor_, _**muchas** iglesias_.
Careful: **después** on its own, at the end or between two actions (_Primero comemos y **después** paseamos_); **después de** + a noun (_después del almuerzo_).
Look at the word next to it: is it an adjective or an adverb? **Muy**. Is it a verb or a thing? **Mucho**.

Al and del in one syllable, and the soft d

**Al** and **del** are a single syllable and join the next word: _al-mer-ca-do_, _del-par-que_. If you hear _a la_ or _de la_, that's two syllables: _a-la-pla-za_. That extra syllable tells you the word is feminine.
A **d** between vowels or after a vowel is **soft**: the tongue lightly touches the teeth, without force, like _th_ in English _this_. It happens in _de_, _del_, _todo_, _mercado_, _a dónde_.
At the start of a sentence or after **n** or **l**, the d is stronger: _¿**D**ónde estás?_, _cuan**d**o_, _el **d**ía_.

**Al** and **del** are always written as one word: never _a el_ or _de el_ (except with the pronoun _él_, with an accent). On the other hand, **a la**, **de la**, **a los**, **de las** are always written separately.
_Del-par-que-al-mue-lle_: all joined, with a soft d in _del_.

From always to never
To say **how often** you do something, use a five-word scale: **siempre** (100 %), **normalmente** (almost always), **a veces** (some of the time), **casi nunca** (very little) and **nunca** (0 %).
These words usually go **before the verb**: _**Siempre** desayuno fruta_, _**A veces** trabajo los sábados_. **Normalmente** and **a veces** can also go at the end: _Ceno en casa **normalmente**_.
**Nunca** has two positions: before the verb, without _no_ (_**Nunca** como carne_), or after it, with _no_ in front (_**No** como carne **nunca**_). Never say _Como nunca carne_ or _Nunca no como_.

For an exact frequency you use longer expressions. They go at the **start** or the **end** of the sentence: _**Todos los días** camino al trabajo_, _Voy al mercado **dos veces por semana**_.
**Una vez**, but **dos veces** (z changes to c in the plural). And **por**: _una vez **por** semana_, _tres veces **por** mes_ (also _al mes_, _a la semana_).

With days: **los lunes** (plural) is a habit, every Monday; **el lunes** (singular) is one single day, for example next Monday. And careful: **todos los días** is every day; **todo el día** is from morning to night.
Key question for talking about habits: **¿Con qué frecuencia…?** or, more simply, **¿Cada cuánto…?**

Many routine verbs are **reflexive**: the person does the action **to themselves**. You find them in the dictionary with **-se**: _levantarse_, _ducharse_, _acostarse_, _vestirse_.

When you conjugate, **-se** becomes a pronoun that agrees with the person and goes **before the verb**: **me**, **te**, **se**, **nos**, **os**, **se**. In the negative, **no** goes before the pronoun: _**No me** levanto tarde_.

Some change their stem like _poder_ or _querer_: _acostarse_ → **me acuesto** (o → ue), _despertarse_ → **me despierto** (e → ie), _vestirse_ → **me visto** (e → i). _Ponerse_ gives **me pongo**. With nosotros and vosotros there's no change: _nos acostamos_.

Me, te, se, nos: the pronoun sticks to the verb

The pronouns **me, te, se, nos** are **weak** words: they have no stress of their own and are said **together** with the verb, like one word: _me-le-**van**-to_, _te-**du**-chas_, _nos-a-cos-**ta**-mos_.
The stress of the phrase goes on the verb, not on the pronoun. If you say _**ME** levanto_, with the stress on _me_, it sounds strange.

If the verb starts with a vowel, the pronoun joins it: _se a-fei-ta_ sounds like **sea-fei-ta**; _nos acostamos_ sounds like **no-sa-cos-ta-mos**. That's why it's important to hear the first syllable well: that's where the person is.

With a conjugated verb, the pronoun is **separate** and in front: _me levanto_. With the infinitive, it's **attached** at the end: _levantarme_, _acostarse_. And remember: **vez** → **veces** (z changes to c before e).

Para mí, contigo: pronouns after a preposition

After a preposition (**para, de, sin, a, con**…), almost all pronouns are the same as the subject: _para **él**_, _de **ella**_, _sin **nosotros**_, _con **ustedes**_. Only two change: yo → **mí** and tú → **ti**.
With **con** there are two special forms, written as one word: **conmigo** (con + yo) and **contigo** (con + tú). Never _con mí_ or _con ti_.

Watch the accent: **mí** (pronoun: _para mí_) has an accent; **mi** (possessive: _mi casa_) doesn't. **Ti** never has an accent. That's why you say _**A mí** me gusta_: it's the preposition _a_ + **mí**.
Trick: if you can swap the word for _él_ (_para él_), it's the pronoun **mí**, with an accent. If you can swap it for _su_ (_su casa_), it's the possessive **mi**.

Gusta or gustan: the final n, and a stressed mí

Between **gusta** and **gustan** there's only one sound: the final **n**. It's short, but it changes the meaning: _me gusta el libro_ / _me gustan los libros_. Listen to what comes next too: _los_, _las_ and the plural **s** confirm there are several things.
**Mí** (pronoun) is a **strong** word: it has its own stress. _A **mí** me gusta_, _para **mí**_. On the other hand, **mi** (possessive) is weak and joins the noun: _mi-ca-sa_.
In **conmigo** and **contigo**, the stress is on the second syllable: _con-**mi**-go_, _con-**ti**-go_.
**Mí** with an accent is a pronoun (_para mí_); **mi** without an accent is a possessive (_mi casa_). **Ti** never has an accent. **Conmigo** and **contigo** are written as one word.

Exactly how much: number, container or measure

When you know the number, you say it before the noun: _tres plátanos_, _ocho personas_. **Uno** loses its -o before a masculine noun (**un** litro) and becomes **una** with a feminine one (**una** lata). The same happens at the end of long numbers: _veintiún kilómetros_, _treinta y una botellas_.

Many things aren't counted one by one (water, rice, cheese). For them you use a **container** or a **measure** + **de** + product: _una lata de atún_, _un litro de leche_, _medio kilo de arroz_, _cien gramos de queso_.
In the plural only the container changes: _dos latas de atún_, _tres paquetes de galletas_. The product stays the same: never _dos latas de atunes_.
If the answer stands alone, use **uno** or **una**: —¿Cuántos litros quieres? —**Uno**. With the noun, **un litro**.

More or less: poco, mucho, bastante; and the whole group: todo

If you don't know the exact number, you use **poco** (not enough), **mucho** (a large amount) or **bastante** (what you need, enough). **Poco** and **mucho** agree with the noun in gender and number; **bastante** only adds -s in the plural.
After a verb, **mucho** and **poco** never change: _Las guías caminan mucho_, _Mi hermana come poco_.
**Todo** talks about the whole group and needs the article in the middle: **todo el** arroz, **toda la** tarde, **todos los** turistas, **todas las** mochilas. _Todos los días_ means _every day_.

**Doler** works like **gustar**: what hurts is the subject and it goes after the verb. If it's one thing, **duele**; if there are two or more, **duelen**. In front goes the person who feels the pain: **me, te, le, nos, os, les**.

The z and the c in cabeza, cinco and cien
**Z** (_zapatos, cabeza, nariz_) and **c** before **e, i** (_cinco, cien, doce_) have the same sound.

In Latin America, the Canary Islands and part of Andalusia that sound is an **s**: _cabesa_, _sinco_. This is called **seseo**. In central and northern Spain it's a sound made with the tongue between the teeth, like _th_ in English _think_. Both pronunciations are correct.
Before **a, o, u**, c sounds like **k**: _calcetines, cuello, botas de agua, paquete_. That's why you write _cuello_ and _cinco_ with c, but they sound different.
Write **z** before a, o, u and at the end of a word (_zapato, arroz_), and **c** before e, i (_cena, cinco_). That's why the plural of _luz_ is **luces** and the plural of _nariz_ is **narices**.

This week you review two classes: how to **identify** an object with several clues (what it is, what it's like, where it is) and how to **compare** two things. You practise it in Panama City, on the metro and in a shop in the Casco Viejo.
Clue by clue: what it is, what it's like, where it is

When there are several similar objects, one clue isn't enough. You add clues in this order: first **the object** (_la mochila_), then **what it's like** (_negra, pequeña, de tela_) and finally **where it is** (_que está en la caja_).
Colour and size go **after** the noun and agree with it: _el paraguas negro_, _la gorra blanca_, _unas llaves pequeñas_. For the material you use **de**: _de tela_, _de cuero_, _de plástico_.
For location you use **estar**, not _ser_: _la que **está** en la caja_. With **ser** you say what it's like: _la mochila **es** negra_.
Before describing, look at what objects there are and find the clue that only your object has.

If the other person already knows which object you mean, you don't repeat the noun: you say **el, la, los, las** + the clue. —¿Cuál es tu mochila? —**La negra**. —¿Y tus llaves? —**Las pequeñas**.
You can also use **el que, la que, los que, las que** + está…: _el que está en la mesa_, _las que están en la caja_. The article says which object it is: **la** = la mochila, **el** = el paraguas.
Remember the adjective forms: ending in **-o**, four forms (_negro, negra, negros, negras_); ending in **-e** or a consonant, masculine and feminine are the same (_grande, verde, azul, gris_).
_Gorra_ is feminine: **la blanca**.
**Azul** has only one form for masculine and feminine.
More … than, less … than
To say A has **more** of something than B: **más + adjective + que**. English has two forms (_bigger, more expensive_); Spanish always uses **más**: _más grande, más caro, más cómodo_.
To say A has **less**: **menos + adjective + que**. Often the opposite adjective with **más** sounds more natural: _menos cara_ = _más barata_.
The adjective agrees with **A**, the first thing: _La mochila verde es más **cara** que el bolso_. With a number you don't use _que_, but **de**: _cuesta **más de** cuarenta dólares_.
Two ways of saying the same thing
With menos
With más + the opposite
With **más**, the partner word is **que**.
The adjective agrees with the first thing: _la maleta_ → **pesada**.
Tan … como: the same
If A and B are **the same** in something, you use **tan + adjective + como**: _La gorra roja es tan barata como la azul_ (both cost five dollars).
In the negative, **no es tan … como** is a very natural way to say _less_: _El bolso no es tan cómodo como la mochila_.
Watch the pairs: **más … que**, **menos … que**, but **tan … como**. And to recognise: **mejor** (better) and **peor** (worse) are special forms.
Before comparing, ask yourself: are they the same? Then, **tan … como**. Are they different? Then, **más** or **menos … que**.

The final vowel that agrees: negro, negra

In Spanish, final vowels are pronounced **full and clear**. They don't turn into a weak sound as in English. That's why you can clearly hear the difference between _negro_ and _negra_, or between _el pequeño_ and _la pequeña_.
That final vowel is the agreement: if you say _la mochila negro_, a Spanish speaker's ear notices the mistake. Open your mouth wide for **-a** and round your lips for **-o**.

In the plural, the final **-s** is also pronounced: _las llaves pequeñas_. In the Caribbean, Panama included, many people aspirate or drop that final s (_la' llave'_), but the article and the context help you understand.
The vowel you hear at the end is the one you write: _rojo_ with **o**, _roja_ with **a**. Adjectives in **-e** (_grande, verde_) don't change: write the same form for el and la.

This week you review three classes for organising time: **the time, the day and the date**, plans with **ir a + infinitive** and what you **want to, can or have to** do. You practise it in Boquete, a mountain town in Panama famous for its coffee and for the Barú volcano.
What time is it? At what time?

For the time **now**: **es la una** (singular) and **son las** dos, tres… doce (plural). Up to half past you add with **y** (_y cuarto, y media_); after that, you subtract from the next hour with **menos** (_las cinco menos cuarto_ = 4:45).
For the time of **something that happens** (a departure, an appointment, a class) you ask **¿A qué hora…?** and answer with **a la** una or **a las** + time: _El tour empieza a las nueve_.
Add **de la mañana**, **de la tarde** or **de la noche** if needed. On tickets and screens you see the 24-hour clock (_17:30_), but in conversation you say _las cinco y media de la tarde_.
In many Latin American countries you also hear _un cuarto para las cinco_ or _quince para las cinco_ (4:45). It's correct; you can use _las cinco menos cuarto_.

For a **plan** or an intention in the near future (tonight, tomorrow, on Saturday), you use **ir** in the present + **a** + **infinitive**: _Mañana voy a visitar una finca de café_.
The present tells what's **normal** (_Los sábados trabajo_); **ir a** tells what you're going to do **this time** (_Este sábado voy a descansar_).

Don't mix up **ir a + place** (_Vamos al mercado_) and **ir a + infinitive** (_Vamos a comprar fresas_). They can go together: _Vamos a ir al mercado_. The negative goes in front: _No voy a salir esta noche_.

Quiero, puedo, tengo que + infinitive

Three verbs + infinitive with three meanings: **querer** is a wish (_Quiero ver el amanecer_), **poder** is a possibility or permission (_Puedo salir a las tres_) and **tener que** is an obligation (_Tengo que trabajar el lunes_).
Only the first verb changes; the infinitive is the same for everyone. **Tener** needs **que**: _tengo **que** salir_. **Querer** and **poder** go straight to the infinitive, without _a_.
Careful with the negative: **no tengo que** = it isn't necessary (_No tengo que trabajar el sábado_); **no puedo** = it isn't possible (_No puedo subir: me duele la rodilla_).
Ask yourself: is it a wish, a possibility or an obligation? Wish: **quiero**. Possible: **puedo**. Necessary: **tengo que**.

Days and months: where the stress falls

Almost all the days of the week are stressed on the **second-to-last** syllable: _LU-nes, MAR-tes, JUE-ves, VIER-nes, do-MIN-go_. But **miércoles** and **sábado** are stressed earlier, on the third-to-last, and that's why they have a written accent: _MIÉR-co-les, SÁ-ba-do_.
Months are stressed on the second-to-last syllable: _e-NE-ro, fe-BRE-ro, a-GOS-to, sep-TIEM-bre, di-CIEM-bre_. Abril is the exception: _a-BRIL_, stress at the end.
In times, the stress goes on the number and on _cuarto_ or _media_: _las DOS y ME-dia_, _las CIN-co menos CUAR-to_.
If the stress is on the third-to-last syllable, the word always has a written accent: **miércoles**, **sábado**. The other days and the months have no accent.

I'm painting: the form
For an action **in progress**, at this moment, you use conjugated **estar** + **gerund**. Estar changes with the person; the gerund never changes: _estoy bailando_, _estamos bailando_.
This is how the gerund is formed: verbs in **-ar** change to **-ando** (_pintar → pintando_) and verbs in **-er** and **-ir** change to **-iendo** (_coser → cosiendo_, _escribir → escribiendo_).
Two special forms: **leer → leyendo** (the i between vowels is written y) and **dormir → durmiendo** (the o changes to u).

Lo, la, los, las: not repeating

When the name of a thing or a person is already in the conversation, you don't repeat it: you replace it with **lo, la, los, las**. The form is like the article: _el tambor → **lo**_, _la máscara → **la**_, _los vestidos → **los**_, _las flores → **las**_.
They also work for people: _Veo a Lucas: **lo** veo_. _Llamo a mi madre: **la** llamo_.
The pronoun goes **before the conjugated verb**: _**La** tengo_, _No **los** encuentro_. With estar + gerund, also before estar: _¿El tambor? **Lo** está tocando mi tío_.

The pronouns **lo, la, los, las** have no stress of their own: they're pronounced joined to the verb, like a single word. _La tengo_ sounds like **la-TEN-go**; _lo está pintando_ sounds like **lo-es-TÁ-pin-TAN-do**.
The stress goes on the verb, not on the pronoun. If you say _LA tengo_ with stress on _la_, it sounds like a contrast (_la tengo yo, no tú_).
In the gerund, the stress is always on the syllable **an** or **ien**: _pin-TAN-do, co-SIEN-do, dur-MIEN-do, le-YEN-do_.
Although they sound joined, they're written separately before the conjugated verb: **la tengo**, **lo está pintando**. And remember the y in **leyendo**.

Who, what they do, what, when: sentence order

The normal sentence follows this order: **who** (subject) + **verb** + **what** + **when** or **where**: _El barco cruza el canal esta tarde_. Often you don't say the subject, because the verb already says it: _Cruzamos el canal mañana_.

The **when** can go at the beginning or at the end without changing the meaning: _Esta tarde el barco cruza el canal_. But with two people, the order decides who does the action: _Rosa llama a Iván_ is not the same as _Iván llama a Rosa_.
To make it **negative**, put **no** right before the verb: _El museo no abre los lunes_. If there's lo, la, los, las, **no** goes before the pronoun: _No lo veo_.

Asking: yes or no, or a piece of information
For a **yes/no** question, you use the normal order with **¿ ?** and your voice goes up at the end: _¿El barco cruza hoy?_

To look for **information**, the question word goes first and the **verb right after it**: _¿Qué ve la gente?_, _¿Cuándo llega el barco?_, _¿Quién vende las entradas?_ Spanish has no word like _does_: never _¿Qué la gente ve?_
With **quién** the verb is singular: _¿Quién quiere un café?_ And if the answer is no, you say **no** twice: _—¿Hay ascensor? —No, no hay_.
Before asking, think: am I expecting a yes or a no, or do I need a fact (a time, a place, a name)?

Describing a place and asking for information: es, hay, está

To describe a place, you combine three verbs: **ser** to say what it is or what it's like (_El centro es moderno_), **hay** to introduce something new or say how many things there are (_Hay un museo y cuatro terrazas_) and **estar** to say where a specific thing is (_El museo está en la planta baja_).
A good order: first **what** the place **is**, then **what there is**, then **where** each thing **is**. That way the other person gets a clear picture.

To ask for information, get a small question kit ready: _¿Qué es esto?_ _¿Hay…?_ _¿Cuántos… hay?_ _¿Dónde está…?_ _¿Cómo es…?_ _¿A qué hora…?_ With something non-specific you can also say _¿Dónde hay un baño?_
Three verbs, three questions
With **la** (something specific), **está**. _Hay_ goes with _un, una_, numbers or plurals without an article.
For the location of something specific, **estar**.

Stating, asking and denying: the voice and the word no

The same words can be a statement or a question: the difference is in the voice. In a **statement** the voice **goes down** at the end (_El barco llega a las dos._ ↘). In a **yes/no question** the voice **goes up** at the end (_¿El barco llega a las dos?_ ↗).
In a **question with qué, quién, cuándo…**, the stress is on the question word and the voice usually **goes down** at the end: _¿CUÁN-do llega el barco?_ ↘
In a **negative**, the word **no** is heard clearly, joined to the verb: _no-a-BRE_, _no-lo-TEN-go_. If you want to insist, give it a bit more stress: _¡NO, no abre!_
In writing, a question needs two marks: **¿** at the beginning and **?** at the end. Question words carry an accent: **qué, quién, cuándo, dónde, cómo, cuánto**.

The Miraflores locks are twenty minutes from the centre of Panama City. It's the best place to see up close how the canal works. The ships go up or down sixteen metres in two locks, and it all happens in less than an hour.

This week you review two classes: what the present perfect is for (**he trabajado**, **has visto**) and how its participles are formed. Here you see it with other examples and in short steps, for studying on your own.
A past that still touches the present

The perfect has two pieces: the present of **haber** (he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, han) and a **participle** (_trabajado_, _comido_). Only haber changes; the participle stays the same for every person.
You use it when you look at the past **from today**: with a period that hasn't finished yet (**hoy**, **esta mañana**, **esta semana**, **este año**) or without saying when it happened.
The two pieces always go together: _no_ and pronouns go before haber. **No lo he visto**, never _he no visto_ or _he lo visto_.
Present of haber + participle
Person
trabajar (to work)
aprender (to learn)
salir (to go out)
The participle in the perfect doesn't change with the person: always **llegado**.
**No** goes before haber; haber and the participle are not separated.
News, experiences and results
**News**: you tell what has happened in a period that is still open. _Hoy he hablado con el jefe._

**Experiences**: you talk about your life up to now, without a date. You ask with **alguna vez** and answer with **nunca**, **una vez**, **dos veces**, **muchas veces**. _¿Has dormido alguna vez en una hamaca? — Nunca._
**Results**: something happened and you can see it right now. _Se ha ido la luz_ (there's no power). _Me he cortado_ (look at my finger).
If you say **when** it happened in a finished period (_ayer_, _en 2019_, _el lunes pasado_), the perfect doesn't fit: you'll review that next week.
Do the clock test: if you can add _hasta ahora_ (so far) or _en mi vida_ (in my life), the perfect works.
**Ayer** is a finished period. With the perfect, use an open period, like **hoy**.
In a question about experience you use **alguna vez**; **nunca** is for the negative answer.
Regular participles: -ado and -ido
Remove the infinitive ending. Verbs in **-ar** take **-ado** (_cantar → cantado_). Verbs in **-er** and **-ir** both take **-ido** (_beber → bebido_, _subir → subido_).
When the stem ends in a strong vowel (a, e, o), the i takes an accent: _leer → leído_, _traer → traído_, _oír → oído_, _caer → caído_.
With haber, the participle doesn't change. But if you use it as an adjective (with **estar** or next to a noun), it does agree: _He cerrado la tienda_ / _La tienda está cerrada_.

After haber comes the participle: vend**ido**, not the present.
After the **e** of _le-_, the i takes an accent: **leído**.
The irregular forms you'll use most
Eight very frequent verbs don't follow the rule. Learn them as a family: **abierto**, **escrito**, **puesto**, **visto**, **vuelto**, **roto**, **dicho** and **hecho**.
Verbs built on them copy the form: _describir → descrito_, _devolver → devuelto_, _deshacer → deshecho_, _proponer → propuesto_, _descubrir → descubierto_.

A memory trick: five end in **-to** after a consonant (abier**to**, escri**to**, pues**to**, vis**to**, vuel**to**), one in **-to** after a vowel (ro**to**) and two in **-cho** (di**cho**, he**cho**).

He, ha and han joined to the participle
In spoken sentences, **he**, **ha** and **han** are short words that stick to the participle: _he-hecho_ sounds almost like one word, because the **h** is silent: [eécho].

If the participle starts with a vowel, the two vowels merge: _ha abierto_ sounds like [abierto] with a slightly long a; _he estado_ sounds like [estado] with a long e. That's why it's easy to confuse _he_ and _ha_: listen carefully to the vowel.
**Han** is easy to tell apart thanks to its final **n**, which joins the next vowel: _han ido_ sounds like [a-ni-do].
Even though it's silent, the **h** of haber is always written: _he_, _ha_, _han_. Without h, _a_ is a preposition (_voy a casa_) and _e_ is a conjunction (_padre e hijo_).

Hablé, comí, salí: the regular forms
The simple past tells **finished** actions in a period that is already over. Verbs in **-er** and **-ir** share endings: _comí_ and _salí_, _comió_ and _salió_.
The **written accent** is part of the form: _yo hablé_, _él habló_. Without it, _hablo_ is present. Always stress the last syllable: ha-**blé**, ha-**bló**.
With **nosotros**, -ar and -ir verbs look the same as in the present: _hablamos_, _salimos_. Context decides: _Ayer salimos tarde_ (past) / _Siempre salimos tarde_ (present).

Three types of verb change a letter only with **yo**, to keep the sound: **-car → -qué** (_buscar → busqué_), **-gar → -gué** (_llegar → llegué_), **-zar → -cé** (_empezar → empecé_). The other persons are regular: _buscó_, _llegaste_, _empezaron_.

The most frequent verbs have a **new stem** in the simple past and endings **without an accent**: _tuv-e_, _tuv-o_. Compare: _llegué_ and _llegó_ have an accent, but _tuve_ and _tuvo_ don't.
**Ir** and **ser** have the same forms: _fui_, _fue_, _fueron_. Context decides: _Fui a Alajuela_ (ir, with **a** + place) / _Fue un día largo_ (ser, an evaluation).
**Hacer** changes c to z with él and ella: _hizo_, to keep the sound. And **decir** loses the i with ellos: _dijeron_, not _dijieron_.

Pidió, durmió: the third-person change

Some **-ir** verbs that change their stem in the present (_pido_, _duermo_) have another change in the simple past, but **only with él, ella, usted and ellos, ellas, ustedes**: **e** becomes **i** and **o** becomes **u**.
**e → i**: _pedir → pidió, pidieron_; also _servir_, _repetir_, _preferir_, _sentir_, _seguir_. **o → u**: _dormir → durmió, durmieron_; also _morir → murió_.
With yo, tú, nosotros and vosotros nothing changes: _pedí_, _dormiste_, _servimos_. If in doubt, ask yourself: am I talking about someone else? Then check the vowel.
Remember the sentence _Él pidió y ellos durmieron_: it has both changes and the two persons where they happen.
With ella, the e of _pedir_ becomes **i**: **pidió**.
With **yo** there's no change: **dormí**. The o → u change is only for él and ellos.

In -ar verbs, the difference between the present for yo and the past for él is only the **stress**: _llego_ (LLE-go, present) and _llegó_ (lle-GÓ, past). If you stress the wrong syllable, you change the tense and the person.

The forms: -aba, -ía and only three irregular verbs

The imperfect is the most regular tense in Spanish. Verbs in **-ar** take **-aba** (_cantaba_); verbs in **-er** and **-ir** take **-ía** (_comía_, _vivía_). The yo and él forms are the same: the context or the pronoun shows who it is.
Watch the accents: **nosotros** with -ar has one (_cantábamos_) and all the -ía forms have one (_comíamos_, _vivían_).
There are only three irregular verbs: **ser** (_era_), **ir** (_iba_) and **ver** (_veía_). Everything else is regular, including _tener_, _hacer_ and _poder_: _tenía_, _hacía_, _podía_.

What it's for: describing, habits and actions in progress
**Describing** people, places and situations in the past: _La casa era blanca y tenía un patio con plantas._ Also the time, age and weather: _Eran las seis_, _Tenía diez años_, _Hacía calor_.
**Telling habits**: what normally happened, many times. Markers: **antes**, **de niño**, **cuando era pequeña**, **siempre**, **todos los domingos**, **a menudo**. _Todos los veranos íbamos al lago._
**Presenting an action in progress**: something was happening at a moment in the past, without saying when it ended. _A las ocho yo cenaba y mi hermana estudiaba._
If in English you can say _used to_ or _was …-ing_, in Spanish it's almost always the imperfect.
Age and stage of life are description: **era** pequeño.
**Todos los días** and **antes** mark a habit: imperfect.
Scene and events: imperfect and simple past together

Imagine a play. The **imperfect** paints the **set**: where we were, what the weather was like, what was going on. The **simple past** tells the **events** that move the story forward: what happened, what each person did.

That's why an anecdote often starts in the imperfect and switches to the simple past with **de repente**, **entonces** or **en ese momento**: _Llovía y todos dormían. De repente, alguien llamó a la puerta._

**Cuando** doesn't decide the tense: look at what happens. _Cuando llegué, mi madre cocinaba_ (my mother's action was in progress). _Cuando llegué, mi madre cocinó_ (first I arrived, then she started cooking).

**Había** describes what existed in the scene: _Había mucha gente en la plaza_. **Hubo** presents something that **happened**: _Hubo una tormenta_, _Hubo un accidente_, _Hubo una fiesta_.
**Era** describes: _Era un día gris_. **Fue** evaluates a complete, finished event: _El concierto fue increíble_. If you're talking about a specific event, don't use _era_: say _hubo_ or _fue_.
Both forms of _haber_ have no plural in this use: _había dos coches_, _hubo tres conciertos_, never _habían dos coches_.

The stressed í of había, tenía, vivía

In **-ía** forms, the **i** is stressed and separates from the next vowel: _te-NÍ-a_, _vi-VÍ-a_, _ha-BÍ-a_. That's **three** syllables, not two. If you say _te-NIA_ in two syllables, it sounds odd or isn't understood.
The same happens with _comíamos_ (co-MÍ-a-mos) and _veían_ (ve-Í-an). The accent on the í reminds you where your voice goes.

Compare with words where the i isn't stressed: _FE-ria_ in two syllables versus _te-NÍ-a_ in three, or _jun-TA-ba_, where the stress is on the a. In the -aba imperfect the stress never falls at the end: _ju-GA-ba_, _ju-GÁ-ba-mos_.
The -ía forms always have an accent (_tenía_, _vivían_) because the í separates from the a. The -aba forms only have one with nosotros: _jugábamos_.

When I was a boy, I spent all my holidays at my aunt Mercedes's house, on Atravesada Street. It was a colonial house with yellow walls, a tiled roof and a huge inner courtyard. In the middle there was a mango tree and around it, four wooden rocking chairs.

My aunt was a short, very serious woman, but she cooked like nobody else. Every afternoon at five, the neighbours brought their chairs out onto the pavement and talked until night. My aunt never went out: she said the pavement was for gossips. We nephews and nieces played in the courtyard while she made dinner.

One night in July, the whole family was having dinner in the dining room. It was hot and the windows were open. Suddenly a bat flew in and started circling over the table. My cousin screamed, my uncle hid under the table and I knocked my bowl of soup onto the floor. Then my aunt, very calmly, stood up, opened the courtyard door and turned off the light. The bat was out in two seconds.
Nobody said a word. Then my aunt turned the light on and served dessert. It was the strangest dinner of my life.

This week you review two classes: how the use of the perfect and the simple past changes from one region to another, and how to describe old habits with **solía**. You already know the forms; now you learn to choose depending on where you are and what you want to say.
Two ways of telling about today

For something that happened **today** or **this week**, Spanish has two habits. In most of Spain the perfect is preferred: _Hoy he comido con mi jefa_. In Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean and the River Plate, and also in the Canary Islands, the simple past is widely used: _Hoy comí con mi jefa_.
Both are **correct**: it's not a mistake, it's a **variety**. A Nicaraguan understands _he comido_ perfectly and a woman from Madrid understands _comí_.

Nor is it simply «Spain versus Latin America»: in parts of Peru or Bolivia you hear the perfect a lot, and in north-west Spain, the simple past. What matters is to recognise both and choose one consistently.
If you live or study in a particular country, copy what you hear there. If not, choose one variety and don't switch halfway through a text.
The same news in two varieties
More frequent in Spain
More frequent in much of Latin America
Don't mix the two forms in the same verb: either **he ido** or **fui**.
What doesn't change: finished time
With a **finished** period (**ayer**, **anoche**, **el lunes pasado**, **en 2018**, **el mes pasado**), all varieties use the **simple past**. _Ayer he ido al médico_ is a mistake in any country.

So the key question is: does the time in the sentence include the present? If you say _hoy_, _esta semana_, _este año_ or don't say when, you can choose according to your variety. If the period is over, there's only one option.
In a conversation between people from different regions it's normal to hear both forms. Don't correct anyone for saying _hoy comí_ or _hoy he comido_.
**El domingo pasado** is a finished period: simple past in every variety.
A finished year: **terminé**.
Solía + infinitive: habits from another time

**Solía** + infinitive tells something that happened **many times** during a stage of the past: _De joven solía correr por las mañanas_. It's like the imperfect for habits, but it stresses the repetition.
Only **soler** changes; the second verb is always in the infinitive: _solía ir_, _solíamos comer_. There's no preposition: never _solía a ir_ or _solía de ir_.
For past habits, **soler** is used almost only in the imperfect. For present habits there's the present: _suelo_, _sueles_, _suele_… _Ahora suelo trabajar desde casa._

To contrast periods, join the sentences with **pero** or **en cambio**: _Antes solíamos hablar por teléfono fijo; en cambio, ahora nos escribimos por el móvil._

The intonation of questions about the past

A **yes/no** question rises at the end: _¿Fuiste a la reunión?_ ↗. The same sentence with the voice falling at the end is a statement: _Fuiste a la reunión._ ↘ Since in Spanish the word order often doesn't change, the **melody** is the only thing that marks the question.
A question with **qué**, **dónde**, **cuándo**, **quién** or **cómo** normally **falls** at the end: _¿Dónde comiste hoy?_ ↘. The question word already shows it's a question.
This applies to both varieties: _¿Has comido?_ ↗ and _¿Comiste?_ ↗ rise in the same way.
In written Spanish, a question opens with **¿** and closes with **?**. The opening mark warns you from the start that the voice is going to change.

Ya, todavía, ya no, todavía no; ayer and antes

**Ya** says something has happened, perhaps sooner than expected: _Ya he comprado los billetes_ / _Ya compré los billetes_ (the two varieties from week 4). **Todavía no** says it hasn't happened, but it's expected: _Todavía no ha llegado el autobús_.
**Todavía** (or **aún**) says a situation **is still the same**: _Todavía vivo con mis padres_. **Ya no** says a situation **changed** and ended: _Ya no fumo_.

**Ayer** places an event on a specific day: it goes with the simple past (_Ayer vendí tres hamacas_). **Antes** on its own talks about **another period**: it goes with the imperfect or solía (_Antes vendía en la calle_; _Antes solía vender en la calle_).
Four markers, four ideas
Marker
Example
Something pending that is expected: **todavía no**. **Ya no** is for something that has ended.
**Ayer** already places the event; **antes** on its own is for another period.
Antes de, después de and cuando
**Antes de** and **después de** go with an **infinitive** (or a noun): _Antes de abrir el puesto, desayuno_; _Después de la comida, descanso_. Never with a gerund or a conjugated verb.

**Cuando** goes with a **conjugated verb**: _Cuando llego al mercado, cuelgo las hamacas_. With the present it tells a routine; with a past tense, a past event or habit (weeks 2 and 3): _Cuando llegué, la tienda estaba cerrada_.

If the sentence starts with **antes de**, **después de** or **cuando**, put a **comma** after that part: _Cuando termino, me voy a casa._ If it comes at the end, you don't need one: _Me voy a casa cuando termino._
Trick: if after the time word you can put _yo_, _tú_ or _ella_, use **cuando**; if there's no person, use **antes de** or **después de** + infinitive.
After **antes de** comes the infinitive: **salir**.
**Cuando** needs a conjugated verb: **llego**.
Desde, desde hace, hace and llevar + gerund
**Desde** + a **point in time** (a date, a year, an event) says when something that **is still going on** began: _Vivo en Masaya desde 2010_; _Trabajo aquí desde que terminé la escuela_.

**Desde hace** + a **length of time** says how long something that **is still going on** has lasted: _Vivo en Masaya desde hace quince años_. The verb is in the present because the situation continues.

**Hace** + a **length of time** with the **simple past** says how long ago a **finished** event happened: _Hace dos años abrí una tienda_. And **llevar** + length + **gerund** stresses how long something has been going on: _Llevo quince años viviendo en Masaya_.

Structure
Question
With a date, only **desde**. **Desde hace** goes with a length of time: _desde hace diez años_.
**Llevar** + time + **gerund**: _viviendo_.
For something still going on, use **hace… que** + present or **desde hace**. **Hace** alone + simple past is for a finished event.

Stress in time words

This week's time words are short and very frequent, and their stressed syllable isn't always the one you expect. _DES-de_ is stressed at the start, but _des-PUÉS_, _a-YER_ and _a-ÚN_ are stressed at the end.
_To-da-VÍ-a_ has four syllables, with the stress on the **í**, like the imperfect forms from week 3. _Ahora_ is said _a-HO-ra_, and _antes_, _AN-tes_.
If you put the stress in the right place, the sentence sounds natural even if you speak slowly: _Lle-vo tres A-ños vi-VIEN-do a-QUÍ._
_Después_ and _todavía_ have a written accent because their stress doesn't fall where the general rule would put it. _Desde_, _antes_ and _ahora_ don't have one.

This week you review two classes about the future: how to choose between **ir a + infinitive** and the **simple future**, and how the future is formed, with its irregular stems. Here you see it in another situation: a weekend in Antigua, with a volcano, an agency and lots of rain.
A decided plan or a promise made right now?

With **ir a + infinitive** you talk about something you decided before speaking: it's in your diary. _Este sábado voy a subir al volcán Pacaya_. You also use it when you see a sign right now: _Mira el cielo: va a llover_.

With the **simple future** you make a promise or an offer on the spot (_Tranquila, te mandaré las fotos_), a prediction with no sign in front of you (_Algún día viviré en Guatemala_) or a formal announcement, as in an email or on the radio (_El autobús saldrá a las seis_).
Often both forms are possible. In conversation, above all in much of Latin America, **ir a** is the most frequent. The future sounds more like a promise, a written text or a distant dream.
Ask yourself: did I decide it before, or am I promising it now? Before → **voy a**. Now, to another person → **future**.

After **voy a** comes the infinitive. Use one form or the other, never both together.

The regular future: the whole infinitive + an ending
The future is easy to form: you don't remove anything. You take the **whole infinitive** (_visitar, volver, subir_) and add the ending. The endings are **the same** for -ar, -er and -ir.
Every person has a written accent except **nosotros**: _visitaré, volverás, subirá, subiréis, visitarán_, but _volveremos_. The stress of the voice falls at the end of the word.
Without the accent, the word changes: _visitara_ or _llamara_ are not future forms. Always write the accent in _visitará_, _llamaré_.

Ten verbs with a changed stem
A small group of very frequent verbs changes its **stem**, but the endings don't change: _tendré, tendrás, tendrá…_

There are three families. Some lose the vowel and add a **d**: _tener → tendr-_, _salir → saldr-_, _venir → vendr-_, _poner → pondr-_. Others just lose the vowel: _poder → podr-_, _saber → sabr-_, _haber → habr-_, _querer → querr-_. And two are very short: _hacer → har-_, _decir → dir-_.
**Habrá** is the future of **hay**. That's why it is always singular: _habrá muchas personas_, never _habrán_.

Si + present, and the future afterwards

For a real condition in the future, after **si** comes the **present**, not the future: _Si llueve, nos quedaremos en el hostal_. The consequence can be in the future or with **ir a**: _Si llueve, vamos a quedarnos_.
The order can change with no problem: _Nos quedaremos en el hostal si llueve_. When the sentence starts with **si**, add a comma.
To recognise: sometimes the future doesn't talk about the future but about a **guess** about now: _—¿Dónde está Sergio? —Estará en el mercado_ (= he's probably at the market).

The final beat of the future
In the future, the stressed syllable is **at the end**: _vi-si-ta-RÉ, vol-ve-RÁS, su-bi-RÁN_. That's why almost all forms have a written accent.
Only **nosotros** has the stress on the second-to-last syllable: _vi-si-ta-RE-mos_. That's why it has no accent.
This final beat helps you tell apart tenses that look alike: _llegará_ (future, stress at the end), _llegaba_ (past, stress on -GA-) and _llega_ (present).
The accent in the future marks the stress at the end: **llamaré, comerás, vivirán**. Without the accent, _llamare_ or _llamara_ are other forms. Nosotros never has it: **llamaremos**.

This week you review the two imperative classes: the **affirmative** (with tú, with usted and, to recognise, with vos) and the **negative**, which uses a different form. Here you practise it in the street: how to get around Guatemala City and how to explain the way to other people.
With tú: the present without the -s

To give an instruction to someone you call **tú**, take the tú present and drop the final **-s**: _caminas → camina_, _bebes → bebe_, _subes → sube_. If the verb changes its vowel in the present, the imperative does too: _cierras → cierra_, _vuelves → vuelve_, _pides → pide_.
Eight very frequent verbs have a short irregular form: **di** (decir), **haz** (hacer), **ve** (ir), **pon** (poner), **sal** (salir), **sé** (ser), **ten** (tener), **ven** (venir).
The imperative sounds kinder with **por favor**, with the person's name or with a reason: _Ana, sube por esta escalera, por favor; es más rápido_.
The eight irregulars fit into one sentence: _Di, haz, ve, pon, sal, sé, ten, ven_. Say it aloud like a rhythm.

With usted: the opposite vowel

With an older person, a customer or someone you don't know, you use **usted**. Start from the **yo** form of the present, drop the **-o** and add the opposite vowel: -ar verbs take **-e** (_camino → camine_); -er and -ir verbs take **-a** (_bebo → beba_, _subo → suba_).

Because you start from **yo**, the irregular yo forms carry over to the imperative: _hago → haga_, _pongo → ponga_, _salgo → salga_, _tengo → tenga_, _vengo → venga_, _digo → diga_. Two are special: **ir → vaya** and **ser → sea**.
For a group (**ustedes**) you add **-n**: _caminen, suban, vayan_. In Spain, with friends, **vosotros** is used (_caminad, subid_), but you only need to recognise it.
From yo to usted
With **usted** the vowel changes: pas**e**. _Pasa_ is for tú.
Start from _yo vengo_: **venga**, with no i.
To recognise: the vos imperative

In Guatemala, in other Central American countries, in Argentina and in Uruguay many people say **vos** instead of tú. It is a correct, normal form; you don't need to use it, but it's useful to recognise it.

The vos imperative looks like the infinitive without the **-r**, stressed at the end: _caminá, comé, subí_. The vowel doesn't change: _cerrá, volvé, pedí_. It has almost no irregulars: _vení, decí, hacé, poné, salí_. For **ir** people say **andá**.
If someone says _Vení, sentate_ to you, understand _Ven, siéntate_.

The negative: no + another vowel

To say what someone should **not** do, it isn't enough to put _no_ in front of the affirmative. The negative uses the opposite vowel, like usted, plus the **-s** of tú: _cruza → no cruces_, _bebe → no bebas_, _sube → no subas_.

It also starts from the **yo** form: _hago → no hagas_, _salgo → no salgas_, _digo → no digas_, _tengo → no tengas_. And again two are special: **no vayas** (ir) and **no seas** (ser). With **usted**, the negative is the same as the affirmative with _no_: _no cruce, no vaya_.

Watch the spelling, to keep the sound: _llegar → no llegues_, _buscar → no busques_, _cruzar → no cruces_. A reason next to it softens the prohibition: _No pagues en efectivo: con la tarjeta es más barato_.
Trick: the negative tú form is the usted form + **s**: _no cruce → no cruces_, _no vaya → no vayas_.

Tú, vos or usted? The stress of the word
With **tú**, the imperative is stressed on the second-to-last syllable: _es-PE-ra, CRU-za, SI-gue_.
With **vos**, the stress jumps to the **end**, so it has a written accent: _es-pe-RÁ, cru-ZÁ, se-GUÍ_. This is the clearest clue to recognise it.
With **usted**, the stress is in the same place as with tú, but the **last vowel** changes: _CRU-ce, SI-ga, es-PE-re_. Listen carefully to the ending.
To keep the sound in the negative and with usted: **c → qu** (_busque, no busques_), **g → gu** (_llegue, no llegues_), **z → c** (_cruce, no cruces_).

This week you review two closely linked classes: **reflexive pronouns** in routines and changes of state, and the **change verbs** _ponerse_ and _quedarse_. Here you see them in Quetzaltenango (Xela), with Spanish students, host families and a trip to the hot springs.
Routine in the past: the pronoun goes in front

A reflexive verb says that the action goes back to the same person: _me ducho_ (I shower myself). In the past, the pronoun **me, te, se, nos, os, se** goes **before** the conjugated verb, in any tense: _me levanté_ (preterite), _me levantaba_ (imperfect), _me he levantado_ (present perfect).
In the present perfect, the pronoun goes before **haber**, never in the middle: _se ha despertado_, not _ha se despertado_.

Verbs that change their vowel in the present (_me despierto, me acuesto, me visto_) don't change it in the preterite with yo: _me desperté, me acosté_. Only -ir verbs change with él and ellos: _se vistió, se vistieron_; _se durmió_.

With infinitive, gerund and imperative: the pronoun attaches

With an **infinitive** or a **gerund**, you have two options: the pronoun before the conjugated verb or attached to the end: _me voy a acostar_ = _voy a acostarme_; _me estoy vistiendo_ = _estoy vistiéndome_.
The pronoun always changes with the person, also when it is attached: _vamos a acostarnos_, _¿vas a ducharte?_, _ellos van a quedarse_.
With the **affirmative imperative** it is attached: _levántate, vístete, tranquilízate_. With the **negative** it goes in front: _no te levantes, no te preocupes_.

Emotion verbs: with se, the person changes inside
Many emotion verbs take a pronoun when they say that **a person changes state**: _preocuparse, tranquilizarse, enojarse_ (in Spain also _enfadarse_), _aburrirse, cansarse, asustarse, relajarse_.
Without the pronoun, the verb says that **another thing or person** causes the emotion: _El ruido asustó al perro_ (the noise did something to the dog), but _El perro se asustó_ (the dog changed).
The same with _dormir_ and _dormirse_: _Dormí ocho horas_ (the action of sleeping) / _Me dormí en la clase_ (I started sleeping, without meaning to).
With se and without se
With se: the person changes
Without se: something causes the change
Your father changes state: **se preocupó**.

**Estar** describes a state: _estaba nerviosa_. **Ponerse** tells a **quick change**, a reaction: _se puso nerviosa cuando la llamaron_. **Quedarse** tells **the result**, how someone ended up after something: _se quedó callada_.

**Ponerse** goes with adjectives of reactions and health: _ponerse rojo, pálido, nervioso, triste, contento, enfermo_. **Quedarse** goes with adjectives and participles (_quedarse sorprendido, dormido, callado_) and **sin + noun**: _quedarse sin batería, sin dinero, sin palabras_.
**Quedarse** + place or time means **not leaving**: _me quedé en el hotel_, _nos quedamos hasta las once_. The adjective always agrees: _se puso rojo_, _se puso roja_, _se pusieron rojos_.
A film in three photos: _estaba tranquilo_ → _se puso nervioso_ → _se quedó sin palabras_.

This week you review two classes that share pronouns: verbs like **gustar** (_interesar, doler, faltar, molestar_), where the verb agrees with the thing, and the **indirect object** (_me, te, le, nos, les_) with verbs like _dar, mandar, decir_. Gustar the other way round: the verb looks at the thing

With **gustar**, the person is not the subject. The subject is **what is liked**, and the verb agrees with it: _me gusta **el mercado**_ (one thing), _me gustan **los mercados**_ (several things). The person appears as a pronoun: **me, te, le, nos, os, les**.

They go in the **singular** (_gusta_): one thing, something uncountable (_el café, la música_) and infinitives, one or several (_me gusta caminar y nadar_). They go in the **plural** (_gustan_): a plural noun or two things together (_me gustan el café y el chocolate_).
**Interesar**, **encantar** and **molestar** work the same way: _nos interesa la historia_, _les encantan las hamacas_, _me molesta el ruido_.

Doler, faltar, molestar: the same pattern

**Doler** follows the pattern of gustar: _me duele **la cabeza**_, _me duelen **los pies**_. With body parts you use the article (**la** cabeza), not the possessive: _me duele la espalda_, not _mi espalda_.

**Faltar** says something isn't there or isn't enough: _me falta **dinero**_, _nos faltan **dos boletos**_. It is also used without a person for what's left: _faltan **cuatro horas** para el bus_. Compare: _necesito tiempo_ (I am the subject) and _me falta tiempo_ (time is the subject).
In the past the agreement doesn't change: _me dolió la rodilla_, _me dolieron las piernas_; _nos gustó el taller_, _nos gustaron las tazas_.
Before conjugating, ask yourself: what is liked, what hurts, what is missing? That word decides whether the verb is singular or plural.

A mí, a ti, a Laura: clarifying and insisting

You can add **a + person** to make clear who it is (_le gusta_ could be he, she or you: **a Laura** le gusta) or to insist, especially when comparing: _A mí me encanta el picante, pero a mi hermano no_.
Even if you say _a Laura_ or _a mí_, the pronoun **doesn't disappear**: _A Laura le gusta_, never _A Laura gusta_.
To react to someone else's taste: **a mí también** (same as me, with yes), **a mí tampoco** (same as me, with no), **a mí sí** and **a mí no** (I'm different).
With _a mis primos_ you also need **les**.
Positive sentence → **también**; negative → **tampoco**.
To whom? Me, te, le, nos, les with dar, mandar, decir

The **indirect object** says **to whom** or **for whom** an action is: _le regalé un pañuelo_ (to my mother). You use it with verbs of giving and communicating: _dar, regalar, prestar, traer, mandar, escribir, decir, preguntar, contestar, explicar_.

It goes before the conjugated verb: _te mando las fotos_, _nos explicó el proceso_. With **le** and **les** it's very common to repeat the person afterwards: _Le di las gracias **a la artesana**_. If the person goes in front, or if you say _a mí, a ti, a él…_, the pronoun is compulsory: _A la artesana le di las gracias_.

Don't confuse it with **lo, la, los, las**, which answer _what?_ or _whom?_ with verbs like _ver, llamar, invitar_: _la llamé_ (Marta), but _le dije la hora_ (to Marta). To recognise: in parts of Spain some people say _le vi_ for a man; it's a variant the RAE accepts.

The -n that changes everything: duele / duelen
Between _me duele el pie_ and _me duelen los pies_ the difference is an **n** at the end of the verb. It's small, but it changes the agreement.

Two pronouns: the person first, then the thing

When we already know which thing and which person we're talking about, we can use **two pronouns** together: the one for the person who receives (**me, te, nos, os**) and the one for the thing (**lo, la, los, las**). The order is always **person + thing**: _¿El cargador? Te lo devuelvo hoy_.
**Lo, la, los, las** agree with the **thing**, not with the person: _¿La mesa? Me la regaló mi tío_. _¿Los platos? Nos los prestó la vecina_.
Both go **before the conjugated verb**, together, and **no** goes in front of both: _No te lo puedo explicar ahora_, _Ya me las han traído_.
Person + thing
Person
The person first (**me**), then the thing (**lo**).
_Las fotos_ is feminine plural: **las**.
Le and les become se
**Le** or **les** can't go before **lo, la, los, las**. In that case, _le_ and _les_ become **se**: _Le di el sofá a Carlos_ → _**Se lo** di_. _Les mandé las fotos a mis padres_ → _**Se las** mandé_.
**Se** doesn't say whether it's one person or several, a man or a woman. If it isn't clear, add **a + person**: _Se lo di **a Carlos**_, _Se lo di **a ellas**_.
Remember: the thing decides _lo_ or _la_. If you give **el** sofá to a woman, it's _se **lo** di_, because sofá is masculine.
Read **se** as «to him, to her, to them…» and look at the second word to know which thing it is.

Before or after? Infinitive, gerund and imperative

With the **affirmative imperative**, the pronouns go **after and attached**, in the same order: _dámelo, llévasela, pásamelos_. With the **negative imperative** they go **in front**: _no me lo des, no se la lleves_.

With **ir a + infinitive**, **tener que + infinitive** or **estar + gerund** you have **two positions**: before the conjugated verb or attached to the end. _Te la voy a llevar_ = _Voy a llevártela_; _Se lo estoy explicando_ = _Estoy explicándoselo_. Never in the middle or repeated.

With an infinitive on its own (after _para, sin, antes de_…) they are attached: _Necesito una caja para guardarlos_. With **usted** it works the same way: _Déjemelo aquí_, _No me lo deje en la puerta_.

The written accent when the word grows
When you attach pronouns, the **stress of the voice doesn't move**: _COM-pra_ → _CÓM-pra-lo_. But the word is longer, and it often needs a **written accent** to mark that stress.
With the imperative: one syllable + one pronoun, no accent (_dame, ponlo, dime_); with two pronouns, accent (_dámelo, pónmelo_). Two syllables + one pronoun, accent (_cómpralo, llévala_).
With the infinitive + one pronoun, no accent (_comprarlo, dejarla_); + two pronouns, accent (_dártelo, llevárselas_). With the gerund, always an accent (_buscándolo, explicándoselo_).
Trick: say the word aloud. If the stress falls three syllables or more from the end (_CÓM-pra-lo_, _DÁ-me-lo_), it has a written accent.
_Di_ + _me_ + _lo_ = three syllables stressed on the first: **dímelo**.
Gerund + pronoun: always an accent, **haciéndolo**.

The stress doesn't move: dame, dámelo
When you attach pronouns to a verb, the stressed syllable **doesn't move**: _LLE-va_, _LLÉ-va-la_, _LLÉ-va-te-la_. That's why, when speaking, the pronouns sound quick and soft at the end.
The typical mistake is to move the stress onto the pronoun: _da-ME-lo_. The natural way is _DÁ-me-lo_, with a beat at the start and the rest light.
With the infinitive the stress stays on the verb's syllable: _lle-VAR-la_, _lle-VÁR-se-la_. Listen to how the ending gets longer, but the stress doesn't change.

The situation: Daniel, a student from Lima, spends a semester in Santa Ana with the Morán family and learns to find his way around his new neighbourhood.
Que: a detail to say which one

Sometimes a noun alone is not enough: _la vecina_… which neighbour? With **que** you add a detail that identifies her: _la vecina **que vive enfrente**_. That way you join two ideas in one sentence and don't repeat the noun.

There are two cases. If the noun **does** the action, the verb comes right after _que_: _el señor **que vende** tortillas_. If **another person** does the action, that person appears: _las tortillas **que compra** doña Carmen_, _el bus **que tomo** cada mañana_.
**Que** works for people, things and places and **never changes**. What changes is the verb, which agrees with the noun before it: _el niño que juega_, _los niños que juegan_.

From two sentences to one, and que versus qué

To practise, think of two sentences that repeat a noun: _Tengo una amiga. **Mi amiga** vive en Santa Ana._ Remove the repeated noun, put **que** in its place and join everything: _Tengo una amiga **que** vive en Santa Ana._

If the repeated noun is not the one doing the action, the rest of the sentence stays the same, but without _lo, la, los, las_: _Compré un mapa. Usé **el mapa** ayer._ → _Ayer usé el mapa **que** compré._
Don't confuse **que** with **qué**. _Qué_, with an accent, asks: _¿**Qué** bus tomas?_ _Que_, without an accent, joins a noun and its detail: _El bus **que** tomo es el 51._
Trick: if you can put the noun first and ask yourself "which one?", the answer starts with **que**: _¿Qué bus? El que va al centro._

Donde for places, cuando for moments
After a **place** use **donde**: _el parque **donde** juegan los niños_, _la ciudad **donde** nací_. It means the same as _en el que / en la que_: _la plaza en la que nos vemos_.

Compare: _el mercado **que** abre a las seis_ (the market does the action) and _el mercado **donde** compro fruta_ (I buy **at** the market). If inside the sentence you would say _in that place_, use **donde**.

For a **moment** you have already named, use **cuando**: _En diciembre, **cuando** hace menos calor, vamos al lago._ With _el día, el año, el momento_ it is more natural to use **que** or **en que**: _el día **que** llegué_, _el año en que empecé_.

Lo que: an idea with no noun
**Lo que** doesn't come after a noun: it means _the thing that_ or _the things that_. Use it when you don't say the noun or you talk about an idea: _**Lo que** necesito es un mapa del centro._

It is very useful for giving opinions: _**Lo que** más me gusta de Santa Ana es el teatro_, _**Lo que** no entiendo es el horario del bus_. And also after a verb: _No sé **lo que** quiere_, _Haz **lo que** quieras_.
Compare: _la comida **que** prepara doña Carmen_ (there is a noun: _la comida_) and _**lo que** prepara doña Carmen_ (no noun: everything she makes).
To describe a word you can't remember, combine everything: _Es una cosa **que** sirve para…_, _Es el lugar **donde**…_, _Es **lo que** usas para…_

Que without stress, qué with stress

The **que** of relative clauses is an **unstressed** word: it attaches to the next word and is barely heard. _la se-ño-ra-que-VEN-de-pan_. The same happens with **donde** and **cuando** inside the sentence.
By contrast, **qué, dónde, cuándo** in questions are **stressed** and have a written accent: _¿QUÉ bus tomas?_, _¿DÓN-de vives?_ Your voice rises or hits that word.
If you say the relative _que_ with a lot of stress, the sentence sounds like a question. Practise with long sentences: join the noun, the _que_ and the verb in a single breath group.
Written accent only in questions and exclamations: **¿qué?, ¿dónde?, ¿cuándo?** No accent in relative clauses: **que, donde, cuando, lo que**.

Comparing two things: más, menos, tan
To say that one thing has **more** or **less** of a quality, use **más / menos + adjetivo + que**: _Este apartamento es **más grande que** el otro_. _El barrio es **menos ruidoso que** el centro_.
To say they are **equal**, use **tan + adjetivo + como**: _El segundo es **tan caro como** el primero_. You can also say **igual de + adjetivo**: _Los dos son **igual de** luminosos_.
The adjective agrees with the thing you're talking about: _La cocina es más **pequeña** que el salón_. With a number, you say **más de**: _Cuesta **más de** diez mil lempiras_.

With **más / menos** you use **que**; **como** goes with _tan_.
Equality: **tan… como**.
Four adjectives have their own form for comparing and **don't take más**: _bueno_ → **mejor**, _malo_ → **peor**, _grande_ (age) → **mayor**, _pequeño_ (age) → **menor**.
They have one form for masculine and feminine, and the plural ends in **-es**: _Esta zona es **mejor** que la otra_. _Los precios aquí son **peores**_. _Mi hermana es **mayor** que yo_.
**Mayor** and **menor** are mainly about **age**. For size, the normal choice is _más grande / más pequeño_: _Mi cuarto es **más grande** que el tuyo_.
To strengthen a comparison, put **mucho** in front: _mucho mejor, mucho más barato_. Never _muy mejor_.

Describing the state of things and talking about groups

To compare houses, cars or places you need to describe **what state they are in**. The participle works as an adjective with **estar**: _La cocina **está reformada**_. _Las paredes **están pintadas**_. _El apartamento **está amueblado**_.
Like any adjective, the participle **agrees**: _el baño está **limpio**_, _la puerta está **rota**_, _los servicios están **incluidos**_. Remember the irregular ones: _roto, hecho, abierto, puesto_.
Words that name a group, such as **la gente, la familia, el equipo**, take a **singular** verb: _La gente del edificio **es** tranquila_.
_Romper_ has an irregular participle: **roto, rota, rotos, rotas**.
_La gente_ is singular and feminine: **es simpática**.
El más… de: picking one out of a group

To say that something is number one in a group, use **el / la / los / las + nombre + más / menos + adjetivo + de**: _Es **el apartamento más barato de** los tres_. _Es **la calle más tranquila del** barrio_.

If we already know what we're talking about, drop the noun: _¿Cuál te gusta? —**El más grande**_. With the special forms, the adjective goes **before** the noun: _**la mejor** vista **de** la ciudad_, _**el peor** día **del** año_, _**el mayor** de los hermanos_.
To say something is among the top ones, use **uno de los / una de las + plural**: _Es **una de las** colonias **más seguras** de Tegucigalpa_.

-ísimo and ¡qué…!: very, very

To say **very, very** without comparing with anything, add **-ísimo / -ísima / -ísimos / -ísimas** to the adjective without its last vowel: _caro_ → **carísimo**, _limpia_ → **limpísima**, _fácil_ → **facilísimo**.

How the diminutive is formed
The most general form is **-ito / -ita**: remove the final vowel and add the ending, with the same gender: _casa_ → **casita**, _perro_ → **perrito**, _abuela_ → **abuelita**.

If the word ends in **-e**, **-n** or **-r**, or is very short, it usually takes **-cito / -ecito**: _café_ → **cafecito**, _camión_ → **camioncito**, _flor_ → **florecita**, _pan_ → **panecito**. The exact form varies a little from country to country.
Watch the **spelling**, because the sound doesn't change: _poco_ → **poquito**, _amigo_ → **amiguito**, _taza_ → **tacita**, _luz_ → **lucecita**.
