Small, affection, politeness
The diminutive doesn't only express **size** (_una mesita_). It often expresses **affection**: _mi abuelita, un perrito precioso, pobrecito_.
It is also used for **politeness**: it softens a request or a wait. _Espéreme **un momentito**_. _¿Le sirvo **un cafecito**?_ _Es **un ratito** nada más_.

Some words with a diminutive have a **life of their own** and don't mean "small": **el bolsillo** (on clothes), **la ventanilla** (at the bank, on the bus). And don't confuse **calentito** (pleasantly warm) with **calentísimo** (too hot, week 12).
With strangers, a polite diminutive (_un momentito, un favorcito_) softens things a lot. But in a formal text or one written for work, use it sparingly.
The one on clothes is **el bolsillo**; _un bolsito_ is a small bag.
Big and ugly: -ón, -azo, -ucho
To exaggerate playfully, Spanish has **augmentatives**. The most common are **-ón / -ona** and **-azo / -aza**: _un problemón_ (a very big problem), _un fiestón_, _un perrazo_, _un exitazo_.
**-azo** sometimes means **a blow**: _un golpazo_, _un portazo_ (slamming the door). **-ucho / -ucha** is pejorative: something ugly or poor quality, _un cuartucho_, _un hotelucho_.

Watch out: some words in _-ón_ are already **something else**: **el cajón** (in a piece of furniture), **el sillón** (a comfortable seat), **el cucharón** (for serving soup). With many augmentatives in **-ón**, the word becomes **masculine**: _una silla_ → **un sillón**.

The stress in -ito and in -ón
The endings **-ito, -ita, -cito** carry the stress on the **i**: _CA-sa_ → _ca-SI-ta_, _ca-FÉ_ → _ca-fe-CI-to_. The word's rhythm changes, even though the base doesn't.

Augmentatives in **-ón** carry the stress at the **end**, which is why they have a written accent: _pro-BLE-ma_ → _pro-ble-MÓN_, _FIES-ta_ → _fies-TÓN_. In **-azo** the stress is on the **a**: _pe-RRA-zo_.
In the plural, **-ón** loses the accent because the word grows: _un sillón_, _dos si-LLO-nes_. Listen: the stress stays in the same place.
Accent on **-ón** in the singular (_sillón, problemón_), no accent in the plural (_sillones_). Changes: **poco → poquito, taza → tacita, amigo → amiguito**.

Travel chronicle on a blog
Clara, a traveller from Guatemala, tells on her blog how she experienced Holy Week in Comayagua.

I arrived in Comayagua on Maundy Thursday afternoon and looked for a hotel near the centre. There was nothing free: everything was full. In the end I found a little room in the house of doña Marta, a really kind lady who welcomed me with a coffee and sweet bread.

In the evening I went out for a walk and didn't see anyone in the main streets. Where was everybody? Suddenly, on a block near the cathedral, I found the whole neighbourhood: children, grandparents and young people were working on the ground with stencils and coloured sawdust.

I asked if anyone needed help and a lady gave me a bucket and a little stencil. "Put a tiny bit of water on it, sweetheart, so the sawdust doesn't blow away," she told me. Nobody talked about sleeping. At three in the morning there was a little problem: a huge dog ran right across the design. Nobody shouted; everybody laughed and fixed it in no time.

**Alguno** asks or states that there is **one or several**; **ninguno** says there are **zero**. They agree with the noun: _alguna tienda, algunos guías, ninguna entrada_.
Before a **masculine singular** noun, they lose the **-o**: _**algún** sitio_, _**ningún** problema_. Without a noun, they are full again: _¿Tienes algún mapa? —No, no tengo **ninguno**_.
**Ninguno / ninguna** is almost always **singular**, even if you'd use the plural in English: _No hay **ninguna** silla libre_ (there are no chairs).
Forms and agreement
Masculine
Feminine
Before a masculine singular noun: **ningún**.
**Ninguna** is almost always singular.
Mucho, poco, demasiado: do they change or not?
Before a **noun**, **mucho, poco, demasiado** agree like adjectives: _**mucha** gente, **pocos** guías, **demasiadas** escaleras, **demasiado** calor_.
With a **verb** or an **adjective** they don't change: _Caminamos **mucho**_, _Los recuerdos son **demasiado** caros_, _Esta tienda abre **poco**_.

**Muy** goes with adjectives and adverbs (_muy alto, muy lejos_); **mucho** goes with verbs and nouns, and also with **más, menos, mejor, peor**: _**mucho** mejor_, never _muy mejor_. **Demasiado** means "more than necessary" and is usually a criticism.
With a noun or without
With a noun (agrees)
With a verb or adjective (doesn't change)
_La gente_ is feminine singular: **mucha gente**.
With an adjective: **muy**.
With a verb: **mucho**.
**Cada** never changes and goes with a **singular** noun: _**cada** escalón_, _**cada** día_, _**cada** persona paga su entrada_.
**Otro / otra / otros / otras** never takes **un** in front: _¿Me das **otra** botella?_ (not _una otra_). To say "one more", _otro_ is enough.
**Todo** agrees and takes **el / la / los / las**: _**todo el** parque, **toda la** mañana, **todos los** templos, **todas las** guacamayas_.
**Otro** doesn't take _un_.
**Cada** + singular noun.
Double negatives: no + verb + nunca, nada, nadie…

In Spanish it's normal to have **two negatives** in a sentence. If the negative word (**nunca, nada, nadie, ningún, tampoco**) comes **after** the verb, you need **no** in front: _**No** fui **nunca** a Copán_, _**No** tenemos **ningún** mapa_.
If the negative word comes **before** the verb, you **don't** use _no_: _**Nunca** fui a Copán_. The meaning is the same; with the negative word first, the sentence sounds a bit stronger.
You can put several negative words in the same sentence, always with just one **no** before the verb: _**No** le dije **nunca nada** a **nadie**_.

no + verb + negative word
negative word + verb

_Nunca_ after the verb needs **no** in front.
También or tampoco, and ni… ni
To agree with someone: if their sentence is **positive**, answer **también**; if it is **negative**, answer **tampoco**. _—Me encanta Copán. —A mí **también**_. _—No tengo agua. —Yo **tampoco**_.
To **disagree**: _—No me gustan las alturas. —**A mí sí**_. _—Yo quiero subir. —**Yo no**_.
To make two things negative together, use **ni… ni**: _No trajimos **ni** agua **ni** gorras_. If it comes before the verb, no _no_: _**Ni** Paula **ni** Tomás conocían Copán_.
Trick: check whether the other person's sentence has **no**. If it does, your answer to agree is **tampoco**.

The stress on the negative word
In a negative sentence, the negative word usually carries the **strongest beat** in the sentence: _No voy NUN-ca_, _NUN-ca voy_, _No vino NA-die_. The initial _no_ is short and soft.
**Ningún** and **algún** carry the stress at the **end** (_nin-GÚN, al-GÚN_), which is why they have a written accent. **Ninguno** and **alguno** have it on **gu**: _nin-GU-no_.
In short reactions, the important word comes at the end and the voice **falls**: _Yo tam-PO-co._ _A mí tam-BIÉN._ If it rises, it sounds like a question.
With an accent: **algún, ningún** (stress at the end). Without an accent: **alguno, ninguno, alguna, ninguna**.

Moving and locating: desde, hasta, hacia, por

For a complete **route** use **desde… hasta** or **de… a**: _Fuimos **desde** la terminal **hasta** el muelle_, _**de** Tegucigalpa **a** La Ceiba_. **A** marks the destination you reach; **hacia**, just the direction: _El barco va **hacia** el norte_. **Hasta** marks the end point: _Caminamos **hasta** la playa_.
**Por** gives the **way** or the place you pass through: _Pasamos **por** el malecón_, _El bus va **por** la costa_. Transport goes with **en** (_en bus, en ferry, en taxi_), but you say **a pie**.

To **locate** things, use these expressions with **de**: _delante de, detrás de, enfrente de, al lado de, encima de, debajo de, dentro de, fuera de, cerca de, lejos de_. And for two reference points, **entre… y…**: _La taquilla está **entre** la cafetería **y** la puerta tres_.

Por and para: why or what for?

**Para** **looks ahead**: **purpose** (_Ahorro **para** viajar_), **destination** (_El ferry sale **para** Utila_), the person who **receives** something (_Este regalo es **para** ti_) and the **deadline** (_Necesito los boletos **para** el viernes_).

**Por** **looks back or around**: the **cause** (_No dormí **por** el calor_, _Gracias **por** todo_), the **way** (_**por** el malecón_), an approximate area (_¿Hay un cajero **por** aquí?_), the **part of the day** (_**por** la mañana_) and the **price** or exchange (_Lo compré **por** seiscientos lempiras_).
For the cause: **por** + noun, **porque** + conjugated verb. _Llegué tarde **por** el tráfico_ = _Llegué tarde **porque** había tráfico_.

Ser, estar and llevar to describe someone

With **ser** you say what a person **is like**: features that identify them. _Nico **es** alto y moreno_, _**es** muy simpático_. With **tener** you describe parts of the body: _**tiene** los ojos verdes_, _**tiene** el pelo rizado_.

With **estar** you say how someone **is** now or what **change** you notice: _**Está** cansada por el viaje_, _**Estás** más delgado_, _¡**Está** muy cambiado!_. The same adjective can go with both verbs: _Es moreno_ (dark-skinned) / _Está moreno_ (tanned).

With **llevar** you say what someone **has on** or how they wear their hair: _**Lleva** gafas de sol_, _**lleva** barba_, _**lleva** una mochila roja_, _**lleva** el pelo largo_. **Ponerse** is the action; **llevar**, the result: _Me puse la chaqueta; ahora la llevo_.

Prepositions link up: desde‿el, por‿el, para‿el

Prepositions almost never carry stress: they **attach** to the next word. If one ends in a vowel and the next starts with a vowel, the two vowels merge into one syllable: _de‿a-QUÍ_, _pa-ra‿el-MUE-lle_, _has-ta‿el-FA-ro_.
If the preposition ends in a consonant, the consonant moves to the next word: _por el_ sounds like _po-rel_; _desde el_ sounds like _des-de‿el_. That way the sentence flows, without breaks.
In fast speech in many countries, **para** is shortened to **pa** (_pa'l muelle_). Understand it when you hear it, but in writing always use **para**.
Always write **para** and **por el** (no apostrophe). _Pa'l_ is only spoken. **Al** and **del** are the only contractions: _vamos al muelle, salimos del puerto_.

Travel diary
Valeria writes in her diary on her first night in Utila.

I left Tegucigalpa on Friday at five in the morning on the bus to La Ceiba. The journey was incredibly long: seven hours along the northern road, between small villages and green mountains. I was nervous because I hadn't seen my cousin Nico for eight years, the boy who taught me to swim when we were children.

At the bus station I looked for him in the crowd, but I didn't recognise anyone until someone shouted: "Vale!". Nico has changed so much. He's as tall as before, but now he has a beard and long hair, and he's very tanned from the sun. He was wearing the yellow T-shirt of the local team, as he promised me. He says I haven't changed at all; for me, that's a compliment. We hugged for a little while and laughed a lot: neither of us could believe we were already twenty-six.

From the bus station we took a taxi to the pier. We went along the seafront, where people walk in the afternoon and vendors sell chilled coconut. We ate some baleadas at a little stall opposite the sea: the best of my life, much better than the ones in the capital. We bought the tickets for Utila at the ticket office for six hundred lempiras each. I paid for them, to thank Nico for the invitation.

The ferry left for the island at four. It was windy and the sea was a bit rough. Inside it was too cold and I didn't have a jacket, so I put on my cousin's sweatshirt, which is huge on me. Neither of us slept: we talked about everything that's happened in these eight years.

Now I'm writing from a hammock in the little house where we're staying, next to the beach. What I like most about this trip isn't the sea or the food: it's being with my cousin again. Tomorrow we're going diving for the first time. I'm so nervous!

Se + verb: what matters is what gets done

In recipes, signs, manuals and rules it doesn't matter **who** does the action: it's information for anyone. That's why we use **se + verb in the third person**: _se pela el plátano_, _aquí se habla inglés_, _¿cómo se escribe tu apellido?_

The verb **agrees with the thing**: one thing or something uncountable → singular (_se lava **el arroz**_); several things → plural (_se lavan **los frijoles**_). The thing can go before or after: _las ollas se guardan aquí_ = _aquí se guardan las ollas_.
If there's no thing, the verb is **singular**: _en esta casa se come temprano_, _en el mercado se regatea_.
One thing, several things or none
What is done
_Los tomates_ is plural: **se pican**.
_Español_ is one thing: **se habla**.
Rules: se puede, no se puede, and who's who

For permission and bans you use **se puede / no se puede + infinitive**. The verb _poder_ is always **singular**, because what follows is an infinitive: _no se puede entrar con sandalias_, _se puede pagar con tarjeta_.
Compare three different sentences: _Se corta el pan_ (an instruction for everyone), _Marcos, corta el pan_ (an imperative to one specific person) and _Marcos corta el pan_ (you say what Marcos does).
Don't confuse it with **reflexive se**: _Marcos se lava las manos_ (himself). In impersonal se there is no person: _primero se lavan las manos_ (everyone, anyone).
Before you write, find the thing: one or several? If an infinitive follows the verb, the verb is singular.
With an infinitive, _poder_ is singular: **no se puede**.
Without _se_, the sentence talks about one specific person (he or she).
Telling things in order: primero, luego, al final
To make a story or instructions easy to follow, mark the order: **primero** → **luego / después** → **entonces** → **al final** or **por último**.
**Al final** says how the story ended (_al final comimos todos juntos_). **Por último** introduces the last step of a list (_por último, se sirve caliente_).

**Después** goes alone or with **de + infinitive**: _después, lavamos todo_; _después de lavar todo, nos fuimos_. Never _después de, llegó_. And **entonces** has two uses: _at that moment_ (_entonces sonó el teléfono_) or _so_ (_no había gas, entonces cocinamos con leña_).

Explaining why: porque, como, por eso, así que, es decir
For the **cause**: **porque** goes after what happened (_llegué tarde porque no había buses_); **como** goes at the start, before what happened (_como no había buses, llegué tarde_).

For the **consequence**: **por eso** and **así que** go after the cause (_no había buses, **por eso** llegué tarde_; _tenía hambre, **así que** compré un vigorón_). Direction matters: first the cause, then the result.
To **clarify** or say the same thing in other words: **es decir** (and in conversation, **o sea**): _el frijol se remoja, es decir, se deja en agua toda la noche_.
Ask yourself: what came first, the cause or the result? Cause at the start → _como_. Result at the start → _porque_. Cause and then result → _por eso_ or _así que_.
Causal **como** goes at the start. To put the cause after, use **porque**.
**Por eso** goes after the cause: first _no había mesas_.

The pause after the connector
Connectors are signals for the listener: _primero, luego, entonces, como, así que_. If you say them fast and without a pause, the story sounds like one long sentence.
After a sequence connector (_primero, luego, al final, por último_) make a **short pause** and keep the pitch **slightly up**: _Primero ↗ | se lava el arroz_. In writing, the pause is the comma.

With causal **como**, the voice rises at the end of the cause and falls at the end of the result: _Como no había gas ↗ | cocinamos con leña ↘_. With **así que** and **por eso**, the pause comes before: _no había gas | así que cocinamos con leña_.
In writing, the pause is a **comma**: after _primero, luego, al final, por último_ and after the cause with _como_ (_Como llovía, …_). A comma is also usually put before _así que_ and _por eso_.

With **si + present** you introduce a possible, real condition: something that may happen. The other part says what we do in that case, also in the **present** or with an **imperative**: _Si hace sol, subimos al cráter_. _Si tienes frío, ponte mi chaqueta_.

Si, sí and cuando

**Si** without an accent is the condition (_si quieres_). **Sí** with an accent is the yes answer or a strong statement (_—¿Vienes? —Sí_; _yo sí voy_). You can hear it: _sí_ is said with stress, _si_ is weak.
**Si** and **cuando** are not the same. With **si** you don't know if it will happen: _si llueve_ (maybe). With **cuando** you know it will happen or always happens: _cuando llego a casa, me ducho_.
For plans with several options you can chain conditions: _Si hace sol, vamos al cráter; si no, vamos a las ruinas_. **Si no** = otherwise.
Ask yourself: is it certain to happen? If it's certain or a habit, **cuando**. If it's only possible, **si**.

Asking without imposing: ¿podrías…?, ¿te importaría…?

With friends you already use _¿puedes…?_ or the imperative with _por favor_. To ask more gently, especially for a big favour or with someone you don't know well, use these fixed phrases + **infinitive**: **¿Podrías…?** (tú), **¿Podría…?** (usted), **¿Podrían…?** (ustedes).
**¿Te importaría…? / ¿Le importaría…?** + infinitive is even softer. Watch the answer: _importar_ means “to mind”, so to accept you say **No, claro que no** or **No, para nada**.
**¿Me harías / me haría el favor de…?** + infinitive is for asking a specific favour. No preposition in the other cases: _¿podrías regar…?_, never _¿podrías de regar…?_

Me gustaría, quería pedirte… and how to answer
**Me gustaría** + infinitive or noun expresses a polite wish now: _me gustaría reservar dos plazas_. It works like _gustar_: **me** gustaría, never _yo gustaría_.

The **courtesy imperfect** softens the request, although it talks about the present: _Quería pedirte un favor_, _Venía a preguntar por el tour_. It doesn't tell about the past: it's a polite way to start.

To **accept**: _Claro_, _Con mucho gusto_, _Sin problema_. To **decline** politely: **Lo siento, es que…** + a reason, and if you can, an alternative with _si_: _Lo siento, es que trabajo el sábado; si quieres, te ayudo el domingo_.
The bigger the favour, the softer the phrase: _¿puedes…?_ to pass the salt, _¿te importaría…?_ to look after your cat for a week.

_¿Te importaría?_ = would it bother you? To accept: **no**.

A polite request rises at the end
A soft request is said like a question: the voice **rises at the end** (_¿Podrías ayudarme? ↗_). If you say it falling, it sounds like an order.

**Sí** has an accent when it's an answer or a statement (_sí, yo sí_). **Si** without an accent is the condition (_si quieres_). _Podrías_ and _importaría_ have an accent on the **í** because that's the stressed vowel.

**Hay que + infinitive** is a general obligation, for everyone, without saying who: _en la finca hay que madrugar_. It never changes and never takes a person: never _yo hay que_.

**Tener que + infinitive** is the obligation of one specific person, and _tener_ is conjugated: _tengo que, tienes que, tiene que, tenemos que, tenéis que, tienen que_. Watch the **que**: _tengo **que** trabajar_.

**Deber + infinitive** says what is right or what I advise you, and it's used a lot in written rules: _debes beber agua_, _los visitantes deben llevar el carné_. With _deber_ there's no **que**: _debo salir_, never _debo que salir_.

In the negative: not necessary or not right
**No hay que** and **no tener que** mean something is **not necessary**: _no tienes que traer sábanas, aquí hay_ (you can bring them, but there's no need).
**No deber** means something is **not right**, bad advice or against a rule: _no debes tocar las plantas con fertilizante_.
And **no se puede** (from week 16) is a clear ban: _no se puede fumar en el beneficio_. Careful: _no tienes que tocar_ is not a ban; it means _it's not necessary to touch_.

When, where, how: the normal order

The information in a sentence answers three questions: **¿cuándo?** (_el lunes, a las seis, por la tarde_), **¿dónde?** (_en la finca, cerca del río_) and **¿cómo?** (_rápido, con cuidado, en grupo_).
A normal, easy order is: **verb + thing + how + where + when**: _Recogemos el café con cuidado en la parte alta por la mañana_.
**Don't separate the subject and the verb** with lots of information: _Los voluntarios desayunan en la cocina_, not _Los voluntarios en la cocina por la mañana desayunan_.

What matters first; two options with o

If the time or the place is the most important thing, put it **at the start** as a frame, with a **comma**: _El viernes, hacemos una cata_. _En la finca, no hay wifi_. That way the reader knows straight away which day or place you mean.
But **don't put everything at the start**: one or two frames are enough. _El lunes, en la finca, empezamos a las seis_ is clear; with four pieces in front, the sentence gets lost.
To offer **two options**, use **o**: _¿Prefieres café o té?_, _¿Trabajamos arriba o abajo?_ The answer is one of the options, not _sí_.

This ↗ or that ↘? The question with two options
When you offer two options with **o**, the voice **rises** on the first and **falls** at the end of the second: _¿Café ↗ o té ↘?_ That way the other person knows they have to choose.
If the voice rises at the very end (_¿Quieres café o té? ↗_), it sounds like an open question: do you want something to drink? That's why sometimes the answer is _sí_.
In a sentence with a frame at the start, make a small pause at the comma: _El lunes ↗ | empezamos a las seis_.
After a frame at the start (_El lunes, …_; _En la finca, …_) a **comma** is usually used. There's no comma between the two options with **o**: _¿café o té?_

The infinitive: after a preposition and as subject
After a **preposition** the verb is in the **infinitive**: _antes de **subir**_, _después de **comer**_, _para **llegar**_, _sin **pagar**_. Never the gerund: not _antes de subiendo_.

**Al + infinitive** means “at the moment when”: _al llegar al muelle, vimos la fila_. And when an action is the **subject** of the sentence, it's also an infinitive: _**Viajar** en ferry es barato_. English uses _-ing_ here; Spanish doesn't.

Three common verb phrases: **acabar de** + infinitive (something very recent: _acabo de comprar los boletos_), **volver a** + infinitive (again: _volvió a llover_) and **empezar a** + infinitive (the start: _empezó a hacer viento_).
Infinitive
Construction
Example
After a preposition, **infinitive**.
Action as subject: **infinitive**, not gerund.
_Acabar de_ + **infinitive**.
The gerund and the participle: what goes on and how things are

**Seguir + gerund** says something continues: _sigue lloviendo_, _seguimos esperando_. Never _sigo a esperar_. The gerund also says **how** something is done: _llegó corriendo_, _aprendí a nadar mirando a mi padre_.

**Estar + participle** describes the **state** or result: _la taquilla está **cerrada**_, _los boletos están **vendidos**_, _el barco está **lleno**_. Here the participle agrees like an adjective: masculine or feminine, singular or plural.

Compare with **haber + participle** (week 1), which never changes: _han cerrado la taquilla_ (action) → _la taquilla está cerrada_ (state). And with posture: _está sentado_ (state), not _está sentando_.
To describe the moment, think of three questions: what has just happened? (_acabar de_), what is still going on? (_seguir_ + gerund), how is everything? (_estar_ + participle).

No sé dónde, ¿sabe cuándo…?: the question inside the sentence

Sometimes the question goes **inside** another sentence: after **no sé, no recuerdo, ¿sabes / sabe…?, ¿me puedes / me puede decir…?, dime / dígame**. The question word **keeps its accent**: _no sé **dónde** está el muelle_, _¿sabe **a qué hora** sale?_

The **verb** comes after the question word, just as in the direct question: _¿Cuándo llega?_ → _No sé cuándo llega_. With a preposition, the preposition goes first: _¿me puede decir **de qué** muelle sale?_
The punctuation changes: _No sé dónde está._ has no question marks, because the sentence is a statement. _¿Sabe dónde está?_ does have them, because the whole sentence asks.
From direct to indirect question
Direct question
Inside the sentence
The question word **keeps its accent**: _dónde_.
Without an accent it means something else (_que_ = that). Question: **qué**.
No sé si…: yes/no questions

When the direct question is answered with **yes or no** (_¿Hay asientos?_), inside the sentence it's joined with **si**, without an accent: _no sé **si** hay asientos_, _¿sabe **si** el ferry lleva carros?_
Don't use _qué_ or _que_ for these questions: _no sé si viene_, not _no sé qué viene_ or _no sé que si viene_.
This **si** (= whether) isn't the condition from week 17 (_si llueve, …_) or the **sí** of an answer. To respond when you don't know, you can say: _No lo sé, pero puede preguntar en la ventanilla_.
Make the direct question in your head: if it starts with _dónde, cuándo, qué…_, use that word with its accent; if it's answered yes or no, use **si**.

How long? How many times? The preterite closes

When a period **ended** and you say **how long it lasted**, you use the **preterite**: _trabajé tres años en una emisora_, _estuve dos meses en Limón_, _viví en Cartago de 2018 a 2021_. Also with _durante_, _toda la tarde_, _de… a…_, _desde… hasta…_.
When you **count the total** number of times, also the preterite: _fui cuatro veces a Tortuguero_, _llamé tres veces y nadie contestó_.
Even if the period was long, if you measure it and it's closed, **don't** use the imperfect: _estuve tres años_, not _estaba tres años_.

A measured, finished period: **preterite**.
**De… a…** or **desde… hasta…**: don't mix them.
Habits of a period and hace + time

If you talk about what you did **often** in a period, without counting the total, you use the **imperfect**: _cada sábado iba al mercado_, _siempre ponía música latina_, _dos veces por semana hacíamos entrevistas_.
Compare: _iba a la radio todos los domingos_ (habit) and _fui a la radio tres domingos_ (counted total).

**Hace + time** says how much time has passed from a moment until today (= _ago_), with the verb in the past: _volví a San José hace dos meses_, _hace cinco años vivía en Limón_. **Hace** goes before the time: _hace dos días_, never _dos días hace_. And don't mix it with _desde hace_, which is for something still going on (week 5).
Ask yourself: am I counting or measuring it (how many times, how long)? → preterite. Was it the normal thing in that period? → imperfect.

Telling it well and then asking: the end of A2

For a **story**: the **scene** and causes in the **imperfect** (_llovía, había tráfico, no tenía batería_), the **events** in the **preterite** (_salí, perdí el bus, llegué_), and **today** with the **present perfect** where that's usual (_hoy he hablado con Rebeca_; in much of Latin America people also say _hoy hablé_). _Ayer_ always goes with the preterite: _ayer llegué_, not _ayer he llegado_. Join everything with connectors: _primero, de repente, como, por eso, así que, al final_.

For a **practical message**: ask with _¿puedes / podrías + infinitive?_ (_¿podrías enviarme el guion?_), give instructions with the imperative and attached pronouns (_envíamelas, llámame, dáselas a Rebeca_) or pronouns before the conjugated verb (_te las envío_). Thank with **gracias por** (_gracias por tu ayuda_) and set a deadline with **para** (_para el viernes_).

Mistakes to avoid at the end of A2: _era mucho tráfico_ (→ _había_), _solía a ir_ (→ _solía ir_), _¿puedes me enviar?_ (→ _¿me puedes enviar?_ or _¿puedes enviarme?_), _gracias para_ (→ _gracias por_), _le las doy_ (→ _se las doy_).

Trabajo, trabajó, trabajé: the stress changes the tense

In the regular preterite, the stress falls on the **last syllable** for _yo_ and _él / ella / usted_: _traba**JÉ**_, _traba**JÓ**_. In the present, it falls earlier: _tra**BA**jo_. If you don't mark the stress, you say a different tense or person.
In the imperfect the stress is on the **-aba / -ía** syllable: _traba**JA**ba_, _le**Í**a_. Comparing _hablaba_ and _habló_ helps you hear whether it's a habit or an event.
In strong irregulars (_estuve, fui, hice_) there's no accent and the stress is on the second-to-last syllable: _es**TU**ve_, _**HI**ce_.

The regular preterite has an accent for _yo_ and _él_: **trabajé, trabajó, leí, leyó**. Strong irregulars don't: **estuve, hice, fui, dijo**. If you attach pronouns to the infinitive and the stress ends up far back, add an accent: **enviármelas**.

Personal email
Tomás writes to his sister Lucía, who lives in Guadalajara, after his first month as a volunteer presenter.

Dear Lucía: sorry for not writing sooner, but this month has been amazing and very intense. As you know, I came back to San José three months ago, after a year and a half in Toronto. I spent several weeks looking for work in radio and in the end Radio Barrio called me, a community station in the Amón neighbourhood. I've been presenting the Saturday programme for a month now.

At the station there are clear rules. You have to arrive an hour early, you can't eat in the studio and the microphones are always switched off at the end. Rebeca, the coordinator, says we shouldn't talk for more than three minutes without playing music. At first I thought it was over the top, but she's right: the audience gets bored quickly.

Let me tell you about my worst day. It was the second Saturday. It was pouring with rain, the traffic was terrible and, to make everything worse, my phone had no battery. I left home at six, but the bus was stopped for twenty minutes because there was a crash on Second Avenue. So I got off and ran in the rain. I got to the studio at ten past seven, soaked. As the programme started at seven, Rebeca put on music and began the interview with our guest, a lady who has been selling flowers at the market for forty years. In the end everything went well, and the guest told me that in her forty years at the market she had never seen such a wet presenter.

Now I leave home at half past five, just in case. Saturdays are long, but I love them. During the week I go to the studio twice to prepare the script, and from time to time I record interviews in the street.

I've also learned a lot. Before, in Limón, I prepared the scripts on my own; here you have to work as a team and decisions are made by everyone. If a guest cancels, it's no problem: we always have a list of songs ready. Last week I interviewed a musician who played for thirty years in the national orchestra. He told me that as a young man he rehearsed six hours a day and that he went on tour in Europe twice.

I'm asking you two favours. Could you send me the photos from Andrés's wedding? I need them for a programme about weddings, so send them to me by Thursday, if you can. And if you talk to Mum, tell her I'm fine; I don't know if she got my last message. Thanks for everything, little sister. A big hug, Tomás.

Three past tenses, three different jobs

When you tell a story, each tense answers a different question. The **imperfect** answers “what was everything like?” and “what did you usually do?”: it describes the place, the weather, the people and habits. The **preterite** answers “what happened?”: it presents finished events, one after another, that move the story forward.

The **present perfect** answers “what balance do you draw today?”. It looks at the past from the present, with time frames that reach up to now: _hoy, esta semana, este año, ya, todavía no, nunca_. If the time frame is closed (_ayer, el lunes, en 2022, el mes pasado_), most of Spain and almost all of Latin America use the preterite.

A trick to check your text: cover the verbs in the imperfect. If the story still makes sense but has no backdrop, you chose well. If the important events disappear, one of those verbs should have been in the preterite.

In some areas (for example, parts of Bolivia, Peru or north-western Argentina) and in spoken Spanish in Spain you will hear more present perfect. For writing, the closed-or-open time frame rule is the safest.

Pluperfect: how it is formed

The pluperfect is formed with **haber in the imperfect** + **past participle**. The participle never changes: it does not agree with the subject or the object. Nothing goes between _había_ and the participle: not _ya_, not _no_, not pronouns. Those words go before it: _ya lo había visto_.

Regular participles end in **-ado** (-ar) or **-ido** (-er, -ir). Review the usual irregular ones, because they come up a lot with this tense: _hecho, dicho, visto, puesto, escrito, abierto, vuelto, roto, muerto, resuelto_.

Pluperfect: three uses in a story

**1. Before another past moment.** First you fix a moment with the preterite and then you look back: _Cuando abrí la puerta, mi compañera ya había hecho la cena_. With **ya** you confirm that the earlier thing happened; with **todavía no**, that it had not happened yet.

**2. An earlier cause.** You explain a past state or event with something that happened before: _Estaba agotado porque había dormido en el suelo_. It is very useful for apologising or justifying yourself.

**3. A discovery.** The moment you find out goes in the preterite (_vi, me di cuenta de, supe, descubrí, me enteré de_) and what you discover, which had happened earlier, goes in the pluperfect: _Me di cuenta de que había dejado la cartera en la furgoneta_.
If everything in your story is in the pluperfect, nobody knows what the reference moment is. Use it only to look back from an event in the preterite.

The stress that separates present and past: compro / compró

Many regular verbs have a present form (yo) and a preterite form (él, ella, usted) that are only told apart by the stressed syllable: **compro** (COM-pro) is present; **compró** (com-PRÓ) is past. If you move the stress, you change the tense and the person.

Also review **había**: it has three syllables, _ha-BÍ-a_, because the _i_ with an accent separates from the _a_. Don't say _ha-bia_ in two syllables. In spoken stories, _había_ joins the participle with no pause: _ha-bí-a-sa-li-do_.

A fact or not yet: the idea of the subjunctive

The **indicative** presents information as a fact: something that is, that happens or that you know. The **subjunctive** presents an action that is **not a fact** yet: something you wish for, ask for or aim at for another person.

Compare: _Sé que abres el sábado_ (I know it: it is a fact, indicative) and _Espero que abras el sábado_ (I hope so: it is not certain, subjunctive). The action is the same; what changes is how you look at it.

That is why the subjunctive almost always comes after a verb of wishing, requesting or purpose, and almost always after **que**. With **para que** you express the goal for another person: _Te dejo la llave para que abras tú_.
I know the premises are on 57th Street.
Information presented as a fact: indicative.
I want the premises to be ready on Friday.
A wish about something that is not real yet: subjunctive.
I put on soft music so that people stay.
Goal for other people: _para que_ + subjunctive.
_Para que_ always takes the **subjunctive**.
Regular forms: the vowel switches teams

Start from the **yo** form of the present indicative, drop the **-o** and switch the vowel: **-ar** verbs change to **e**; **-er** and **-ir** verbs change to **a**. It is as if each group used the other group's vowel.
The **yo** form and the **él, ella, usted** form are the same: _que yo hable, que ella hable_. The context tells you who it is.
If you already know the negative imperative (_no hables, no comas_), you already know the tú subjunctive: they are the same forms.

Irregular verbs: the yo stem and the six special ones
Many irregular verbs **keep the yo irregularity** in all persons: _tengo_ → _tenga, tengas, tengamos_; _hago_ → _haga_; _conozco_ → _conozca_; _salgo_ → _salga_; _digo_ → _diga_; _pongo_ → _ponga_.

Stem-changing verbs (**e → ie**, **o → ue**) change in every person except nosotros and vosotros: _quiera, quieras… queramos_; _pueda… podamos_. -ir verbs like **pedir** also close the vowel in nosotros: _pida, pidamos_; **dormir** gives _duerma, durmamos_.

Six verbs don't follow the yo rule and have to be memorised: **ser** (sea), **estar** (esté), **ir** (vaya), **haber** (haya), **saber** (sepa) and **dar** (dé). And watch the spelling: _buscar_ → _busque_, _llegar_ → _llegue_, _empezar_ → _empiece_.

Querer, esperar, desear: one person or two?

Look at who wishes and who does the action. If it is **the same person**, use the **infinitive**: _Quiero abrir a las diez_ (I want, I open). If it is **another person**, use **que + subjunctive**: _Quiero que abras tú_ (I want, you open).
**Esperar** works the same way: _Espero llegar a tiempo_ / _Espero que llegues a tiempo_. **Desear** is more formal or more intense: it appears in cards, speeches and written messages.
After **espero que** you don't use the future: _Espero que te guste_, not _espero que te gustará_.

Different subject: que + subjunctive

Ojalá and ¡que…!: short wishes

**Ojalá** is not a verb: it doesn't change and it always takes the **subjunctive**, even when the wish is for yourself: _Ojalá aprenda rápido_. You can say _ojalá_ or _ojalá que_. On its own it works as an answer: _—¿Vendrá mucha gente? —¡Ojalá!_

To say goodbye or congratulate someone, Spanish uses short phrases with **¡Que + subjunctive!**: they are the second half of _espero que…_ or _deseo que…_. The most frequent: _¡Que te vaya bien!, ¡Que tengas suerte!, ¡Que lo pases bien!, ¡Que te mejores!, ¡Que disfrutes!_
_Ojalá_ comes from Andalusian Arabic and meant something like “God willing”. Today believers and non-believers use it alike.

A wish about a thing: _ojalá que_ + subjunctive.

The final vowel that changes the mood: habla / hable

In the subjunctive, a single vowel often decides the meaning: _Sé que Camila **habla** con los vecinos_ (a fact) and _Quiero que Camila **hable** con los vecinos_ (a wish). If you don't pronounce the last vowel clearly, your listener won't know what you mean.

Spanish vowels are short and tense: don't lengthen them or turn them into a neutral sound at the end of the word. Say **-e** with your mouth slightly open and your lips spread; **-a**, with your mouth wide open.
Also be careful with **esté** (es-TÉ, subjunctive of estar) and **este** (ES-te, demonstrative). The accent marks the stress and changes the word.
Some verbs change a letter to keep the sound: _buscar_ → **busque**, _llegar_ → **llegue**, _empezar_ → **empiece**, _coger_ → **coja**.

News item from a neighbourhood newsletter
Text published in «Chapinero al día», the digital newsletter the neighbourhood's residents receive.

Next Saturday La Taza de Papel opens its doors on 57th Street: a bookshop with a café that Camila Rojas, a 34-year-old engineer, has spent almost two years preparing. «I want people to come and read without hurrying and for nobody to tell them they have to order something to stay», she explains while placing novels on a shelf made of recycled wood.

The premises used to be an old stationery shop. Camila kept the original counter and decorated the walls with old photos of the neighbourhood lent to her by the neighbours. «I don't expect to get rich», she says, laughing. «I hope the business will be sustainable and that we can run writing workshops for children on Saturday mornings.»

The neighbours have already left their messages in a notebook by the door. Don Hernando, who has been selling fruit on the corner for thirty years, wrote: «I hope it goes very well for you and I hope you sell lots of books, but don't put up the price of the coffee». A student signed with a drawing and a sentence: «May the wifi never fail». And the owner of the bakery opposite left a practical note: «If you'd like me to bring you fresh bread in the mornings, let me know».
The opening will be at ten, with live music and a table of second-hand books. Camila asks visitors for just one thing: that each of them bring a book to swap.

In your last three classes you used the subjunctive to advise, to judge and to react with emotions. Advising and recommending: who, to whom and what

The formula has three pieces: **who advises** (the main verb), **to whom** (the pronoun _me, te, le, nos, os, les_) and **what that person has to do** (_que_ + subjunctive): _Te aconsejo que riegues por la mañana_.

With **recomendar, aconsejar** and **sugerir** you can also use the infinitive, because the person who receives the advice is the one who acts on it: _Te aconsejo regar por la mañana_. Without a pronoun, the infinitive gives general advice: _Recomiendo usar compost_. Never put _de_ in front: not _te aconsejo de regar_.

Be careful with **decir que**: if it passes on information, it takes the indicative (_Amparo dice que el agua está cortada_); if it passes on an order or advice, it takes the subjunctive (_Amparo dice que cerremos la puerta_). And to ask for something you use **pedir**, not _preguntar_: _Le pido que me preste la azada_.

Judging or stating: not the same thing

When you **judge** someone's action, you use an evaluative expression + **que + subjunctive**: _es importante, es necesario, es mejor, es normal, es una pena, es una buena idea, me parece bien_. The subjunctive is used even if the action is real: _Es una pena que Pilar deje el huerto_ (she really is leaving, but you are judging it).

If you are not talking about anyone in particular but about something that applies to everyone, use the same expression + **infinitive**, without _que_ and without _de_: _Es importante regar al atardecer_.

Expressions that **state** that something is true do not judge: _es verdad, es cierto, es evidente, está claro, es obvio_ + **que + indicative**. _Está claro que este año llueve poco._ But in the negative they change: _No es verdad que llueva poco_ (you will look at this in detail next week).

Emotions and reactions: me alegra que, me molesta que

Emotion verbs work like **gustar**: the person who feels is _me, te, le, nos, os, les_, and what causes the emotion is the clause with _que_ + **subjunctive**: _Me alegra que vengas al huerto_. The emotion verb stays **singular** even if a plural follows: _Me molesta que los perros entren en las parcelas_.
If the person who feels and the person who acts are the **same person**, use the infinitive: _Me alegra verte aquí_ (not _me alegra que yo te vea_).

Other forms: **estar contento / harto / cansado de que**, **alegrarse de que**, **tener miedo de que**, **sentir que** (to express regret). And in conversation, the quickest reaction: **¡Qué bien / qué pena / qué raro / qué suerte que** + subjunctive!
_Siento que_ + subjunctive expresses regret (_Siento que te vayas_); _siento que_ + indicative is a perception (_Siento que algo no va bien_).

Soft g and strong sound in the subjunctive: riegue, recoja

When forming the subjunctive, some verbs change a letter to **keep their sound**. _Regar_ has a soft _g_ (as in _gato_): to keep it before _e_ you write **gu**: _riegue_. _Recoger_ has a strong sound (like the _j_ in _jardín_): before _a_ you write **j**: _recoja_.

First listen to whether the sound is soft, with the back of the tongue relaxed, or strong, with air rubbing the throat. Then repeat. Remember that the voice is synthetic and helps you perceive the sound; it is not a regional model.
Quick rule: **g + e/i** sounds strong (_recoge_), so for a soft _g_ before _e_ you write **gue** (_riegue_); and for the strong sound before _a_ you write **ja** (_recoja_).

Stating your opinion: indicative

With **creo que, pienso que, opino que, me parece que** and **estoy seguro de que** you present your opinion as true. That is why the verb that follows is in the **indicative**, in whatever tense you need: _Creo que el equipo **rinde** más los lunes_; _Pienso que **fue** una buena decisión_; _Me parece que **va a funcionar**_.

Don't confuse **me parece que** (opinion, indicative) with **me parece bien que** (judgement, subjunctive, as you saw last week): _Me parece que Luisa **tiene** razón_ / _Me parece bien que Luisa **tenga** el viernes libre_.
With **estar seguro** don't forget the **de**: _Estoy segura de que podemos hacerlo_.
I think the clients aren't going to notice the difference.
Stated opinion: indicative.
In my opinion we should try it for three months.
_Opinar que_ + indicative (here, conditional).
I'm sure there's a solution.
_Estar seguro de que_ + indicative.
_Creo que_ states: **indicative**.
_Pensar que_ doesn't take _de_.
Denying your opinion: subjunctive

When you **deny** the opinion verb, you are not stating what comes after: you are questioning or rejecting it. That is why it is in the **subjunctive**: _No creo que el equipo **rinda** más_; _No pienso que **sea** tan fácil_; _No estoy segura de que los clientes lo **acepten**_.
It also works when you are the one acting: _No creo que **pueda** terminar el informe hoy_.
Compare the two sentences. Stating: _Creo que **llegan** a tiempo_. Denying: _No creo que **lleguen** a tiempo_. Only the _no_ changes… and the mood.

I state: indicative
I deny: subjunctive
Denied opinion: **subjunctive**.
Asking, seeking agreement and correcting

In a normal question, **¿crees que…?** takes the **indicative**: _¿Crees que es buena idea?_ And with **¿no crees que…?** you aren't denying anything either: you want the other person to agree with you, so it also takes the **indicative**: _¿No crees que trabajamos demasiado?_

To **correct** what someone else has understood, use **no es que + subjunctive** (you reject that interpretation) and then **es que + indicative** (you give the real reason): _No es que no **quiera** el viernes libre, es que **tengo** miedo de perder clientes_.
Do you think the bosses are going to accept it?

Don't you think it's worth trying?
You are seeking agreement: indicative.
It's not that I'm against it, it's that I need more data.

Certainty and possibility: seguro que, a lo mejor, puede que
For **certainty** use the indicative: **seguro que, está claro que, es evidente que, estoy convencido de que**. _Seguro que_ also works for a strong assumption: _Seguro que Valeria ya lo sabe_.
**A lo mejor** means “maybe”, but it has a fixed rule: it always takes the **indicative**: _A lo mejor probamos en enero_.

For **possibility** and **doubt** use the subjunctive: **es posible que, es probable que, puede que, dudo que, no es seguro que**: _Puede que el piloto empiece en febrero_; _Dudo que todos estén de acuerdo_.

With **quizás, quizá, tal vez, probablemente** before the verb, both options are correct: _Quizás funciona_ / _Quizás funcione_ (the subjunctive sounds a bit more doubtful). If the adverb comes after the verb, only the indicative: _Funciona, quizás, mejor en verano_.
_Dudo que_ + subjunctive, but _no dudo de que_ + indicative: if you have no doubt, you are sure.

In Spanish, a yes/no question can have exactly the same words as a statement: _Crees que funciona._ / _¿Crees que funciona?_ The only thing that changes is the **final melody**: in a statement the voice falls at the end; in a question, it rises.

With **¿no crees que…?** the voice also rises, but it usually starts higher: it is an invitation to agree. With **no es que…, es que…** there are two parts: the first is left hanging and the second falls firmly.
Listen and decide; then repeat, slightly exaggerating the rise or fall. The voice is synthetic: use it to perceive the difference, not as a regional model.
In writing, Spanish opens and closes questions: **¿…?**. If the question starts in the middle of the sentence, the opening mark goes where the question begins: _Si te parece bien, ¿lo probamos?_

Opinion column
Column published in the online magazine of an association of small businesses in Antioquia.

More and more companies are talking about the four-day working week. Some have already tried it in Europe and Latin America, and the first results look positive: less stress, fewer sick days and, in many cases, the same productivity. But is it an idea for everyone? Honestly, I don't think there is a single answer.

I'm convinced that rest improves creative work. An exhausted designer doesn't have good ideas, and anyone who has ever spent a Friday afternoon staring at a blank screen knows that. I also think a day off helps people balance work and life, especially those who look after children or elderly people.

However, I don't think the model works the same way in a restaurant, a hospital or a shop that opens six days a week. Those sectors may need to hire more people, and I doubt all small businesses can take on that cost. Maybe the solution isn't a fixed day off, but more flexible hours.

Fad or future? Perhaps both. What is clear is that the conversation has already begun. My advice to business owners: it's not that you have to change everything tomorrow, it's that it's worth running a serious trial before saying no.

Just one question: who does the second action?

Many verbs you already know (_querer, preferir, necesitar, esperar, desear_), emotions (_me alegra, me molesta, me da miedo_) and judgements (_es importante, es mejor_) follow the same rule. If the second action is done by **the same person**, use the **infinitive**. If it is done by **another person**, use **que + subjunctive**.
_Prefiero subir temprano_ (I prefer, I go up). _Prefiero que subas temprano_ (I prefer, you go up). _Me alegra estar aquí_ (I'm glad, I'm here). _Me alegra que estés aquí_ (I'm glad, you're here).
With judgements, the infinitive is a general rule and _que_ + subjunctive points to someone specific: _Es importante beber agua en la altura_ / _Es importante que Hannah beba agua_.
Same person or another
Type of verb
Same person: infinitive
Another person: que + subjunctive
The same person wants and gets to know: **infinitive**.

Permitir, prohibir, dejar: two correct forms

With **permitir, prohibir, dejar, aconsejar, recomendar** and **obligar a**, the person who receives the permission or prohibition appears in the pronoun (_me, te, le, nos, les_). That is why you can use the infinitive even though there are two people: _Rocío le prohíbe salir_ = _Rocío le prohíbe que salga_.
Don't put **de** before the infinitive: _te prohíbo salir_, not _te prohíbo de salir_. With **obligar** you do need **a**: _El guía nos obliga a llevar casco_.

The imperative: only one form of its own

Only the **affirmative tú** order (and the vosotros one) has its own form: _espera, sube, ven, di, haz, pon, sal, ten, ve, sé_. **All the others** are the present subjunctive you already reviewed in week 2: negative tú (_no subas_), usted (_suba, no suba_), ustedes (_suban, no suban_) and nosotros (_subamos_).

Pronouns go **after and attached** in affirmative orders (_siéntese, dímelo, tráiganlas_) and **before** in negative ones (_no se siente, no me lo digas, no las traigan_). When you attach pronouns, many forms need a written accent to keep their stress: _di_ → _dímelo_.

Passing on an order: dile que venga

When an order **passes through another person**, the imperative becomes **que + subjunctive**: _«Ven a las siete»_ → _Dile que venga a las siete_; _Patricio dice que vengas a las siete_; _Te pide que vengas a las siete_.
When you pass on the order, **the person of the verb** and **the pronouns** change: Patricio says to Hannah _«Mándame el documento»_ and Rocío passes it on like this: _Dice que se lo mandes_.

In conversation, **que** at the beginning is enough: _Que pase_ (an order for someone who isn't talking to you), _—¿Qué dice? —Que subas_ (repeating an order). Remember: **decir que** + indicative passes on information (_dice que hace frío_); **decir que** + subjunctive passes on an order (_dice que te abrigues_).

Stress in the imperative with pronouns: siéntese, dímelo

When you attach pronouns to an affirmative order, the word grows, but **the stressed syllable doesn't move**: _siente_ → **sién**-te-se; _di_ → **dí**-me-lo; _explica_ → ex-**plí**-ca-me-lo. That's why many of these forms have a written accent.

In negative orders the pronouns go before and each word keeps its own stress: _no se **sien**-te_, _no me lo **di**-gas_. Listen to the difference between the affirmative order with an attached pronoun and the negative one with separate pronouns.
The voice is synthetic: use it to perceive where the stress falls, not as a regional model.

Practical rule: if, after attaching pronouns, the stress falls on the third-to-last syllable or earlier, the word takes an accent: _explica_ → _explícamelo_; _pon_ → _ponlo_ (no accent, it is still stressed on the second-to-last syllable).

“Haya + past participle”: the form

The perfect subjunctive is built just like the present perfect indicative, but with the auxiliary “haber” in the present subjunctive: haya, hayas, haya, hayamos, hayáis, hayan. The past participle comes after it and never changes, neither in gender nor in number.

The irregular participles are the usual ones: hecho, dicho, visto, puesto, escrito, vuelto, abierto, roto. Nothing goes between “haya” and the participle: “que ya haya terminado”, “que no lo haya visto”.
If you can say “han vendido”, you can already say “hayan vendido”: only the auxiliary changes.

Looking back from now: reaction, doubt and possibility

You use “haya + past participle” when the main verb calls for the subjunctive (an emotion, an evaluation, a doubt or a possibility) and the action you are talking about has already happened, or may have happened, before this moment. The reaction is now; the event came earlier.

Compare three sentences. “Han vendido todas las entradas” states a fact. “Qué bien que hayan vendido todas las entradas” reacts to that fact which has already happened. “Ojalá vendan todas las entradas” looks towards a future action: that is why it uses the present subjunctive.

“Cuando” with the future: subjunctive; with habits or the past: indicative

After “cuando”, the verb goes in the subjunctive if the action has not happened yet. The other part of the sentence can be in the future, the present, with “ir a” or in the imperative, but what follows “cuando” never goes in the future.

If you talk about a habit or something that already happened, you use the indicative: “cuando termina la función, cenamos todos juntos” (always), “cuando terminó la función, cenamos” (yesterday). In questions, “¿cuándo…?” does allow the future: “¿cuándo estrenarán?”.
Ask yourself: has this already happened, or does it always happen? If the answer is “not yet”, put the subjunctive after “cuando”.

After “cuando” you never use the future tense, even if the action is in the future.

These connectors work like “cuando”: with a future action they take the subjunctive and with a habit or a past event they take the indicative. “En cuanto” means something happens right after; “hasta que”, the end of an action; “mientras”, two actions at the same time.

“Antes de que” always takes the subjunctive, even in the past. If both parts of the sentence have the same subject, you use the infinitive: “antes de salir a escena, respiro hondo”, not “antes de que yo salga”.

Silent h: “que ha” and “que haya” are linked, but they don’t sound the same

The “h” is not pronounced in Spanish. That is why “que ha” and “que haya” are said linked, with no pause between the words: [ke‿a], [ke‿á.ʝa]. What lets you tell them apart is the final syllable: “haya” has two syllables and the second starts with the “y” sound.

The same happens with “han” and “hayan”: “sé que han llegado” versus “dudo que hayan llegado”. When you speak, don’t break the sentence between “que” and the auxiliary; say it like one long word and keep the stress on “ha” in “haya”.
Remember that “haya” (from “haber”) is spelt with h and y; don’t confuse it with “halla” (from “hallar”, to find) or with “allá” (place).

Dear friends of Telón Sur: there are three days to go until the opening of “La casa de los relojes” and we want to tell you how we got here. It has been a long week, but we are delighted that the play has grown so much in so little time. On Monday we still didn’t have the set; today there is a four-metre wooden staircase in the middle of the stage.

Not everything went perfectly, of course. We are sorry that Clara, our violinist, has injured her hand and can’t play live. We recorded her music on Tuesday and, although we don’t think it sounds the same, the audience may not even have imagined it. We are also surprised that so many people have written to ask about extra performances: thank you for your patience.

What will happen now? When we finish painting the staircase, we will do the last rehearsal with an invited audience. As soon as we have the date of the second season, we will publish it here and on social media. And until sales open, please don’t buy tickets on other websites: we only sell at the theatre’s box office.
One last request: on Saturday, before the curtain goes up, switch off your phones. After the show, stay for a while; the actors will come out to chat with you while we take down the stage.

“Para” + infinitive or “para que” + subjunctive

Purpose answers the question “what for?”. If the person doing the main action is the same as the one achieving the goal, you use “para” + infinitive: “Ahorramos para comprar muebles” (we save, we buy).

If the goal is achieved by someone else, you need “para que” + subjunctive: “Ahorramos para que nuestros hijos tengan un cuarto cada uno”. With the main verb in the present, future or imperative, the subjunctive goes in the present. The negation goes before the verb: “para no perder”, “para que no se pierdan”.
Test it: who does the second action? If it is the same person, delete “que” and use the infinitive.

Subjects
Structure
Example
The subject is the same (“I” look, “I” pay): infinitive.
“Para que” is always followed by the subjunctive.
Asking “¿para qué?”, moving “a” and speaking formally
The question “¿para qué…?” takes the indicative, also in indirect questions: “¿Para qué necesitan la garantía?”, “No entiendo para qué sirve este papel”. The answer can take “para que” + subjunctive.

With verbs of movement (ir, venir, salir, bajar, subir, entrar), purpose usually goes with “a” + infinitive: “Vengo a firmar el contrato”, “Bajo a abrir la puerta”. In letters, notices and official documents you find “a fin de (que)”, “con el fin de (que)” and “con el objetivo de”, with the same rules as “para (que)”.

“Que” identifies; “, quien…,” adds a detail

“Que” joins a noun (the antecedent) with the information that identifies it: “la vecina que tiene perro”, “el barrio que nos gustó”, “la escuela que está junto al parque”. Without that information, we wouldn’t know which one you mean, and no commas are used.

If the person is already identified, for example by their name, the detail is only added, like a bracket, between commas. There you can use “que” or “quien” (more formal): “Gonzalo, quien trabaja en la inmobiliaria, nos ayudó mucho”. “Quien” never goes without commas after a noun for a person: you don’t say “la señora quien vive arriba”.

Known or sought antecedent: indicative or subjunctive

When you talk about something that exists and that you know, the relative clause goes in the indicative: “Conozco una escuela que tiene comedor”. When you describe something you are looking for, need or ask for and you don’t yet know if it exists or which one it is, the relative clause goes in the subjunctive: “Buscamos una escuela que tenga comedor”.

The same happens with negation and questions: “No hay ningún apartamento que acepte mascotas”, “¿Conoces a alguien que arregle persianas?”. Look at the article: “el / la” usually points to something known; “un / una / alguien” usually goes with what is being looked for.
Ask yourself: can I point to it? If you can, indicative; if you are still looking for it, subjunctive.

The commas of a relative clause that adds a detail can be heard: before “que” or “quien” there is a short pause, the voice drops slightly during the detail and rises again at the end, as in a bracket. “Aunque” + indicative: I accept the obstacle and carry on

With “aunque” + indicative you present an obstacle as a real fact and say that it doesn’t prevent the main idea: “Aunque tengo poco tiempo, entreno cuatro días”. It can go first, with a comma, or after, as a final reservation: “Me encanta correr, aunque me cuesta madrugar”. It also works in the past: “Aunque llovía, salimos a correr”.

The obstacle goes with “aunque”; the result can go with “pero”, “sin embargo” (more formal, after a full stop or semicolon) or “aun así”. Don’t combine “aunque” and “pero” in the same sentence. “A pesar de” takes a noun or an infinitive (same subject), and “a pesar de que”, the indicative.
This week you use “aunque” with the indicative because the obstacle is a fact you know. If you don’t know whether it is true, later on you will see that the subjunctive can be used.
One obstacle, five ways to say it
Structure
Example
“Aunque” already introduces the contrast; “pero” is not needed.
As with “aunque”, you don’t add “pero”.
“Si” + present: possible conditions

In a real or possible condition, “si” is always followed by the present indicative. What changes is the result, depending on your intention: a general truth or a habit (present), a prediction or a promise (future or “ir a”), an instruction (imperative), a permission or an obligation (“poder”, “tener que”).

Never use the future or the present subjunctive after this “si”. Also distinguish “si” from “cuando”: “si llueve” leaves the possibility open; “cuando llueva” takes for granted that it will rain (and takes the subjunctive, as you saw in week 6). When “si” means “whether” (“no sé si…”), it does allow the future: “No sé si llegaré a la meta”.

The conditional: an easy form and twelve irregulars

The conditional is formed with the whole infinitive plus the endings -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían, the same for all three verb groups. Irregular verbs have the same stem as in the future: tendr-, saldr-, podr-, pondr-, vendr-, sabr-, querr-, habr-, dir-, har-, cabr-, valdr-.

“Correría” or “corría”: the “r” that separates the conditional from the imperfect

In -er and -ir verbs, the conditional and the imperfect are very similar: “corría / correría”, “salía / saldría”, “tenía / tendría”. The difference lies in the “-rí-” syllable of the conditional, which keeps the “r” of the infinitive or the irregular stem. Listen for that syllable before the final “-ía”.

In both forms the “í” is stressed and forms a hiatus with the “a”: co-rre-RÍ-a, co-RRÍ-a. Don’t turn it into a diphthong (“correrya”); pronounce two clear syllables at the end. In “-ríamos” the stress stays on the “í”: co-rre-RÍ-a-mos.
All conditional forms have an accent on the “í” because it breaks the diphthong: entrenaría, tendríamos, saldrían.

Your first half: a guide to not giving up
A running club’s guide
The Corredores de la Malagueta club hands out this guide to people who are going to run their first half marathon.

Running 21 kilometres seems crazy when you start. However, every year hundreds of beginners cross the finish line on the Paseo del Parque, and most of them are not athletes. Although you don’t have to suffer to improve, you do need consistency: if you go running four times a week for three months, your body will adapt.

The most frequent doubts have simple answers. If something hurts for more than two days, stop running and see a physiotherapist. If it’s very hot, train early or at sunset. If one day you feel you have no energy, you can walk for a while: walking is not failing. And if you get bored of always running alone, join our Wednesday evening runs, which start by the lighthouse.

And our advice for the big day? If we were you, we would have a light dinner the night before and arrive at the start forty minutes early. We wouldn’t change anything either: not breakfast, not clothes, not trainers. Many runners tell us afterwards that, in a second race, they would go more slowly at the beginning.
Finally, a request: could you let us know if you drop out of the plan? Although we completely understand, we would like to know so we can give your place to someone else.

Condition, agreed plan or rule

You already know that “si” is followed by the present. In real situations, the result tells you what kind of sentence it is. With the future, you make a prediction or take a decision now: “Si el río está alto, tomaremos otra lancha”. With the present, you present a plan already agreed: “Si llueve, salimos a las diez” (the group has already decided it).

When both parts are in the present and the situation repeats, it is a rule or a habit: “Si encuentras un nido, avisas al guardaparques”. For plan B, use “si no” (with no pause between “si” and “no”) or “en ese caso”: “Si el autobús llega a tiempo, comemos en Cariari; si no, comemos en la lancha”.

Advising without giving orders: “yo + conditional”

A very natural way of giving advice is to say what you would do: “Yo llevaría botas de goma”, “Yo no dejaría la mochila en la playa”. The other person decides; you only suggest. It sounds softer than the imperative (“Lleva botas”) and less direct than “tienes que”.

You can combine it with a real condition to make a friendly suggestion: “Si tienes tiempo, podrías ayudarnos con los nidos”, “Si vas al mercado, yo compraría frutas para el viaje”. For a compulsory rule, on the other hand, use the present, “tener que” or the imperative.
Ask yourself: who decides? If the other person decides, advise with “yo + conditional”; if it is a rule, use the present or the imperative.

“Por” looks back or along the way

“Por” expresses the cause, what lies behind an action: “Cerraron la playa por la tormenta”, “Gracias por venir”, “Lo hago por las tortugas”. Also the route or the place you go through (“Fuimos por la Ruta 32”, “Paseamos por el pueblo”) and an approximate time (“por la mañana”, “por diciembre”).

In addition, “por” marks the means (“Te aviso por mensaje”), the exchange and the price (“Pagamos quince mil colones por la excursión”, “Cambié mis botas por unas sandalias”) and the amount per unit (“dos litros de agua por persona”).

“Para” looks ahead

“Para” points to the goal (“Vinimos para cuidar los nidos”, “para que las crías lleguen al mar”, as you saw in week 7), the recipient (“Este informe es para la bióloga”), the destination of a movement (“Salimos para Limón a las seis”) and the deadline or time limit (“Necesito la lista para el viernes”).

It is also used to give an opinion (“Para mí, es el mejor viaje”) and to compare with what is expected (“Para ser julio, llueve poco”). A trick: if you can ask “¿para qué?”, “¿para quién?” or “¿para cuándo?”, the answer usually has “para”.

“Por”, “para” and “pa’”: little prepositions in fast speech

“Por” and “para” are unstressed words: they have no stress and they stick to the next word (“porla mañana”, “parael lunes”). That is why they are easy to miss. Pay attention to the vowel: “por” has a single syllable with “o”; “para” has two syllables with “a”.

In the informal speech of many countries, Costa Rica included, “para” is reduced to “pa’”: “pa’ la playa”, “pa’ que veas”. It is normal in a conversation between friends, but it is not written that way in a formal text. When you speak, pronounce “para” in full and mark the soft final r of “por”.
The form “pa’” is spoken. In texts always write “para”, and remember that “si no” (condition) is written as two words and “sino” (but rather) as one.

Empezar a, ponerse a, echarse a: three ways of starting

“Empezar a” (or “comenzar a”, more formal) + infinitive marks the start of an action, a state or a process, with no further nuance: “Empecé a trabajar en la librería en marzo”, “Empieza a hacer frío”. “Ponerse a” + infinitive shows that someone decides to start, or suddenly starts, an activity: “Llegué a casa y me puse a escribir”. It is not used with states: we don’t say “se puso a saber”.

“Echarse a” is used almost only with reír, llorar, correr and temblar, for a sudden, uncontrolled start: “Cuando vio el cartel, se echó a llorar”. And if the action hasn’t started yet but is about to, you say “estar a punto de” + infinitive. Pronouns go before the conjugated verb or attached to the infinitive, never in between: “me puse a ordenarlos” or “los empecé a ordenar”.

With “empezar”, “ponerse” and “echarse” the preposition “a” is compulsory.

Seguir + gerund and soler + infinitive

“Seguir” (or “continuar”) + gerund says that an action that started before has not been interrupted: “Sigo dando clases por las mañanas”. The opposite, that something you expected still hasn’t started, is said with “seguir sin” + infinitive: “Seguimos sin tener calefacción”. Careful: “seguir” changes “e” to “i” (sigo, sigues, siguió) and never goes with an infinitive: you don’t say “sigo trabajar”.

“Soler” + infinitive talks about what you normally do: “Suelo abrir a las cuatro”. It is only used in the present (“suelo”) and the imperfect (“solía”), and always with an infinitive. The gerund is formed with -ando (-ar) and -iendo (-er, -ir); some verbs change the vowel (durmiendo, pidiendo, diciendo) or use “y” (leyendo, oyendo, yendo).
If in English you say “still + -ing”, think of “seguir + gerund”; if you say “still not”, think of “seguir sin”.

The gerund: -ando, -iendo, -yendo and the changing vowel

The gerund is always stressed on the syllable “-an-” or “-ien-”: tra-ba-JAN-do, a-pren-DIEN-do. In -ir verbs that change their vowel in the present, “e” becomes “i” and “o” becomes “u”: pidiendo, sintiendo, diciendo, siguiendo, durmiendo, muriendo. That vowel can be heard clearly and it is easy to mix it up if you aren’t expecting it.

When the stem ends in a vowel, the “i” of “-iendo” becomes “y”: leyendo, oyendo, cayendo, construyendo; and the gerund of “ir” is “yendo”. Pronounce that “y” as a soft consonant, just like in “haya” from week 6.

A profile in a local newspaper
The “People of Rosario” section of the city newspaper publishes this profile for the bookshop’s first anniversary.

A year ago, on a corner in Pichincha that had been empty for some time, Paula Ferraro hung up a handwritten sign: “Second-hand books, coffee and conversation”. Nobody expected much from such a small shop. However, within a few weeks the neighbours started dropping in to have a look, and many of them stayed.

Paula, who is a literature teacher, still works at a secondary school in the mornings. “Although I end up exhausted, I don’t want to give up teaching,” she explains. In the afternoons she usually serves alone, although on Saturdays her brother Tomás, who takes care of the book launches, helps her. The best attended was the one by a poet from the neighbourhood: when she finished reading, the audience started a standing ovation and she burst out laughing from nerves.

Not everything was easy. The paperwork for the licence took four months and the shop still has no heating. “In July we gave the workshops wearing gloves,” she remembers, laughing. To stay afloat, Paula sells coffee and home-made cakes from a neighbour, and every month she organises a book-swap fair on the pavement: if you bring two books, you take one.

The project keeps growing. “Acabar de”: a moment ago or already finished

In the present, “acabar de + infinitive” places an action in the very recent past: “Acabo de apagar el móvil” (a minute ago). In a story in the past, the imperfect does the same: “Acababa de salir de clase cuando me llamó mi hermana”.

In the preterite, the present perfect or the future, however, “acabar de” means the same as “terminar de”: completing something that was already under way. “Ayer acabé de leer la novela” means I read the last pages, not that I read it a moment ago.
One periphrasis, two meanings
Form
What it means
Example
To say that something happened a moment ago, use the present “acabo de”.
“Acabo de” is a recent past: it does not combine with a distant time like “hace dos años”.
Terminar de, dejar de, llegar a and acabar + gerund

“Terminar de” completes a task: “Termino de fregar y salgo”. “Dejar de” interrupts or abandons an activity or a habit, even if it is not finished: “Dejé de mirar el móvil en la cama”. With “no” in front, “no dejar de” means to keep on without stopping (“No deja de llover”), and in the imperative it is a friendly invitation: “No dejes de visitar el Albaicín”.

For the end of a story you have two more tools. “Llegar a + infinitive” marks the highest point, sometimes a surprising one: “Llegué a pasar seis horas al día con el móvil”. “Acabar + gerund” (or “acabar por + infinitive”) tells the final result after a process: “Al final acabé apagándolo todo”.
Ask yourself: was the action completed (terminar de) or cut off before it finished (dejar de)?

To abandon a habit you need “de”. Without “de”, “dejar + infinitive” means “to let”.

“Volver a + infinitive”: again, in any tense

“Volver a + infinitive” means “again”: an action is repeated or taken up again after a break. Only “volver” is conjugated; the infinitive does not change: “vuelvo a leer”, “volví a leer”, “he vuelto a leer”, “volveré a leer”, “espero que vuelvas a leer”.

Pronouns go before “volver” or attached to the infinitive, never in both places: “Lo volví a instalar” or “Volví a instalarlo”. With pronominal verbs the same thing happens: “Se volvió a caer la red” or “Volvió a caerse la red”.
Volver a in the tenses you already know
Tense
The pronoun goes in only one place: before “volver” or after the infinitive.
After “volver a” the verb is always in the infinitive.
No volver a, otra vez, repetir and the prefix re-

In the negative, “no volver a” means “never again”: you use it to promise (“No volverá a pasar”), to warn (“No vuelvas a contestar ese correo”) or to say that something did not happen again (“Nunca volví a verla”). Don’t confuse it with “dejar de”: “dejé de ir al gimnasio” says that a habit ended; “no volví a ir al gimnasio” says that, after one time, I never went again.

To repeat you also have “otra vez” and “de nuevo” (“Lo leí otra vez”), “repetir” + noun (“Repetí el examen”; never “repetí a hacer”) and the prefix “re-” in some verbs (releer, rehacer, reenviar). Careful: “volver a + a place” means to return: “Volví a Granada en 2020”.
If you can add “otra vez” at the end of the sentence without changing the meaning, “volver a” is the natural choice.

Acabo / acabó, dejo / dejó: the stressed syllable changes the tense

In this week’s verbs, a single strong syllable separates the present from the past. “Acabo de” (a-CA-bo) talks about you right now; “acabó de” (a-ca-BÓ) says that someone else finished something. The same happens with “dejo / dejó” and “termino / terminó”. If you change the stress, you change the tense and the person.

With “volver” the difference is also in the vowel: “vuelvo” and “vuelve” have “ue” in the strong syllable, but “volví” and “volvió” have “o” because the stress moves to the end. Also, “a” joins the next vowel without a pause: “vuelvo‿a‿hacerlo”, “acaba‿de‿empezar”.
The written accent marks the difference in writing: “acabo / acabó”, “dejo / dejó”, “termino / terminó”. If you forget it in a message, you change the tense and the person of the verb.

Day 31: what I gave up and what I got back
Personal blog post
Nuria writes a blog about life in Granada. This is the post she published the day after finishing her challenge.

Today is day 31 and I’ve just opened my laptop to write this, not to look at social media. A month ago I decided to do an experiment: thirty days without Instagram or TikTok. My screen time had reached five hours a day, and the worst thing wasn’t the hours, but the feeling of never finishing anything.

The first thing I stopped doing was looking at my phone as soon as I woke up. The first few days I picked it up anyway, out of sheer habit, and stared at a screen with nothing to see. I had a relapse on day twelve: I installed an app again “just for a moment” and ended up spending a whole hour swiping. That night I deleted it again and never fell back into it.

What I’ve got back has surprised me. I’ve started reading before bed again, I’ve started phoning my friends again instead of sending them a heart, and on Sunday I walked up to the Sacromonte again, something I hadn’t done since university. I also finished sorting the photos from my trip to Morocco, which had been waiting for two years.

And now? I don’t intend to go back to my old life. I’ll keep just one social network and look at it in the afternoon. If you’re thinking of doing something similar, be sure to try: the first week is hard, but it’s worth it.

By the end of this week you can tell the story of a change of life: what you got used to, what you realised, what you dream of, and whether you became, turned into or changed into a different person.

This week you review two classes that help each other a lot. The first is about verbs that always take the same preposition: if you change the preposition, the sentence sounds wrong or changes its meaning. The second is about the verbs that express, in Spanish, the idea of “changing and becoming something else”. Your guide is Carmen, an engineer from Quito who moved to Cuenca ten years ago and now weaves toquilla straw hats.
Each verb with its preposition

Some verbs always take the same preposition before a noun or an infinitive. The most practical thing is to learn them as a block, like a single word: “acostumbrarse a”, “tratar de”, “pensar en”, “soñar con”. If you change the preposition, the listener notices the mistake straight away.

Grouping them by preposition helps you remember them. With “a” there are usually verbs of starting or daring (aprender a, atreverse a, negarse a). With “de” there are many verbs of memory and emotions (acordarse de, olvidarse de, quejarse de). With “en”, verbs of the mind and trust (pensar en, confiar en, fijarse en). With “con”, verbs of desire and company (soñar con, contar con, casarse con).

Preposition
Verbs
Example

The preposition doesn’t disappear: before “que” and in questions

When a clause with “que” follows the verb, the preposition stays: “Me di cuenta de que el taller era pequeño”, “Confío en que lo terminemos a tiempo”. Dropping it is a frequent mistake (queísmo). The opposite mistake is adding “de” where it isn’t needed (dequeísmo): “Pienso que…”, not “Pienso de que…”. A trick: replace the clause with “eso”. If you say “me di cuenta de eso”, you need “de que”; if you say “pienso eso”, just “que”.

In questions, the preposition goes first: “¿En qué piensas?”, “¿Con quién cuentas?”, “¿De qué te quejas?”. And watch out with “pensar”: “pensar en” is to have someone or something in your mind; “¿qué piensas de…?” asks for an opinion; “pensar + infinitive” is to intend.
Before writing “de que”, test it with “eso”: if the sentence needs “de eso”, keep the preposition; if not, remove it.

Hacerse, volverse and convertirse en

In Spanish there isn’t a single verb for “to change and become”. “Hacerse” + adjective or noun without an article tells a change that depends on a decision or a long process: profession, beliefs, ideas, age, money (“Se hizo artesana”, “Se hizo vegetariano”, “Nos hacemos mayores”).

“Volverse” + adjective tells a change of character or personality that the person doesn’t fully control: “Con los años se volvió más paciente”. “Convertirse en” + noun tells a complete transformation of people, things or places: “La casa de mi abuelo se convirtió en un taller”. Notice: “convertirse” always takes “en”, and “volverse” never does.
