“Convertirse” always takes “en”.
“Volverse” doesn’t take “en”; with a noun, it takes “un” or “una”.
Llegar a ser, pasar a ser, and volverse versus volver a

“Llegar a ser” tells the goal of a long road, almost always with effort: “Llegó a ser la mejor tejedora del barrio”. “Pasar a ser” is more neutral: a change of category, post or status, frequent in the news (“El pueblo pasó a ser parte del municipio”).

Don’t confuse “volverse” with “volver a”, which you reviewed in week 11. “Se volvió desconfiado” is a change of character; “volvió a confiar” means he trusted again; and “volvió serio” means he came back from somewhere looking serious.
Ask yourself three questions: did they decide it or seek it? (hacerse), did their character change without them wanting it? (volverse), is it now something else? (convertirse en).

The preposition that hides when you link words: “me acostumbré‿a”, “pienso‿en‿ti”

Many of this week’s prepositions are a single vowel or start with a vowel: “a”, “en”. In speech they join the word before and the word after, and almost disappear: “me acostumbré‿a‿esto” sounds like a single word. That is why many students don’t hear them and then don’t write them.

So as not to lose them, pronounce the link without a pause but without deleting the vowel: “pienso‿en‿ella”, “se convirtió‿en‿un taller”, “me atreví‿a‿hablar”. When two identical vowels meet (“voy‿a‿aprender”), lengthen the sound a little instead of saying it twice.
Even if the preposition is barely heard in speech, it always appears in writing: “me acostumbré a”, “pienso en”, “se convirtió en”. Remember the contractions too: “a + el = al”, “de + el = del”.

It is Wednesday afternoon in a toquilla straw hat workshop in the centre of Cuenca. Julián, a Colombian student making a documentary about crafts, interviews Carmen, who left engineering ten years ago.

Thank you for having me, Carmen. I was told you were an engineer before you took this up. Is that true?
Yes, I worked for twelve years at a construction company in Quito. I earned well, but one day I realised I didn’t think about anything but work. I had become a very nervous person.
And why did you choose hats, of all things?
Because of my grandmother. She used to weave here in Cuenca and I had dreamed of learning since I was a child. So I dared to leave my permanent job and came here with a suitcase and a lot of fears.
Was it hard for you to get used to life here?

And now look: this house has become a workshop with four apprentices.

Yes, my grandmother’s house became the headquarters of a small cooperative. I don’t know if I’ll ever be as good as she was, but I’ve become a real craftswoman. And I’ve become much calmer, that’s for sure.
What would you say to someone who is thinking about changing their life?
Not to try to do it all in a month. And to trust the people who know more than you.

Profile in a travel magazine
An Ecuadorian travel magazine publishes every month the profile of a person who changed their life. This month it’s Carmen’s turn.

Ten years ago, Carmen Ordóñez calculated the strength of bridges in an office in Quito. Today she spends eight hours a day sitting by a window in the San Sebastián neighbourhood, in Cuenca, weaving toquilla straw hats. “People think I went mad,” she says, laughing. “I think I became more sensible.”

The change was not sudden. Carmen remembers the exact afternoon she decided: she was stuck in a traffic jam, thinking about a report, and she realised she had gone months without thinking about anything else. That weekend she travelled to Cuenca, visited her grandmother’s empty house and dared to ask a question she had never asked herself: what if I stay?

Getting used to her new life was hard. She had to learn to work with her hands, to earn a living with much less money and to trust a master who only spoke to her when she made a mistake. For months she complained of pain in her fingers. But little by little she became a craftswoman, and her grandmother’s house became a workshop open to visitors.

Today she has four apprentices and dreams of a weaving school for young people in the neighbourhood. Will she become one of Cuenca’s great masters? “That doesn’t depend on me,” she answers. “I just try to weave each hat better than the last one.”

The topic first: “El pescado lo compré yo”

In Spanish you can start the sentence with what you are talking about, especially when you contrast it with something else: “El pescado lo compré yo; los limones, Diego”. If the direct object goes before the verb, you have to pick it up again with “lo, la, los, las”. It isn’t a pointless repetition: it is compulsory. If it goes after the verb, it isn’t repeated: “Compré el pescado”.

The pronoun agrees with the topic: “La salsa la preparamos el viernes”, “Los platos los lavó Ana”, “Las mesas las trae el ayuntamiento”. After the topic you can make a short pause when speaking; in writing, it is sometimes marked with a comma.
Direct object after and before the verb
Normal order
Topic first
What changes
If the direct object goes first, the pronoun is compulsory.
With the object after the verb, it is not doubled with “lo”.
Le and les in front, “a mí me” and “lo es”

Something similar happens with the indirect object. Before the verb it needs “le” or “les”: “A los proveedores les escribí ayer”, “A Diego le encanta el ají”. After the verb, the doubling is optional but very frequent: “Le di la receta a Rosa”. With verbs like “gustar”, the pronoun always appears. Use “les” when the person is plural.

Stressed pronouns (a mí, a ti, a ella…) always come with the unstressed pronoun: “A mí me lo contó Diego”, “La vi a ella en el mercado”. And to pick up an adjective or a noun with “ser”, “estar” or “parecer”, use “lo”, which doesn’t change: “¿Es caro el puesto? — Sí, lo es”, “Parece fácil, pero no lo es”.
Before writing a topic first, ask yourself: is it direct (lo, la, los, las) or indirect (le, les)?

Quien, el que and el cual

“Quien” and “quienes” refer only to people. You use them with no noun before them (“Quien prepara las salsas es Diego”, “Busco a quien organizó el puesto”), after a preposition (“la proveedora con quien hablé”) or between commas (“Rosa, quien abrió el local en 2015, …”). They aren’t used without a preposition to identify: “el cocinero que vino”, not “el cocinero quien vino”.

“El que, la que, los que, las que” work for people and things, after a preposition (“el mercado al que vamos”, “la mesa en la que trabajo”) and with no noun before them (“La que lleva las cuentas es Rosa”). “El cual, la cual” appears mostly in formal texts (“el local, en el cual se celebró la feria”): recognising it is enough.

Lo que, lo de and lo + adjective

“Lo” with no noun after it talks about ideas or topics, not concrete things. “Lo que” means “the thing that”: “Lo que me preocupa es el transporte”, “Haz todo lo que puedas”. With “lo que + verb + es / son” you highlight one element: “Lo que necesitamos son más manos”.

“Lo de” + noun, infinitive or adverb sums up a topic both people know: “lo del pedido”, “lo de abrir los lunes”, “lo de ayer”. And “lo + adjective” presents one aspect of the situation: “Lo bueno es que hay mucha gente; lo malo, que no tenemos sombra”. Don’t confuse “lo que” (an idea) with “el que / la que” (a specific person or thing).
If you can say “the thing that” or “the matter of”, use “lo que” or “lo de”.

Pauses that change the meaning: commas in relative clauses and the topic first

A relative clause between commas (non-defining) is said with a pause before and after, and in a slightly lower tone, like a comment: “Los cocineros, que estaban cansados, se fueron a casa” (they were all tired and they all left). Without pauses, the relative clause picks out only some: “Los cocineros que estaban cansados se fueron a casa” (the others stayed).

When you put the topic first, it is also normal to make a short pause and raise your tone a little at the end of the topic: “El pescado… lo compré yo”. That pause tells the listener they are going to hear something about that topic.
In writing, the pauses of a non-defining relative clause are marked with two commas: one before the relative and one at the end. If you forget the second comma, the sentence becomes confusing.

A Lima newspaper publishes on Monday a report on the weekend’s food fair in the Parque de la Exposición.

Anyone who went past the Parque de la Exposición on Saturday already knows what it is to wait forty minutes for a ceviche. What nobody disputes is the atmosphere. The visitors we spoke to all said the same thing: eating well and cheaply in Lima is possible. Is this the best fair of the year? Many believe it is.

“Ni… ni”: ruling out two things at once

“Ni… ni” denies two elements at the same time: “El hostal no tenía ni wifi ni agua caliente”. If the sentence starts with “no”, the first “ni” is optional in some cases, but with “ni… ni” the idea is clearer. If “ni… ni” comes at the start, before the verb, you don’t need “no”: “Ni el precio ni el horario son un problema”.

With two singular subjects before the verb, the plural is normal: “Ni el guía ni el conductor hablaban inglés”. It also works to rule out two explanations or two options: “No fue ni por la lluvia ni por el tráfico”.
There were neither clean sheets nor towels.
“No” + verb + “ni… ni”.
Neither the bus nor the train goes as far as the village.
Before the verb: no “no” and in the plural.
I don’t want coffee or tea, thanks.
Turning down two options.
With “ni” you repeat “ni”: it isn’t mixed with “o”.
If “ni… ni” goes before the verb, “no” is not added.
Pero, sin embargo and aunque: the weight of the ending

“Pero” joins two opposing ideas within one sentence: “El trayecto es largo, pero el paisaje es increíble”. “Sin embargo” does the same with more force and usually starts a new sentence or goes between commas: “El hostal era barato. Sin embargo, las camas eran muy incómodas”. It can also go inside the second idea: “El desayuno, sin embargo, era excelente”.

“Aunque” can add a short reservation at the end, often with just an adjective: “Es una excursión cansada, aunque muy bonita”. Remember the golden rule: what comes last weighs more. “Es bonito, aunque caro” leaves an impression of “caro”; “Es caro, aunque bonito” leaves an impression of “bonito”.

Porque, como and es que: causes in conversation

“Porque” goes after the result and answers “¿por qué?”: “Llegamos tarde porque el bus se averió”. In a short answer it can stand alone: “¿Por qué no fuiste? — Porque estaba enfermo”. “Como”, for its part, always goes at the beginning, before the result: “Como el bus se averió, llegamos tarde”.

“Es que” is very colloquial: it presents a cause as an excuse or explanation when someone asks you to account for something: “Perdona el retraso, es que no encontraba las llaves”. And “por” + noun or infinitive gives the cause briefly: “Cerraron por la nieve”, “Perdón por llegar tarde”.
As there were no seats on the bus, we rented a car.

We rented a car because there were no seats on the bus.
“Porque” after the result.
—Aren’t you coming to dinner? —The thing is, I’ve got a headache.

Ya que, puesto que, debido a, gracias a and por culpa de

“Ya que”, “puesto que” and “dado que” present a cause the listener already knows or accepts. They are more formal than “porque” and can go at the start or after, with a comma: “Puesto que la carretera está cerrada, la excursión se aplaza”, “La excursión se aplaza, ya que la carretera está cerrada”.

“Debido a” and “a causa de” go with a noun and are typical of notices and news: “debido a la nieve”. If a conjugated verb follows, you need “que”: “debido a que nevó”. Finally, “gracias a” presents a cause with a positive result and “por culpa de”, with a negative result: “Vimos los cóndores gracias al guía”, “Perdimos el bus por culpa del tráfico”.
Ask yourself who you are talking to: with a friend, “como” or “es que”; in a formal email or a notice, “ya que”, “puesto que” or “debido a”.

Como / cómo, porque / por qué and the pause of “sin embargo”

Causal “como” is unstressed: it leans on the next word and is hardly marked (“como‿no había plazas…”). Interrogative “cómo” is stressed: it is said with force and has a written accent (“¿Cómo llegaste?”). The same happens with “porque” (one word, soft stress on “-QUE”: por-QUE) and “por qué” (two words, strong stress on “QUÉ”).

“Sin embargo” usually goes between pauses and with a small change of tone, like a door opening to the opposite idea: “Era caro. | Sin embargo, | valió la pena”. That pause helps the listener notice the counterweight.

“Porque” (cause) is one word without an accent; “por qué” (question) is two words with an accent; “el porqué” is a noun (“el porqué de la cancelación”). Causal “como” has no accent; “cómo” in questions does.

The second day was the best. We got up early again, although this time for a good reason: at eight, at the Cruz del Cóndor viewpoint, we saw six condors flying very close. Since they don’t always appear, the guide told us we had been very lucky.

Do I recommend it? Yes, but with two pieces of advice. First, take warm clothes, because at night it goes down to several degrees below zero. Second, don’t pay for the cheapest package: the value for money of the middle one is much better. It’s a tiring excursion, but an unforgettable one.

Así que, por eso, por lo tanto: from cause to consequence

Result connectors come after the cause and present the result. In conversation, the most frequent are “así que”, “por eso” and “entonces”: “Me ofrecieron un sueldo mejor, así que acepté”. In a formal text, “por lo tanto”, “por tanto” and “en consecuencia” are preferred, usually after a full stop or semicolon and followed by a comma: “El alquiler ha subido un 30 %; por lo tanto, muchas familias se han ido del centro”.

Remember the direction: “como” and “ya que” (week 14) present the cause; “así que” and “por eso”, the consequence. You can tell the same thing both ways: “Como no había vuelos, fuimos en bus” = “No había vuelos, así que fuimos en bus”.

“Así que” introduces the consequence, not the cause: it comes after.
“Por lo tanto” comes after a full stop or semicolon, and is followed by a comma.
“De modo que”: result or purpose, and “¿así que…?”

“De modo que” and “de manera que” with the indicative tell a result: “El teleférico une El Alto con el centro, de modo que mucha gente ya no usa el minibús”. With the subjunctive, however, they express purpose, like “para que” (week 7): “Pon el horario en la puerta, de modo que todos lo vean”.

At the start of a turn in conversation, “¿Así que…?” draws a conclusion from what you have just heard and asks for confirmation: “—Me han ofrecido un puesto en Santa Cruz. —¿Así que te vas?”. It is said with question intonation.

To add arguments in the same direction you have “además”, “también” and “es más” (which adds a stronger one): “Santa Cruz tiene mejor clima. Además, el sueldo es más alto. Es más, la empresa paga la mudanza”. “Encima” also adds, but it is colloquial and usually goes with a complaint: “Me subieron el alquiler y encima no arreglan la calefacción”.

“Incluso” and “hasta” present the most surprising item in a series: “Vinieron todos a despedirme, incluso mi abuela de noventa años”. In the negative, you use “ni siquiera”: “Ni siquiera me preguntaron mi opinión”. To order a text, you can use “en primer lugar”, “por otro lado” and “por último”.

“En cambio” and “mientras que” compare two different people, things or positions: “En La Paz hace frío; en Santa Cruz, en cambio, hace calor todo el año”, “Mi padre quiere quedarse, mientras que mi madre prefiere probar”. “Así que” and “¿así que…?”, “sino” and “si no”

“Así que” as a consequence is said in the middle of the sentence, with a tone that falls at the end: “No había vuelos, así que fuimos en bus”. By contrast, “¿Así que…?” at the start of a turn rises at the end, because it asks for confirmation: “¿Así que te vas a Santa Cruz?”.

Why I haven’t left La Paz (yet)
Opinion column in a newspaper
A La Paz newspaper publishes a reader’s column every Sunday. This week Daniela writes, a year after that Sunday lunch in Sopocachi.

A year ago I was offered a job in Santa Cruz and, like so many people from La Paz my age, I was about to pack my bags. I didn’t, and this column isn’t a complaint against those who leave, but an explanation of why some of us stay.

First of all, La Paz has changed. Fifteen years ago, crossing the city could take two hours by minibus; today the cable car has become the backbone of transport, so living in El Alto and working in the centre is no longer torture. Besides, the cultural offer has grown: there are theatres, festivals and even a book fair that fills the streets every August.

On the other hand, what weighed most in my decision wasn’t the city, but the people. My parents are getting old and my brother works away almost all year. In Santa Cruz, by contrast, I had nobody to count on. It’s true that the salary there was better and the climate milder. However, money wasn’t going to give me back Sundays with my family.

Does this mean I will never leave? No. My company opened an office here, so I was able to accept a similar project without moving. Neither the altitude nor the cold has stopped bothering me, but I’ve got used to them. Therefore, my advice is simple: before taking the plunge, ask yourselves what you would lose. Sometimes the answer is “nothing”, and then you have to go. Other times, the answer is everything.

Reporting in the past: the verb takes a step back

When you report today what someone said at another time, the reporting verb is in the past (“dijo”, “contó”, “explicó”) and the verb of the quote usually moves back one tense. “Tengo prisa” becomes “dijo que tenía prisa”; “Ya lo pagué” or “Ya lo he pagado” becomes “dijo que ya lo había pagado”; “Volveré el viernes” becomes “dijo que volvería el viernes”.

The imperfect does not change (“Antes vivía en Cholula” → “dijo que antes vivía en Cholula”). If what was said is still true now or hasn’t happened yet, you can keep the original tense: “Me dijo que el taller abre a las nueve” (and it still opens at nine).
Before reporting, ask yourself: is what they said still true today? If not, move the verb back.

Who, where, when: references change too

When you report, you change the point of view. “Mi taller” in the teacher’s mouth is “su taller” in yours; “aquí” may become “allí”; “hoy” becomes “ese día”, “mañana” becomes “al día siguiente” and “ayer” becomes “el día anterior”, if you are no longer on that day.

Questions are reported without question marks. If the question is answered with yes or no, use “preguntó si”: “¿Hacen envíos?” → “Preguntó si hacíamos envíos”. If it has a question word, you repeat it with its accent: “¿Cuánto cuesta?” → “Preguntó cuánto costaba”. For requests, use “me pidió que” or “me dijo que” with three forms learnt as a chunk: “viniera”, “llamara”, “hiciera” (if you speak to someone as tú: “vinieras”, “llamaras”, “hicieras”).
“I’ll bring the design tomorrow.” → She said she was bringing the design the next day.

“Se” that agrees with the thing: se vende, se venden

When it doesn’t matter who does something, but what is done, you use “se” + a third-person verb. The verb agrees with the thing: “Se pinta cada plato a mano”, “Se pintan los platos a mano”. It’s what you see on signs and adverts: “Se vende local”, “Se reparan bicicletas”.

If the thing is not specific, it goes without an article and without “a”: “Se buscan aprendices” (any apprentices). It works in every tense: “El taller se fundó en 1924”, “Las piezas se entregarán en marzo”.

Impersonal “se”: always singular

When there is no thing to agree with, the verb is always singular: “En Puebla se come muy bien”, “En el taller se trabaja en silencio”, “Se prohíbe tocar las piezas”, “Se dice que la talavera llegó de España”. With specific people “a” appears and the verb stays singular: “Se busca a los dueños del perro”.

There are other ways of not saying who: the third person plural (“Dicen que va a llover”, “Me cobraron de más”) and “uno”, which is required with verbs that already carry “se”: “Al principio uno se cansa mucho”.

Direct question and reported question: the intonation changes

A direct yes/no question ends with a rising tone: “¿Hacen envíos?”. When you report it (“Preguntó si hacían envíos”), it’s no longer a question but information: the sentence ends with a falling tone, like any statement.

Something similar happens with a question word: in “¿Cuándo abren?” the stress is on “cuándo”; in “Quería saber cuándo abrían”, “cuándo” keeps its stress, but the sentence ends falling. If you raise your tone at the end when reporting, it sounds as if you were the one asking.
In the reported question the “¿?” marks disappear, but the question word keeps its accent: “preguntó qué quería”, “no sé dónde vive”. “Si” in “preguntó si” has no accent.

It’s Monday morning at the workshop. Andrés, an apprentice like Ximena, didn’t come in on Saturday. Ximena tells him what happened with a client from Monterrey and how they are going to make her order.
workshop apprentice
How was Saturday? I saw there’s a new card on doña Rosario’s table.

And when does she want them for?

And did she accept?

Great! OK, I’ll start right now. Did she leave a photo?

This is how a piece is made at Casa Pájaro Azul
Craft workshop web page
The workshop where Ximena works explains on its page how its pieces are made and collects what some visitors tell it.

At Casa Pájaro Azul talavera is made as it was a hundred years ago. The clay is brought from two mines near Puebla and mixed by hand. Then it is left to rest for about three months, because that makes it easier to work. The pieces are shaped on the wheel or in moulds and dried in the shade for several weeks.

Then they are fired for the first time and covered with a white glaze. On that base the design is drawn with a paper stencil and painted by hand with donkey-hair brushes. Only six traditional colours are used. Finally, each piece is fired again and checked one by one: if a flaw is found, it is not sold as a first-quality piece.

In the workshop nobody works in a hurry, and it shows. Many visitors tell us so. A teacher from Oaxaca told us she had bought her first cup here thirty years before and still used it every morning. A Japanese student asked us whether he could stay for a week to learn, and we told him to come back in summer. Last week a little girl wanted to know why the plates were so expensive. We explained how many hands touch each piece, and her dad told us he would never haggle at a market again.
Visits are accepted from Tuesday to Saturday. Please arrive on time and do not touch the pieces that are drying.

“Estar” + participle: the state an action leaves

When someone does something, it leaves a result: limpiaron el baño → el baño está limpio; abrieron la ventana → la ventana está abierta. With “estar” + participle you describe that result, not the action. The participle works like an adjective and agrees with what it describes: “la puerta está cerrada”, “los cajones están cerrados”, “las luces están apagadas”.

For a past state, use “estaba”: “Cuando llegué, la calefacción estaba encendida”. Remember the most frequent irregular participles: abierto, roto, hecho, escrito, puesto, vuelto, muerto, dicho, cubierto. With “limpiar”, “llenar”, “vaciar” and “secar” the adjective is preferred: “está limpio”, “está lleno”, “está vacío”, “está seco”.
Ask yourself: am I talking about what someone did or about how the thing is now? If it’s how it is, “estar” + agreeing participle.

Don’t mix up three things. “He pintado la puerta” tells the action and the participle doesn’t change; “la puerta está pintada” describes the state and agrees; “estoy pintando la puerta” talks about the action in progress. With “quedar” or “quedarse” + participle you talk about the final state, often unexpected: “La persiana se quedó atascada”, “La reunión queda aplazada”.
For progress so far, use “tener” + participle, which agrees with the object (“Tengo las maletas deshechas, pero no los libros”), and “llevar” + amount + participle (“Llevo tres cajas ordenadas”).

“Ser” + participle: the action, with a date or an agent

In news, history texts and official signs you’ll see “ser” + participle. It doesn’t describe a state but an action that happened, almost always with a date or with “por” + whoever did it: “El colegio fue fundado en 1611 por los jesuitas”, “La biblioteca fue inaugurada ayer por la alcaldesa”. The participle agrees here too: “Las obras fueron terminadas en marzo”.

In conversation it is much more common to say the same in the active or with “se”: “Los jesuitas fundaron el colegio en 1611”, “El colegio se fundó en 1611”. At this stage what matters is that you understand “ser” + participle when you read or hear it, and that you can rephrase it.

The participle in -ado: careful and relaxed forms

In spontaneous speech in much of Spain, the “d” between vowels in the “-ado” participle weakens a lot or disappears: “estoy cansado” sounds almost like “estoy cansao”, “he terminado” sounds like “he terminao”. It’s normal in a conversation among friends, but in a formal situation or when reading aloud the soft “d” is pronounced.

In “-ido” the “d” is kept more (“comido”, “salido”), and in feminine participles (“cansada”, “terminada”) it hardly ever disappears. When you speak, pronounce a soft “d”, with the tongue between the teeth and without closing completely: that way you sound natural in any register.
Always write “-ado”, even if you hear “-ao”: “cansado”, “terminado”. The forms “cansao” or “terminao” only appear in texts that imitate speech.

Residence website (history of the building)
Lucía’s residence tells the history of the building on its website for new residents.

The building where you live was built between 1611 and 1630 with Villamayor stone, the same golden stone as the cathedral. It was founded by a canon of the city as a college for students without means, who lived here for free in exchange for helping in the church next door. For two centuries the college was full of young people from all over Castile.

In the 19th century the building’s life changed completely. It was turned first into barracks and then into a grain store. By the mid-20th century it was already almost empty, and in 1978 it was closed because of the danger of collapse. It stood abandoned for almost forty years: the cloister roof had caved in, the windows were bricked up and the façade was covered in ivy.

In 2017 the City Council and the University signed an agreement, and the building was restored by a team of local architects. The work was finished in the summer of 2020, and the residence was opened in September, with the first forty students.

Today the cloister is restored and open to residents, the rooms are equipped with heating and wifi, and the library is housed in the old chapel. Only the north wing is still closed: it is reserved for a future museum. If you look closely at the entrance, you’ll see that the canon’s coat of arms is still carved above the door.

Adjectives that change meaning with “ser” and “estar”

You already know that “ser” presents a characteristic and “estar” a state. With some adjectives, changing the verb changes the meaning of the word. “El abuelo es listo” means he is clever; “El abuelo está listo”, that he is ready. “La familia es rica” is about money; “la carne está rica”, about taste.

With “estar”, several of these adjectives take a preposition: “estar orgulloso de”, “estar seguro de”, “estar interesado en”, “estar listo para”. Other adjectives, such as “tranquilo”, “nervioso” or “serio”, don’t change meaning: with “ser” they describe what someone is like in general; with “estar”, how they are today.
Ask yourself whether you are talking about what the person or thing is like, or how it is now. If the adjective is in the table, also check which meaning you want.

Two pronouns together: order and position

When two pronouns appear, the order is fixed: first “se”, then “te” or “os”, then “me” or “nos”, and finally “lo, la, los, las”. In practice: the person pronoun goes before the thing pronoun (“me lo”, “te la”, “nos los”). And “le” or “les” become “se” before “lo, la, los, las”: you don’t say “le lo”, but “se lo”. To make clear who “se” is, add “a” + person: “Se lo damos a la abuela”.

With a conjugated verb, in any tense, both pronouns go in front: “se lo di”, “se lo he dado” (never between “he” and “dado”), “te lo diría”. In the negative imperative they go after “no”: “No se lo digas”. In the affirmative imperative, the infinitive and the gerund they are attached at the end and almost always need a written accent: “dáselo”, “dárselo”, “dándoselo”. With verb phrases you can choose: “se lo voy a dar” or “voy a dárselo”, but never in the middle and never twice.

Collectives and quantities: “la gente dice”, “la mitad votó / votaron”

A collective noun on its own, even if it refers to many people, takes a singular verb: “La gente dice”, “La familia decidió”, “El público aplaudió”. When a collective or a quantity is followed by “de” + plural noun (“la mayoría de los primos”, “la mitad de los invitados”, “un grupo de vecinos”, “el setenta por ciento de los votos”), the verb can be singular or plural: both options are correct, and the plural is very common.
If the noun after “de” is singular, the verb is singular: “La mitad de la torta desapareció”. With “cada uno de” + plural, the verb is singular: “Cada uno de los nietos trajo algo”.
Most of the cousins came by car.
Also correct: “vino”.
A group of grandpa’s friends sang a zamba.
Also correct: “cantaron”.
Half of the barbecue got burnt.
“Del asado”: singular.
Each of the guests wrote a sentence in the book.
“Cada uno”: singular.
“La gente”, on its own, takes a singular verb.
Coordinated subjects, “ni… ni” and “haber”

Two subjects joined with “y” take a plural verb, and the first person takes priority: “Mi hermano y yo llevamos las bebidas” (nosotros). With “tú y él”, in the Americas and parts of Spain “ustedes” is used (“Tú y Facundo traen la torta”); in the rest of Spain, “vosotros” (“traéis”). “Usted y Marta” always go with “ustedes”. If an adjective refers to masculine and feminine nouns, it goes in the masculine plural: “La torta y el vino estaban buenísimos”.

With “ni… ni” before the verb, the plural is normal: “Ni la abuela ni el tío sabían nada”. And remember that “haber” meaning that something exists never changes: “Había cuarenta personas”, “Hubo tres discursos”, “Va a haber música”. The form “habían cuarenta personas” is heard in many regions, but it is not the educated standard.

Pronouns attached to the verb: the stress doesn’t move

When you attach one or two pronouns to the end of a verb, the word gets longer, but the strong syllable is still the same one in the verb: “da” → “dá-se-lo”, “contando” → “con-tán-do-se-lo”, “preparar” → “pre-pa-rár-se-la”. The pronouns are weak syllables: don’t stress them.

That’s why these words carry a written accent: the strong syllable is far from the end. When listening, the strong syllable of the verb tells you the action; the weak syllables at the end tell you to whom and what: “dámelo” (to me), “dáselo” (to him or her), “dánoslo” (to us).
Write an accent when the strong syllable is three or more syllables from the end: “dáselo”, “decírselo”, “contándoselo”. “Dame” and “decirlo” don’t have one.

Account in a neighbourhood club newsletter
The newsletter of the club in the Alta Córdoba neighbourhood, where grandpa Cacho has played bocce for fifty years, publishes an account of the party.

Last Saturday, don Cacho Ferreyra turned eighty and his family threw him a surprise party in his daughter Inés’s courtyard. There were more than forty people: children, grandchildren, neighbours and a group of club mates, who arrived wearing the bocce team’s shirts. Most of the guests hid behind the plants, and when don Cacho walked in, everyone started singing.

“I was sure they were up to something,” the birthday boy said afterwards; he is famous at the club for being very sharp. “My granddaughter is very clever, but uncle Rubén can’t hide anything.” Apparently, on Friday someone mentioned the barbecue to him and he told his wife about it, and she denied everything with a smile.

The barbecue, in the hands of grandson Facundo, was delicious, although half of the empanadas disappeared before everyone sat down. At the toast, the grandchildren gave him a watch; they gave it to him with a letter signed by each of them. Don Cacho, who is not a man of many words, just said he was proud of his family and his friends from the club.

The party ended with a zamba. Neither don Cacho nor his wife had danced in public since their wedding, but that night they danced twice. From the club, we wish him many more years… and many more games of bocce.

The noun you don’t repeat: “la gris”, “la de Tomás”, “la que…”

When everyone knows what you’re talking about, you can drop the noun and keep the article with whatever describes it. The article agrees with the missing noun: “Tengo dos maletas: la gris es mía y la azul, de mi hermana”. It works with an adjective (“la grande”), with “de” + something (“la de Tomás”, “la de las ruedas rotas”) and with “que” + clause (“la que tiene una cinta roja”).

Without a noun, the short possessive (“mi”, “tu”, “su”) doesn’t work: you need the long form with an article: “el mío”, “la tuya”, “los suyos”, “las nuestras”. Since “el suyo” can be his, hers, yours (formal) or theirs, if there’s any doubt use “el de” + person: “el de Camila”, “el de ustedes”.
Only drop the noun if the reader knows what you mean: if there are two candidates, add “de” + person or a clause with “que”.

Explaining or selecting: apposition and modifier

An appositive explains who someone is or what something already identified is; it goes between commas and, if you remove it, the sentence still works: “Tomás, mi compañero de oficina, me llevó al aeropuerto”. It lets you introduce someone without writing another sentence.

A modifier, on the other hand, picks one out of several and goes without commas: “El compañero que vive en Ñuñoa me llevó al aeropuerto” (not the other one). That’s why commas change the meaning: “Los pasajeros, que tenían maletas grandes, esperaron una hora” (all of them) versus “Los pasajeros que tenían maletas grandes esperaron una hora” (only those).
My boss, a very calm woman, laughed at the story.

Telling an anecdote: opening, moving forward and surprising

An anecdote usually starts with a hook: “¿A que no sabes qué me pasó?”, “Resulta que…”, “Una vez…”. Then you paint the scene in the imperfect or with “estaba” + gerund (“Estaba esperando la maleta y había muchísima gente”) and move forward with the events in the preterite, ordered with “al principio”, “entonces”, “luego”, “al rato” or “a los diez minutos”.

The surprise comes in with “de repente”, “de pronto”, “en ese momento” or “justo cuando” + preterite: “De repente vi una maleta igual que la mía”. For what had happened before, use the pluperfect: “Cuando llegué a la cinta, el señor ya se había llevado la mía”.

The background scene with “mientras” goes in the imperfect.

Closing and reacting

To close, use “al final” (what happened at the end), “por fin” (something you were waiting for that finally came), “total, que…” (informal summary) and “menos mal que” + indicative (relief): “Menos mal que tenía la etiqueta con mi teléfono”. Don’t use “por fin” for something bad: “Al final perdí el vuelo”, not “por fin perdí el vuelo”.

The intonation of a story: keeping the listener waiting

When you tell an anecdote, not all sentences end the same way. If the story continues, the voice stays suspended at mid-height or rises a little at the end (“Estaba esperando la maleta…”), and the listener knows something more is coming. When you finish a part or the story, the voice clearly falls (“…y era la de otro señor”).

Before the key moment, many speakers make a short pause and stretch the marker a little: “Y de repeeente…”. Appositives between commas are said in a lower tone and a bit faster, like a parenthesis: “Tomás, mi compañero de oficina, me llamó”.
In writing, appositives and relative clauses that explain go between commas; those that select go without commas. Ellipsis dots (“…”) mark the suspense of the voice in writing.
Rise at the end: it’s a hook to make them ask.

Three red backpacks on the bus
Post on a travel anecdote blog
A Chilean blog publishes an anecdote sent in by its readers every week. This one was written by Ignacio, a student from Temuco.

Once, in my first year at university, I travelled to Santiago for a national team match with two friends from school, Matías and Benja. The three of us had almost identical red backpacks: mine had a key ring from La U, Matías’s was a bit torn and Benja’s, since he’s always been the tidiest one, had his name embroidered on it.

It turns out that after the match we got on a bus full of fans. While we were standing, squashed like sardines, someone started singing and the whole bus began jumping. At that moment the backpacks fell on the floor and got mixed up with other passengers’ bags. A while later we got off, each with a red backpack, and went to the hostel without looking.

That night, when I opened mine, I realised it wasn’t mine: inside there was a nurse’s uniform, a recipe book and an avocado sandwich. Matías had his own, but Benja had a lady’s who, according to the card inside, lived in Maipú. What a pain! My backpack, with my wallet, had disappeared.
Luckily the lady, a very friendly nurse, found my ID card in the pocket and called me the next day. In the end we met at a metro station and swapped backpacks. Since then, mine has a yellow ribbon.

Real option, imagined option and advice

To talk about a possible, concrete option, use “si” + present and a consequence in the present or future: “Si nos quedamos en la sala, mantenemos el público fiel”. To imagine an option you haven’t chosen yet and see what would happen, use the conditional: “En una gira llegaríamos a gente que nunca va al teatro”. Never put the conditional after “si”: “si iríamos” is wrong.

To give advice, put yourself in the other person’s place: “Yo que tú, aceptaría”, “En tu lugar, hablaría con el elenco”, “Sería mejor esperar a marzo” (with the infinitive). If you want to name the person, use “es mejor que” + present subjunctive: “Es mejor que lo decidan todos juntos”.

What is likely and what is better

To say how likely you think something is: “a lo mejor” + indicative (“A lo mejor nos dan la subvención”), “quizás” + indicative or subjunctive, “puede que” + subjunctive (“Puede que el público del interior responda bien”) and “lo más probable es que” + subjunctive (“Lo más probable es que la sala esté llena en verano”).

To compare the two options: “Es mejor X que Y”, “Prefiero la gira a la temporada en la sala”, “Por un lado…, por otro…”, “Lo bueno es que…”, “Lo malo es que…”. That way the listener sees the pros and cons before your conclusion.

Arguing and deciding as a group

A good argument has four parts: the thesis (“Creo que debemos salir de gira”), the arguments with connectors (“ya que”, “además”, “incluso”), a counter-argument you acknowledge (“Es verdad que es caro, pero…”, “Aunque perdemos la sala dos meses, …”) and the conclusion (“Así que propongo que…”, “Por eso…”).

Watch the mood: “creo que”, “me parece que”, “está claro que” and “es verdad que” go with the indicative; “no creo que” and “no me parece que”, with the subjunctive; “es importante que”, “propongo que” and “sugiero que”, also with the subjunctive. To disagree politely: “Entiendo tu idea, pero…”, “No estoy del todo de acuerdo”, “Yo lo veo de otra manera”.
Before you speak, write your thesis in one line and prepare a concession with “es verdad que…, pero…”: people who acknowledge the other side’s argument are more convincing.

Emphasis for arguing: the contrasting word and the concession

When you argue, your voice marks which word matters. In “No creo que sea CARO, sino que es arriesgado”, the stress falls on the word that contrasts with another. If you put the emphasis somewhere else, the message changes: “No creo que SEA caro” sounds as if you doubt that it is.

In a concession with “es verdad que…, pero…”, the first part ends with the voice up, suspended, and the part with “pero” falls firmly: the listener understands that the important thing comes afterwards. Something similar happens with “aunque”: “Aunque es caro ↗, vale la pena ↘”.
In writing, the comma marks the pause of the concession: “Es verdad que es caro, pero…”, “Aunque es caro, …”.

Opinion column in a cultural magazine
A week after the meeting, a Montevideo theatre critic publishes this column about La Rambla Teatro’s decision.

Last week La Rambla Teatro, one of the best-loved independent companies in Ciudad Vieja, put to a vote a question many companies ask themselves: stay in the theatre or go on tour? Most of the cast voted for the tour, and in February they will travel to Salto, Tacuarembó and Rocha. I think it’s a brave decision, and I want to explain why.

On the one hand, it is clear that independent theatre in Montevideo has a problem: people always perform for the same audience. In an eighty-seat theatre, the people who go are almost always the same, and that, although it is comfortable, doesn’t help anyone grow. On the other hand, in the interior there are magnificent theatres that stand empty for months. The one in Salto, for example, was opened in 1882 and today is perfectly restored, but it receives very few plays a year.

It is true that a tour costs a lot of money and that the Ciudad Vieja theatre will be closed for two months. Some spectators may get annoyed, and the company will most likely earn less than in a normal season. However, I don’t think culture should be measured only in money. If companies don’t leave the capital, the rest of the country will go on seeing theatre only on television.

That is why I suggest that the Montevideo council also support these tours, and that other theatres follow the example. If I were them, I would also record the shows in the interior to show them on their return. That way, the regular audience wouldn’t be left without its company, and the new one would have a reason to visit it in the capital.

A form born from the preterite

To form the imperfect subjunctive you do not need to memorise a new list: start from the third person plural of the preterite, drop «-ron» and add the endings. If the preterite is irregular, the irregularity carries over entirely: tuvieron → tuviera, pidieron → pidiera, durmieron → durmiera, leyeron → leyera.

There are two sets of endings, in -ra and in -se, and they mean the same. The -ra form is the most frequent in conversation across Latin America and Spain; the -se form appears above all in writing and careful speech. The «nosotros» form always carries a written accent, because the word becomes stressed on the third-to-last syllable.
If you are unsure about a verb, first say the preterite «ellos» form aloud. If you get that right, you will get the imperfect subjunctive right too.

Uses without «si»: unlikely wishes and politeness

Before reporting other people's requests, it is worth remembering two short uses. With «ojalá», the imperfect subjunctive presents a wish that the speaker sees as difficult or impossible in the present: «ojalá abriera» sounds more remote than «ojalá abra». And «quisiera» is a very common polite form in shops, offices and emails: it softens a request without changing its content.
Although it is called «imperfect», in these uses the form does not talk about the past: it talks about now or later, seen from a distance or with politeness.
I hope the café has room for everyone on Saturday.

Reporting in the past what someone asked, wanted or felt

You already know that verbs of influence (pedir, aconsejar, exigir), wish (querer, esperar, preferir) and emotion (alegrar, molestar, preocupar) take the subjunctive when the other action has a different subject. What is new is the tense: if that main verb is in the preterite, imperfect or pluperfect, the verb that depends on it moves to the imperfect subjunctive.
If the subject is the same, there is no «que»: the infinitive is used. «Delia quería abrir temprano» (she wanted and she opened); «Delia quería que abriéramos temprano» (she wanted, we opened).

Dejar, hacer, prohibir; «decir» with two meanings; pending requests

With «dejar», «hacer», «prohibir» and «permitir» there are two correct patterns: a pronoun plus an infinitive («no nos dejaba tocar el piano») or «que» plus the subjunctive («no dejaba que tocáramos el piano»). The first is more common in conversation.

«Decir», «insistir en» and «escribir» either inform or request. If they inform, they take the indicative: «insistió en que el piso era de pinotea». If they request, the subjunctive: «insistió en que lo encerásemos cada mes». And if someone asked for something in the past but the request is still pending today, the present subjunctive is also possible: «me pidió que la llame el jueves» (Thursday has not come yet).

Right, let's make the list before we forget anything. Grandma asked us for three specific things: not to change the name, to keep the marble tables and to keep opening at seven, even if only four people come at that hour.

The name and the tables are done. The seven o'clock part is harder for me. She wanted the café to be the first lit-up place on the block, I understand that, but she also told me not to work myself to death. Both things at once are not easy.

That's why I'm suggesting shifts. And remember what used to bother her: people waiting on their feet. She was really embarrassed when someone left without sitting down. If we hire one more person for the mornings, we meet both wishes.

All right. Another thing: on Monday Ramón asked me to send him the new menu before Friday, because he wants to give his opinion. I haven't sent it yet. And he insisted that the piano was in tune, that he had checked it himself.

In tune? Grandma never let anyone touch it without permission, and now it turns out Ramón checks it on his own. Anyway. If only she could see how the room turned out. She would like to see that the lamp is the same one from her day.
Sure. You send Ramón the menu tonight, he listens to you more. And ask him to tell us what he thinks without beating about the bush: Grandma always wanted things to be said openly.

Original SpanishCue text written as a feature for the fictional magazine «Vecinos de San Telmo». The people and the café are invented.

For sixty years, the corner of Defensa and Carlos Calvo kept a fixed schedule: at seven sharp, Delia Ferraro raised the shutter and switched on the lamps of Café Delia. When it closed two years ago, many of us thought the corner would become another souvenir shop. We were wrong. On Saturday, her grandchildren Martina and Joaquín reopened the premises, and they did it with a list of requests that Delia herself left them in writing.

The list wasn't long, but it was precise. Delia asked them not to change the name, to keep the marble tables and for the waiters to keep calling customers by their names. She also wanted the menu always to include a cheap dish, «so that nobody would be left out for lack of money». Martina says that at first this condition seemed impossible to her with today's prices: «I told my brother we needed to make money, and he reminded me that Grandma had never wanted to get rich from the café».

Not everything was obedience. Joaquín admits they argued a lot about the music. Delia disliked bars playing songs at full volume, and she would not allow anyone to play the piano without her permission. The siblings decided the piano would be played only on Fridays, with a guest pianist, and that the rest of the week the noise would be the usual: cups, newspapers and conversation. «I don't know whether she would agree with everything», Joaquín admits, «but I think she would be glad that people were staying for hours again».

We at this magazine allow ourselves an opinion. A list of requests can become a cage if it is read to the letter, and Café Delia has avoided that. The grandchildren did not copy their grandmother: through her papers, they asked her what she wanted to survive. If only more businesses in the neighbourhood had that luck, or that patience. For now, the shutter goes up at seven again.

In class you saw how the main verb decides the tense of the subjunctive and how «si» can present a plan or a dream. Here you review it with a neighbourhood project in Rosario: what the council asks for, what it asked for, what the neighbourhood hopes for and what it would do if things were different.
Two frames: the main verb sets the tense

If the verb that asks, wishes, evaluates or needs is in the present, future, imperative or present perfect, the subjunctive goes in the present. If it is in a past tense (preterite, imperfect, pluperfect) or in the conditional, the subjunctive goes in the imperfect. The same happens after «para que», «antes de que» and «cuando» with future meaning.
Watch out for the conditional: even though it talks about the future, it belongs to the past frame. «Me gustaría que vinieras», not «me gustaría que vengas», in the most widespread standard.

Looking back from now: perfect and imperfect

From a main verb in the present you can also talk about something earlier. If that action is close to the present or its result is still alive, use the perfect subjunctive: «me alegra que hayan votado tantas personas». If it is a closed past, with a marker such as «ayer» or «el año pasado», use the imperfect: «me alegra que votaran tantas personas el año pasado».

The two-frame rule has a useful exception: if someone asked for something in the past and that content is still pending, the present is also accepted: «la concejala pidió que mandemos el plano esta semana».

In the most general standard, with «ayer» the past is closed: imperfect. The perfect is also heard in some areas.
«Si»: a possible plan or an imagined world

With «si + present indicative» you present an open condition: you believe it can be fulfilled and you set up a real consequence in the present, future or imperative. With «si + imperfect subjunctive» you distance the condition from the current reality, and the consequence goes in the simple conditional. The choice depends not only on the facts but on how the speaker sees them.

Although it is called «imperfect», in these sentences the subjunctive does not talk about the past: it talks about now or the future. And the order is free: you can start with the consequence without changing the tenses. When «si» comes first, separate the two parts with a comma.

Negotiating with hypotheses without mixing the worlds

Hypotheses are very useful for making cautious proposals: «si pusiéramos el taller junto al muelle, ¿no sería más visible?». They sound less imposing than «pongamos el taller junto al muelle». But each sentence must stay in a single world: if the condition is possible, the consequence is real; if it is imagined, so is the consequence.

To offer alternatives in a negotiation, combine both attitudes: «si nos dan el permiso, empezamos en mayo; si no nos lo dieran, buscaríamos otro terreno». That way you show what you expect and what you see as less likely.
What if we held the vote online?

A possible plan: indicative in both parts.
An imagined condition needs a consequence in the conditional.

Original SpanishCue text in the form of a newsletter from a fictional residents' association in Rosario. The data and people are invented.

Dear neighbours: as every September, the City Council has opened the call for participatory budgeting. This year the rules changed a little. Until 2024 they required each proposal to have fifty signatures; now they require us to gather a hundred and to submit three quotes from different companies. The committee also asked us to keep the project under ten per cent of the district fund. We think this is reasonable, although it forces us to work faster.

Our proposal is a bike workshop on the riverside. If we get the signatures before the twentieth, the committee will review the project in October and, if it approves it, the neighbourhood will be able to vote on it in November. We want all residents to know about it before that date, which is why we are organising a talk at the club on Thursday. It is important that people who don't ride a bike come too: we also need their opinion.

We allow ourselves to dream a little. If the workshop worked well for a year, we could ask the council to include it in its permanent programme. If we also found experienced volunteers, we would run mechanics courses for older adults. And if the river didn't rise so much every autumn, which is a lot to ask, we would keep the bikes stored by the water instead of taking them to the club's shed.

Not everyone agrees, and it is good that it should be so. At the last meeting, some residents preferred the money to go towards lighting the inner streets of the neighbourhood. We are glad they raised it openly. We propose that both ideas be submitted and that the vote decides. What we don't want is for the neighbourhood to end up without a project because we didn't agree in time.

One last practical request. The committee has reminded us that the signature sheets must be complete, without crossings-out and with each resident's ID number. Last year several signatures were not counted because someone wrote their address instead of their ID number. We kindly ask you to check your details before signing, so that this year we don't lose a single supporter.

The form: «hubiera» or «hubiese» + past participle

The pluperfect subjunctive is formed with «haber» in the imperfect subjunctive plus the past participle, which never changes. The -ra and -se forms are equivalent; «hubiera» predominates in conversation. Irregular participles are kept: hecho, dicho, puesto, vuelto, visto, escrito, roto, abierto.

Regret: three kinds of «ojalá» and other expressions

With the pluperfect subjunctive you express regret or sorrow about something that can no longer be changed. The coach's letter after the season
Open letter to the team published in the club newsletter
Original SpanishCue text written as a letter from a fictional rowing club in Santa Fe. The people and results are invented.

Dear team: the season is over and I want to thank you for your effort before talking about results. We came second in the regional final, eight tenths of a second behind first place. I know many of you went home thinking about those eight tenths. So did I. But second place is not a failure, and I ask you to look at it with a cool head.

I'll start with what didn't go well. If we had checked the order of the heats on Friday, we would have known that we were due to start in the wind. Nobody did, and I am the one most responsible. I also believe that, if we had practised more starts during the winter, we wouldn't have lost so much ground in the first few metres. It hurt me that some of you blamed each other on the jetty, because we lost the race together.

Now, what went well. I was moved that Paula, who couldn't row, had travelled anyway to help with the boat and cheer from the shore. I was pleasantly surprised that the youngest rowers had learned in just a few months to coordinate their strokes with the rest. And I was glad that, the next day, nobody missed training.

I also want to be fair to the Rosario team. They won because they rowed better in the final stretch, not through luck. Their coach told me afterwards that they had spent the whole winter practising in a crosswind. If we had done the same, the margin would probably have been different. I'm not saying this so that we feel sorry for ourselves, but because it is the most useful piece of information the final left us with.

Would we have won with different preparation? Maybe, maybe not. If only we had had another chance that same afternoon, but regattas aren't rerun. What we can do is use this experience. That's why I propose three changes: checking the official programme two days in advance, practising starts once a week and training on windy days, even if they are uncomfortable. See you on Monday in the shed.

The form and its first use: what never happened

The conditional perfect is formed with the conditional of «haber» plus the past participle: habría, habrías, habría, habríamos, habríais, habrían + terminado. Its best-known use is to present a past consequence that did not happen. The condition can come with «si + hubiera», but also with a phrase: «con un buen arquitecto», «sin la lluvia», «en tu lugar».
Don't confuse it with the pluperfect indicative: «la obra había terminado» reports a real earlier fact; «la obra habría terminado» imagines or calculates something that was not confirmed.

The conditional perfect also moves the future perfect into the past. If in March the builder said «para junio habremos terminado», today we report it like this: «dijo que para junio habrían terminado». Look for the deadline: «para», «antes de», «a fin de mes».

It also serves to reproach gently: instead of an impossible order about the past, it describes the expected alternative that wasn't taken. «Habrías podido avisarme» or «habrías debido consultar» point out a failing without attacking. «Tendrías que haber…» and «podrías haber…» have the same value.
For reference: you will also hear the conditional perfect used for guesses about the past, as in «cuando llegó el camión, habrían sido las diez».

Present-time markers are the clue: «ahora», «hoy», «todavía», «ya no». If you remove them and the result stays in the past, you are back to the pure hypothesis of week 3.

Inés, two years ago you left Buenos Aires. If you hadn't made that decision, where would you be today?

Probably in the same two-room flat, commuting two hours a day and working late. If we hadn't come back, we wouldn't have this house with a garden today, that's for sure. And we probably wouldn't have a dog either, which was Federico's dream.
But I know the renovation of the house wasn't easy.

Honestly, it was a nightmare. In February the building firm assured us that by June they would have finished everything. In June they didn't even have the windows. What annoyed me most wasn't the delay, because unforeseen problems happen, but that nobody told us. They could have called us once, even if only to say they didn't know when.
And did you do anything wrong?

Yes, of course. If I were less impatient, I wouldn't have had a shouting match with the builder the day the pipe burst. It wasn't his fault. And if we had asked for a contract with dates and penalties, we wouldn't still be paying for repairs now.
Last question: was it worth it?

Yes. If Federico hadn't got the post at the university, maybe we wouldn't have dared, and today we'd have the same life as before, only more tired. To anyone thinking of moving, I'd say: get everything in writing and don't fall out with the builder.

A year in the house on Urquiza Street
Personal blog post
Original SpanishCue text written as a post on Inés Ortiz's fictional blog. The people, the house and the company are invented.

Today it is a year since we first slept in the house on Urquiza Street. That day there was no hot water, the kitchen ceiling was dripping and the front windows were two sheets of plastic tied with tape. If someone had shown me a photo of that night when we were living in Buenos Aires, we probably wouldn't be here. Luckily, nobody took one.

The renovation taught us a lot, almost always the hard way. The building firm had promised us that in four months they would have finished; they took nine. I understand that a house from 1940 hides surprises, but they could have explained to us from the start that the estimate was optimistic. We, for our part, should have asked for a contract with dates. If we had signed one, today we wouldn't still be arguing about who pays for the pipe that burst in August.

I also learned things about myself. If I were a calmer person, I wouldn't have spent the nights of April looking at photos of kitchens we couldn't afford. Federico, on the other hand, is patient by nature; if he weren't, I think the builder would have walked off the job in May. We divided the roles without saying so: I worried and he negotiated.

The neighbours were another surprise. Doña Rosa, from the house opposite, let us use her bathroom for three weeks without us asking. If we hadn't met her, I don't know how we would have survived September. Today she invites us for mate on Sundays and tells us what the street was like when it wasn't paved. If we were still living in a twelve-storey building, we probably wouldn't even know the name of the neighbour next door.

What would have happened if we had stayed? I don't know. Maybe I would have got a promotion, maybe not. What I do know is that today I have breakfast in the garden, I cycle to work and on Sundays we look at the river from the riverside walk. If we hadn't made that change, I would still be waiting for the perfect moment to change my life. And that moment, I know now, never comes on its own.

Beyond «si»: the necessary condition

«Siempre que», «siempre y cuando», «con tal de que» and «a condición de que» present an essential condition: they are equivalent to «only if». With this meaning they always take the subjunctive. «A condición de que» is the most formal; «con tal de que» is common in conversation. If the subject is the same, you can use «con tal de» or «a condición de» + infinitive.

Be careful with «siempre que»: with the indicative it means «whenever» and sets no condition. «Siempre que llueve, se moja el pasillo» describes a habit; «les dejo la terraza siempre que la limpien» sets a condition. Agreement follows the week 2 rule: with a main verb in the past or conditional, the connector requires the imperfect subjunctive.
Necessary condition (= only if)
Connector
Register
Example

Past frame: imperfect subjunctive.

«Whenever»: indicative.
As a necessary condition, «con tal de que» always takes the subjunctive.
Exceptions, foreseen cases and warnings

«A no ser que», «a menos que», «salvo que» and «excepto que» introduce the only exception: they are equivalent to «unless». They also take the subjunctive. «Salvo que» with the indicative, on the other hand, means «except for the fact that» and presents a real fact: «the flat is perfect, except that the lift breaks down every week».

«En caso de que» + subjunctive anticipates a possibility and says what to do if it happens; «por si» + indicative explains a precaution taken now. Finally, «como» + subjunctive at the start of a sentence is a colloquial warning or threat, often in jest; with the indicative, «como» is causal.
In a formal text, avoid «como» + subjunctive: it sounds like a threat. Use «en caso de que» or «si».

«Como si»: comparing with something imagined

«Como si» compares what you see with an unreal or unconfirmed situation. It allows only two tenses: the imperfect subjunctive if the imagined thing happens at the same time («Nico habla como si fuera el dueño») and the pluperfect if it is earlier («entró como si no hubiera pasado nada»). The tense of the main verb does not change this choice: he talks, talked or will talk «como si fuera el dueño».

After «como si» there is never a present subjunctive, indicative or conditional. For a real, known manner «como» + indicative is used («hazlo como te expliqué»). And to protest in a colloquial tone there is «¡ni que…!»: «¡Ni que fuera tu empleada!» means «you are behaving as if I were, but I'm not».
Camila cleans the kitchen as if the inspectors were coming.
Imagined and simultaneous: imperfect.
He looked at us as if we had broken something.
Imagined earlier cause: pluperfect.
Anyone would think you'd paid for the sofa!

Multi-word connectors are pronounced without internal breaks: «siempre_y_cuando», «a_no_ser_que», «con_tal_de_que», «como_si». If you pause in the middle, the listener loses the relationship. Sharing a home without losing friends: a guide for students
Information guide from a university office
Original SpanishCue text written as a guide from the accommodation office of a fictional university in Córdoba. The cases and names are invented; it is not legal advice.

Every March, thousands of students arrive in Córdoba and share a flat for the first time. The experience is usually good, as long as some basic rules are followed from the start. This guide brings together the most frequent questions we received last year and some real cases, with the names changed.

Before signing, read the whole contract. Many landlords accept students without a guarantor on condition that they pay a two-month deposit. Don't sign unless the contract states when and how that money will be returned. If the flat has prior damage, take photos of it on the first day and send them to the landlord in writing. Lucas, a medical student, wrote to us in November: «If I had taken photos of the stain on the ceiling, they wouldn't have deducted half my deposit». Just in case you ever need them, keep all the receipts too.

Living together requires explicit agreements. We recommend that, during the first week, each group writes a chore rota and decides how it will split the costs. Rules work best if nobody imposes them: when one person runs the house as if they were the owner, the others stop feeling that the rules are theirs. An exchange student told us that her flatmate behaved as if he had lived there all his life and she had just arrived on a visit. She felt like a guest in her own home.

Money deserves a section of its own. The fairest approach is to split fixed costs equally, unless someone has a much bigger room; in that case, they can pay a little more. Open a shared account or a shared spreadsheet in the first week, in case questions come up later. A student from Jujuy told us that, for months, her flatmate paid the electricity late as if the bills arrived by themselves. «If only I had said something in April», she wrote to us. «If I had, they wouldn't have cut off the service in the middle of winter».

The most common conflicts have to do with noise, cleaning and visitors. Whenever there's a problem, it's best to talk about it in person and soon. A third-year group explained their method to us: anyone can invite someone to stay the night, as long as they give a day's notice and it isn't more than twice a week. «If we had agreed on it from March», one of them admitted, «we wouldn't be so tired of arguing today».

Finally, think about leaving right from the moment you move in. If a student has to leave before the contract ends, they can usually do so by giving a month's notice, unless the contract says otherwise. Our office checks contracts free of charge: if people had brought them to us earlier, many of the cases in this guide would never have happened. Book an appointment; there's no need to wait until there is a problem.

«Aunque»: the mood depends on what you do with the fact

After «aunque», the subjunctive does not mean the fact is false or doubtful. The mood shows how you use the information you concede. If you present it as something new for the other person, you assert it, and it goes in the indicative. If you both already know it and you only mention it to move on to your answer, you can use the subjunctive. If you are talking about something that may or may not happen, and you mean "whatever happens", you use the subjunctive.

With facts already known you have a choice: the indicative asserts them again and the subjunctive sets them aside. With new information, however, the subjunctive sounds odd, because you take for granted something the other person does not know.
Try the news test: if you could start the sentence with «te cuento que…» (let me tell you that…), use the indicative.

What does not go after «aunque»

To talk about a future possibility, «aunque» is not combined with the future or the conditional: the future asserts that something will happen and the conditional imagines a result; neither concedes an obstacle. The natural form is the present subjunctive.

Nor do you need «pero» in the main clause. «Aunque» already marks the contrast; if you add «pero», the sentence breaks in two and loses force. And do not confuse «aunque» with «sino»: the first accepts an obstacle, the second corrects a negated idea.
Even if diesel goes up, we will keep the price of the grapes.
Possibility: present subjunctive, never «subirá» or «subiría».

For a future possibility after «aunque», use the present subjunctive; the future would assert it.
«Aunque» already expresses the contrast: the main clause does not take «pero».
The closure has already happened and is being reported: «aunque la cierren» would turn it into something that might happen.
Conceding more strongly: «por mucho que», «por más que», «por muy… que»

These structures say that the intensity of the obstacle does not change the result: "no matter how much". That is why they almost always take the subjunctive. Only when you describe something that really happens, again and again, can you use the indicative: «por más que lo limpiamos, el filtro se tapa».

Look at the pieces. With a verb: «por mucho que» or «por más que» + verb. With an adjective or adverb: «por muy» + adjective + «que», and here the subjunctive is the rule. With a noun: «por mucho / mucha / muchos / muchas» + noun + «que», with agreement.

Register and position: «a pesar de que», «si bien», «aun cuando»

«A pesar de que» and «pese a que» work like «aunque» and follow the same mood logic. Without «que», «a pesar de» takes a noun, or an infinitive if the subject is the same: «a pesar de la sequía», «a pesar de trabajar de sol a sol».

Formal texts use «si bien», which concedes a real fact and takes the indicative, and «aun cuando», which with the subjunctive sets up a hypothesis: «aun cuando el Gobierno aumentara el cupo». «Aun» without an accent also combines with a gerund: «aun sabiendo el riesgo, invirtieron».
Position changes the effect. In front, the concession prepares your conclusion; after it, it sounds like a reservation or a retort added at the end.
In a report or a formal letter, alternate «si bien», «pese a que» and «aun cuando» instead of repeating «aunque» three times.
Although the harvest was smaller, the wine came out with more body.

Hearing the mood in the last vowel and marking the concessive pause

In many verbs, the difference between indicative and subjunctive is a single final vowel: «sube / suba», «llega / llegue», «baja / baje». When you listen, that vowel tells you whether the speaker is announcing a fact or leaving a possibility open. When you speak, if you pronounce it weakly, the listener will not know what you meant.

When the concession comes first, the voice stays suspended at its end, pauses briefly and falls at the end of the decision: «Aunque suba el gasoil… | mantenemos el precio». If the concession comes after, the pause comes before «aunque» and the ending sounds like a reservation.

Opinion column
Column by Inés Lucero, an agronomist, in the opinion section of a regional newspaper in Mendoza. The author and the newspaper are fictional.

Every summer, when the irrigation turn gets longer and the city's channels run almost dry, the same debate reappears in Mendoza. Growers ask for more water, residents ask for living trees and the province asks for patience. Although we all know that the Andes have less snow every year, we keep arguing as if the problem were temporary.

It is worth starting with what nobody denies. Although drip irrigation saves up to half the water, it is not within reach of every farm. A family with ten hectares cannot take on debt blindly, however reasonable the technical proposal may be. Even though credit exists, the terms are short and the interest rates high. Anyone who says small growers do not change out of stubbornness has not done the sums.

That said, however much I understand those difficulties, I do not share the conclusion some draw from them: that it is better to wait. Even if next winter brought heavy snowfall, the problem would still be there, because every year more land is irrigated with the same river. Waiting is not neutral; it is choosing to let scarcity decide for us.

Nor am I convinced by the opposite argument, that of those who believe technology will solve everything. However modern the systems may be, the water a farm saves does not go back by itself to the canal or to the city's trees. We need a clear rule about who it is allocated to, and that rule is political, not agronomic.

I therefore propose three modest measures. First, that the province finance drip irrigation for small farms with long repayment terms, even if that means cutting other spending. Second, that part of the water saved go back to the city's trees, which are also Mendoza's heritage. Third, that the turns be published in advance, so that nobody finds out at the gate of their farm.
I know some will call me naive. I accept it. Even though the debate comes back every year, we still have time for the next drought to find us prepared.

«Por muy» + adjective + subjunctive: the intensity does not change the result.
Formal hypothesis with the imperfect subjunctive and a consequence in the conditional.
«Pese a que» + indicative: real fact in written register.

Dear members: I am writing to propose that the cooperative buy, all together, a set of soil moisture sensors that we can share in turns. Although many of you already know it, I will repeat it: from March the irrigation turn will be every sixteen days, and watering by eye is going to cost us more and more.

I know there are reasonable objections. Although the sensors cost almost a million pesos, divided among forty members the expense is small and pays for itself in two seasons. Some say experience is worth more than any device, and it is true that nobody knows their farm like the person who works it. But however much experience we have, we cannot see how much moisture is left fifty centimetres down. I have also been told it is better to wait for a winter with more snow. Even if that winter came, the quota would not go back to what it was, because the province has already shared out the water in the basin.

That is why I ask the assembly to vote for a one-year trial with ten volunteer farms of different sizes, and for the results to be presented at the autumn assembly. However small a farm may be, it should be able to take part. If the trial does not work, I will admit it; if it works, we will have gained time and water. Yours faithfully, Rodrigo Aguirre, member number 112.

Has it happened, does it always happen, or not yet?

Time connectors («cuando», «en cuanto», «tan pronto como», «apenas», «una vez que», «hasta que», «después de que», «cada vez que») do not decide the mood by themselves. The time does. If you tell something that has already happened or something that always happens, you use the indicative. If you talk about something in the future that has not yet happened, you use the subjunctive, even if you are almost sure it will happen.

The same goes for «siempre que» and «mientras»: with the indicative they talk about time ("every time", "while"); with the subjunctive they can express a condition ("as long as"). «Siempre que nos den el permiso» does not mean "every time", but "if they give it to us".
Ask yourself: has this already happened, or is it a habit? If the answer is no, subjunctive.

The future seen from the past, and the infinitive

When you report what someone promised or planned in the past, the future of that moment becomes the imperfect subjunctive: «Nos dijeron que nos avisarían en cuanto llegaran los cascos». It does not matter whether it happened later or not: from the moment of the promise, it was still in the future.

«Antes de que» always takes the subjunctive, even with past facts, because what comes next had not happened yet: «Salimos antes de que empezara la réplica». If the subject is the same, use the infinitive: «antes de salir», «después de revisar», «al llegar», «nada más sonar». In «no salimos hasta que no nos avisen», the second «no» denies nothing: it means the same as «hasta que nos avisen».

What for: «para que», «con el fin de que», «a fin de que»

To explain a purpose, look at who does each action. If the subject is the same, use the infinitive: «Practicamos para salir rápido». If it changes, use «que» + subjunctive: «Practicamos para que los chicos salgan rápido».

The subjunctive tense follows the main verb. With the present, future or imperative: present subjunctive. With a past tense: imperfect subjunctive: «Pintaron flechas en el piso para que nadie se perdiera». In formal texts you will find «con el fin de que», «a fin de que» and «con vistas a» + infinitive. «De manera que» and «de modo que» with the subjunctive express purpose; with the indicative, result.

«Sin que» + subjunctive says that one thing happens and another does not: «Evacuamos el edificio sin que nadie se lastimara». Since «sin» already negates, it combines with «nadie», «nada» or «ningún», not with «alguien» or «algo». With the same subject, the infinitive again: «salieron sin correr».

«No vaya a ser que» (and, in the past, «no fuera a ser que») presents a precaution: you do something just in case what you fear happens. In conversation you also hear «que» + subjunctive after an order: «Habla más alto, que te oigan los de atrás».
If you can add «por si acaso» (just in case) in front, «no vaya a ser que» fits.

Connectors as a single block

Multi-word connectors are pronounced as a single unit, with no pauses in the middle: «en-cuan-to», «tan-pron-to-co-mo», «a-fin-de-que», «no-va-ya-a-ser-que». If you pause inside the connector, the listener loses the thread and the sentence sounds read out.

Also, identical or similar vowels link together: in «no vaya a ser que» you hear almost «no-va-ya-ser-que», and in «una vez que estemos» the «e» of «que» joins the one in «estemos». The natural pause comes at the end of the subordinate clause, before the main action: «En cuanto suene la sirena | salimos».

Thanks for coming. The drill is on Thursday and I want it to go better this time than in April. Hugo, how shall we organise it?

The same as always, with two changes. As soon as the long siren sounds, the children drop, cover and hold on. They don't leave until it stops sounding, even if it takes a minute. Once everything is silent, each teacher opens the door and leaves with her group.
In Mexico we did almost the same. What worries me is the first-graders: at my other school, last year, they started crying before the siren even began, just from nerves.

That's why this year we are going to tell the families in advance, so that they talk to the children at home. And the first-grade teacher is going to tell a story about earthquakes, so that nobody gets scared.
