Article by deputy head Laura Quiroga in the monthly newsletter of a primary school in San Juan. The school and the people are fictional.

In San Juan, grandparents still tell where their parents were on the night of the 1944 earthquake, and almost every family has a memory of some more recent tremor. We live in an earthquake zone and there is no point denying it. What we can do is prepare ourselves, so that fear does not decide for us when the moment comes.

With that aim, on Thursday the 14th we will hold the second drill of the year. We will not announce the time to the pupils, because an earthquake does not give warning either. We do want to tell you, the families, so that you can talk with your children at home and explain that it is a rehearsal. Experience tells us that children who have talked about the drill before going through it get through it much more calmly.

The protocol is simple. As soon as the long siren sounds, each pupil will crouch next to their desk, cover their head and hold on to the leg. Nobody will leave the classroom until the siren stops. Once there is silence, the teacher will open the door and the group will go down the evacuation route marked with arrows, without running or talking, so that everyone can hear the instructions.

This year we have changed the meeting point. In April the groups gathered in the middle of the playground, too close to the gym. Now each grade will have its place in a green rectangle painted next to the court. As soon as the group is there, the teacher will take the register and raise a green sign if everyone is there or a red one if someone is missing, so that the emergency team knows instantly where to look.

We also ask you for a small effort at home. Prepare an emergency backpack and agree on a meeting place with your children, in case an earthquake catches you apart. And if anyone comes home a little nervous on Thursday, listen to them before they go to sleep.

No drill is perfect, but each one brings us closer to a quick, calm response. When the earth moves again, and in San Juan we know it will move again, we want our pupils to know exactly what to do without fear paralysing them.

How is it done? A known way or an open way

«Como», «según», «tal como», «tal y como» and «de la manera que» introduce the way something is done. If that way already exists and you know it (someone explained it, it is on a plan, it is the custom), you use the indicative. If it is still open and someone else decides it, you use the subjunctive: «Lo tejemos como usted quiera».

«Según» sometimes adds the idea of dependence: «Teñimos la lana según esté el tiempo» means the result depends on something we do not know yet. With the indicative, «según» also shows the source of information: «Según me contó mi tía, el poncho era de su padre».
Ask yourself: can I point to that way of doing it (a photo, an explanation, a custom)? If you can, indicative.

Comparing with an idea: «de lo que», «del que», «de la que»

When you compare with an idea or an expectation, not with another concrete thing, you use «de lo que»: «El encargo llevó más tiempo de lo que pensábamos». If what you compare is a noun, the article agrees with it: «más lana de la que compramos», «menos ovillos de los que hacían falta», «más trabajo del que imaginaba».

After «de lo que» you can use the indicative if the expectation is concrete («de lo que calculamos») or the subjunctive if it is open and undefined («va a quedar mejor de lo que te imagines»). Remember that «más que» compares two elements («teje más que su hermana»), not an idea.

Comparing with the unreal: «como si», «igual que si», «tanto como si»

In week 5 you reviewed «como si» + imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive. The same idea of comparing with something unreal is expressed with «igual que si», «lo mismo que si», «tanto como si» or «más que si». They are always followed by the imperfect subjunctive (simultaneous) or the pluperfect (earlier), never the present.
This lets you judge a result forcefully: «El tapiz quedó igual que si lo hubiera tejido mi abuela».

After «como si» the present subjunctive is never used.
The preposition travels with the relative

If the verb in the relative clause requires a preposition (hablar con, aprender de, confiar en, depender de, referirse a), that preposition goes in front of the relative: «la tejedora de la que aprendí», never «la tejedora que aprendí de». To find it, go back to the original sentence: «Aprendí de esa tejedora».

After the preposition, use «el que, la que, los que, las que» (the article agrees with the antecedent) or «quien, quienes» for people, always without an article. In formal register you also find «el cual, la cual». For places, «en el que» and «donde» are usually interchangeable.
If in doubt, undo the relative clause and say the original sentence aloud: the preposition appears by itself.

The «preposition + relative» group has no stress of its own

In «la lana con la que tejemos», the words «con la que» have no stress of their own: they are said quickly and joined to the strong syllable of the verb, «con-la-que-te-JE-mos». The same happens with «de quien», «en el que», «a las que». The main stress falls on the antecedent noun and on the verb.

That is why there is no pause after the preposition. If you say «la lana con… la que tejemos», it sounds as if you are searching for the word. The natural pause, if needed, comes before the preposition or at the end of the relative clause.

Magazine feature
Feature published in a travel and culture magazine about a weaving workshop in San Luis. The people and the workshop are fictional.

Half an hour from the city of San Luis, in an adobe house with a veranda, Elsa Lucero has woven every morning since she was twelve. The loom she works on takes up half the room and creaks every time she passes the shuttle. «My father made it out of carob wood», she says, «and it is better than many new looms I have seen».

Elsa did not study the craft at any school. She learned it from her mother, who in turn had learned it from a neighbour from Renca of whom only one photograph survives today. That is why, when someone asks her about her method, the answer is always the same: «I do it just as I was taught». She warps the threads in the courtyard, dyes the wool with plants from the hills and weaves the way people wove a century ago.

However, not everything in the workshop is tradition. Her grandson Joaquín, who studied design in Buenos Aires, came back three years ago with an idea that at first seemed to the family riskier than they could afford: selling online. Today the Luceros' ponchos and blankets reach shops in Mendoza, Córdoba and Valencia, and sales have grown much more than anyone expected.

The change also brought problems nobody had counted on. The first large order, forty blankets for a hotel, took them twice the expected time and they needed more wool than they had bought. «We learned to calculate», Joaquín admits, «and to explain to the customer that a handmade piece is not manufactured as if it were a T-shirt».

What has not changed is the relationship with customers. Elsa insists that each buyer choose the colours as they prefer and on sending them photos of the samples before starting. Buyers who find it hard to wait always get the same answer: the wool is dyed according to the weather, and the weather cannot be hurried.
At the end of the visit, Elsa gives us a table runner with jarilla stripes. She wraps it with enormous care, just as if she were handing us a family heirloom. Perhaps, in a way, it is one.

We are three siblings from Paraná and we work with clay in the same courtyard where we played as children. We learned the craft from our aunt Nélida, a potter with whom we spent every summer of our childhood and from whom we inherited the wood-fired kiln we still use. We work just as she taught us: we knead the clay by hand, throw each piece separately and leave it to dry in the shade for a week. We prepare the glazes ourselves, depending on the earth we bring from the river, and that is why no two cups come out the same. When someone commissions a piece, we choose the shape and colour together, and then we make it however the customer prefers, even if their choice sometimes surprises us.

When we opened the online shop four years ago, we expected to sell a few pieces a month. We sold many more than we could make and had to learn to say no, something that was harder for us than we imagined. Today we prefer to make fewer pieces and make them well. Every time we send a parcel, we wrap it just as if it were a present for someone in the family. Thank you for coming along with us on this journey.

«Cuyo»: it looks forward

«Cuyo» links a possessor with what belongs to it: «el arquitecto cuyos planos se conservan». It goes between the two nouns and agrees with what is possessed, that is, with the noun that follows, not with the possessor. That is why we say «la ciudad cuyo trazado» (masculine, because «trazado» is) and «el barrio cuyas casas» (feminine plural).

«Cuyo» is never followed by an article: «cuyo el balcón» is wrong. If the verb requires a preposition, it goes in front, as with the other relatives: «la casa de cuyo patio salía música», «la familia para cuya tienda trabajaba».
Cover the possessor and read only «cuyo» + noun: they must agree with each other, like an adjective and its noun. What comes after is in charge.

Writing and speaking: correct alternatives to «cuyo»

«Cuyo» belongs to careful texts: guides, articles, fact sheets, speeches. In speech it is rarely used, and it is natural to rephrase. You can use «del que / de la que / de quien» with a different order («una casa de la que conozco la historia»), make two sentences («Es un edificio precioso. Su fachada es de 1890») or use «que tiene» («una casa que tiene un balcón enorme»).
What is not considered correct in careful language is «que su»: «el vecino que su casa está restaurada». And do not confuse «cuyo» with «¿de quién?»: «cuyo» never asks a question.
Text: «la pintora cuyos murales decoran la estación». In speech: «la pintora que hizo los murales de la estación».
Same information, different register.
Text: «el club cuyo estadio se inauguró en 1907». In speech: «el club que inauguró su estadio en 1907».
«Que su» is not standard; in a careful text use «cuya».
«Cuyo» agrees with what is possessed: «fuentes» is feminine plural.
«Cuyo» is not a question word; to ask about the owner you use «¿de quién?».
«…, lo que» and «…, lo cual»: commenting on a whole fact

When you want to comment on everything said before (a whole fact, not a noun), you use «lo que» or «lo cual» after a comma: «Llovió toda la mañana, lo cual retrasó la grabación». The antecedent is the whole sentence. «Que» alone does not work, because it needs a noun to refer to.

With a preposition in front you chain consequences and reactions: «por lo que» (and so), «con lo cual» (so), «a lo que» (to which), «de lo que» (about which). The preposition depends on the meaning or on the verb that follows: «…, a lo que respondió…», «…, de lo que se quejó…».
Do not confuse this use with «lo que» without a comma, which means "the thing that": «Lo que más me gusta es el trazado».

To refer to a whole fact you need the neuter: «lo cual» or «lo que».
Ideas without a name: «lo + adjetivo + que», «aquello que», «eso de que»

«Lo + adjective or adverb + que» talks about the intensity of something: «No sabes lo bonita que está la fachada». Here the adjective agrees with the noun, even though the article is «lo»: «lo caras que son las entradas», «lo bien que lo explicó».

«Aquello que» and «aquello de» + infinitive refer to ideas that are distant in time or were mentioned long ago: «¿Te acuerdas de aquello de grabar de noche?». «Eso de que» + clause quotes someone else's idea, often with distance or scepticism: «No me creo eso de que nadie visita el museo». And «lo que» + subjunctive leaves the choice open: «Graba lo que te parezca interesante».

The pause before «lo cual» and «lo que»

When «lo cual» or «lo que» comment on a whole fact, you can hear the comma: the voice falls at the end of the fact, pauses briefly and starts the comment in a slightly lower tone, as if adding a remark: «Se cortó la luz | lo cual nos obligó a parar».

By contrast, «lo que» without a comma («lo que más me gusta») is said in one go, with no pause, as part of the same group. When listening, that pause helps you know whether someone is commenting on a fact or naming a thing.

«Cuyo» is pronounced with a «y» like the one in «yo», and its stress falls on the first syllable: «CU-yo», «CU-yas». The audio uses the browser's speech synthesis: it does not certify a regional accent or assess your pronunciation.

Audio guide script
Text of the first three stops of an audio guide prepared by a residents' association in La Plata. The association and the private houses are fictional.

Welcome to La Plata, a city whose plan was drawn before a single house existed. In 1882, when Buenos Aires became the national capital, the province needed a new capital, and a team of engineers and architects designed it from scratch. The result is a perfect grid crossed by diagonal avenues, which lets you cross the city in a straight line and, according to the locals, get lost with surprising ease.

Our first stop is the main square, on whose sides stand the two powers of the time: the cathedral and the town hall. It is no coincidence. The founders wanted the Church and the government to face each other, so the axis joining the two buildings is also the symbolic centre of the city. Notice how tall the cathedral is: its towers were not finished until 1999, more than a century after the first stone was laid.

We now walk along 51st Street to a «casa chorizo» with a plain façade. Its first owners were a family of Italian engineers, whose children went on living here for seventy years. The house was about to be demolished in the nineties, to which the neighbours responded with a campaign that ended with it being declared a listed building. Today you can visit the courtyard, whose tiles are the originals.

The third stop is the station, whose platforms keep the iron roof brought from Europe. For decades the train connected the city with the national capital, so many workers lived here and commuted every day. When the service was cut back, the building was abandoned, which sparked protests from those who saw it as part of their history.

Before we go on, a word of warning. You may have heard the idea that in La Plata all the streets are the same. It is not entirely true: each block has its details, and the interesting thing is to discover them. We ask you to notice what does not appear in the guidebooks: a plaque, a stained-glass window, a jacaranda planted by a neighbour whose name nobody remembers.

The old covered market in my neighbourhood is a 1912 building whose iron structure arrived by ship from Belgium. For fifty years it was the centre of neighbourhood life: grandparents did their shopping there and many immigrant families worked there, whose surnames can still be read on some of the stalls. It was so important that residents organised their timetables around the time it opened.

The building keeps almost intact the central dome, the tiles of the stalls and a clock whose hands stopped, so they say, on the day it closed. Notice how tall the columns are: they were designed so that the air would circulate and food would stay fresh without fridges.

In 1978 the market closed, which left dozens of people out of work and the neighbourhood without its meeting place. The building was abandoned for twenty years, so many residents took it for granted that it would be demolished. However, an association got it declared a listed building, which was followed by a long restoration. Today it houses a farmers' market and a library. Cualquiera que, dondequiera que: when you don't know who or where

When you talk about a person, place or thing you cannot identify, because it could be any, you use «cualquiera que», «quienquiera que», «dondequiera que», «comoquiera que» or «cualquier + noun + que», always with the subjunctive: «Cualquiera que encuentre un animal herido debe avisar a la coordinadora».

«Cualquiera» stands alone when it works as a pronoun and drops the «a» before a noun: «cualquier bolsa», «cualquier persona». The plural, «cualesquiera», is formal and rare. In conversation people prefer «el que», «quien» or «donde» + subjunctive, with the same meaning: «El que llegue primero abre el depósito», «Plantamos donde diga el guardaparques».

«Pase lo que pase», «sea cual sea» and mood in relative clauses

Reduplicated formulas say that the decision doesn't change, whatever happens: «pase lo que pase», «digan lo que digan», «vayas donde vayas», «hagas lo que hagas». With «cual» there is agreement: «sea cual sea el resultado», «sean cuales sean los resultados». With two options: «llueva o no llueva», «quieras o no».

In any relative clause, the mood depends on the antecedent. If it is known and exists, indicative: «Busco a Lidia, que tiene la llave». If it is sought or you don't know whether it exists, subjunctive: «Busco a alguien que tenga la llave». If its existence is denied, also subjunctive: «No hay nadie que tenga la llave».

Reported speech: stating, asking, requesting

Before thinking about tenses, decide what the other person did. If they stated something: «dijo que», «explicó que», «aclaró que». If they asked: «preguntó si» (yes/no question) or «preguntó qué, dónde, cuándo». If they requested or ordered: «pidió que», «nos dijo que» + subjunctive.

When the verb introducing the message is in the past, tenses shift back: present becomes imperfect, present perfect or preterite becomes pluperfect, future becomes conditional and the imperative becomes imperfect subjunctive. If what was said is still true when you report it, you can keep the present: «Dijo que la reunión es los lunes».

A reported request takes the subjunctive; with «pidió», the imperfect subjunctive.

References that change and verbs that add precision

When you report a message at another time or in another place, the references change too: «hoy» may become «ese día», «mañana» «al día siguiente», «ayer» «el día anterior», «aquí» «allí», «este» «ese», «venir» «ir» and «traer» «llevar». Always think from where and when you are speaking.

«Decir» works for everything, but other verbs convey the intention better: «aclaró», «advirtió», «insistió en que», «recordó», «recomendó», «prometió», «propuso». With verbs of influence (recomendar, proponer, insistir en que meaning a request) the message takes the subjunctive.
On Tuesday, the coordinator warned that there would be a storm that night and recommended that we not go to the breakwater.
«Esta noche» → «esa noche»; recommendation in the subjunctive.

Switching voice between the narrative and the quotation

When you tell what another person said in direct speech, your voice changes: you make a short pause after «dijo» and the quotation sounds in another tone, sometimes imitating the intention («¡No se metan al agua!»). In reported speech, on the other hand, everything is in your voice, with no pause after «que»: «dijo que no nos metiéramos al agua».

Reduplicated formulas («pase lo que pase», «sea cual sea», «digan lo que digan») are pronounced as a single block, with the strong stress on the first verb and a pause afterwards: «PA-se-lo-que-pa-se | empezamos».

Newspaper chronicle
Chronicle published in the local section of a Mar del Plata newspaper at the end of the summer season. The people and the organization are fictitious.

On Sunday, while the last tourists were loading their suitcases into their cars, some forty volunteers met at the headquarters of the Costa Limpia network, in the harbour district, to take stock of the season. Its coordinator, Graciela Ibarra, a biologist whose campaigns began six years ago with just five friends, opened the meeting with a figure: between December and March, the network removed almost four tonnes of waste from the beaches, quite a lot more than anyone had calculated.

Ibarra explained that half of what was collected was cigarette butts and plastic bottle caps, which, she said, «shows that the problem isn't just the big dumps, but the small gestures of every day». She clarified that, although the figure may look like a success, it isn't entirely one: «If we collect so much, it's because a lot was thrown away». However much the network grows, she insisted, without a change of habits the work has no end.

It wasn't all figures. The head lifeguard of the southern area, Ramón Etcheverry, reminded the volunteers that nobody was to go into the water to collect waste, whatever happened. He said that in February a young man had gone in with a red flag to rescue a fishing net and that the rip current nearly carried him away. «Anyone who sees something floating, let a lifeguard know», he asked. «That's what we're here for».

Then it was time for plans. Ibarra proposed that next year the network also work on the southern beaches, where access is harder and rubbish piles up for weeks without anyone removing it. To do that, she said, a van is needed and someone to drive it. She asked if there was anyone present with a professional licence, which was followed by an awkward silence. Two days later, as the coordinator herself confirmed to this newspaper, a volunteer who hadn't been able to attend offered to drive, and a harbour shopkeeper, whose name he preferred not to give, lent the van.

There were disagreements too. Some volunteers complained that the shift started at seven in the morning. Ibarra replied that, although she understood the tiredness, it was the only time when the tide was low and the beach empty, so she had no intention of changing it. She did promise, however, that as soon as she had the calendar she would send it so that each volunteer could choose their days in advance.

At the end, the coordinator thanked everyone as if they had saved the whole ocean, and more than one person was moved. Wherever you look, this network's work is small compared with the size of the problem. But anyone who has walked along Varese beach this morning, without a single cigarette butt in sight, knows that the difference exists.

Recalculating time from your own day

Words like «hoy», «mañana», «ayer», «ahora» or «esta semana» have no fixed value: they point to a day starting from the moment someone speaks. When you report what another person said, do not copy them or change them mechanically. Ask yourself which specific day they pointed to and what that day is called from your moment.

If you report the message shortly afterwards, sometimes the word stays the same or changes to a nearby one («mañana» can become «hoy» or «ayer»). If a lot of time has passed, use expressions that look at the day back then: «ese día», «al día siguiente», «el día anterior», «en ese momento». And if there is a risk of confusion, name the day: «el martes».
Before passing on a message, write two dates in the margin: the day it was said and the day you report it. With those two dates, every «mañana» sorts itself out.

Place, people and movement: where are you?

«Aquí» and «acá» point to the speaker's place; «este» points to something close to the speaker. If you report from somewhere else, that place is far from you: «allí» or «allá», «ese» or «aquel». «Aquel» adds distance, in space or in time, which is why it appears a lot in memories. In the River Plate area and in much of Latin America, «acá» and «allá» are preferred in conversation.

Pronouns and possessives adjust to the new conversation: another person's «mi» is «su» for you, and the «te» said to you becomes «me». With «venir/ir» and «traer/llevar», decide from your current position: if you are at the destination, «venir» and «traer»; if not, «ir» and «llevar». And if the place and the day match yours, change nothing.

You are not in Bahía Blanca: the destination is «allá» and the movement is «ir».
Ser + past participle: what receives the action comes first

The «ser» passive turns what receives the action into the subject. «La intendenta inauguró la muestra» puts the mayor in the foreground; «La muestra fue inaugurada por la intendenta» puts the exhibition in the foreground. The verb «ser» carries the tense and agrees in number; the participle agrees in gender and number with the subject.

The agent appears with «por» only if it adds information. If it is obvious, unknown or not important, it is left out: «El techo fue reparado en 2022» is enough. The passive works in all tenses, and also in the continuous form «está siendo + participle», useful for processes that are still open.

When the passive helps and when it feels heavy

The «ser» passive is typical of the press, history, reports and official documents. In conversation it sounds stiff: among friends people say «abrieron el galpón» or «lo abrió la intendenta». If the agent is important and known, the active is usually more direct. Next week you compare these forms with the «se» passive.

Also remember the difference with «estar + participle»: «ser» presents the action («La puerta fue pintada ayer»), and «estar» presents the result you see now («La puerta está pintada»). And do not build passives with the person who receives something: with «dar», «regalar» or «preguntar», the person cannot be the subject of the passive.
Ask yourself who reads the text. If it is a report or a news item, the passive gives order; if it is a message to a friend, change it to the active.

Informative register: the passive fits.

Among friends: active with a general subject.
The clock is already fixed: it tells the exact time.
«Estar» describes the resulting state.

In the passive, the key information is at the end of the participle: «restaurado», «restaurada», «restaurados», «restauradas». It is Thursday in the newsroom of a digital newspaper in Bahía Blanca. Editor of the newspaper
Photographer, spoke to Lucas on Monday
Tomás, Lucas still has a fever and the shed article comes out on Saturday, so we'll finish it ourselves. On Monday he called you from the port, didn't he? What exactly did he tell you?

He called me from White at about eleven. He told me that at that moment he was inside the shed with the guide and that it still smelled of locomotive grease in there. He asked me to go there the next day with the big camera and to take him the recorder, because he had left it here.
So you went on Tuesday. And what did he say about the building?

That the shed was built in 1907 by a British company and that it was closed in the early nineties. The guide explained to him that the yard tracks were taken up before privatisation, but that the repair pits were preserved by the neighbours themselves, who cleaned them every spring.
That's gold. And the opening? The press release says «tomorrow», but the press release is from Monday.

Right, careful with that. That «tomorrow» was Tuesday, that is, the day before yesterday. The exhibition was opened on Tuesday afternoon by the mayor; I was there and took the photos. What still hasn't been decided is the winter timetable.
Perfect. So we don't write «opens today», we write «was opened on Tuesday». Anything else Lucas said?
Yes. He said the guide had promised him a list of the railway workers who worked in that workshop, and that she had asked him to go back there on Friday to collect it.

White's locomotive shed opens its gates again
News story from a regional online newspaper
Original SpanishCue text written as a news story from the fictional newspaper «La Ría Digital». The building and the people are invented.

The locomotive shed in Ingeniero White, built in 1907 and closed for almost thirty years, was reopened on Tuesday as a cultural centre. The opening exhibition, devoted to the port's railway workers, was presented by the mayor to some four hundred people, many of them children and grandchildren of those who worked in that workshop.

The restoration was not quick. The roof was repaired in 2022 with provincial funds; the iron gates were taken down, cleaned and put back by a cooperative of local blacksmiths; and the pits where the engines were inspected were only partly covered, so that the public could see what they were like. According to the architect in charge of the works, Paula Rivas, every decision was discussed with the residents' association, which for years had looked after the building on its own.

During the ceremony, Rivas recalled that the first time she went into the building, in 2019, there was no electricity or water there and that roof let the rain in. «That day I thought it couldn't be saved», she admitted. Néstor Salas, one of the blacksmiths, said that his father had started working in that very shed at fifteen and that that afternoon, for the first time, he had felt that his family's history was in a museum and not in a drawer.

The centre's guide, Mirta Ojeda, announced on Tuesday that school visits would begin the next day and that the following week a list with the names of the workshop's railway workers would be published on the website. The list has not been published yet: as she explained to this newspaper yesterday, it is being checked by the families, who asked for some surnames to be corrected before it comes out.

Visits are free. The winter opening hours will be announced at the end of the month; until then, the centre opens from Wednesday to Sunday, from 2 p.m. to 7 p.m. Anyone who has photos or documents from the workshop can take them to the entrance: they will be digitised and returned to their owners the same day. According to Ojeda, the aim is for the exhibition not to be closed, but to grow every month with what the neighbours bring, because «this shed was built by them, and they have to keep telling its story».

The architect is speaking in the shed, but she is remembering 2019: «aquel» marks distance in time.
Continuous passive: the process is still open when the story is published.

One event, four ways of telling it

The same event can be told by putting in the foreground either whoever acts or what receives the action. The active names the agent; the «ser» passive, which you reviewed last week, puts it in the background; the passive «se» and the impersonal «se» remove it. The key question is: does it matter who did it?

Each form has its typical text. The active is the normal one in conversation and when the agent is news. The «ser» passive belongs to the press and reports. «Se» is the form of notices, recipes, rules and descriptions of processes, because what matters is the action itself.

Agreement or not? Passive «se» versus impersonal «se»

With the passive «se», the thing is the subject and the verb agrees with it: «se vende una entrada», «se venden entradas». With the impersonal «se» there is no subject, and the verb is always singular: «se vive tranquilo en Neuquén», «se trabaja con guantes», «se recomienda llevar agua». Specific people take «a» and, for that reason, the verb does not agree either: «se entrevistó a los voluntarios», «se busca a dos padres acompañantes».

On signs in many areas you see «se alquila departamentos», but the academic norm recommends agreement: «se alquilan departamentos». When there is a periphrasis, the auxiliary verb also agrees: «se pueden reservar visitas». And if you need to talk about something general with a verb that already carries «se» («quejarse», «levantarse»), use «uno» or «la gente»: «uno se levanta temprano».
Do the «a» test: if «a» appears in front of the people, the verb with «se» stays singular.

Se me rompió: the thing controls the verb

To report something that happened unintentionally, Spanish uses «se» + pronoun of the person affected + verb. It works like «gustar»: the person goes in the pronoun (me, te, le, nos, os, les) and the verb agrees with the thing. «Se me cayó el casco», «se me cayeron los guantes». With an infinitive, singular: «se nos olvidó avisar».

If you name the person, the pronoun is still obligatory: «a Mateo se le cayó el celular». Possession is already in the pronoun, so the article is normal: «se le rajó la pantalla», not «su pantalla». The order is always «se» first: «se me», never «me se».

Rompí, se me rompió, se rompió: how much blame do you take?

There are three ways of reporting the same damage. «Rompí el molde» takes ownership of the action. «Se me rompió el molde» presents it as involuntary, but includes me as the person affected. «Se rompió el molde» mentions nobody. Something similar happens with «olvidar»: «olvidé» and «me olvidé de» are personal; «se me olvidó» softens.

The accidental «se» is very useful in excuses and apologies, but it does not erase responsibility. If the problem was your decision, or if another person suffered the consequences, it sounds evasive: in that case, first person. Also, it only works with verbs that describe something that can happen by itself (caerse, perderse, romperse, acabarse, quedarse, borrarse); with verbs that require someone who acts, it does not: «escribí mal la dirección», never «se me escribió».
Ask yourself: did I do it on purpose, did it happen to me or did it happen without me? That answer chooses between «rompí», «se me rompió» and «se rompió».

Field diary: what breaks and what we break
Column in a palaeontology museum's magazine
Original SpanishCue text written as a column by a field technician in the fictional magazine «Huellas del Comahue». The people and the site are invented.

In an excavation season you work at dawn, when the plateau sun is not yet scorching. You get to the site by pickup, the grid squares are shared out and, for hours, people speak little. From the outside it looks like slow work, and it is: last season two hundred and fourteen fragments of a sauropod were extracted, and each one was recorded with a photograph, coordinates and a handwritten record sheet.

Visitors often ask who finds the bones. The honest answer is that the wind finds them. Then Dr Laura Funes's team finishes uncovering them, consolidates them and wraps them in plaster bandages. In official reports we write that «remains were found in the northern sector»; in the camp kitchen we say that the wind left them exposed for us.

There are mishaps in the field too, and over the years I learned to report them properly. Every one of us at some point drops a brush into the grid square, runs out of plaster too early or forgets to note down the depth of a piece. Nobody goes looking for them. Once, a vertebra split in two in a student's hands as he was lifting it. He did not speak for half an hour; the vertebra was already cracked and would have split just the same in anyone's hands.

But there is another kind of mistake. Last summer I decided to remove a block without waiting for the plaster to dry, because I wanted to finish before the afternoon wind. The block came apart. For days, in conversations, I said that «the block had broken on us». It was a lie, or almost: I broke it, by being in a hurry. When I finally said it that way, the director did not reproach me at all; she just asked me to note it on the record sheet so that nobody would repeat the decision.

Since then I tell the volunteers the same thing on the first day: «se me rompió» is for what really slips out of our hands; for what we choose, the first person is better. In a museum bones are displayed, but behind every display case there are record sheets, and a good record sheet says what was found, where it was found and, when necessary, who made a mistake and why.
Notice how the column changes form depending on what it wants to say.

Accidental «se» with a named person: the pronoun «le» is still necessary.
Active in the first person, with «yo» at the end to highlight responsibility.
the plateau
a raised plain, like the one in Patagonia
to consolidate a bone
to harden it with a product so that it does not fall apart
out of haste
because of being in a hurry; «apurado» is common in Latin America

The preposition travels with the verb

Many verbs take a preposition that is not chosen: it comes with them. «Depender de», «darse cuenta de», «acordarse de», «quejarse de», «arrepentirse de», «confiar en», «insistir en», «pensar en», «contar con», «soñar con». That preposition stays whatever the complement: a noun, a pronoun, an infinitive or a «que» clause.

In questions, the preposition goes before the question word: «¿De qué depende?», «¿Con quién cuentas?», «¿En qué piensas?». And with pronouns, the stressed form is used: «confío en ella», «cuento contigo», «depende de ti».
Always learn these verbs with their preposition, as one piece: «contar con», never «contar» on its own.

Before «que», the preposition is still there

If the subject is the same, the infinitive is normal: «Insisto en ir el lunes» (I insist, I go). If it changes, «que» appears: «Insisto en que vayas el lunes». In both cases the preposition stays. Dropping it before «que» («me di cuenta que») is called queísmo and is avoided in careful language. The opposite error, adding «de» where it does not belong («pienso de que»), is dequeísmo.

The most useful test is to replace the clause with «eso»: «me di cuenta de eso» → «me di cuenta de que»; «creo eso» → «creo que». Watch out also for verbs that change meaning with the preposition: «pensar en» (to have on your mind) and «pensar de» (to have an opinion, in questions); «quedar en» (to agree) and «quedar con» (to arrange to meet); «acabar de» (just now) and «acabar con» (to finish something off, to eliminate it).

First the fact, then the comment

You already know how to say «me molesta que lo anunciaran por correo». If you want the fact to be the topic of your sentence, you can put it at the beginning: «Que lo anunciaran por correo me molesta» or, more formally and more clearly, «El hecho de que lo anunciaran por correo me molesta». The fact works as the subject, so the main verb is singular, even if there are plurals inside.

The normal choice in this position is the subjunctive, even when the fact is real and known, because what matters is the comment: «El hecho de que la sede esté lejos explica muchas quejas». With verbs like «demostrar», «significar» or «explicar» it is also the usual choice. In texts that assert the fact as new information the indicative may appear, but for your own writing the subjunctive is the safe option.

Noun + de que: fact or possibility?

Many nouns take «de que» + a clause that explains their content. The mood depends on the noun. Those that present something possible, feared, wished for or necessary call for the subjunctive: «la posibilidad de que», «el riesgo de que», «el miedo de que», «la esperanza de que», «la necesidad de que». Those that present information or certainty call for the indicative: «la noticia de que», «el rumor de que», «la certeza de que», «la impresión de que».

Do not confuse content with a relative clause: in «la noticia que leí», «que» is relative (I read the news) and takes no «de»; in «la noticia de que cierran la sede», the clause says what the news says. In conversation, «lo de que» takes up something that was said: «Lo de que nos cambian de piso, ¿es seguro?».

Unstressed «de que» versus stressed «¿de qué?».

In «depende de que haya metro», the words «de» and «que» are unstressed: they carry no force and join what follows, «dequeaya». In contrast, in the question «¿De qué depende?», «qué» is stressed: it has an accent, force and a tone that clearly rises or falls. If you stress the unstressed «que», your sentence sounds like a question.

Three days at the office: what the email does not say
Opinion column in a newspaper
Original SpanishCue text written as a column in the fictional newspaper «La Hora de Santiago». The author and the companies mentioned are invented.

In recent weeks, several companies in Santiago have sent the same email with different signatures: from March, three days in the office. The news that the office is compulsory again has filled messaging groups, and not always with complaints. Many young workers confess that they missed learning by watching their colleagues, something a screen does not fully achieve.

The problem is not the measure, but how it is taken. The fact that most of these decisions are communicated without a single prior consultation says a lot about how trust is understood in some companies. For three years, teams showed that they could meet their deadlines from home; that they are now not even asked which days they prefer is, to say the least, inelegant.

Moreover, the success of the return depends on factors that do not appear in the emails. It depends on transport: in a city where thousands of people spend more than two hours a day on the metro or the bus, starting at eight is not the same as starting at ten. It depends on space: there are offices that shrank during the pandemic and where there are now not enough desks for everyone. And it depends, above all, on the bosses going in too; nobody believes in a rule that only others follow.

There is also the risk that companies will lose their best professionals, who today can work remotely for firms in any country. It is not an empty threat: in industry surveys the idea that flexibility is worth as much as a pay rise appears again and again. Anyone who does not realise this in time may regret having won an argument and lost a team.

I am not arguing that everything should go back to being remote. I am arguing for something more modest: that people talk before deciding. Companies that have consulted their teams now have agreements that are kept without supervision. Those that have not complain that nobody respects the in-office days. Perhaps the difference lies not in the number of days, but in the conversation that came before.

«La idea de que» with the indicative: the idea is presented as something stated in the surveys.
«Arrepentirse de» + compound infinitive: the action comes before the regret.

No porque…, sino porque…: the action happens, the cause is another

When someone attributes a mistaken cause to something that did happen, you reject it with «no porque» + subjunctive and give the real cause with «sino porque» + indicative. The action is real; what you deny is the reason. The subjunctive marks that the cause is not accepted. The tense follows the frame: present («no porque falten clientes»), perfect («no porque haya bajado la venta») or imperfect if you are talking about the past («no porque estuviera cansada»).

Pay attention to the scope of the negation. «No abrió porque estaba enferma» says that she did not open, and why. «Abrió, pero no porque quisiera, sino porque se lo pidieron» says that she opened and denies the reason. With a noun or an infinitive it works the same with «por»: «no por dinero, sino por cansancio»; «no por ser turista, sino por no avisar».
Before writing, ask yourself: did the action happen? If it did and you only deny the reason, «no porque» + subjunctive.

«No es que…, es que…» and connectors according to their position

«No es que» + subjunctive rejects a possible interpretation; «es que» or «sino que» + indicative give the real explanation. It is very common for softening a refusal: «No es que no quiera ayudarte, es que el sábado trabajo». You can also use it to correct an exaggeration: «No es que el barrio esté mal; es que ha cambiado muy rápido».

Causal connectors have a position and a register. «Como» always goes at the start: «Como suben tantos turistas, abrimos antes». «Porque» usually comes after the main idea. «Ya que», «puesto que» and «dado que» present a known cause and are more formal; «debido a» + noun and «a causa de» belong to informative texts. In conversation, after an order, «que» introduces the cause: «Abrígate, que en el cerro corre viento».
It's not that the music in the street bothers me; it's that at three in the morning I can't sleep.

Tan, tanto, tal: intensity has consequences

When a consequence comes from an intensity, the intensity is marked in the first part and the consequence arrives with «que». «Tan» goes before an adjective or an adverb: «la calle es tan empinada que…», «subían tan despacio que…». «Tanto» agrees with the noun: «tanta gente», «tantos cruceros», «tantas mochilas». After a verb, «tanto» does not change: «llovió tanto que…».

«Tal» + noun highlights the kind or degree of something: «había tal ruido que no oíamos el timbre», «dijeron tales cosas que nadie volvió». «De tal manera que» or «de tal modo que» refer to the manner: «lo explicó de tal manera que todos lo entendieron». The consequence is in the indicative because it is a fact.
Look at the next word: adjective or adverb → «tan»; noun → «tanto» with agreement; nothing (after the verb) → «tanto».

«Así que»: consequence without intensity

If the consequence does not depend on an intensity but on a fact, «así que» is enough, and it comes after a comma: «El ascensor estaba cerrado, así que subimos por la escalera». Do not confuse consequence with cause or purpose: «porque» explains what came before, «para que» states the goal and «así que» reports what resulted.

In more formal texts you will find «por lo tanto», «por consiguiente» or «de modo que», with the same value. And when the main sentence is negative, the imagined consequence can go in the subjunctive: «No es tan caro que no puedas pagarlo». For your own writing, remember the basic rule: real consequence, indicative.
The power went off on the hill, so we closed early.
Consequence of a fact: «así que».

Pauses and focus: when the voice separates the cause and when it joins it to the negation.

Intonation helps you understand what is being denied. In «No abrió, porque llovía», there is a pause after «abrió»: the action is denied and then the cause is given. In «No abrió porque lloviera, sino porque estaba enferma», there is no pause between «abrió» and «porque»: the negation reaches the cause, and the voice rises on «lloviera» and marks the contrast on «sino».

In result clauses, the intensity word («tan», «tanto», «tal») carries an emphatic stress and the voice rises up to it; then a short pause before «que» announces the consequence. So beautiful it wears you out: a Sunday on Cerro Alegre
Chronicle in a cultural magazine
Original SpanishCue text written as a chronicle in the fictional magazine «Puerto Escrito». The people quoted are invented.

At eleven on a Sunday morning in February, Templeman street is so full that you have to walk sideways. Groups arrive from the pier, couples with paper maps and students who come up from the flat part of the city with soaking T-shirts. Since the nearest funicular has been under repair for months, almost everyone walks up, so the last stretch turns into a small procession of breathless people.

The residents tell it without bitterness. «It's not that we're against tourism», explains Ester Valdés, who has lived on the hill for forty years. «It's that the neighbourhood changed so fast that we didn't have time to get used to it». In a decade, half the houses on her block became hostels or souvenir shops, and rents went up so much that several families left for other hills.

It would be easy to blame the cruise ships, but the explanation is more complex. The ships do not bring so many passengers that the hill cannot receive them; the problem is that almost all of them arrive at the same time and walk along the same four streets. Since the guided tours always follow the same route, there are corners of the hill that get saturated and others, two hundred metres away, where nobody goes all day.

Local shops are finding their own way to hold out. A bookshop on Almirante Montt street stopped opening on Sundays, not because it was selling little, but because its owners were exhausted. A bakery does the opposite: it opens at six to serve residents before the groups come up. «There are days with such a crowd that we can't even sweep», says its owner, «but in winter, when nobody comes, it's the residents who save us».

At seven in the evening, when the last group goes down towards the port, the hill gets back some of its silence. You can hear the seagulls and the dogs again. It is so beautiful at that time that you understand why so many people want to see it, and also why those who live here ask, without shouting, for someone to think of them when the routes are designed.

Cuanto más…, más…: two things that change together

To say that one thing increases or decreases at the same time as another, use two parts: «cuanto más / menos…» and then «más / menos / mejor / peor…». It takes no article and no «que»: «cuanto más se pedalea, más se conoce la ciudad», never «lo más… lo más». The subject usually goes after the verb: «cuanto más crece la ciudad…».

«Cuanto» does not change before a verb, an adjective or an adverb, but it agrees with a noun: «cuanta más gente», «cuantos más árboles», «cuantas más bicicletas». With «mayor», «menor», «antes» or «después», «más» is not added: «cuanto mayor es el río…», «cuanto antes, mejor». In many Latin American countries you also hear «mientras más…, más…», with the same meaning.

The mood depends on time. For what is general, habitual or past, indicative: «Cuanto más llueve, más sube el río». For what is future or hypothetical, present subjunctive in the first part: «Cuanto antes empiecen las obras, antes estará el parque». In a past narrative about something that was future at the time, imperfect subjunctive: «Dijeron que cuanto más esperáramos, más caro saldría».
To talk about a single thing that changes over time, you do not need two parts: «cada vez más», «cada vez menos», «cada vez mejor» (never «cada vez más mejor»).

Linking paragraphs: conceding without giving in

In week 6 you reviewed «aunque», «a pesar de que» and «por mucho que» within a single sentence. Now the level is the text: connectors that link a sentence or a paragraph to the next. «Sin embargo» and «no obstante» (more formal) present a contrast: they go after a full stop or a semicolon, and take a comma after them. They can also go in the middle, between commas. Never «pero sin embargo».

«Aun así», «con todo» and «así y todo» say that the result holds despite what came before. «De todas formas», «de todos modos» and «de todas maneras» indicate that, whatever the previous point, what follows holds. «Pese a» + noun or infinitive and «pese a que» are formal. In conversation, «y eso que» + indicative adds, after the main idea, a fact that would lead you to expect the opposite: «Llegó en bici, y eso que llovía».

Objecting in a debate: ahora bien, eso sí and other phrases

«Ahora bien» accepts what has been said and opens an important objection or condition: «El parque es necesario. Ahora bien, ¿dónde estacionarán los feriantes?». «Eso sí» adds a condition or a nuance, often in a friendly tone: «Apoyo la ciclovía; eso sí, con buena iluminación». «Aunque» can work like «pero» to correct yourself: it always comes after and takes the indicative: «Me gusta el plan, aunque no me convence el plazo».

In an oral debate, conceding before objecting makes your position more convincing. The most useful phrases: «Tienes razón en que + indicative, pero…», «No digo que no + subjunctive, pero…», «Puede que tengas razón, pero…», «Es cierto que…; ahora bien…», «Ya, pero…» (colloquial).
Concede first and object afterwards: your partner listens to the objection better if you have acknowledged their point first.
You are right that shops need customers, but cyclists buy things too.

Connectors with their pause and the two-beat rhythm of «cuanto más…, más…».

Concessive connectors form a group of their own: there is a pause before and a short pause after, and the voice stays suspended on them: «El proyecto es caro. | Sin embargo, | tiene apoyo». «Ahora bien» and «eso sí» are usually said on a slightly higher pitch, because they announce something important.

In «cuanto más…, más…» the sentence has two beats: the voice rises at the end of the first part and falls at the end of the second, with a pause in between. Both words «más» carry stress. The riverside under debate

It is Wednesday afternoon on a local radio station in Concepción. The programme «Ciudad abierta» devotes half an hour to the public consultation on the plan to turn a car park by the Biobío river into a park with a bike path. Javiera, an engineering student and cyclist, and Héctor, owner of a nearby hardware shop, take part. Paula is the host. Listen first without the transcript. The voices are synthetic and do not represent a verified regional variety.
Programme host

Owner of a nearby hardware shop, with doubts
Good afternoon. Up to yesterday more than nine hundred submissions had been received, so many that the council extended the deadline to the end of the month. Javiera, why do you support the park?

Because the more people can reach the river without a car, the better the city will be. Today the bank is a car park, and the fact that the most beautiful place in Concepción is full of cars seems absurd to me. I'm not saying it because I hate cars, but because the river belongs to everyone.

You're right that the riverbank could be better; nobody disputes that. That said, my customers carry bags of cement and wooden boards. I'm not saying the park shouldn't be built, but if they remove the parking, my business depends on there being another solution.
Héctor, at Monday's meeting you said the council had never asked you anything. Do you still think the same?

Partly. That day the councillor promised me that she would come to the hardware shop on Tuesday to listen to the shopkeepers, and she came, that has to be said. However, she forgot to bring the plans, so we were talking in a vacuum.
And that's despite the plans being published online a month ago. Anyway, I understand the point about loading. A loading and unloading zone could be set aside in the street behind.
That interests me. Even so, I'm worried about the winter: when the river rises, the bank floods so much that nobody will go for a walk there in July.
That's precisely why the design includes a wetland: the more space the water has to spread out, the less damage it will do in the neighbourhoods. It's an idea that's used in many cities with rivers.
A listener writes to us: «I have been parking there for twenty years and nobody asked me if I wanted a park». Héctor, do you feel represented?
Not entirely. That nobody asked him is true, but now the consultation is open, and the more people take part, the harder it will be for them to decide without us.
We have one minute left. Is there any common ground?
Yes: the park, but not at the expense of local shops. Mind you, I want to see the loading zone on the plans before I sign anything.
That seems fair to me. The sooner they include it, the sooner we'll stop arguing and start building.

Feature in a university magazine
Original SpanishCue text written as a feature in the fictional magazine «Campus Biobío». The project, the data and the people quoted are invented.

Anyone walking along the banks of the Biobío today, a few blocks from the main square, comes across a curious image: one of the widest rivers in Chile flows behind a row of parked cars. The land, almost four hectares, was handed over to the council in 2019 and has worked as a free car park ever since. In March, the project to turn it into a park with a bike path and a wetland was approved by the city council, and that same month a public consultation was opened to collect submissions.

The response exceeded all expectations. More than nine hundred submissions were received in three weeks, so many that the deadline had to be extended to the end of the month. Residents, local market stallholders and the two nearby universities were consulted. According to the technical team, the more opinions are gathered before putting the works out to tender, the fewer changes will have to be made during the works, which is when changes cost more.

The arguments in favour are well known. The city has few green spaces by the water and, in summer, the centre gets so hot that many families look for shade outside the district. The fact that the most central riverbank is occupied by cars, the supporters say, shows that the city has turned its back on its river for decades. In addition, the wetland is not decoration: the more space the water has to spread out during floods, the less risk the low-lying neighbourhoods will face.

The objections, however, do not come only from those who defend the car. The shopkeepers on Barros Arana street are not against it because they distrust the park, but because their business depends on customers being able to load goods nearby. «I'm not saying a park isn't needed», a local hardware shop owner explained on Monday at the community centre, «but nobody remembered us when the plans were drawn». That same afternoon, the councillor in charge promised that she would go to listen to the shopkeepers the next day. She went; however, according to several witnesses, she forgot the plans and the meeting ended without specific agreements.

There are also technical doubts. A civil engineering academic points out that the land floods almost every winter and that, therefore, the bike path will have to be built on an embankment. Even so, she considers the project viable. «It's more expensive than was said at first», she admits; «that said, the sooner it's done, the less it will cost, because construction prices keep going up».

Despite the differences, in recent weeks a compromise has begun to take shape: keeping a loading and unloading zone in the street behind, planting more trees than planned and opening the park in stages. It is nobody's proposal in particular, even though nobody presented it as such. Perhaps that is the lesson of this consultation: the more you listen before deciding, the less you have to correct afterwards.

To the technical team: I am making this submission as a resident of the Centro neighbourhood and a regular user of the Biobío riverbank. The park project was approved by the council in March and, according to the published information, two hundred trees will be planted and a two-kilometre bike path will be built. I think it is a valuable proposal and I want to support it with some conditions.

The meeting took place; however, she forgot the plans, so the shopkeepers still do not know where they will be able to load goods. They are not against it because they distrust the park, but because their work depends on there being a loading zone nearby.

I have to acknowledge that the project is expensive and that the land floods almost every winter. Even so, the fact that a wetland is included seems a sound decision to me: the more space the river has during floods, the less damage the low-lying neighbourhoods will suffer. That said, the current design concentrates the trees at one end, and the rest is so exposed to the sun that it will be hard to use in summer.

For this reason I propose three changes: setting aside a loading zone in the street behind, spreading the trees along the whole bike path and opening the park in stages. The sooner they are incorporated into the project, the less they will cost. I trust these comments will be useful, and I remain available to the team to take part in the next meetings. Yours faithfully, Carolina Muñoz.

The result in your hands: tener, llevar and dejar + participle

With «haber» you report an action that was done and the participle never changes: «hemos revisado las fichas». With «tener», «llevar» and «dejar» you present the result of that action, and then the participle behaves like an adjective of the direct object: it agrees with it in gender and number. «Tengo revisadas las fichas», «llevamos embaladas doscientas cajas», «dejé cerrada la bodega».

Each verb adds a nuance. «Tener» presents something ready, available. «Llevar» adds up what has been done so far and leaves the task open, so it usually comes with a quantity. «Dejar» tells how something was left when you went away or let go of it. There are also fixed forms that don't agree because they have no visible object: «tengo entendido que…», «tengo pensado mudarme», «te tengo dicho que no…».
Before you write the participle, underline the direct object. If the auxiliary verb is «tener», «llevar» or «dejar», copy its gender and number.

How it all ended up: quedar, quedarse, ir and andar + participle

With «quedar» and «quedarse» the participle agrees with the subject. «Quedar» is used mainly with things and situations, often without anyone wanting it: «la puerta quedó abierta toda la noche». «Quedarse» appears more with people and usually expresses something involuntary: «me quedé dormida en el bus». «Ir» and «andar» describe how someone or something is while moving or during a phase: «el seguro va incluido», «anda preocupado desde el lunes».

Some verbs have two participles. With «haber» both are valid («han imprimido» and «han impreso», «ha freído» and «ha frito»), but as an adjective the irregular one is preferred: «los folletos impresos». Other adjectives look like participles but aren't: you say «estoy despierto» but «me he despertado». And several participles gained a new meaning as adjectives: a «leída» person has read a lot, an «atrevida» person takes risks and someone «agradecido» feels grateful.

Obligation or deduction: deber, deber de and tener que

«Deber + infinitive» expresses an obligation or firm advice: «debes devolver el libro el viernes». «Deber de + infinitive» expresses a deduction: you don't know something for sure, but you assume it from what you see. «Debe de ser el camión: ya son las nueve». Grammars also accept «deber» without «de» for deducing, but advise against using «deber de» to oblige.

Deduction can look at the past: «debía de ser muy tarde», «debió de olvidarse», «debe de haber llovido toda la noche». When the deduction is almost certain, «tener que» is used: «tiene que haber una gotera en el techo, el suelo está mojado». That way you can rank how sure you are: «tiene que» (almost certain), «debe de» (probable), «a lo mejor» or «quizás» (possible).
Ask yourself whether someone is giving an order or making an assumption. If it's an assumption, add «de» and the sentence becomes clear to any reader.

Haber de, hay que in every tense, and venir a

«Haber de + infinitive» is an obligation typical of formal or written texts: «los libros han de devolverse en buen estado». In Mexican speech and in other areas it is also used to make assumptions: «ha de estar en la oficina». «Haber que» is impersonal and is conjugated in every tense, always in the singular: «hubo que», «había que», «habrá que», «habría que», «aunque haya que». «Debe de haber» is also singular when «haber» means to exist: «debe de haber cien cajas», never «deben de haber».

«Venir a + infinitive» is used to approximate a figure («la mudanza viene a costar trescientos mil pesos») or to sum up an equivalence («lo que propone viene a ser cerrar un mes»). And if you want to soften an obligation, put the verb in the conditional: «deberías», «tendrías que», «habría que».
On Saturday it took six people to carry the shelves.

Diary of a move: the Rayen changes house
Entry from a community library's newsletter
Original SpanishCue text written as the newsletter of the fictional Rayen library in Temuco. The people and places are invented.

For twelve years, the Rayen Library operated in the neighbourhood parish hall. When the parish told us it needed the space, many of us thought we would have to close. That didn't happen: the neighbourhood council offered us a wooden house three blocks away, with a courtyard and a large room that used to be a sewing workshop. The contract was signed in September and we haven't stopped since.

Today we can take stock for the first time. We have almost four thousand books inventoried and three hundred boxes packed so far, each one labelled by section. The metal shelves are dismantled in the hallway, and the wooden ones, which were too heavy, we left installed in the parish as a donation for catechism classes. The volunteers from the carpentry workshop plan to build new furniture from salvaged boards.

Not everything has gone well. In the first week we found a damp patch in the kitchen of the new house. For days we argued about the cause: some said there had to be a leak; others, that the neighbour must be watering against the wall. In the end a builder climbed onto the roof and found a loose zinc sheet. It had to be replaced before we brought in the books, because wet paper can't be saved. The repair came to about the same as two months of electricity.

We also learned something about ourselves. A project like this must have clear rules, but it can't depend on just one person. That's why every Saturday someone writes on the whiteboard which boxes were moved and what's missing. Nobody should take keys home, and every night the last person to leave turns off the heaters. It seems obvious, but one Friday the courtyard door was left open and a dog came in and fell asleep on the children's section.

If all goes well, we will open the new house on the first Saturday of December. We'll have to paint the front and finish the shelves, and there must still be about a hundred boxes at the parish. If you have a free afternoon, come along: you don't need to know about books, just bring some enthusiasm and, if you can, a flask of tea.
Notice how the newsletter separates what is done, what needs to be done and what is only assumed.

How long you've been at it: llevar + time + gerund

«Llevar» + amount of time + gerund measures an action from when it began up to the moment you are talking about: «llevamos ocho meses lijando el casco». It works in the present, the imperfect and the future: «llevaba dos años trabajando en Castro cuando la conoció», «en abril llevaré un año viviendo aquí». It isn't used in the preterite; for a closed duration say «estuve dos años viviendo en Castro» or «viví dos años en Castro».

If what you are measuring is time without doing something, use «llevar» + time + «sin» + infinitive: «lleva tres semanas sin venir al astillero». And with a place or a state no gerund is needed: «lleva un año en Puerto Montt», «llevo una semana resfriado». Pronouns can go before «llevar» or attached to the gerund: «lo llevamos pintando dos días» or «llevamos dos días pintándolo».
Before using «llevar», ask yourself whether the action is still open at the moment you are talking about. If it has finished, change the verb.
Rocío has been building boats for thirty years.
Present: the action continues.
When the wood arrived, we had been waiting for it for a month.
Imperfect: duration up to a point in the past.
Tomás hasn't shown up at the workshop for two Saturdays.
«Sin» + infinitive: time without doing something.
«Llevar» + gerund doesn't take the preterite: a closed duration is expressed with «estar» or with the verb alone.
After «sin» comes the infinitive.
How it is progressing: ir, venir and andar + gerund

«Ir» + gerund presents gradual, step-by-step progress: «el casco va tomando forma», «ve preparando las herramientas mientras llego» (start and keep going). «Venir» + gerund looks from a point in the past up to today and usually indicates that something is repeated or insisted on: «la cooperativa viene pidiendo un muelle nuevo desde 2019». It is very common in the press.

«Andar» + gerund is colloquial: it describes an activity done here and there, without order, and often carries criticism: «anda diciendo que la lancha no flotará». In Mexico and other areas it is used a lot and is usually neutral: «ando buscando trabajo».

The phases of an action at a glance

You already know the phase verb phrases. Here we just put them in order so you can choose quickly. «Echarse a» and «romper a» mark a sudden start, especially with llorar, reír or correr: «se echó a reír», «rompió a llover». «Volver a» indicates repetition. «Estar a punto de» marks something imminent; «estar por» means the same in many parts of Latin America, and in others, to feel like doing something. «Acabar» + gerund and «terminar por» + infinitive tell the outcome after a process.
Notice that they can all be combined with the previous ones: «llevábamos un mes sin lijar y volvimos a empezar»; «después de tanto discutir, acabamos aceptando su propuesta».

The future perfect: looking back from the future and guessing

The future perfect is formed with the future of «haber» and the past participle: «habré terminado». Its main use is to place yourself at a future moment and look back: what will already be done by then? That reference point almost always appears: «para marzo», «antes de la regata», «cuando llegue el invierno», «dentro de un año». It is also used to take stock up to a future date: «cuando me jubile, habré construido cuarenta botes».

Without a future reference point, the same form is usually read as a guess about something that has already happened: «Tomás no contesta; habrá dejado el teléfono en el taller». It is a hypothesis, not a fact, so it's best to check it before acting.
Look for the reference point. If there is one, it's a forecast; if there isn't and you are talking about something that has already happened, it's a guess.

«Ha terminado» or «habrá terminado»: one syllable that changes the tense.

The present perfect and the future perfect start the same way, but the future has one more syllable and the stress falls at the end of that form of «haber»: ha / ha-BRÁ, hemos / ha-bre-MOS, han / ha-BRÁN. Auntie, do you know how long we've been at this boat? Eight months. Eight months sanding, changing planks, caulking. And the people on the pier are going around saying it won't be ready for the regatta.

Let them say what they like. The hull is coming along nicely, plank by plank. I've been doing this for forty years and I've never launched a boat before it was ready. By the end of January we'll have finished the bottom, and in February there'll only be the painting left.
And the engine? Don Aurelio has been warning since the summer that it's rusty, and the truth is he hasn't come to check it for weeks.

He must have had trouble with his back again. Last month he was about to have an operation. Don't worry: the mechanic from Calbuco is coming by again on Thursday, and by the time he finishes, Aurelio will have recovered and will want to have his say about everything.
Right. Listen, another thing. The cooperative has been asking for progress photos for the website. Shall I send them the ones from last Saturday? You can see the new bow.

Done. I'll also tell them we were about to give up in July, with all that rain. That explains why we're a month behind. You know what? When we launch her, I'm going to cry like a child.
Me too. The last time I launched a boat, my dad burst out laughing in the middle of the pier and didn't stop for half an hour. Right, back to sanding, the oak won't sand itself.

Story for a fishermen's cooperative newsletter
Original SpanishCue text written as a story in the fictional newsletter of the Angelmó Fishermen's Cooperative. The people and the boat are invented.

By the time this newsletter reaches your homes, the «Esperanza» will have turned sixty-two. She is a larch and oak boat that for decades carried shellfish from Chiloé to Puerto Montt, and which has been abandoned in a corner of the boatyard since 2015. This year, a group of members decided she wasn't going to rot there. Since March, every Saturday, the cooperative has been gathering volunteers to restore her.

The work is going at a slow pace. It is led by Rocío Aguilar, a wooden-boat builder who has been building and repairing vessels for forty years. «At first I thought it would be enough to change ten planks», she says. «We ended up changing forty-three». Each new plank has to be bent with steam, fitted and caulked by hand, with oakum and pitch, as it used to be done. Her nephew Tomás, an engineering student in Puerto Montt, hasn't missed a Saturday in eight months, although he admits that in July he was about to give up: «It rained three weekends in a row and you couldn't work».

Not everything depends on the group. The original engine, a 1970 diesel, has been causing problems since day one. Don Aurelio Mancilla, who was the boat's last skipper, knows it better than anyone, but he hasn't shown up at the boatyard for weeks. «He must have had to take care of himself», they say on the pier, and nobody dares call him so as not to bother him. Meanwhile, a mechanic from Calbuco comes back to check it every fortnight.

The deadlines are tight, but Rocío is clear about them. By the end of January they will have finished the bottom; in February they will paint the hull blue and white, the colours of the first owner; and before the regatta on 10 March they will have tested the engine in the bay. If all goes well, that day the «Esperanza» will leave the Angelmó pier with twelve volunteers on board.

And afterwards? Nobody has decided yet. Some propose using her for school trips; others, keeping her as a floating museum. What is clear is that, when they launch her, the cooperative will have recovered more than a boat: it will have brought three generations of the cove together again around the same work. If you want to help, on Saturdays from nine there's coffee, homemade bread and always a free piece of sandpaper.

In class you worked on these two tools with your teacher. Here you review them another way: with a trunk from 1912 that turns up in a museum in Punta Arenas, tables to consult and the mistakes that come up most when someone guesses about the past or writes an informative text.
Guessing: the verb moves one step forward

To present something as a guess and not as a fact, Spanish moves the verb one tense forward. What would be present becomes simple future: «serán las ocho» (I suppose it's eight). What would be present perfect becomes future perfect: «habrá llegado». What would be imperfect or preterite becomes simple conditional: «tendría veinte años cuando se embarcó», «se conocerían en el puerto». And what would be pluperfect becomes conditional perfect: «ya habría salido de Split cuando empezó la guerra».

Questions with these tenses express doubt or curiosity; they don't ask anyone for a fact: «¿Quién será la mujer de la foto?», «¿Por qué guardaría estas cartas?». They are very useful when you are thinking out loud.
First say the sentence as a fact. Then move the verb one step: present → future, past → conditional.

Conceding, comparing and not confusing it with a hypothesis

With «pero», these tenses are used to concede something and set another idea against it: «será muy antiguo, pero está perfecto» (I accept that it's old); «tendría dinero, pero vivía con muy poco». You also have other ways to guess, each with its own mood: «a lo mejor» + indicative, «quizás» or «tal vez» + indicative or subjunctive, «seguramente» + indicative, «debe de» + infinitive and «puede que» + subjunctive.

Don't confuse the conditional of guessing with that of a hypothesis. «Tendría veinte años» guesses at something real in the past; «si tuviera veinte años, viajaría» imagines an unreal condition. In many parts of Latin America the simple future is little used for plans («voy a viajar»), but the future of guessing is alive everywhere.
It may be expensive, but it's worth every peso.

Precise noun phrases: ellipsis and relative clauses

When you leave out a noun («las de 1912», «los del puerto»), the reader must be able to recover it without hesitation. If you previously mentioned photos and postcards, «las de 1912» could be either: repeat the noun. If you only talked about photos, the ellipsis is clear.

Relative clauses without commas select a part: «las cartas que están escritas en croata» (there are others that aren't). Relative clauses between commas comment on the whole group: «las cartas, que están escritas en croata, …» (all of them are). «Quien» and «el cual» without a preposition only appear in the comma type; in a restrictive clause use «que».

What relationship «de» expresses, gender that changes meaning, and nominalisation

«De» can express many relationships: «el retrato de Ana» can be the one Ana made, the one that shows her or the one that belongs to her. If the context doesn't make it clear, make it explicit with a participle or a preposition: «el retrato realizado por Ana», «el retrato de Ana hecho por su hermano», «el libro sobre Magallanes». Gender and plural also carry information: «el orden» (organisation) and «la orden» (command), «el capital» (money) and «la capital» (city), «el cometa» (comet) and «la cometa» (kite); «los paraguas» doesn't change in the plural.

Nominalisation turns an action into a noun to condense information: «cuando el barco llegó en 1912» becomes «la llegada del barco en 1912»; «decidieron restaurar las fotos» becomes «la decisión de restaurar las fotos». It is typical of titles, reports and labels. Use it in moderation: if you chain too many nouns with «de», the text becomes opaque.

Original SpanishCue text written as wall text for a fictional museum in Punta Arenas. The family and the objects are invented, although Croatian immigration to Magallanes is a historical fact.

Ivo Marinovic's arrival in Punta Arenas, in the winter of 1912, does not appear in any newspaper. What we know comes from a wooden trunk that his descendants donated to the museum in 2023 and which held a passport, fourteen letters and twenty-two photographs. This exhibition brings those objects together and offers a cautious reading: it separates what the documents prove from what we can only suppose.

The passport, which was issued in Split, confirms that Ivo was born in 1893 on the island of Brač. He would therefore have been nineteen when he set sail. We don't know the name of the ship; like so many young men from the Dalmatian coast, he probably travelled on a steamer that stopped in Buenos Aires before crossing the Strait of Magellan. The crossing would have taken about forty days.

The letters he wrote to his sister Marija between 1912 and 1930 form the core of the exhibition. They are in Croatian and have been translated by volunteers from the community. In the first ones, Ivo talks about the cold, about working in a bakery and about missing the Adriatic Sea. In the last ones, by then married with three children, he barely mentions going back. He had probably decided to stay long before he wrote it; the letters show that he put down roots without announcing it.

The photographs raise more questions. In one of them, taken around 1915, a young woman in a dark dress poses in front of a stone house. Could it be Marija? The dedication only says «so that you don't forget me». The family believes it is; we prefer to present it as a hypothesis. The portrait of Ivo made by his son Pedro around 1950, on the other hand, is signed and dated.

The donation of the trunk came with a request: that Ivo's story be told without embellishment. We have tried to respect it. That is why each label in this room clearly indicates which information comes from a document and which is an interpretation by the museum team, which may change if new evidence appears. If you recognise any of the people in the photos that are not identified, we would be grateful if you would let the museum reception know.
