Pronoun compulsory, recommended or impossible?

When you put a known direct object at the beginning, you have to repeat it with a pronoun: «el escenario ya lo armamos», not «el escenario ya armamos». The unstressed pronoun is also compulsory when the object is a stressed pronoun: «me lo dijo a mí», never «lo dijo a mí». With the indirect object after the verb, the pronoun is highly recommended and is the most natural option: «le di las llaves a Martín». With verbs like «gustar», «molestar» or «importar» it is always needed: «a la vecina le molesta el ruido».

On the other hand, there is no pronoun when you bring a word forward to highlight it as new or surprising information (focus): «ESO te dije yo», «algo sabrá Martín», «tres años llevamos con el tablado». Notice that the subject usually goes after the verb. A noun without an article isn't repeated either: «sillas no tenemos», «entradas ya no quedan».
If the object comes first, ask yourself: is it something already known (the pronoun goes in) or is it the new information I want to highlight (it doesn't)?

Contrast, «a mí me» and variation

To contrast two topics, the pronoun appears with the first one and the second is reduced: «a Olga la llamé ayer; a su hijo, no». «A mí me parece» is not a faulty redundancy: «a mí» marks the contrast with other people and «me» is compulsory. That's why you don't say «yo me parece», because «parecer» doesn't have «yo» as its subject. When «se» doesn't make clear who you are talking about, add «a ella», «a usted» or «a ellos»: «se lo expliqué a ella».

In speech in many areas «le» for «les» with a plural object is common («le dije a los vecinos»); the norm recommends «les», especially in writing. Also very common in much of Latin America is «se los dije» to indicate that «ellos» or «ustedes» received something («se lo dije a ellos»); you hear it a lot, but in a formal text «se lo dije a ellos» is better.

The scale of politeness: three ways to create distance

A direct order («baja la música») works between people who know each other well. To create distance you have three grammatical tools. The first is to ask instead of ordering: «¿puedes bajar la música?». The second is to move the verb away from the present: conditional («¿podrías…?»), imperfect of politeness («quería pedirle un favor») or «quisiera». The third is to remove the person: «se ruega moderar el volumen», «se agradece la puntualidad», or an infinitive on a sign: «no estacionar».

Notice the difference between «¿te importaría + infinitive?» (the other person does something: «¿te importaría cerrar la puerta?») and «¿le importaría que + imperfect subjunctive?» (you ask permission or someone else acts: «¿le importaría que pusiéramos el escenario frente a su casa?»). «Me gustaría que», «quisiera que» and «le agradecería que» also take the imperfect subjunctive: «le agradecería que me informara antes del viernes».

Ordering without the imperative and choosing the form of address

Not all orders use the imperative. The present can sound blunt: «tú te quedas en la puerta». The infinitive appears on signs and general instructions («no fumar») and in familiar exclamations («¡a ensayar!»). «¡Que + subjunctive!» insists on or repeats an order: «¡que bajes el volumen!». And «haz el favor de + infinitive» sounds like a reproach: «haz el favor de llegar puntual».

Choosing the form of address is also choosing the distance. In Latin America, «ustedes» is the only plural; in much of Spain «vosotros» (familiar) is distinguished from «ustedes» (distant). In Costa Rica and in many Colombian families «usted» is used even within the family. In Uruguay and Argentina many people use voseo among friends: you'll hear «cerrá», «vení», «pasame»; recognise it, even if you use «tú». With an older neighbour you don't know, «usted» is the safe option.

Before asking for something, think about three things: how close you are, how much it costs the other person and whether it is spoken or written. The higher each one is, the more grammatical distance.

Focus can be heard: strong stress on the highlighted word and a friendly tone in requests.

Club column in a neighbourhood newspaper
Original SpanishCue text written as the column of a fictional neighbourhood club in a Montevideo community newspaper. The people and the club are invented.

Every February, for twenty-two years, our club has set up a carnival stage on the corner of the square. This year we're going to do it again, but not in the same way. Last year we received three formal complaints, and all three we read carefully. The neighbours who signed them, we called one by one; the city government, on the other hand, we answered in writing. This column sums up what we learned and what we commit to changing, because a neighbourhood party only makes sense if the whole neighbourhood feels it is theirs.

First of all: the murga is not the problem. That's what everyone told us, even those who complained most. Most of the neighbourhood loves watching the groups rehearse in the street. What bothers people is what comes afterwards: recorded music at full volume, cars in front of garages and Sunday's rubbish. A lot of noise we made, it's true, and few solutions we offered.

That's why this year we have changed several things. The recorded music, we'll cut it at one. The speakers, we'll point them towards the square. There will be signs with a clear message: «No parking in front of garages». And in every neighbour's letterbox on the block we'll leave the phone number of a person in charge, so that they call us before calling the police. On Sundays at nine, a group of members will go round the square to leave it clean.

We also have something to ask of you. We would like neighbours who have a complaint to tell us directly; we assure you we will listen. We would also be grateful if you kept the pavements clear while the stage is being set up, on Friday afternoon. And if anyone wants to help, any help is appreciated: members we don't have too many of, and hands neither.

We know that a street party is always a difficult balance. To some it seems too little and to others, too much. To us it seems worth trying, as long as we can all sleep on Sunday. We look forward to seeing you on Saturday the 14th from eight o'clock. Those who come with small children will have a reserved area near the club entrance.

Ordering, adding, giving examples and rephrasing

A presentation is easier to follow when the listener knows where they are. To order, use «en primer lugar… en segundo lugar… por último», «para empezar» or «a continuación»; to present two sides, «por un lado… por otro (lado)» or «por una parte… por otra». To add, «además» and «asimismo» (more formal); «es más» and «incluso» raise the strength of the argument; «encima» also adds, but it is colloquial and usually sounds like a complaint.

To give examples, «por ejemplo», «es el caso de» or «pongamos por caso». To rephrase, «es decir», «o sea» (more spoken) and «en otras palabras»; «mejor dicho» corrects what you have just said: «son trescientos comercios, mejor dicho, doscientos ochenta». In writing, these connectors usually go between commas or after a semicolon.
Before writing, number your arguments on a piece of paper. Then choose one connector for each step and don't repeat the same one twice in a row.

Concluding, refuting and attributing

To draw consequences, «por (lo) tanto», «por consiguiente» and «así que»; «de ahí que» takes the subjunctive: «el tránsito se duplicó; de ahí que los vecinos pidan cambios». To close, «en resumen», «en definitiva» or «en conclusión»; «total, que…» is colloquial. To refute, remember the mood: «no es cierto que + subjunctive» denies, and «es cierto que + indicative» concedes before objecting. «Al contrario» comes after a negated idea; «no…, sino (más bien)…» replaces one idea with another; «lejos de + infinitive» presents the opposite of what was expected; «en absoluto» is a flat «no»; «nada más lejos de la realidad» denies emphatically.

To attribute an idea to someone else, «según + noun» (or «según tú»), «de acuerdo con» and «como señala…». Attributing well is part of refuting well: first you state fairly what the other person thinks and then you argue against it.

A community radio station in Almagro, Buenos Aires, holds a debate on the proposal to pedestrianise the market street at weekends. Inés moderates; Paula, a teacher, is in favour; Ricardo, owner of a hardware shop, has doubts. Listen first without the transcript. Programme moderator
Teacher, member of the residents' association
Owner of a hardware shop on the market street
Good afternoon. Today we're debating a proposal that has been causing a lot of discussion: closing the market street to traffic on Saturdays and Sundays. Paula, you support it. You have the floor.

Thank you, Inés. Firstly, I want to clarify something: it's not that we want to close off the neighbourhood, but to open the street to people. We've been asking for a solution for the pavements, which are extremely narrow, for two years. In addition, according to the university report, almost half of the market's customers arrive on foot. Consequently, the street already belongs, in practice, to pedestrians.

It's true that the pavements are narrow, but I don't think the solution is to close the street. My hardware shop sells heavy materials, and customers come by car. If nobody can park, who's going to carry a bag of cement away on foot? On top of that, nobody consulted us.

I understand the concern, Ricardo, but far from harming the shops, a pedestrian street usually attracts more people. That's the case with several streets in the centre. And loading and unloading would be kept in the mornings, from six to ten.

The streets in the centre, I know them, and they're nothing like ours. Look, I'm not against it at all. What I'm asking for is a trial with data. If the council had done a study beforehand, today we wouldn't be arguing blindly.

There's a message from a listener, Marta, who says she has lived on the street for forty years and on Saturdays she can't open the window any more because of the noise from the cars. Paula, would you accept the trial Ricardo is proposing?

Of course. In fact, we have more than eight hundred signatures collected asking for exactly that: a six-month trial and a consultation at the end. By March the council will have published the traffic study, and there should be time to organise the trial in autumn.

Well, we agree on that. So, in the end, we both want the same thing: to decide with information. Now, I'd be grateful if the association invited us to the meetings, because we shopkeepers find out about everything from the papers. And another thing: on Sunday mornings, or rather, until midday, my shop is open. That should be taken into account too.
To sum up: agreement on the pavements, doubts about parking and a joint proposal for a trial. Thank you both. Listeners can leave their opinion on our answering machine.
Listen to the whole debate. How does the discussion develop?
Choose the answer that sums up the debate.
How does the debate end?
Both accept a six-month trial and deciding on the basis of data.
What is Ricardo's position?
Listen again and find the specific details.
Answer with the exact information from the audio.
According to the report Paula quotes, how do customers get to the market?
Why is Ricardo worried about the proposal?
He talks about bags of cement and parking.
What does Ricardo ask for at the end?
Now focus on the form. You can read the transcript after answering.

Ordering, adding or concluding
Refuting, conceding or correcting
Structure reviewed in weeks 16 to 19
Ordering connector.
Corrects an interpretation.
Rebuttal with «lejos de».
«Tener» + agreeing participle (week 16).
Future perfect with a reference point (week 17).
Concluding connector.
Known topic picked up with a pronoun (week 19).
The market street: less noise and more data
Opinion column in a neighbourhood newspaper
Original SpanishCue text written as an opinion column in a fictional Almagro newspaper in Buenos Aires. The people, the figures and the report are invented.

Few proposals have divided the neighbourhood as much as the one to pedestrianise the market street at weekends. Since the residents' association presented it in March, meetings fill up, messaging groups are ablaze and, at the market entrance, there's more arguing than shopping. This column doesn't aim to close the debate, but to put it in order: to separate what we know from what we suppose and to answer the arguments that circulate most.

Firstly, it's worth remembering where the idea comes from. The association has been calling since 2019 for a solution for the pavements, whose width in some stretches is no more than a metre and a half. On Saturday mornings, when the market is full, walking with a pushchair is almost impossible. Consequently, the problem exists and nobody has invented it. What is being discussed is the solution, and on that it's worth listening to everyone who lives and works on the block, not only to those who shout loudest at meetings.

The most repeated argument against it is that the pedestrian street would empty the neighbourhood. According to the shopkeepers who hold this view, customers would stop coming if they can't park. It is not true, however, that most of them arrive by car. The study carried out by the Universidad del Oeste last year, and not the one commissioned by the council, shows that almost half of customers arrive on foot and only one in five comes by car. It is true that this fifth spends more, which is why shops selling materials, such as Ricardo Benítez's hardware shop, have reason to be worried.

The second argument holds that the proposal is improvised. Nothing could be further from the truth: the text the association presented is twenty pages long, includes a loading and unloading schedule from six to ten in the morning and provides for exceptions for residents with reduced mobility. That said, a good document is no substitute for a consultation. If the council had asked the shopkeepers from the start, there wouldn't be so much distrust today, and many of them wouldn't have found out about the proposal from the papers.

Far from being a dead end, the debate has produced a reasonable idea: a six-month trial, with measurements of sales, traffic and noise, and a binding consultation at the end. By March, as the councillor for mobility has announced, the traffic study will have been published, so the trial could begin in autumn. There must also be intermediate formulas: closing only on Sundays, for example, or providing a loading area for shops that sell heavy goods.

In short, the pedestrian street is neither the panacea some imagine nor the disaster others predict. It is a tool, and as such it must be measured. Of the residents who support it we ask patience; of the shopkeepers who fear it, that they agree to look at the data. And the council, we would be grateful if, for once, it did not decide behind closed doors what will be lived in full view of everyone.
Notice how the column combines connectors and structures from the whole level.
Rebuttal with the subjunctive; «sin embargo» between commas links it to the previous argument.
Mixed conditional: an unrealised past with an effect on the present.
Precise noun phrase (week 18): the participle clarifies authorship and the ellipsis «el que» is recovered without doubt.
Topic placed first and picked up with «les» (week 19), and a final request with distance.
to be ablaze
here, to be very heated or full of arguments
a binding consultation
a vote whose result the authorities must follow
the panacea
a remedy that supposedly solves everything
Answer according to the column.
What aim does the column state?
First paragraph: «no pretende cerrar el debate, sino ordenarlo».
Which figure from the university study does the writer use to refute the shopkeepers?
Third paragraph.
What does the column propose as a way forward?
Fifth paragraph.
Whom does the column ask not to decide «behind closed doors»?
Last paragraph.
Interpret the text in your own words and support it with quotations.

Explain in 80–100 words how the writer refutes the two arguments against and whether you find their position balanced. Use at least two refuting connectors and a concession, and quote a sentence from the text.

The writer refutes the first argument with data: it isn't true that most people arrive by car, because almost half walk. To the second he replies emphatically, «Nada más lejos de la realidad», and describes the twenty-page document. Even so, he concedes that shops selling materials have reason to worry and that a good document is no substitute for a consultation. I find it balanced, because, far from ridiculing the shopkeepers, he asks them to look at the data and also criticises the council.
I explain how each argument is refuted.
I quote a sentence from the text word for word.
I use two refuting connectors and a concession.

Write a letter to the editor (230–300 words) for your neighbourhood newspaper about a proposal that divides residents (pedestrianising a street, opening a shopping centre, closing a market). Present your position in order, refute at least two opposing arguments while attributing them fairly, concede something and finish with a proposal and a request to the authorities.

The letter will be published with your name and will be read by neighbours who don't think like you. It has to be firm but respectful, and well organised into paragraphs. You can use the case of the Almagro market street or a real issue in your town.
Write your thesis in one sentence and note down the two strongest opposing arguments, with who holds them.
Organise the letter: introduction of the topic and thesis, your own arguments, rebuttal with concession and closing with a proposal and a request.
Use connectors for ordering, refuting and concluding, and at least three structures from weeks 16 to 19.
Revise the mood after each connector («no es cierto que», «de ahí que», «es cierto que») and correct ambiguous pronouns and noun phrases.

Dear Editor: I am writing as a resident of Almagro to give my opinion on the proposal to pedestrianise the market street at weekends, an issue we have been discussing in the neighbourhood for months. I will state my position from the outset: I am in favour, provided that a serious trial is carried out first.

Firstly, the pavements on that street are dangerously narrow; anyone who has tried to get through with a pushchair on a Saturday knows it. Secondly, according to the Universidad del Oeste study, almost half of customers arrive on foot. Consequently, the street already works as a pedestrian street, even though nobody has decided it.

Some shopkeepers argue that the measure would empty the neighbourhood. It is not true that customers are going to disappear; on the contrary, sales grew on other streets in the city. Others claim the proposal is improvised, and nothing could be further from the truth: the document provides for loading times and exceptions. It is true, however, that businesses selling heavy goods have a real problem, and there must be solutions for them, such as a reserved loading area.

In short, I propose a six-month trial with public measurements and a consultation at the end. If the council had consulted from the start, there would not be so much distrust today. In the meantime, it would be useful for the shopkeepers and the association to meet every month. That is why we would be grateful if the councillor for mobility published the traffic study before March and invited the shopkeepers to every meeting. Yours faithfully, Paula Ferreyra.
I present my thesis at the beginning and return to it at the end.
I attribute opposing arguments fairly before refuting them.
I use the correct mood after each refuting and consequence connector.
I include at least three structures from weeks 16 to 19.
The letter is firm, respectful and organised into paragraphs with clear functions.

This checkpoint closes the B2 level with two speaking tasks that integrate the last five weeks. Speak from notes, without reading. If you record yourself, the recording stays on your device and is not assessed automatically.
Debate on the neighbourhood radio

Your teacher defends the opposite position to yours on a change in your town (pedestrianising a street, banning cars from the centre, closing a market). Present your position in order, listen to their argument, attribute it fairly, refute it with data, concede a point and together propose a middle way.
Prepare three ordered arguments and a figure attributed to a source.
Prepare two rebuttals: «no es cierto que…» and «lejos de…».
Prepare a concession and a polite request to close.
I listen and respond to the other person's real arguments.
I use varied connectors and the correct mood after each one.
We finish with a concrete proposal or I explain why there is no agreement.
Taking stock of my B2

Speak for about three minutes about your journey through the B2 level. Say how long you've been studying, what you have already mastered, what has been hardest, what you would have done differently and what you will have achieved a year from now. Organise your presentation with connectors and finish with a clear conclusion.
Note down one structure from each week from 16 to 20.
Order your review: situation, achievements, difficulties, hypotheses and conclusion.

I've been studying Spanish for almost two years and this level has been the most demanding. Firstly, I've got the subjunctive fairly well mastered, although I still hesitate with some connectors. In addition, I now understand radio debates that a year ago seemed impossible to me. What I've found hardest are focus pronouns; if I had read more newspapers, I'd probably use them more naturally. In short, I'm happy: a year from now I will have started C1, and by then I hope to have lost my fear of speaking in public.
I use at least one structure from each week from 16 to 20.
I pause after ordering connectors.
My review has a beginning, a middle and a clear conclusion.
Take your checkpoint work to class and use it to check with your teacher what you have mastered as you finish the B2 level.
Bring your letter to the editor with the connectors marked in colours (ordering, refuting, concluding) and the structures from weeks 16 to 19 underlined.
Suggest a controversial issue in your town to your teacher and debate it for five minutes: you defend one position and they defend the opposite.
Read your teacher an argument from your letter to the editor and ask them to refute it; then reply to their rebuttal.
Choose the class from weeks 16 to 20 that you find hardest and ask your teacher for three sentences to practise it before starting C1.
It isn't true that the new bus line ___ (tardar) longer than the old one.
«No es cierto que» + subjunctive.
Rents went up by 60%; hence many families ___ (ir) to the outskirts.
«De ahí que» + subjunctive, with the tense depending on the frame.
The project doesn't aim to cut costs, ___ to improve the service.
«No…, sino…» replaces the negated idea.
The committee has ___ (revisar) all the proposals received.
«Son quince manzanas, mejor dicho, catorce.» What does «mejor dicho» do?
Self-correction.
Which sentence concedes a fact before objecting?
«Es cierto que» + indicative concedes.
According to the audio, what is the speaker's position?
«No es que… sino que…» corrects an interpretation and adds a demand.
«Por mucho que» with a general meaning: subjunctive.
«Al contrario» already contrasts the ideas: it isn't combined with «pero».
Future perfect with a future point (week 17) and impersonal «haber» in the singular (week 16).
In short, we propose a six-month trial.
Concluding connector at the beginning.
Write a short paragraph (three sentences) refuting an argument about your town: attribute it, refute it with a connector and close with a consequence.

According to some neighbours, the new park will attract crime. Nothing could be further from the truth: in neighbourhoods with more squares, robberies went down. Consequently, far from fearing it, we should demand that it be finished as soon as possible.
I attribute the argument to the people who hold it.
I use one refuting connector and one consequence connector.
The paragraph progresses clearly.
I can organise a presentation with connectors for ordering, adding, giving examples, rephrasing and concluding, with suitable punctuation.
I can refute precisely (no es cierto que + subjunctive, al contrario, lejos de, no… sino) and attribute ideas to the people who hold them.
I can choose at each moment the B2 structure I need and combine the classes from weeks 16 to 19 in the same text.
Tomorrow, without looking at the tables, write one connector for each function and a sentence with each one.
In three days, listen to a radio or TV debate and note down three refuting connectors you hear.
Before starting C1, reread your texts from weeks 16 to 20 and choose two structures you want to use more naturally.

changes.text: By the end of this week, you can greet people, introduce yourself and ask someone's name, informally or formally.

_Buenos días_ = good morning; _buenas tardes_ = good afternoon (from lunchtime until it gets dark); _buenas noches_ = good evening AND good night. Spanish uses the same phrase to say hello and goodbye at night.
_Día_ is masculine (buen**os** días) but _tarde_ and _noche_ are feminine (buen**as** tardes, buen**as** noches).
Spanish verbs show who is acting, so subject pronouns are usually dropped: _Soy Ana_ (I'm Ana). Use _yo, tú, él_… only for contrast or emphasis.
_Tú_ is informal 'you'; _usted_ is polite 'you'. _Usted_ takes the same verb form as _él/ella_ (he/she).
_Me llamo_ literally means 'I call myself'. Never drop _me_: say _me llamo_, not _yo llamo_.
_Encantado / encantada_ agrees with the person who speaks, not with the person you meet.
What's your name? — My name is Diego.
Nice to meet you, I'm Laura. (a woman speaking)
Pleased to meet you. (man / woman speaking)
a ≈ the 'a' in _father_, but short · e ≈ the 'e' in _met_ · i ≈ the 'ee' in _see_, short · o ≈ the 'o' in _or_, without a glide · u ≈ the 'oo' in _food_, short.
Keep every vowel full, even in unstressed syllables: _ca-sa_, not 'cass-uh'.
Nice to meet you, I'm Elena.
By the end of this week, you can say where you're from, your nationality and which languages you speak, ask other people the same, and give or note down a phone number.
_Nosotros_ = we, _vosotros_ = you all (informal, only in Spain), _ustedes_ = you all (formal in Spain; formal AND informal in Latin America), _ellos/ellas_ = they.
The feminine forms _nosotras, vosotras, ellas_ are only for all-female groups. A mixed group uses the masculine form, even if there's only one man.
If you learn Latin American Spanish, you never need to produce _vosotros_ — but you will hear it in films and series from Spain.
Camila and I are from Colombia.
Are you the new students? — Yes, that's us.
Spanish negation is simple: put _no_ right before the verb. No 'do not', no 'am not' — just _no soy_, _no es_, _no somos_.
_No, no soy de aquí_ is not a mistake: the first _no_ means 'no' (the answer), the second means 'not'.
With _me llamo_, _no_ goes before the little word _me_: _No me llamo Ana_, never _Me no llamo_.
I'm not from Guadalajara, I'm from Monterrey.
Are you Argentinian? — No, we're not Argentinian. We're Uruguayan.
His name isn't Mario, it's Darío.
Nationalities agree with the person: _Pedro es mexicano_, _Ana es mexicana_, _Pedro y Ana son mexicanos_.
Unlike English, nationalities and languages are NOT capitalised in Spanish: _soy inglés_, _hablo español_. Countries are: _Inglaterra, España_.
The name of the language is usually the masculine singular nationality: _el francés, el alemán, el inglés_.
Lukas is German and Hanna is German.
_¿De dónde eres?_ literally 'From where are you?'. The preposition _de_ goes first: never _¿Dónde eres de?_.
_Hablo, hablas, habla_ are forms of _hablar_ (to speak). In week 4 you'll learn the whole pattern; for now learn them as fixed chunks.
Where are you from? — I'm from Lima. I'm Peruvian.
Where are you from? (formal) — I'm from Toronto, I'm Canadian.
What languages do you speak? — I speak English, French and a little Spanish.
11–15 are irregular: _once, doce, trece, catorce, quince_. 16–19 are 'ten and six' written as one word: _dieci-séis_.
_Cero_ is zero. In phone numbers you'll hear each digit clearly: _cero, cero, cinco…_
Portuguese, German, Chinese, Japanese (languages are masculine)
English is stress-timed: some syllables are long and others are swallowed. Spanish is syllable-timed: tap each syllable with your finger and give it the same time.
I'm not from here, I'm from Lima.
I speak English and a little Spanish.
By the end of this week, you can name everyday objects, say what there is in a place, understand a short ad and ask for help when you don't understand a word.
Every Spanish noun is masculine or feminine — even objects. It's a grammar category, not a meaning.
Rule of thumb: -o → masculine, -a / -ción / -dad → feminine. Words ending in -e or a consonant: memorise them with _el_ or _la_.
Don't learn 'mesa = table'. Learn '**la mesa** = table'. The article is part of the word.
the notebook, the window, the room

Accent marks can disappear (_habitación → habitaciones_) or appear (_joven → jóvenes_) in the plural. The stressed syllable doesn't move; only the spelling rule changes. You'll understand why in the pronunciation section.
_Un/una_ ≈ 'a/an': something new or one of many. _El/la_ ≈ 'the': something both speakers can identify.
First mention → _un/una_. Second mention → _el/la_: _There's a lamp. The lamp is on the table._ = _Hay una lámpara. La lámpara es de la casa._
No article with _ser_ + profession: _Soy profesora_ (I'm a teacher).
There's a lamp. The lamp is doña Rosa's.
The keys? — They're some keys from the school.
She's a student, she's not a teacher.
_Hay_ = there is / there are. Same form for one or many: _hay una silla, hay cuatro sillas_.
Never _hay el / hay la_. Use _hay un / una_, a number, or a plural noun alone.
Pronunciation: the h is silent and _ay_ sounds like the 'i' in _hi_: _hay_ sounds exactly like _ay_ (ouch!).
In the room there are two beds and a table.
Is there wifi? — Yes, there's wifi in the whole house.
There's no TV in the room.
_¿Cómo se dice X en español?_ = How do you say X in Spanish? _¿Qué significa X?_ = What does X mean?
Choose _puedes_ (tú) or _puede_ (usted) to match the person, just like _eres / es_.
Use these phrases in your live class every time you need them: that's real communication, not a failure.
There's a closet. — Sorry, what does 'clóset' mean?
How do you say 'key' in Spanish?
Can you repeat, please? More slowly. (usted)
How do you say … in Spanish?
Stress = one syllable is longer and louder. In Spanish the vowel quality never changes when unstressed (no 'uh' sound).
Written accent (tilde) = 'the rule doesn't predict the stress here, so I mark it'. Learn the two rules and the tilde stops being random.
This is why _habitación_ has a tilde but _habitaciones_ doesn't: the stress stays on _-cio-_, but now the word ends in -s, so rule 1 already predicts it.
In the backpack there are some keys.
Is there a pharmacy in the centre?
There's no map in the classroom.
By the end of this week, you can say what you do, where you work or what you study, ask and answer five questions in a short interview, and use numbers up to a hundred.
Regular -ar verbs: remove -ar and add -o, -as, -a, -amos, -áis, -an. Learn this once and you can use hundreds of verbs.
_Trabajo_ alone means 'I work'. The ending tells you who: -o = I, -as = you, -a = he/she/you (usted), -amos = we, -an = they/you all.
The Spanish present also covers English 'I'm working / I'm studying' for current situations: _Estudio ingeniería_ = I'm studying engineering.
I work in an office and I study English in the evening.
They teach maths at a university.
No article with professions after _ser_: _Soy profesor_ = I'm a teacher. Saying _Soy un profesor_ sounds odd unless you add a description.
Professions agree with the person, like nationalities: _Pedro es abogado, Ana es abogada, Pedro y Ana son abogados_.
_¿A qué te dedicas?_ (literally 'What do you dedicate yourself to?') is the most natural way to ask 'What do you do?'.
What do you do? — I'm a programmer. I work from home.
Ana and Luis are doctors. They work in a hospital.
What are you studying? — I'm studying engineering at university.

Question words always have a written accent: _qué, dónde, cuándo, cómo, quién, cuánto_. Without the accent they're different words (_que_ = that, _donde_ = where as a connector, _como_ = like / I eat).
Spanish questions don't use 'do/does': _¿Dónde trabajas?_ = Where do you work?
Prepositions go first: _¿De dónde…?_ (Where… from?), _¿Con quién…?_ (Who… with?).
How many students are there in the class?
21–29: one word (_veinti-_). 31–99: three words (_treinta y dos_). Only the 'y' joins tens and units — never between hundreds and tens.
Don't confuse _sesenta_ (60) and _setenta_ (70): _se-sen-ta_ comes from _seis_, _se-ten-ta_ from _siete_.
I work forty-two hours a week.
There are twenty-one engineers in the office.
_y_ = and · _pero_ = but · _también_ = also / too · _tampoco_ = neither / not either.
Use _pero_ only when the second idea contrasts with the first: _Soy profesora, pero ahora no trabajo._
_Yo también_ = me too. _Yo tampoco_ = me neither.
I study Spanish and I work in a restaurant.
I'm from Spain, but I work in Mexico.
How many hours do you study at night?
Who do you work with at the office?
to work at a school / at the university
in the morning / afternoon / at night
to work with clients / with a team
Yes/no question ↗ (rise at the end). Statement ↘ (fall). Question-word question ↘ usually (fall), with a strong question word.
English uses 'do/does' to signal a question; Spanish uses only melody. Exaggerate the rise at first.
_¿Qué?_ with accent = what? (stressed). _que_ without accent = that (unstressed connector).
By the end of this week, you can give a full introduction of yourself (name, origin, languages, work or studies) and say what there is around you, both in speech and in writing.
_Ser_ is your identity verb: name, origin, nationality, job. Nationalities are not capitalised in Spanish: _mexicano_, _española_.
No article before a job after _ser_: _Soy profesor_ = I'm a teacher. _Vosotros sois_ is Spain only; Latin America uses _ustedes son_ for any group, formal or informal.
Learn every noun with its article: _el día_, _la clase_. The ending is a clue, not a rule.
_Hay_ = there is / there are, one form for both. Use it with _un/una_, numbers or no article — never with _el/la/los/las_.
In the room there are twelve tables and a printer.
The printer is new. (we already know which one)
Regular -ar verbs: drop -ar, add -o, -as, -a, -amos, -áis, -an. With _vos_ the ending is stressed: _vos hablás_.
Negation is simply _no_ before the verb. Question words always carry an accent mark, and in a yes/no question your voice rises at the end.
What languages do you speak? — I speak Spanish and German.
Do you study here? — No, I don't study here.
How many languages do you speak? (formal)
_Y_ adds, _pero_ contrasts, _también_ means 'too / also'. _Y_ becomes _e_ before an 'i' sound: _español e inglés_.
16–29 are one word (_veintitrés_); from 31 they are three words (_treinta y uno_). Phone numbers are often read in pairs.
I'm a designer, but now I'm studying Mayan.
I speak French and a little English.
What do you do (for a living)?
I'm not working at the moment.
How do you say 'charger' in Spanish?
Spanish rhythm is syllable-timed: every syllable gets roughly the same time, and vowels are never reduced, even in unstressed syllables.
Yes/no questions rise at the end (↗). Questions with a question word usually fall at the end (↘).
a Mexican sandwich in a bread roll
How many languages do you all speak?
I speak English, but I don't speak French.
My colleague isn't Chilean, she's Argentinian.
By the end of this week, you can introduce your family members, say how old they are and describe them with two or three physical and personality traits.
_Tener_ = to have. Spanish uses it for age: _Tengo 30 años_ = I am 30 (literally 'I have 30 years'). Never _soy 30_.
For hair and eyes, use _tener_ + definite article: _tiene el pelo largo_ (she has long hair), _tiene los ojos azules_ (he has blue eyes).
How old are you? — I'm twenty-six.
I don't have any brothers or sisters: I'm an only child.
My sister has short hair and dark eyes.
Possessives agree with the thing owned, not with the owner: _mis padres_ (my parents) — one owner, plural thing.
_Su/sus_ can mean his, her, its, your (usted/ustedes) or their. Add _de él / de ella / de usted_ when it's ambiguous.
My parents are from Tuxtla and my brother is from San Cristóbal.
Ana and I are sisters: our mother is a teacher.
Pedro and his wife have three children.
Adjectives agree with the person in gender and number. Mixed groups use the masculine plural.
_-o_ adjectives have four forms; _-e_ and most consonant adjectives have two (singular/plural). _-or_ adjectives add _-a_ for the feminine.
My cousin is tall, slim and very funny.
His sisters are shy but very kind.
My mother is hard-working and has curly hair.
_Los padres_ = parents; _los hermanos_ = brothers or siblings; _los tíos_ = uncles or uncles and aunts. Masculine plural includes everyone.
Use _de_ for 'of / 's': _el hijo de mi tía_ = my aunt's son.
I have three siblings: two boys and a girl.
My father's father is my grandfather.
I'm an only child, but I have a lot of cousins.
c + a/o/u = [k]. c + e/i and z = [θ] (like English _th_ in _think_) in most of Spain, or [s] in Latin America (seseo). Both are standard.
Spelling follows the sound: _z_ changes to _c_ before e/i (_lápiz → lápices_, _feliz → felices_).
My older sister has two children.
My father has short white hair.
By the end of this week, you can describe what you usually eat and drink, say how often you do things and ask about other people's habits.
-er and -ir verbs share the same endings except for _nosotros_ (-emos / -imos) and _vosotros_ (-éis / -ís).
Compare with -ar verbs: the 'a' endings (-as, -a, -an) become 'e' endings (-es, -e, -en). _Habla_ → _come_, _vive_.
My parents live in Puebla and eat at home every day.
We share a pizza and drink water.
_Nunca_ before the verb = no extra _no_. _Nunca_ after the verb = you need _no_ before the verb: _No como nunca carne_. Two negatives are correct in Spanish.
Never say _Nunca no como_: when _nunca_ comes first, it does the negative job alone.
I read the newspaper once a week.
How often do you eat fish? — Twice a month.
Meal names vary: _almuerzo_ is lunch in much of Latin America, a late breakfast in Mexico and a mid-morning snack in parts of Spain. _La comida_ is both 'food' and 'the main midday/afternoon meal'.
You don't need to learn every variant: use one, recognise the others.
I have coffee with milk and sweet bread for breakfast.
At home we have tortillas with beans for dinner.
I almost always have fruit for breakfast.
We eat mole twice a year.
lunch, the main midday meal (varies by country)
a white coffee / a black coffee
a beer / a glass of wine
What do you usually have for breakfast?
How often do you eat out?
B and V are the same sound in Spanish. Never use the English lip-teeth V.
After a pause and after m/n: lips fully closed [b]. Elsewhere, especially between vowels: lips almost closed [β], a soft sound.
From time to time we have dinner at a restaurant.
By the end of this week, you can say where a place is, ask whether there is a service nearby, and give or understand simple street directions.

Spanish has two verbs for 'to be'. _Ser_ tells you WHAT something is (identity, origin, profession). _Estar_ tells you WHERE something is. Location always uses _estar_: _El museo está en la zona 1_ (The museum is in zone 1).
Watch the written accents: _está_ (is) vs _esta_ (this). The accent changes the stress and the meaning.
Where are you? — I'm at the market.
The National Palace is on the square.
My friends are in a café.
_Hay_ = there is / there are. It introduces something new: _Is there a pharmacy around here?_ → _¿Hay una farmacia por aquí?_
_Está_ = is (located). It locates something both speakers already know: _Where is the pharmacy?_ → _¿Dónde está la farmacia?_ Never put _el, la, los, las_ after _hay_.
Is there a supermarket nearby? — Yes, there's one on the corner.
And where is the supermarket? — It's next to the bank.
There are no restaurants on my street.

Most location phrases end in _de_ (of): _cerca de_ = near, _lejos de_ = far from, _al lado de_ = next to, _enfrente de_ = opposite, _delante de_ = in front of, _detrás de_ = behind, _entre_ = between.
_de + el_ always becomes _del_, and _a + el_ becomes _al_. These are the only two contractions in Spanish, and they are not optional.
The stop is opposite the hospital.
The bookshop is between the bakery and the bank.
In Guatemala, as in most of Latin America, a city block is _una cuadra_; in Spain people say _una calle_ or _una manzana_.

Giving directions with the present tense (_cruzas, giras_) is completely natural. You will also hear commands like _gira, cruce, siga_: you will learn them later, but you can already understand them from the verb.
Excuse me, is there a bank around here? — Yes, walk two blocks and it's on the right.
You cross the square and the museum is opposite.
It isn't far: it's five minutes away.
the bus stop (in Guatemala the city bus is also called _camioneta_)
the shop (in Guatemala and Mexico, also the small corner shop)
on the right / on the left
Single r = one quick tap, like the 'tt' in American English _better_ or _water_. Double rr = a trill: several taps in a row.
If you can't trill yet, don't panic: a long, strong single tap is understood. Practise the trill a little every day; it comes with time.
Don't use the English r (tongue curled back, not touching anything). In Spanish, the tip of the tongue always touches the ridge behind your top teeth.
Excuse me, is there a bakery around here?
The museum is opposite the park.
You cross the square and turn left.
Where are the pharmacy and the bank?
By the end of this week, you can describe your normal daily routine, say what time you do things and ask about someone else's schedule.

Reflexive verbs describe actions you do to yourself: _me ducho_ (I shower = I shower myself). The small pronoun (me, te, se, nos, os, se) always matches the subject and goes BEFORE the conjugated verb.
With vos the pronoun is _te_ and the verb has the vos ending: _vos te levantás_. With usted: _usted se levanta_.
Use the article with body parts: _me lavo el pelo_ (I wash my hair), not _mi pelo_.
I get up at seven and have a shower.
What time do you go to bed?
My kids don't wake up early on Sundays.
_¿Qué hora es?_ = What time is it? → _Es la una_ / _Son las dos_. Only 1:00 (and 1:xx) takes singular _es la_.
_¿A qué hora…?_ = At what time…? → _A las dos_. Don't answer _Son las dos_ to a question about when something happens.
Spanish counts down after half past: 7:45 = _las ocho menos cuarto_ (eight minus a quarter).
What time is it? — It's twenty past eleven.
The class is at half past one.
I have dinner at nine in the evening.
Days are not capitalised in Spanish. Use _el_ for one specific day and _los_ for a habit: _el martes_ (on Tuesday) vs _los martes_ (on Tuesdays).
_Lunes_ to _viernes_ already end in -s, so the plural looks the same: _el lunes_ / _los lunes_. _Sábado_ and _domingo_ add -s: _los sábados_.
I work from Monday to Friday.
On Sundays I get up late.
In the morning I study and in the afternoon I work. (Latin America)
_Primero_ (first), _después / luego_ (then, afterwards), _más tarde_ (later), _por último / al final_ (finally). They make a list of actions sound like a story.
_Empiezo_ (I start) also changes its root vowel (_empezar_): learn _empiezo a trabajar_ as a chunk for now.
First I shower, then I have breakfast and then I walk to work.
Finally, I read a little and go to bed at eleven.
Do you work on Saturdays? — No, but I study.
I shower / I take a bath (in much of Latin America, _bañarse_ also means to shower)
I comb my hair / put on make-up / shave
I have lunch (_comer_ in Spain and Mexico, _almorzar_ in many other countries)
in the morning (Spain and others / Mexico, Central America / Río de la Plata)
Spanish j (and g before e, i) ≈ the 'ch' in Scottish _loch_ or German _Bach_; in Guatemala and much of Latin America, softer, like a breathy English 'h'. Never the English 'j' of _job_.
g before a, o, u = hard 'g' as in _go_. _gue, gui_ = hard 'g' with a silent u: _guitarra_ sounds 'gee-TAH-rra'.
Final j is very weak or silent in everyday speech: _reloj_ often sounds like 'relo'.
On Saturdays I don't get up early.
What time do you go to bed? (formal)
First I shower and then I have breakfast.
My son brushes his teeth at night.
By the end of this checkpoint, you can describe your family, your neighbourhood and your week in writing and aloud, and pick out the place, time and plan from a voice message.
English uses 'to be' for age (_she is 30_) but Spanish uses _tener_: _tiene treinta años_ (she has thirty years).
English 'is' can be _es_ (what/how it is) or _está_ (where it is). And 'there is' is always _hay_.
My cousin is dark-haired, has long hair and is in Panajachel.
There's a bakery on my street. It's opposite my house.
How old is your son? — He's six.
_Su_ can mean his, her, its, your (usted), their or your (ustedes). Context usually makes it clear; if not, say _de él / de ella_.
Adjectives come after the noun and match it: _mi hermana pequeña_, _mis abuelos simpáticos_.
Our family is big: we have twelve cousins.
My sisters are tall and friendly.
Diego lives with his mother. Her house is near the lake.
-er and -ir verbs share all endings except _nosotros_ and _vosotros_: _comemos_ but _vivimos_.
If _nunca_ comes after the verb, you need _no_ before it: _No bebo café nunca_. This 'double negative' is correct in Spanish.
On Sundays we get up late and have breakfast in the garden.
My brother never drinks coffee, but he always drinks atol (a warm corn drink).
Do you live near work? What time do you get back home?
Voice messages are fast and informal, but they follow a pattern: greeting → reason → details → goodbye. Focus your attention on the details in the middle.
Write only key words while listening: a number, a place, a time. You can build the full sentences afterwards.
Hi, it's Camila! I'm writing about Saturday…
…the boat leaves the pier at half past eight…
…but better at one, behind the church. See you!
uncles and aunts, cousins, nephews and nieces
children: a son and a daughter
the pier and the boat (on Lake Atitlán, boats connect the villages)
the market, the church, the square
the stop, the bank, the pharmacy
I wake up, get up, shower
Seseo (Latin America) = c/z sound like s. Distinción (central/northern Spain) = c/z sound like English 'th'. Choose one and be consistent.
b and v: same sound. Never bite your lip for v.
r = one tap; rr = trill. j = breathy sound at the back of the mouth, never English 'j'.
a Mayan language spoken around Lake Atitlán
We're waiting for you! / Come and see us!
Our house is behind the church.
My grandfather never goes to bed late.
What time do your children have breakfast?
My cousins are tall and have green eyes.
By the end of this week, you can suggest a weekend plan, accept one, or politely say you can't and suggest something else.
Some verbs change their stem vowel when it is stressed: _querer_ → _quiero_ (I want), _poder_ → _puedo_ (I can). The endings stay regular.
_Nosotros_ and _vosotros_ never change, because the stress moves to the ending: _queremos, podéis_. This is often called the 'boot' or 'shoe' pattern.
Write new verbs in your notebook with the change in brackets: _dormir (ue)_, _pedir (i)_.
On Sundays I sleep until ten.
The class starts at six thirty.
What time do you go back home?
_Querer_ = to want, _poder_ = can / to be able to, _preferir_ = to prefer. After them, use the infinitive: _quiero ir_ (I want to go). Never add 'a' or conjugate the second verb.

With reflexive verbs, the pronoun can go at the end of the infinitive or before the first verb: _Prefiero acostarme temprano_ = _Me prefiero acostar temprano_ (the first one is more common with _preferir_).
Do you want to go to the cinema tonight?
I can't go out, I'm studying for an exam, you see.
I prefer running in the morning.
On Saturday I want to get up at nine.
I want to go to bed early today.
_Vos_ is an informal 'you', used across Central America and the River Plate. Its present forms are stressed on the ending and keep the infinitive vowel: _querés, podés, jugás_ — no stem change.
You don't need to produce _vos_ yet. Just recognise it: _¿Vos querés venir?_ = _¿Tú quieres venir?_
Do you want to climb the volcano on Saturday? (vos)
Can you make it at eight? (vos)
And what do you prefer, cinema or football? (vos)
To suggest: _¿Quieres + infinitive?_ (Do you want to…?), _¿Por qué no + nosotros form?_ (Why don't we…?).
To say no politely: _Lo siento, no puedo. Es que…_ + reason + an alternative. A bare 'no' sounds rude in Spanish.
Regional 'OK!': _¡Va, pues!_ (El Salvador, Honduras), _¡Dale!_ (Central America, Argentina, Uruguay), _¡Vale!_ (Spain), _¡Sale!_ (Mexico).
—Do you want to play basketball on Saturday? —Sure! What time?
—Why don't we eat pupusas? —OK, let's do it! (El Salvador)
—Can you make it at six? —Sorry, I'm working. How about eight?
to play football (in Latin America also _jugar fútbol_)
to swim in the pool (_alberca_ in Mexico)
to ride a bike (_montar en bici_ in Spain)
to go hiking (Central America; _hacer senderismo_ in Spain)
to watch a series at home
to eat pupusas (El Salvador's favourite dish)
Can you make it on Saturday?
The thing is… (to give a reason)
ñ ≈ 'ny' in _canyon_, but as one single sound. Practise: _año, señor, España, mañana_.

ll and y sound the same for most speakers ('yeísmo'), close to English 'y' in _yes_ but with more friction. In Argentina and Uruguay they sound like 'sh'. In Central America they can be very soft between vowels.
At the end of a word, **y** is a vowel sound: _hoy, muy, soy_ sound like 'oi', 'mui', 'soi'.
five dollars: El Salvador uses the US dollar
Do you want to ride a bike on Sunday?
On Saturdays I prefer to get up late.
I can't, I have class, you see.
By the end of this week, you can talk about your likes and hobbies, ask about other people's tastes and react: me too, me neither, I do, I don't.
Think of _gustar_ as 'to be pleasing to'. _Me gusta el té_ = tea is pleasing to me. The verb agrees with the thing, so: _gusta_ (one thing or activity), _gustan_ (plural things).
Never use _yo_ with _gustar_: say _me gusta_, not _yo gusto_. Use _a mí_, _a ti_, _a Ana_ for emphasis or to make clear who you mean, especially with _le_ and _les_.
Use the article with things in general: _Me gusta el chocolate_ (not _me gusta chocolate_).
I really like punta, the Garifuna music of Honduras.
My sister likes painting and drawing.
_Encantar_ = to love (things, activities): _Me encanta cocinar_. It already means 'like a lot', so don't add _mucho_.
_Interesar_ = to interest: _Me interesa la historia_ (I'm interested in history).
Negative: _no_ goes before the pronoun: _No me gusta_. _Nada_ at the end makes it strong: _No me gusta nada_ (I don't like it at all).
I'm not interested in golf at all.
Are you interested in animal documentaries?
Agreeing: 'me too' = _a mí también_ (after a positive sentence); 'me neither' = _a mí tampoco_ (after a negative sentence).
Disagreeing: _a mí no_ (after a positive), _a mí sí_ (after a negative).
Use _a mí_ with _gustar_-type verbs and _yo_ with normal verbs: _—Me gusta el sushi. —A mí también._ / _—Cocino mucho. —Yo también._
—I don't like getting up early. —Me neither.
—I'm not interested in video games. —No? I am.
_Muy_ = very, before adjectives and adverbs: _muy bueno, muy tarde_. It never changes.
_Mucho_ = a lot / much / many. After a verb it doesn't change (_trabajo mucho_). Before a noun it agrees: _mucha gente, muchos amigos, muchas fotos_.
Tegucigalpa has a lot of mountains around it.
Horror films are very boring for me.
My brother plays video games a lot.
punta: Garifuna music and dance from the Caribbean coast of Honduras
to play the guitar / the piano
to play video games (_jugar videojuegos_ in much of Latin America)
h is always silent: _hola_ = 'ola'. The English 'h' sound is written with **j** in Spanish (_jugar_).
The /k/ sound: c + a/o/u (_casa_), qu + e/i (_queso_, the u is silent), k only in foreign words (_kilo_).
I support Olimpia (a Tegucigalpa football club; Motagua is its rival)
Honduran flour tortilla with beans, cheese and cream
I don't like horror films at all.
I have a lot of very old books.
By the end of this week, you can buy clothes in a shop: point at what you want, ask the price, ask for another size or colour, try things on and decide what to buy.
_este_ = this (near me), _ese_ = that (near you / not far), _aquel_ = that over there (far from both of us).
They agree like adjectives but go before the noun: _esta falda, estos zapatos, esas camisetas, aquellos sombreros_.
Watch the masculine singular: _este, ese, aquel_ — they don't end in -o.
I like those trainers you've got in your hand.
And that hat over there, the one on the wall?
—Which T-shirt do you prefer? —That one, the green one.
_esto, eso, aquello_ = this, that, that over there — for unknown things, groups of things or ideas. They never go with a noun.
_¿Qué es esto?_ = What's this? (I don't know what it is). _¿Cuánto cuesta este?_ = How much is this one? (I know it's a hat).
Sorry, what's this? —It's a hammock from Masaya.
A thousand córdobas? That's a lot of money.
_cien_ = exactly 100; _ciento_ = 101–199 (_ciento veinte_). Never put _y_ after the hundreds: _ciento veinte_, not _ciento y veinte_.
200–900 agree with feminine nouns: _trescientas personas_. Irregular: _quinientos_ (500), _setecientos_ (700), _novecientos_ (900).
_mil_ never takes -es: _tres mil_. _Millón_ does: _dos millones de dólares_.
This shirt costs six hundred and fifty córdobas.
There are two hundred rooms in the hotel.
Granada has about a hundred and thirty thousand inhabitants.
The palm hat costs one thousand two hundred córdobas.
Colours go after the noun and agree: _una camisa blanca, unos zapatos blancos_. Colours ending in -e or a consonant only change for plural: _verde/verdes, azul/azules_.
_Llevar_ = to wear: _Hoy llevo una camiseta azul_.

Regional words: T-shirt = _camiseta_ (Spain, Central America), _playera_ (Mexico), _remera_ (Argentina). Trainers = _tenis_ (Mexico, Central America), _zapatillas_ (Spain, Argentina). Brown = _marrón_ (Spain) / _café_ (much of Latin America).
Today I'm wearing blue jeans and a white T-shirt.
I'm looking for black sandals, size 38.
That grey jacket is very nice.
Trying on: _probarse_ (o → ue): _¿Puedo probarme esta falda?_ Fit: _quedar_ works like _gustar_: _Me queda grande_ (it's too big for me), _Me quedan bien_ (they fit me).
Deciding: _Me llevo este_ (I'll take this one). Browsing: _Solo estoy mirando_ (I'm just looking).
How much are those sandals over there?
Can I try this dress on in size S?
It fits me perfectly. I'll take this one.
brown (_café_ in much of Latin America)
How much is it? / How much are they?
Do you have this shirt in blue?
Can I try on this dress?
It's too big / too small / It fits.
Can you give me a discount?
Hard d [d]: at the start after a pause and after _n_ or _l_ (_dos, tienda, falda_). The tongue touches the back of the upper teeth, like a soft English 'd' but with the tongue further forward.
Soft d [ð]: everywhere else, especially between vowels (_todo, vestido, cada_). It sounds close to 'th' in _this_, but lighter.
In fast speech (Spain, Caribbean) _-ado_ often sounds like _-ao_: _cansado_ → 'cansao'. Final _-d_ is very weak: _ciudad_.
Can I try on this grey jacket?
These shoes are a bit big for me.
How much is that red dress over there?

By the end of this week, you can order a full meal politely, ask about a dish, sort out a small problem and ask for the bill. You can also talk about quantities (a little, quite, too much) and use hago, pongo, traigo, salgo, conozco and sé.
Spanish uses _Para mí…_ (For me…) and the question _¿Me trae…?_ (Will you bring me…?) to order. A literal translation of 'Can I have…?' (_¿Puedo tener…?_) sounds strange: nobody says it.
_De primero_ = as a starter, _de segundo_ = as a main course, _de postre_ = for dessert.
Use _usted_ with waiters. In Nicaragua, friends use _vos_ with each other (_¿Vos qué querés?_), but the waiter will usually treat you as _usted_.
I'll have the set menu, please.
For the main course, chicken with rice and beans.
Could you bring me another fork, please?
Excuse me, does the soup have meat in it?
_poco_ = little / not much (negative); _un poco de_ = a little, some (positive); _bastante_ = quite a lot, enough; _demasiado_ = too much / too many; _nada de_ = no … at all.
Before nouns these words agree like adjectives (_poca leche, demasiados turistas_). Before adjectives they never change (_demasiado caras_, not _demasiadas caras_).
The rice and beans don't have much salt.
Could you bring me a bit of cheese, please?
There are too many people in this place.
The salad has no meat at all.
Only the _yo_ form is irregular. Don't let it spread: it's _sales_ (you go out), not _salges_.
_Conocer_ = to know / be familiar with a place, dish or thing. _Saber_ = to know a fact, or to know how to do something (_Sé nadar_ = I can swim).
On Sundays I make rice and beans for the whole family.
I know a very cheap place near the cathedral.
Do you know how much the set menu costs? — I don't know.
the set menu of the day
the menu (the full list of dishes)
fish with rice as a main
the set menu including a drink
Could you bring me a glass of water, please?
Could you bring me another napkin?
Does the rice have meat in it?
rice and beans fried together (Nicaragua, Costa Rica)
a big tamale wrapped in banana leaf
a tortilla with soft cheese, cream and onion (León area)
A diphthong is two vowels in one syllable: the weak vowel (i, u) glides quickly into the other one. _Bueno_ has two syllables, not three: _bue-no_.
A written accent on _í_ or _ú_ breaks the diphthong: _día_ has two syllables (_dí-a_). So the accent tells you how to pronounce the word.
The soup as a starter and the chicken as a main.
Could you bring me a bit of bread?
This dish is too spicy for me.

By the end of this checkpoint, you can organise a whole day out in Spanish: suggest a plan, talk about likes and react, buy a present and order in a restaurant. You can also choose between two places by reading short reviews.
Stem-changing verbs change in four forms (yo, tú, él, ellos) — think of a boot shape in the table. _Nosotros_ and _vosotros_ stay regular: _podemos_, not _puedemos_.
Yo-irregular verbs only change in the _yo_ form: _salgo_ but _sales, salimos_.
No preposition between _querer/poder/preferir_ and the infinitive: _Quiero ir_, never _Quiero a ir_.
Can you (all) make it on Saturday afternoon?
I'm ordering the casado and she's ordering a salad.
I finish work at five: do you want to have dinner afterwards?
_Gustar_ works like 'to please': _Me gustan los conciertos_ = concerts please me. The verb agrees with the thing you like, not with you.
Agree with a positive statement: _a mí también_. Agree with a negative statement: _a mí tampoco_. Disagree: _a mí no_ / _a mí sí_.
I don't like noise at all. — Me neither.
Are you interested in art? — Yes, a lot. (Costa Rican usted between friends)
Quick test: if the word next to it is an adjective (_caro, grande, rico_), use _muy_ (or _bastante, demasiado, un poco_ without agreement). If it is a noun, use _mucho/mucha/muchos/muchas_.
_Demasiado_ means 'too much': it signals a problem, not just a big amount.
The Central Market is very big and has lots of small eateries.
There are too many people on the avenue on Saturdays.
This T-shirt is a bit expensive, but I really like it.
_Este_ = this (near me), _ese_ = that (near you), _aquel_ = that over there. _Esto / eso_ are for things you can't or don't name: _¿Qué es esto?_
Shops and restaurants share a lot of language: _¿Cuánto cuesta…?_, _¿Puedo pagar con tarjeta?_. What changes: _Me llevo…_ (shop) vs. _Para mí…_ / _¿Me trae…?_ (restaurant).
How much are those national team T-shirts over there?
This one is very small. Do you have a size M?
Thank you very much. — You're welcome. (Costa Rica)
Do you want to go to the theatre on Saturday?
Can you come on Sunday? (usted between friends, Costa Rica)
to go on a guided tour
I don't like noise at all.
Do you have a bigger size?
Do you have this T-shirt in red?
set plate: rice, beans, salad, plantain and meat or fish
You're welcome (common reply to _gracias_ in Costa Rica).
All good! / Hi! / Thanks! (Costa Rican all-purpose phrase)
This is a review: listen for the difference, then say each phrase slowly and then at normal speed.
Remember the pairs: _caña_ (ñ) vs. _cana_ (n); _pollo_ (ll) vs. _polo_ (l); _todo_ (soft d) vs. _toro_ (r).
Do you prefer to eat at the soda or at the market?
I don't like shopping centres at all.
I'll take that red T-shirt, please.

By the end of this week, you can talk about your weekend plans with ir a + infinitive, place them in time (tomorrow, on Saturday, in two days), talk about the weather and say how you're going to get there.
_Ir a_ + infinitive = 'going to' + verb. Only _ir_ is conjugated; the second verb stays in the infinitive.
Don't forget the _a_: _Voy a comer_, not _Voy comer_.
_Ir a_ + place = going to a place. _Voy a ir a_ + place = I'm going to go to a place.
On Saturday I'm going to go for a hike in the forest.
What are you going to do tonight? — Nothing, I'm going to rest.
My friends are going to go to Monteverde by bus.
We aren't going to cross the bridges: it's too windy.
_La semana que viene_ = _la próxima semana_ = next week. _Próximo/próxima_ agrees with the noun: _el próximo sábado, la próxima semana_.
_Dentro de_ + time = in + time from now: _dentro de tres días_ = in three days.
No preposition before days: _el sábado_ = on Saturday.
Spanish says 'it makes heat' (_hace calor_), not 'it is hot'. Because _calor_ is a noun, intensify it with _mucho_: _hace mucho calor_ (never _muy calor_).
_Está nublado_ (it's cloudy) is a fixed weather chunk with _estar_.
Transport: _en_ + vehicle, but _a pie_ (on foot) and _a caballo_ (on horseback).
In Monteverde it's cool and it rains quite a lot.
Today there's too much fog to see the volcano.
We're going to go by bus and then on foot.
Tomorrow it's going to be sunny, but in the afternoon it's going to rain.
On Saturday we aren't going to leave the hotel.
What are you (all) going to do tomorrow?
In two days I'm going to go back to San José.
The weather is good. / The weather is bad.
to go for a hike in the forest
to watch birds, like the quetzal
to do a zip-line tour (also: la tirolesa / el tirolino)
Linking (enlace): a final consonant joins the next word's first vowel. Think of the phrase as one long word: _vamosaír_.
This is why Spanish sounds fast to learners: there are no small pauses between words.
By the end of this week, you can describe your home or the flat you are looking for: what there is, where it is, what it is like and what state it is in.
_Hay_ = there is / there are. It introduces new things and never changes for plural: _hay un baño, hay dos baños_.
_Estar_ = location of something already known (with _el, la, mi_…). _Ser_ = what something is like (size, style, age, colour) and identification.
Quick test: am I mentioning it for the first time? → **hay**. Do we already know it and I'm saying where? → **está**. Am I describing what it's like? → **es**.
In my building there's a gym.
The gym is on the ground floor.
_Estar_ + adjective describes a temporary state or condition: how someone feels, or how something is right now (dirty, open, broken).
_Ser_ + adjective describes what something is like in general. _La casa es bonita_ (it's a pretty house) vs _la casa está bonita_ (it looks nice today, e.g. after decorating).
The adjective agrees: _cansado_ (man), _cansada_ (woman), _cansados_ (group with at least one man), _cansadas_ (only women).
Today I'm happy: my new flat is ready.
Ordinals agree like adjectives: _primero / primera_. Before a masculine noun: _primer piso, tercer piso_ (not _primero piso_).
In Spain people often drop the noun: _Vivo en el tercero_ = I live on the third floor.
I live on the third floor, door B.
In my flat there are two bedrooms and a small living room. (Mexico)
A good description moves from outside to inside: type and location, general description, rooms, your opinion, and a plan.
_Tener_ and _hay_ can express the same idea: _the flat has two bathrooms_ / _there are two bathrooms in the flat_.
I live in a small flat. It's in the centre, near the metro.
It's old, but it gets a lot of light. There's a living room, a kitchen and a bedroom.
There's too much noise at night. This summer I'm going to look for another one.
We watch TV in the living room.
I cook in the kitchen every day.
We eat in the dining room on Sundays.
The bathroom is at the end of the corridor.
The corridor is long and narrow.
I have breakfast on the balcony.

Sinalefa = linking a final vowel to the next initial vowel in one syllable. _La amiga_ has 3 beats, not 4. The letter h is silent, so _mi hijo_ links too.
Same vowels merge into one slightly longer vowel; different vowels glide into each other. Don't insert a pause or a glottal stop between the words.
The flat is on the fifth floor.
In the kitchen there's a new fridge.
My room is small, but it gets a lot of light.
This summer we're going to paint the terrace.
By the end of this week, you can say what you have to do, share out household chores and write a message to organise them.
_Tener que_ = have to (a specific person). _Hay que_ = one has to / it's necessary (general rule, nobody named). _Necesitar_ = need.
_Hay que_ never changes and never takes a subject: not _yo hay que_, not _hay que limpiamos_. Always _hay que_ + infinitive.
I can't go out today: I have to study.
In the library you have to speak quietly.
Do you need help with the bags?
_Lo, la, los, las_ = it / them, for something already mentioned. Choose by the gender and number of the noun: _la basura → la_, _los platos → los_.
Position: before a conjugated verb (_lo compro_), never after it (not _compro lo_). With an infinitive you can also attach it: _voy a comprarlo_.
Have you got the key? — Yes, I've got it in my backpack.
And the documents? — I'm going to sign them tomorrow.
The towels are dirty. They need washing.
Spanish marks a specific person who receives the action with _a_: _veo **a** María_ (I see María). It has no English translation. Don't use it with things: _veo la casa_.
After _tener_ and _hay_ we usually don't use personal _a_: _tengo dos hermanos_, _hay un médico_.
Today I have to call the owner of the flat.
Where's Diego? — I don't know, I can't see him.
I'm going to pick up the children at five.
_Me toca_ = it's my turn. _¿A quién le toca?_ = whose turn is it?
Offering to do something: object pronoun + verb + _yo_: _Lo hago yo_ (I'll do it).
Who's buying the water? — I'll buy it.
This week it's your turn to clean the bathroom.
Guys, you have to set the table. (Latin America)

Two consonants + vowel form one syllable: _tres_ = 1 syllable. Don't insert a vowel between them, and don't add a vowel at the end.
The r in tr, pr, cr, gr, br, dr, fr is a single quick tap, like the tt in American English 'better'. Never a rolled rr.
The bread? I'm going to buy it now.
My mother — I call her on Sundays.
This week it's your turn to take out the rubbish.
By the end of this week, you can invite someone to a party with the date, time and place, accept an invitation enthusiastically or turn it down with a polite excuse.
Date order is day + _de_ + month: _el 9 de julio_ (July 9th). In numbers, the day comes first: 9/7.
Spanish uses cardinal numbers for dates (_el dos, el veinte_), not 'second' or 'twentieth'. The only exception is day 1: _el primero_ (Latin America) or _el uno_ (Spain).
Months and days of the week are not capitalised in Spanish.
Portobelo's Black Christ festival is on October 21st.
Ordinals are used for 'the first week', 'the third Sunday', but not for the day of the month: _el tres de junio_, not _el tercero de junio_.
We're going on holiday the first week of August.
The third Sunday of June is Father's Day in many countries.
_¿Por qué?_ (two words, accent) = why? _Porque_ (one word, no accent) = because.
_Es que…_ ≈ 'the thing is…'. It softens an excuse or explanation, so it's ideal for saying no politely.
Why are you buying balloons? — Because Sunday is Leo's birthday.
Are you coming to the concert? — What a shame! The thing is, I'm ill.
Saying just 'No' to an invitation sounds rude in Spanish. Thank, show regret, give an excuse with _es que_ and suggest an alternative.
Careful: in many countries _te invito_ can mean 'I'm paying'. _Te invito a un café_ = the coffee is on me.
Events take _ser_ for place and time: _La fiesta es en mi casa a las ocho._ Objects and places take _estar_ for location.
Do you want to come to my birthday party on Friday the 23rd?
I'd love to! Shall I bring anything? — Yes, bring the ice. — OK, I'll bring it.
The party is on the roof terrace, but the terrace is on the top floor.
carnival: four days of music and costumes
to turn: I'm turning thirty in May.
to celebrate your birthday with the family
to have a party at home
to give flowers as a present
to make a toast with friends
Merry Christmas and a happy New Year!
Exclamations start high, stress the key word strongly and fall clearly at the end. Flat exclamations sound bored or sarcastic in Spanish.
In lists, each item stays slightly up (more to come); only the last item, after _y_, falls.
Do you want to come to my party on Saturday?
The party is at my house at nine.
Sorry, the thing is I have to work.
Why don't we celebrate your birthday at the beach?

By the end of this checkpoint, you can introduce yourself, describe your home and your week, talk about your plans, organise chores, and invite people or answer an invitation: everything the A1 level promises.
Ser: identity, characteristics, and where/when an event takes place. Estar: location of people and things, and temporary states. Hay: existence of something new. Hace: most weather expressions.
Contrast pairs to remember: _la casa está en el centro_ / _la fiesta es en el centro_; _la cocina es pequeña_ / _la cocina está sucia_.
It's sunny today, but tomorrow it's going to rain.
The concert is in the park; the park is near the canal.
I'm happy: my new flat is bright and quiet.
_Ir a_ + infinitive = plans (going to). _Tener que_ = have to. _Querer_ = want to. _Poder_ = can. All are followed directly by an infinitive.
Don't forget the little words: _voy **a** ir_, _tengo **que** ir_, _dentro **de** dos días_.
In three days we're going to cross the canal by boat.
Next weekend I can't go out: I have to clean the house.
Pronoun position: before a conjugated verb or attached to the end of an infinitive. Never _tengo que lo comprar_ and never _compro lo_.
Have you got the tickets? — Yes, I've got them on my phone.
And your parents? — I'm going to visit them in December.
A polite refusal = thanks + regret + _es que_ + alternative. Dates: day before month, cardinal numbers (except day 1).
Why don't you come on Friday the 16th? — The thing is, I'm going back to Buenos Aires that day.
What a good idea! I'll be there on Wednesday at eight.

Linking (consonant + vowel) and synalepha (vowel + vowel) remove the gaps between words. Clusters like tr/pl stay in one syllable with no extra vowel. Exclamations start high and fall.
I've been in Panama for three months
This weekend I'm going to paint my room.
Whose turn is it to wash the dishes?
My birthday is on the first of March.
Sorry, the thing is that day I'm ill.

Why don't we go to the canal by boat?
The perfect uses a present form of haber plus an unchanged participle. Ya means it has happened; todavía no means it remains pending.
find there are no tickets left
Use the preterite to report completed events in a finished time period. Stress distinguishes hablo from habló.
at the end of the day
Fui and fue can mean was or went. The surrounding words tell you which verb is intended; irregular preterite roots do not need written stress marks.
The imperfect describes what life was like and what people used to do. Solía is followed by an infinitive, not a second conjugated verb.
Choose the past form for its job: experience linked to now, completed event, or past habit. Keep dates and background separate in your exhibit.
The imperfect sets the scene; the preterite moves the story forward. A long event can still be presented as completed.
Tan compares qualities; tanto agrees with the quantity being compared. Better and worse already express comparison, so do not add más.
it is colder than on the coast
The receiver pronoun comes before the object pronoun. Le and les become se before lo, la, los or las.
Attach pronouns to affirmative commands. Keep the same form of address throughout instructions and check the stress when pronouns are added.
Combine what happened, what you prefer and what people must do. A useful group plan makes responsibilities and return dates explicit.
Estar + gerund tells what is happening or temporarily in progress. Seguir + gerund means continue; acabar de + infinitive means have just done.
A plan, a prediction and a promise are different messages. In a real condition, use present after si even when the result refers to the future.
The body part controls duele or duelen. Practise describing symptoms and confirming an appointment; the scene does not prescribe treatment.
Quería, me gustaría and podría soften requests. State the concrete problem, ask for a possible solution and confirm the final price.
Keep confirmed information separate from an option still being discussed. On the phone, repeat times and agreements before ending the call.
Porque and como give a cause; por eso and así que give a result. Antes de and después de are followed by an infinitive in these patterns.
Para commonly gives purpose, recipient, destination or deadline; por can give reason, means, exchange or a route through a place.
Use no when a negative word comes after the verb: no viene nadie. Describe an unknown object with its material, shape and function.
Give a position, reasons and an example. You can disagree at A2 with no estoy de acuerdo followed by a clear affirmative explanation.
Use both sources, distinguish what is confirmed and ask for missing facts. Your final message should allow another person to act on the plan.
